title: Help is not without hurdles
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
It is early days, but a recent report on Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave shows that the program served thousands of people in its first quarter. The trust fund is projected to remain stable for the next 10 years.
The report covered claims submitted and processed from March 30 (when applications could first be filed) through June 30. The program, which provides up to 12 weeks of paid leave, received 8,376 applications. The most common type of leave was for health reasons, followed by time taken to welcome a new child or to care for a family member. The average weekly benefit amount was approximately $816.

title: High schools Monday: Leavitt boys soccer shades Cony
text:
Carter Berube’s goal with 4:40 remaining broke a tie and gave the Leavitt boys soccer team a 4-3 win over Cony on Monday in Turner.
Derek Fortin, Tyler Mates and Sam Dunn also scored for the Hornets (6-1-3), while Kalix Marquis and Everett Michaud each had an assist.
Manny Stevenson and Liam Lemieux scored for the Rams (0-9), whose first score was an own goal that deflected off a Leavitt player and gave Cony a 1-0 lead.
GIRLS SOCCER
HALL-DALE 2, MONMOUTH ACADEMY 0: First-half goals by Clare Sturtevant and Robin Asch carried the Bulldogs (6-2-2) to a Mountain Valley Conference win over the Mustangs (4-4) in Farmingdale.
Sturtevant scored first, in the sixth minute, then Asch netted her first goal of the season on a direct free kick with 25 seconds to play in the first half. Goalie Genevieve Ciccarelli made four saves to earn her second straight shutout.
Lily Carlton stopped 10 shots for Monmouth.
LAKE REGION 4, GRAY-NEW GLOUCESTER 1: Abbigail Nadeau netted three goals to lead the Lakers (6-4) to a road win over the Patriots (3-8) in Gray.
Helena Sheldrick also scored and had an assist for Lake Region, and goalie Quinn Doucette stopped seven shots.
Khloe D’Andrea scored Gray-New Gloucester’s goal off an assist by Ida Waterman. Mallory Hardiman made three saves.
FIELD HOCKEY
WINTHROP/MARANACOOK 3, HALL-DALE/MONMOUTH 0: Natalie Irwin scored twice to propel the Ramblers (9-1) past the Bulldogs (2-7) in Farmingdale.
Addie Daigle also scored for Winthrop. Evelyn Mortimer assisted on both goals.
Hall-Dale goalie Haylie Stevens finished with four saves.
LEAVITT 4, YORK 0: Ainsley Barry scored two goals and the visiting Hornets (8-1) defeated the Wildcats (1-8) in York.
Sarah Orso stopped 15 shots for York.

title: Why I’m out canvassing for Troy Jackson
text:
Sandra Smith Congdon is a Maine Democrats campaign volunteer and Saco Democratic Committee member.
I’m out every weekend canvassing for Troy Jackson in York County with the hope that we can flip the U.S. Senate because Maine is central to that fight.
I grew up in a working-class family in the ’70s and ’80s. My father worked in construction and my mother worked in retail, both in unions that provided them with fair wages and good healthcare. They worked hard to put food on the table for our family and made sure we had what we needed and sometimes could even afford things that we “wanted.”
The reason I’m supporting Troy is because I see a lot of working-class people today who can no longer afford basic needs. Troy wasn’t my first pick to run against Susan Collins but the more I hear him speak and hear others talk about him, the more I believe he’s the right choice for Maine. His working-class roots and his experience in the Maine Senate show that he is a fighter and will work hard for Mainers.
Mostly I’m out knocking on strangers’ doors because I cannot believe what I’m seeing every day in our Capitol. The bombastic man occupying the Oval Office has staffed his cabinet with sycophants whose only qualifications are blind loyalty and public praise of their boss. His only consistent policy is maximizing financial gain for himself and the billionaires who understand his pay-to-play mindset.
He isn’t listening to, nor does he care about, working-class people. He doesn’t see that the average American is struggling to afford food, fuel, healthcare, childcare, housing and other basic needs. He doesn’t even try to hide the corruption or his all-important ego, focusing on buying or bullying his name onto whatever he can in an attempt to paint himself a legacy in D.C. vs. earning it from the American people.
But worst of all is the lack of accountability, because Republicans in Congress are unwilling to stand up to his schoolyard bullying and brazen grift. They are showing the American public very clearly that their hold on power is far more important to them than the well-being of our great nation.
We need to flip the House and the Senate in the midterms to bring back checks and balances (not to mention basic accountability) to this administration. We cannot afford another two years of expensive pet projects, a continuing war in Iran driving up fuel costs, the whittling away of our education system, legislation that makes it harder to vote, abuse and alienation of our allies, deaths of U.S. citizens at the hands of ICE and tariffs that are being passed on to American consumers. We cannot afford children going hungry because of SNAP cuts, an EPA that is enabling the destruction of the planet, whitewashing or erasing U.S. history and a lack of AI regulation that could quickly get out of human control.
I encourage you all to tune out the negative campaign ads that stretch the truth and look at how we can be better humans and get back to having an American dream again where basic needs are met and working people can even afford some wants. This will not happen with the current administration or Susan Collins’ consistent enabling. As everyone can clearly see, Collins votes with the Republicans 95% of the time and only doesn’t when her vote won’t make a difference. Collins may have been a moderate at some point during her career, but she no longer fits that definition.
Please vote for Troy Jackson and other Democratic candidates so working-class people, not just billionaires, have a shot at the American dream.

title: Mother, godmother charged in death of 4-year-old
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - Two people are facing charges in connection with the death of a 4-year-old in South Carolina.
The Richland County Sheriff’s Department said Zokeiyah McCray, 36, and Helen Benbow, 59, were arrested Friday and charged with homicide by child abuse.
The department said the investigation stemmed from deputies responding Friday morning to a hospital, where a child, identified as Kameron Howell, 4, was pronounced dead.
Medical staff reportedly told investigators that the child was seriously hurt, with lacerations seen throughout their body. The child had also suffered multiple head injuries that caused internal bleeding, as well as burn marks that deputies said “appeared consistent with contact from a lit smoking material.”
It was also found that McCray and Benbow had been the child’s legal guardians and caretakers since May 2026. McCray was the child’s godmother, while Benbow is McCray’s mother. Authorities said the two lived in the same apartment with the child.
McCray and Benbow were booked at the Alvin S. Glenn Detention Center.

title: Gas prices drop slightly in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The average price of gas and diesel in Maine has gone down slightly in the past week.
According to AAA, the average price of regular unleaded gas is $4.40, a three cent drop from last Monday.
This is four cents above the national average which sits at $4.36 as of October 5th.
Diesel has gone down by more than a nickel; the average price for a gallon now stands at $6.45 but still is well above the national average.
The national average for diesel currently sits at $6.32 as of October 5th.

title: Firefighter had to ‘gnaw’ his way free after being handcuffed by girlfriend, 911 call reveals
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG/Gray News) - An Ohio firefighter appeared in court Monday, three days after her arrest for allegedly refusing to remove a man from handcuffs, stealing his car and phone, and breaking into his home.
The alleged victim is a fellow Toledo firefighter and a captain within the department.
Kenasia Guilford, 33, faces multiple charges, including abduction. The two firefighters were in a relationship, according to a 911 call.
Guilford’s attorney, Richard Mitchell, spoke in court earlier this week.
“This series of incidents stems from a paramour situation, where some information was learned by the defendant that would make anyone have substantial concern and was traumatic,” Mitchell said.
In a 911 call from the captain’s friend, the victim’s friend detailed a call for help at four in the morning.
“I had a friend call me. He showed up at my house at four, saying his girlfriend handcuffed him,” the caller said.
Police say Guilford handcuffed the man to a staircase, with his consent, but affidavits say she later refused to let him go. The caller described how his friend broke free.
“And he said he had to gnaw — she handcuffed him to some railing or something. He said he had to fight his way off of there, so he might be injured, I don’t know,” the caller said.
The caller also told dispatchers he picked up his friend and drove him home.
Investigators say Guilford stole the man’s car, broke into his house, and was later found hiding inside.
“He told me to hover around so he could go and get his keys, and I can take him to go get his truck. But as I was waiting, I see her walking down the street in the pitch dark, running toward his house. I was on the phone with my wife, and she was like, ‘You might need to call 911,’ but I don’t even know what to say,” the caller said.
The alleged victim was walking down the street still in handcuffs, according to the 911 call. Police later had to cut the handcuffs off. It’s not clear how the alleged victim was able to contact his friend in the first place.
“You said he has no phone on him?” a dispatcher asked.
“No, I got his bag. He had a bookbag on him, but she had the phone. I think that’s why he was — why she handcuffed him — to get to his phone or something like that. And that’s why he didn’t have his phone on him,” the caller said.
Monday, a judge set Guilford’s bond at $10,000, with a no-contact order, and ruled she must wear an ankle monitor while the case is pending.

title: Special education needs growing more complex, Farmington schools find
text:
FARMINGTON — Regional School Unit 9 is seeing increasingly complex special education needs, even as its overall identification rate remains relatively steady, driving expansion of specialized programs, staffing, training and transportation services.
Director of Special Services Cynthia Bernstein said the district has seen significant changes in the types of services students require over the past five years.
Identification of students with specific learning disabilities has decreased by nearly 31% during that period, while autism identification has increased nearly 26%. Identification under other health impairments, including attention challenges or anxiety, has increased 67%.
Bernstein said the local increase in autism reflects a broader rise in diagnoses as well as students entering the district with existing needs.
“Each year students who transfer into the district come to us with these challenges, including new kindergarten students and this year pre-K students,” Bernstein said.
She also pointed to the effects of disrupted education during the COVID-19 pandemic and difficulty accessing services outside school.
“Families are struggling with accessing necessary community support, rural options are few, to help their children learn and use the life skills we are teaching in school,” she said.
While the overall percentage of RSU 9 students identified for special education has remained relatively consistent, Bernstein said the level and type of support needed has changed.
Life skills program services have increased, and include adaptive behavior services for eligible students. Speech and language, occupational therapy and physical therapy services expand as students’ developmental needs require them, while day treatment services continue across grade levels as students grow older.
The changing needs are shifting resources toward behavioral, adaptive and executive-functioning supports and have required smaller, more individualized programs.
RSU 9 has also reduced out-of-district placements by 50% over five years, although additional students would be placed outside the district if space were available.
Asked how the district is serving students whose needs might otherwise require an outside placement, Bernstein said the number changes from year to year.
“The district is focusing on solutions for students whose skills require a program that is more specialized than what can be provided in a public school building,” she said.
That work includes development of such a program as part of the special education services offered by Mt. Blue. The district’s special services budget has increased 19.5% over five years, from about $7.02 million in fiscal 2022 to about $8.38 million for fiscal 2027.
Bernstein identified staffing, training and transportation as the primary factors behind the increase. “The necessary expansion of programs has increased the need for skilled staff,” she said.
Training is provided before and throughout the school year so employees can develop and practice skills needed to serve students. The district also contracts with staffing companies when required positions cannot be filled by educators hired directly by RSU 9.
Transportation needs have also become more specialized. Based on student needs many times this is individualized in separate vehicles.
Staff preparation has been another major focus. More than 135 employees received SafetyCare training before the school year began, 22 educational technicians were being trained as behavioral health professionals, and nine professional staff members were receiving training to administer the Woodcock-Johnson V Test of Achievement.
Bernstein said staff training is one of the department’s strengths.
“I would say the things that we do best … are probably getting staff trained,” she said. The district is also evaluating whether its current safety training adequately addresses staff needs.
Bernstein said RSU 9 moved more training from the school year to the summer two years ago to reduce staff absences from classrooms and programs, a change that increased costs. During the past year and a half, the district has gathered staff feedback, reviewed administrator observations and examined changing student needs.
“These factors influenced the district’s investigation of additional behavior support programs that provide a more specific focus on student trauma and functional backgrounds and skills,” Bernstein said.
RSU 9 is also expanding services for younger children. The district is providing special education services for 4-year-olds through school-based pre-K programs, an adaptive skills pre-K and kindergarten program and community settings.
Bernstein said the district is preparing to take on services for 3-year-olds next year as well. The combination of younger students entering services and more students requiring intensive programming means the district will continue tracking staffing, space and program needs as it plans for future years.
RSU 9 includes Chesterville, Farmington, Industry, New Sharon, New Vineyard, Starks, Temple, Vienna, Weld and Wilton.

title: Grieving family fights fake obituaries for teenage son
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - The details in the obituaries were vague, some were totally wrong. Brett Tinch found himself correcting lies about his teenage son Noah’s life.
“I started seeing these posts, obituaries, and none of the information was accurate. The middle name was wrong,” Brett Tinch said. “There’s one out there that says he’s 32 years old.”
The rising sophomore was actually one day away from his 19th birthday, in Colorado with his mother. The family says he was helping grandparents clean out a property they had just sold, and he was doing what he loved - fly fishing.
“They believe that he had gotten a fly stuck in a rock and he had bent down to pick it up, he hit his head and lost consciousness and he drowned,” Brett Tinch said.
The father of two wasn’t planning on sharing those difficult details, but he knew he had to fight the fake facts with the painful truth.
“It’s an unfortunate situation, and it’s the last thing a family wants to deal with when a loved one has passed,” Dr. Lisa Blue, the director of the Artificial Intelligence Strategies for Eastern Kentucky University, said. “The family’s best strategy is to be proactive, and control the narrative by posting an obituary on an official news site, or a platform, or a funeral home website as soon as possible.”
Blue said the AI-generated obituaries are published anonymously, some overseas, with no repercussions for inaccurate information.
“These fake obituaries are then published to these low-quality, high-volume content sites in the hopes of generating ad revenue. So the more odd these obituaries seem, the more likely they’re gonna get clicks, and every one of those clicks generates a small income stream for the poster,” Blue said.
Blue said grieving families should publish the real obituary early and widely.
Use the funeral home’s website or a reputable obituary platform and ask friends to share that link only.

title: 🍗🔥 MAINE MADE THE LIST! This Thomaston Fried Chicken Gem Is Getting National Attention!
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Restaurant Named Among U.S.’s Most Popular Fried Chicken
If you love fried chicken, you may want to add a stop in Thomaston, Maine, to your food bucket list.
That’s because Honey's Fried Chicken Palace has landed on a nationwide list highlighting the most popular fried chicken spots in every state, and it’s representing Maine!
The list comes from Finance Buzz, a website best known for personal-finance and consumer content, including topics like credit cards, banking, shopping, travel, and budgeting. But FinanceBuzz also covers lifestyle topics, including food.
For this particular feature, Finance Buzz looked at fried chicken spots across all 50 states and selected a restaurant to represent each state. Honey’s Fried Chicken Palace was the Maine pick, giving this Thomaston favorite some fun national exposure.
Read More: This Maine Gem Ranks Among America's 20 Best Chinese Restaurants
And there’s plenty to love about the menu.
Honey’s specializes in fresh, made-to-order fried chicken, with its sandwiches being a major attraction. Popular options include The Classic, Hot Honey, Pimento, Nashville Hot, China Fortune, and Stinger, so there’s definitely more than one way to get your fried chicken fix.
Then there are the sauces. Lots of them.
Honey’s currently offers a whopping 17 housemade sauces, along with its famous oversized Super Tendies, wings, loaded tots, fries, and other sides. The restaurant says its chicken is fresh, never frozen, hand-trimmed, and seasoned with a custom blend of 12 herbs and spices.
It’s pretty cool to see a Maine restaurant from a small Midcoast town getting national attention for something as universally loved as fried chicken.
So, have you tried Honey’s yet? Which sandwich is your favorite?

title: US monitoring suspected plague death in Russia. Here's what to know
text:
US monitoring suspected plague death in Russia. Here's what to know
A Russian lab worker who worked in an anti-plague institute died recently from an undisclosed disease, prompting questions, quarantines and an investigation.
Here's what you need to know:
What happened?
A 28-year-old female staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and Far East died last week from pneumonia of an "undetermined" origin, according to Igor Kobsev, the regional governor.
According to Axios, unconfirmed local media reports state that on Sept. 25, the staffer — identified as Darya Shipilova — accidentally broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen.
Shipilova reportedly became ill while at work and was admitted to a local hospital on Sept. 29. She died overnight on Oct. 2.
Did she contract the disease from the facility where she worked?
Nothing has been confirmed or ruled out at this point. However, Kobsev said that no "microorganisms linked to the employee's professional activities were detected" in her body, adding that there were no other cases among employees at the facility.
Where did this happen?
The anti-plague lab is in the city of Irkutsk, and the hospital where the staffer was treated is in the nearby town of Shelekhov; both are in eastern Russia, over 3,000 miles from Moscow.
What is the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and Far East?
It is a public health and research facility that studies infectious diseases, specifically the plague. Its research is used to monitor and prevent diseases from forming and spreading in the region.
According to the institute's website, it employs roughly 95 workers, including "13 doctors and 40 candidates of medical and biological sciences."
How are Russian authorities responding?
Maxim Modin, the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district where the lab and hospital are located, said that authorities are implementing a “comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures."
The hospital's inpatient facility where the worker was treated has been quarantined, and several departments have suspended patient admissions and discharges, Modin said. Other hospitals in the region have also closed, according to local media reports.
Local media has also reported that the institute is locked down, forcing staff to sleep on the floor and in chairs. "They've been isolating everybody since Friday – more than 60 people," a relative named Roman told the news outlet Siberia.Realities.
Unofficial reports, including those from the independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala, say that nearly 200 people are under observation.
Modin said that there have been no reported cases of infectious diseases among institute staff over the past 10 days, and all of the late employee's recent contacts are being tested and examined.
Is there a threat to the U.S.?
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration was watching the situation closely.
"I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it," Rubio said.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said that it is in contact with Russian authorities and is attempting to verify details.
"Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low," it said.
What is pneumonic plague?
There are three forms of plague, an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
Bubonic affects the lymph nodes, septicemic infects the blood and pneumonic impacts the lungs.
Scientists consider pneumonic plague the most dangerous form of the infection.
How is pneumonic plague transmitted?
Pneumonic plague is the only form of the infection that can spread directly from person to person, typically through respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit the disease.
What are the symptoms?
Pneumonic plague can trigger severe pneumonia, causing intense breathing problems.
Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Symptoms usually begin within 24 hours of the infection, and without immediate treatment, it is almost always fatal.
The last person in the U.S. to die from pneumonic plague was a resident of Flagstaff, Arizona, in July 2025. It was the first U.S. death from the infection since 2007.
CNN contributed to this report.

title: ‘Days of Our Lives’ actor Robert Kelker-Kelly dead at 62
text:
(Gray News) — “Days of Our Lives” actor Robert Kelker-Kelly died Saturday. He was 62.
TMZ was the first to report his death.
Kelker-Kelly was best known for playing Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives” from 1992 to 1995, according to his IMDb page.
His character arc often revolved around Lisa Rinna’s character Billie Reed.
Earlier this year, Rinna revealed in her memoir “You Better Believe I’m Gonna Talk About It” that the two did not get along on set, going so far as to say Kelker-Kelly was “verbally abusive” and “manipulative.”
Kelker-Kelly also appeared in other series including “Port Charles,” “Touched by an Angel” and “General Hospital.”
According to TMZ, Kelker-Kelly was also a professional pilot.
Kelker-Kelly died at his home in St. Peters, Missouri, according to Deadline. St. Peters police responded to his home for a report of an unconscious man who was not breathing.
Deadline reported the actor complained of chest pain shortly before coming unresponsive, police said. His official cause of death has not been revealed.

title: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Dennis Hastert, whose congressional legacy as the longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.
Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007 and spent more than a year in prison later in life, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.
When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.
In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP’s poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job in 1999, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton’s impeachment trial.
After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush’s legislative agenda.
A post-congressional scandal lands Hastert in prison
In 2015 he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified “prior misconduct.” Nearly a year later, prosecutors said Hastert’s alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in Yorkville, a small town west of Chicago.
Prosecutors said Hastert sexually abused at least four team members during his coaching career, which lasted from 1965 to 1981.
The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them.
Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.
Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.
At the sentencing hearing, where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a “serial child molester.”
In a statement, Hastert said he was “deeply ashamed” and admitted that he “mistreated” some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.
He knew how hard being speaker would be
When he became House speaker, Hastert was aware of the pitfalls of holding the powerful position.
“You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn’t be,” Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. “But you come back home, and you’re home. You’re back where you’ve always been, and your feet are back on the ground.”
As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert’s aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.
“I really didn’t want to be president, temporary or otherwise,” Hastert wrote in a 2004 memoir.
Hastert’s journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.
In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.
Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.
In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995.
Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.
He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year.
Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor’s degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master’s in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.
In 2007, Wheaton named its new public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert’s indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.
Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago’s suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family’s feed business.
Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.
___
Tarm and McCann are former Associated Press reporters. Associated Press reporter Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, contributed to this report.

title: UMSG approves $2,080 funding request for consent awareness events
text:
The University of Maine’s Student Government (UMSG) held its 1,619th meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 22, at 6 p.m. in the Bangor Room at the Memorial Union. 16 senators attended as the Senate considered student organization recognition, funding requests, executive reports and several new initiatives.
The meeting began with the approval of the agenda and minutes from the Sept. 15 meeting. Sen. Rivera’s resignation was also announced at the beginning of the meeting.
Ski & Snowboard Club Receives Preliminary Recognition
The Ski & Snowboard Club received preliminary recognition from the Senate following a presentation from club president Flynn Barden.
The club meets biweekly to discuss skiing and snowboarding. Once there is enough snow, meetings will transition into trips to Sugarloaf Mountain. The organization also takes an annual trip to Canada, which typically includes between 25 and 30 students.
The club has been active for approximately six years and previously had more than 300 members on CampusGroups. Barden said the organization currently has about 200 students registered through Google Classroom and approximately 2,000 followers on Instagram.
The club also works with a local brewing company to raise money for the Maine Adaptive program, which provides adaptive skiing experiences for people with disabilities.
Senators asked about potential future funding requests. Barden said the club hopes to organize a Beginners Day event in February that would include transportation, lift tickets, equipment and other expenses. The exact cost of the event had not yet been determined.
The Senate approved the committee’s recommendation for preliminary recognition without discussion or debate.
Student Organizations Receive Final Recognition
The Maine College of Engineering and Computing Student Advisory Board received final recognition after Sen. Delorme spoke on behalf of the organization.
The advisory board is made up of engineering and computing students and reports directly to the dean of the Maine College of Engineering and Computing. The board provides students with an opportunity to give feedback about the college and gives students direct access to the dean without having to go through faculty.
Delorme said nine students, in addition to the executive board, attended the previous meeting. The organization plans to increase its advertising efforts over the next several weeks, primarily by speaking to students in classrooms before classes begin. The Senate approved the board’s final recognition.
The Caribbean and Latinx Student Association also received final recognition. Club president Sofia Carrasquillo said the organization is intended to provide an inclusive environment for all students, including students who are not Caribbean or Latinx.
The organization meets every Monday and typically has between seven and 15 students at meetings, with more than 15 students on its email list. The club does not charge member dues and collaborates with other student organizations.
Carrasquillo said the organization is hoping to restart a Carnival Day and host a Culture Fest in November. The group anticipates requesting between $400 and $500 for the events and plans to fundraise for costs beyond that amount. The Senate approved the organization’s recognition without debate.
The Bedazzling Club was also approved for recognition. Club president Natalie Murdoch described the organization’s goal as making “the campus sparkle a little more.”
The club bedazzles personal items and other objects and has collaborations planned with the American Chemical Society and the Mushroom Club. The organization currently has 30 members, six of whom joined within the previous 24 hours. The club meets every other week in the Den at the Memorial Union and expects to request funding for general supplies. The Senate approved the committee’s recommendation.
Senate Approves Funding for Consent Awareness Events
The Senate approved a $2,080 funding request from Sigma Phi Epsilon for two events: Concert for Consent and Walk a Mile in Her Shoes.
Mason Hartery, chair of the project, Brandon Mastrianno, the organization’s treasurer, and two other representatives presented the request.
Concert for Consent brings local bands together to raise awareness of sexual assault. The event partners with Rape Response Services and Partners for Peace.
Walk a Mile in Her Shoes is a relay event in which participants walk around the mall wearing high heels. Representatives explained that the event is intended to represent the experience of women walking home after a night out.
The two events have previously been held separately but will be combined this year and held on the mall on the same day.
Hartery said Concert for Consent has been held for more than a decade. Last year, the concert drew approximately 350 people, while the walk had about 150 participants. Organizers expect similar attendance this year.
Funding will go toward food, sound and lighting equipment, the band stage, performers, flyers and shoes for the event.
Representatives said donations are welcome for the walking event, although teams are not required to pay to participate. Proceeds from the event will go to Rape Response Services.
The Senate approved the funding request following debate. Sen. Farnsworth spoke in support of the importance of the events to the campus community.
Executive Reports
President Cynthia Shelmerdine reported on several upcoming meetings and projects. She said she would meet with the president of the Black Student Union and serve as a guest speaker at a Student Athlete Advisory Council meeting. Shelmerdine also said she met with the vice president of research about developing a council with equal representation between graduate and undergraduate students.
She said she would work with the university’s director of communications to create a post addressing the university’s funding situation. The goal, according to the minutes, is to provide information and prevent what Shelmerdine described as false narratives or unnecessary concern.
Shelmerdine also announced plans for “Beat UNH” shirts for the women’s hockey team ahead of its Dec. 4 home game against the University of New Hampshire. The event will include a Fan Fest outside with food trucks, and the Student Government plans to distribute shirts to attendees.
Vice President Hazel Sparks reported that she had completed her senator meetings and was beginning work on the next projects for the semester. She also said she was working on the Sports Club Representative Board and restarting the Syllabus Bank Project.
Vice President of Financial Affairs Matthew Webber reported that he had spent much of the previous week helping student organizations begin the funding process, holding hiring meetings and working to ensure the university’s transition to Bangor Payroll goes smoothly.
Vice President of Student Organizations Alayna Dana said five clubs had appeared before her committee during the week. She also reminded club officers that update forms were due Sept. 22 and said she would soon begin an audit of student organizations.
University Budget Discussed
Student Government advisor Lauri Sidelko addressed questions surrounding the university’s budget situation.
Sidelko said the university’s financial situation has been developing for more than a year and encouraged senators to seek information about university funding and how different sources of money can be used.
According to Sidelko, university leadership is working to communicate about the situation and provide transparency. She noted that while enrollment and tuition have increased, university expenses have also risen.
New Policy and Student Government Election
The Senate also considered a new policy concerning pronouns in Student Government’s governing documents.
The proposed resolution, titled “Pronoun Standardization Across Documents,” would change remaining gendered pronouns in governing documents to gender-neutral pronouns. The Policy and Procedure Committee recommended approval, and the Senate approved the resolution without discussion or debate.
Sen. Braun was also elected to the Student Organization Committee after Sen. Noble-Brown resigned from the committee because of another time commitment. Several senators declined nominations before Braun accepted the position.
The meeting concluded with several announcements, including the Concert for Consent and Walk a Mile in Her Shoes events scheduled for Oct. 1. After a final roll call, Sen. Delorme moved to adjourn. The motion passed, and the meeting ended at 7:17 p.m.

title: Early voting begins in Maine ahead of November election
text:
Early voting begins in Maine ahead of November election
Mainers can start voting early, in-person at town offices across the state on Monday ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
Early voting begins in Maine ahead of November election
Mainers can start voting early, in-person at town offices across the state on Monday ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
Mainers can start voting early, in person at town offices across the state on Monday ahead of the November election.
Registered voters can also request, complete and return an absentee ballot.
Voters do not need to provide a reason to vote absentee, and those voting in person at the clerk's office do not have to fill out an application in advance.
Voters also can request an absentee ballot online or by mail.
The deadline to request a no-excuse absentee ballot is Thursday, Oct. 29.
Voters must submit completed absentee ballots to their municipality by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Maine residents who are not yet registered to vote still can participate. The state allows same-day voter registration, meaning eligible voters can register and cast a ballot during the early voting period or on Election Day.
In September, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said that absentee voting by mail would continue as normal, after the U.S. Supreme Court rejected a Trump administration effort to dramatically overhaul the system in the name of election integrity.
"We know that many Mainers – particularly seniors and people with disabilities – appreciate the convenience of voting from home, and we are thrilled that our joint legal efforts with states across the country to protect the right to vote by mail have succeeded," Bellows wrote in a news release on Sept. 15. "This is good news for voters and for democracy."
Despite criticizing absentee voting and falsely blaming fraud associated with mail-voting for his 2020 election loss, President Donald Trump is now imploring Republicans to use "every appropriate tool," including mail-in ballots, to vote in the midterms.
The Secretary of State’s Office says Maine is coming off record turnout during the June primary election and is a national leader in voter turnout.
During the June primary, Maine Democrats outnumbered Republicans 3:1 in the turnout of unenrolled early and absentee voters.
On Election Day, Mainers will cast ballots to decide the race for Maine Governor, U.S. Senate, House, and every seat in the Maine Legislature.
Visit WMTW's Maine Voter Guide for everything you need to know before you cast your ballot.

title: Spruce Mountain field hockey defeats Lisbon in C South battle
text:
LISBON — Things weren’t going Spruce Mountain’s way before the first whistle even blew.
“I think everything was against us,” said coach Alex Bessey. “Our bus was late, didn’t pick us up, so we showed up (at) about 3:50 for a (4:15) start. And then it was hailing. So there were a lot of things against us.”
The Phoenix were able to overcome those challenges, however, and defeat Lisbon 1-0 on Monday in a battle between Class C South field hockey contenders.
“Our record’s (now) 9-1 but I think behind the scenes, it’s been a little painful and a little bit bumpy roads,” Bessey said. “So this (win) was really huge for us.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
This was the first time Spruce Mountain (9-1) and Lisbon (8-1) faced off since last year’s Class C South semifinal game — which the Phoenix won, 1-0 — so it felt appropriate that the score was 0-0 until the second half.
Alaina Kachnovich eventually scored a couple minutes into the third period off an assist from Maddie Grimaldi.
“Lots of adrenaline,” Kachnovich said. “There wasn’t much defense back there, so I was just ready to go for it. And (Grimaldi) had my assist and we just all worked super hard to get (the score).”
The Greyhounds (8-1), like Spruce Mountain, came close to scoring several times, but they never found the back of the cage.
“I don’t think they were a bad team,” Lisbon forward/midfielder Julia Quagliaroli said. “They had good defense, they had good shots, they had good aerials, good drives, and you have to work with that, you have to block it up, stuff like that.”
UNSUNG HERO
Spruce Mountain’s Maddie Grimaldi averaged two steals per game for the Phoenix this past basketball season, so it’s little surprise that she knocked the ball away from a Lisbon defender to find Kachnovic for the game’s lone goal.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “I’m super happy for my team. We’ve been working really hard this season, and it finally all came together and we were able to finish today with a win.” — Spruce Mountain forward Alaina Kachnovic
• “(Playing a team like Spruce Mountain) brings us fire because we just want it more and more every single day, and we work hard at practice, we work hard in preseason. We work hard for our wins.” — Lisbon forward/midfielder Julia Quagliaroli.
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Spruce Mountain: Alaina Kachnovic (goal), Maddie Grimaldi (assist)

title: New brewery opens at former Lone Pine space in Old Orchard Beach
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An Old Orchard Beach motelier has opened a brewery and restaurant in the former home of Lone Pine Brewing Company.
Joe Rousseau, who owns The Executive Motel and Crosswinds Cottages, opened Old Orchard Brewing Company last week.
“It’s a great location,” Rousseau said. “So far, it’s been actually really great.”
Old Orchard Brewing Company, located at 32 E. Grand Ave., offers beer on tap, plus cocktails, pizza, soup, salad and nachos. There’s an outdoor patio, too.
Lone Pine Brewing Company, which Rousseau helped bring to town, closed in late September.
Rousseau celebrated Old Orchard Brewing Company’s opening with a “pretty big” first day. He said the first weekend was steady, and he expects the brewery to become a hangout spot for locals.
“There aren’t a lot of breweries down here,” Rousseau said. “It’s something to bring down to Old Orchard Beach and add to the community. We’ve had a lot of locals come in excited to see it open.”
In the future, Rousseau hopes to begin brewing his own beer. (Right now, he’s waiting on permits from the state.) It’s not something he’s well-versed in, but he’s excited to try it.
“It’ll be a new experience,” he laughed.
As tourist season comes to a close, Rousseau plans to offer game nights, open mic nights and trivia events as a way to get people through the door and connect with the community during the winter.
And next summer, he plans to bring live music to the brewery.
“The sky’s the limit,” Rousseau said.
Old Orchard Brewing Company is open 3 p.m. to 8 p.m. Sunday-Thursday, and 3 p.m. to 9 p.m. Friday and Saturday.

title: Cornell building sprayed with graffiti blasting school's response to gang rape complaint
text:
A crowd of students protests Cornell's response to gang rape allegation
Cornell students thronged a campus plaza to protest the university's response to allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity house, and the school's main administration building was splashed with graffiti and damaged overnight.
At a demonstration that overflowed the large space in front of the school's student center, students, faculty members and others wore purple ribbons and held signs with such messages as “support survivors, expel rapists” and “Justice 4 every Jane Doe" — the name by which the woman who reported the assault is known in court papers. Other people watched from pathways, windows and a nearby hill.
“Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support,” student Athena Holloway told the crowd. “How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”
Hispanic studies professor Julia Chang added to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.”
Calls for Cornell president's resignation
Speakers faulted fraternities, the university trustees and Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff, saying he and his administration have prioritized protecting the university's reputation over students' safety.
“Kotlikoff, resign!” demonstrators chanted, among other slogans, as they marched to the damaged administration building to present a list of demands. They included changes to how the student code of conduct defines sexual consent, an overhaul of the student discipline system and expulsions or degree revocations for all students involved in the alleged 2024 assault of the woman known as Jane Doe, among other things.
The woman's account of being sexually assaulted by several fraternity brothers has made clear, on and beyond campus, that “for all the strong feelings about sexual assault, .... we do not do enough to prevent it, nor to support survivors after it happens," student Madeline Gage said.
The group began disbanding with chants including “Ban the frats!”
Graffiti and broken glass at an administration building
The Ivy League school has been trying to quell a firestorm over its handling of the alleged 2024 gang rape. Early Monday, the university found signs of the anger on the very walls of its administrative headquarters.
Holes were knocked into one of the building's glass doors, and the walls beside them were marked with red-painted messages condemning patriarchy and the Ivy League school’s handling of sexual assaults, news media photos showed. Later Monday, the graffiti was removed and the door was boarded up.
Cornell spokesperson Kyle Kimball said in a statement that the university was investigating and that “damaging property is not the answer” to Cornellians' “frustration and strong emotions.” Campus police referred questions to his office, which declined to provide more detail on the incident.
Jane Doe alleges that she was sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity members in October 2024 after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs. She was a Cornell student at the time.
The woman recently sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others. Her lawsuit said that she became fully incapacitated as fraternity members assaulted her, and that one man sent others a message inviting them to participate.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told Cornell investigators last year, according to records reviewed by The Associated Press.
Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that some of the accused students, when interviewed by Cornell investigators, described the sexual activity as consensual.
Shortly before she went to Cornell police in November 2024, Jane Doe recorded a phone call with one of the men she says raped her. ABC News broadcast portions of that call Monday, containing only what it said was his voice, and recounted other parts of the conversation in writing.
“What y’all did would be classified as gang rape,” she told him at one point, according to the network, which said she had provided the recording to the university.
Students are demanding transparency, accountability
The suit has drawn national attention to what Cornell, its police force and the local district attorney did after she told the campus police in November 2024 she “can say with 100% confidence I was raped.”
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others. In a statement last week, the administration bristled about the “false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case.”
Students, however, have demanded more accountability and transparency, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has said Jane Doe was “failed by people and institutions" including the Cornell police and local District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.
Hochul appointed the state attorney general last week to take over a criminal investigation that Van Houten had reopened days earlier, and the governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter.
After the week's developments, Kotlikoff released an apologetic video Saturday, saying that Jane Doe's account “raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.”
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his support for an independent review of the university's actions and vowed more transparency and a commitment to "finding the answers our community deserves.”
Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz contributed from New York.

title: Part I: An Interview with Jim Gilbert
Supreme Court weighs local governments' climate change lawsuits against oil and gas companies
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court grappled Monday with whether local governments can sue oil and gas companies to help cover costs associated with climate change, an issue with potentially billions of dollars at stake.
Key justices appeared wary about the potential sweep of litigation, but torn over the complex legal interplay of federal and state laws raised by the case.
Officials in Boulder argue their lawsuit is an attempt to hold energy companies Suncor and ExxonMobil accountable for their contributions to climate change.
They say that worsening disasters such as floods and wildfires put a heavy financial burden on local communities, and the industry should bear part of that cost.
Governments from largely blue-leaning areas around the country have filed similar lawsuits seeking damages that could total billions of dollars, part of a wave of legal action worldwide seeking to leverage action through the courts.
“If you prevail, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit,” said Chief Justice John Roberts. “How do you think that will work out on the ground?”
A win for the oil and gas companies at the Supreme Court could shut down dozens of similar cases.
Suncor and Exxon argue that the Clean Air Act gives the federal government – not the states – the power to regulate emissions.
They have the support of the Trump administration, which argues the lawsuits are an unconstitutional attempt to regulate planet-warming emissions and impose Colorado’s state law beyond its borders.
But Roberts and other justices raised skeptical questions about why they should bar civil lawsuits in state courts now. The court is also weighing a jurisdictional question that allows it an “off-ramp” to avoid deciding the issues now.
The case was heard without Justice Samuel Alito, who recused himself just a week before arguments after facing calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies. That raises the possibility of a tie vote, which would allow the Colorado case to proceed.
The companies asked the justices to reverse a decision from Colorado’s highest court allowing the case to proceed. Attorney Kannon Shanmugam, representing the industry, said the Boulder case was attempting to use the courts to decide a public policy issue that is properly up to Congress and other elected officials.
“Climate change is certainly one of the most pressing issues” facing the country, but the lawsuit “is exactly the wrong way to go about” addressing it, he said.
Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris said Boulder’s case “egregiously exceeds” the state’s authority. The county essentially declares itself a victim of actions that occurred largely out of state, she said.
But Kevin Russell, an attorney representing Boulder, argued that state lawsuits can address damage in Colorado, regardless where the fossil fuels are produced.
Trump’s Republican administration has rolled back environmental regulations, including a move last month by the Environmental Protection Agency to repeal rules that limit emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. States and cities have already sued the Trump administration over the repeal of the power plant rule.
The conservative-majority Supreme Court has been skeptical of environmental regulations in the past, including in a 2022 decision limiting the EPA’s authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions from power plants.
A decision is expected in the coming months.
___
Associated Press writer Nicholas Riccardi in Denver contributed to this story.

title: Family prepares to donate son’s organs after devastating high school football injury
text:
SWEET HOME, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — A 15-year-old Oregon high school student who suffered a severe brain injury during a football game is preparing to donate his organs, his family said.
Mason Flores was injured during a home game at Sweet Home High School on Monday. He had a seizure and a brain bleed, and he was flown to Portland for surgery.
His family said doctors worked to treat him, but his condition did not improve. Now, his family is saying their goodbyes.
Monday would have been Mason’s 16th birthday.
In an update shared by the family, Mason’s loved ones said he was preparing to donate his organs to help other families. They asked the community to remember him for his love of football, humor and the joy he brought to those around him.
“With the full blessing of Mason’s family, our school district will proceed with our scheduled homecoming ceremonies and events,” Superintendent Terry Martin said in a message to the community. “Continuing with homecoming is a direct reflection of the family’s request to celebrate life, joy and community.”
Martin said counselors and support staff will be available to students and employees.
A GoFundMe page has been set up to help Mason’s family with medical expenses.

title: Local students participate in Socktober
Midcoast Maine boarding home closes after 50 years
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
THOMASTON, Maine — The Lucette Boarding Home, which has provided assisted care living for residents for 50 years, has closed.
Administrator Brian Holmes said that it had become increasingly difficult to retain and attract employees. He said workers would call out and some would simply not call and not show up to work. He said he and the owner have filled in for shortages but that it turned out not to be a temporary problem.
“If it was temporary we could do it, but it became overwhelming,” Holmes said.
The home spent $7,000 to advertise for workers on Indeed, which he said has been successful in the past. But lately, there are no or few responses to such advertisements.
Lucette’s staff was able to find homes for the 14 residents who remained at the home at the end. The capacity of the house was 18 residents.
He said that the longest resident of Lucette began living there in September 1997. He said it was difficult for some people to move but that they have heard feedback that the residents are happy in their new assisted living homes.
Holmes said the state was prepared to renew Lucette’s license but that the staffing issues and low reimbursement rates from the state led to the decision to close.
But he said the state was constantly clawing back finding money for the services provided at Lucette. He said reimbursement is not sufficient to hire qualified staff.
Lucette provided meals, dispersed the medication to residents, took them to appointments, and personal care services such as laundry.
Lucette opened at 61 Main St. in 1976, but he said it had served in similar capacities under different businesses prior to Lucette. The house has been at the location since the 1800s.
Michelle McLean of Waldoboro is the owner, Holmes is treasurer of the company as well as administrator, and Kristen Lee of Jefferson is listed as a director.
The town has the property valued at $566,300 for tax purposes.

title: Trump says he may visit Maine
text:
Before departing for a campaign event in Nebraska, President Donald Trump told members of the media on Monday that he may be making a stop in Maine in the near future.
“I don’t know about Maine,” Trump told reporters who asked whether the state was among his upcoming stops. “I think we’re going to Maine, too, but I’m going to Michigan in about a week and a half.”
A spokesperson for Sen. Susan Collins said her office is unaware of any plans for Trump to come to Maine and referred a reporter to the White House.
When asked whether any formal plans were taking shape for a visit, a White House spokesperson deferred a reporter to the Republican National Committee. The RNC did not immediately reply to a request for comment on Monday.
Trump plans to visit at least 10 states ahead of the midterm elections, Politico reported last week, though Maine was reportedly not on the list at that time.

title: No arrests announced in shootings that killed 2, left dozens injured at Georgia block party
text:
No arrests announced in shootings that killed 2, left dozens injured at Georgia block party
Authorities in rural southern Georgia were still searching Monday for suspects in weekend shootings that killed two people and left nearly three dozen others injured when gunfire erupted during a sprawling block party to celebrate a homecoming football victory.
No arrests have been announced in Dooly County, where the sheriff says more than 50 shots were fired early Sunday in the small city of Vienna as more than 1,000 people were still outside celebrating long after midnight.
Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy identified the two people killed as Ja’Quavion Jackson, 21, of Cordele, and Macaleb Jackson, 23, of Hawkinsville. The two men don't appear to be related, said Sara Lue, a spokesperson for the Georgia Bureau of Investigation.
An additional 35 people were injured — most of them by gunfire, though others were hurt in the chaotic scramble to flee, authorities told reporters at a Sunday news conference. The sheriff said an unspecified number were hospitalized with critical injuries.
Authorities haven't said what may have motivated the shootings or precisely how many people were shot.
“At large parties with people from different places, not just your locals, sometimes problems come,” Peavy said Sunday.
Local officials say the block party wasn't a school-sponsored event and didn't have a city permit. Peavy said he had extra deputies working over the weekend in anticipation of homecoming drawing large numbers of alumni and other out-of-town visitors.
The sheriff did not immediately return a phone message Monday. Lue said no further updates were available from state investigators, who customarily assist Georgia's rural communities in major cases.
The violence marred what Peavy said had been a large but otherwise peaceful celebration of Dooly County High School winning its homecoming football game in Vienna, a city of about 3,000 people located about 50 miles south of Macon.
Crowds of revelers gathered across an area covering four blocks, and Peavy said that he had deputies patrolling the area. When the first shots were fired and deputies rushed to the scene, he said, more gunfire sounded about a block away.
“It was so many people,” Peavy said. “And it was just hard to figure out what was going on.”
Among this weekend's visitors was Antoria Felton of Jonesboro, who drove two hours to bring her daughter and six other girls to Vienna. She told WMAZ-TV that everything seemed peaceful when suddenly “bullets were going everywhere.”
Felton said she saw that “kids laying on the ground had been shot” as she scrambled to find her daughter and the other girls.
“The only thing I’m trying to do is find these girls,” Felton said. “Everybody scattered out everywhere, everybody running. It was terrifying.”

title: Maine SAT scores reach five-year high and outscore the national average
text:
Maine students scored higher on the SAT this year than they have in any of the past five years.
According to new data from the College Board, Maine high schoolers scored higher on the SAT than any graduating class since 2021 and outscored the national average by more than 40 points.
Still, less than half met the college and career readiness benchmarks, which the College Board says predict future success.
The number of Maine students meeting these benchmarks has declined by nearly 10% post-pandemic.
Maine’s SAT participation rate has remained steady since the pandemic, and the College Board said a majority of students are submitting their scores to colleges in Maine, even though most don’t require them for admission.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Nicaragua torture victim imprisoned for second time after being deported by U.S.
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — A Nicaraguan exile who was imprisoned and tortured after protesting against the government was deported by the U.S. back to his country, where he was immediately imprisoned once again by authorities, family members and his lawyer confirmed Monday.
Upon climbing off the U.S. deportation flight in Managua, Nicaragua’s capital, last week, 35-year-old Jeffrey Jarquín was taken by authorities back to the same prison where he was once tortured, confirmed one family member.
The family member spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity, fearing persecution by the government. Local media first reported on Jarquín’s deportation and detention.
Jarquín was a prominent figure in anti-government protests in 2018, which set off a yearslong campaign by husband-and-wife co-Presidents Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo to crush dissent.
The government’s crackdown on critics, civil society, religious groups and virtually anyone who raised their voice has fueled the flight of more than 800,000 people from the country, according to U.N. figures.
Osley Sallent, Jarquín’s lawyer in the U.S., confirmed the Nicaraguan exile was deported after seeking asylum in the United States.
Jarquín was detained in 2018 with other protesters and thrown into a maximum-security prison known as El Modelo. Until he was released a year later and fled to the U.S., Jarquín and others were tortured in chambers known as “tiny hell,” according to a 2019 report by the Organization of American States.
Sallent said Jarquín was living in Miami when he was detained. Before Jarquín’s asylum case was rejected by a Louisiana court in July, Sallent said he was held in Alligator Alcatraz, the Florida immigration detention center in the Everglades plagued by reports of harsh conditions. Sallent wasn’t able to provide more details of the asylum case.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Following a request by the AP for more details on why Jarquín was imprisoned for a second time, a spokesperson for Nicaragua’s government responded: “Thank you very much! Hugs.”
The Trump administration has long criticized the Nicaraguan government and labeled it a dictatorship, especially after authorities there canceled elections scheduled for next year. Just last week, Deputy U.S. Secretary of State Christopher Landau said in remarks before the OAS that what was happening in Nicaragua was “intolerable.”
“Murillo and Ortega’s dictatorship has no place in our hemisphere,” he added.
Despite that, ICE has ramped up deportations to the Central American country in recent months, according to a recent Human Rights Watch report, which said the Trump administration had deported 6,300 Nicaraguans between January and July 2026.
The organization documented that ICE had detained least eight Nicaraguan exiles who were stripped of their citizenship in a move observers say was intended to punish critics, the report said. Some of those detained had pending asylum applications.
Juan Pappier, deputy director of the Americas for Human Rights Watch, said the simultaneous criticisms of Nicaragua’s government and deportations of those forced to flee its repression “makes Washington look hypocritical.”
“Nicaragua has the most brutal government in the Western Hemisphere, and any government critic who is sent back is at real risk of torture or persecution,” Pappier said.
——
Associated Press reporter Gisela Salomon contributed to this report from Miami.

title: Varsity Maine football honor roll for Week 5
text:

Dustin Maley, Massabesic: Maley carried the ball six times for 77 yards, highlighted by a 75-yard touchdown run, made big plays on defense and blocked a field goal in the Mustangs’ 14-7 win over Noble.

Miles Provost, Lawrence: Provost was a force all over the field in the Bulldogs’ 35-27 victory over Cony in a showdown of unbeaten Class B North teams. Provost caught two passes for 45 yards and two scores, and had a sack and a fumble recovery.
Logan Stout, Edward Little: Stout rushed for three touchdowns, including two in overtime, and threw for a score in the Red Eddies’ 27-21 double-overtime win over Scarborough.
Isaac Vail, Gorham: The Rams’ captain caught a 33-yard touchdown pass from Wyatt Walker with 30 seconds to go for the go-ahead score, then sealed a 19-17 win at Cheverus with an interception as time expired.
Ethan White, Kennebunk: White ran for all five of the Rams’ touchdowns in a 34-6 home win against Deering. White finished with 22 carries for 191 yards.

title: 1 CMMC nurse reinstated after September firings at Lewiston hospital
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
One Central Maine Medical Center nurse will return to work this week after being fired in mid-September, according to union officials in a press release issued Monday night.
The nurse, who was not identified, was among 20 who had been disciplined last month for “documented violations of established hospital policies and standards,” according to CMMC officials last month.
At the time, several city leaders criticized the hospital, which is owned by California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation, saying the terminations were retaliation for a unionizing effort among the nurses.
Local leaders from across the political spectrum said the firings appeared to be related to recent union activities at the hospital, which would be in violation of state and federal law, and demanded the nurses be reinstated.
“Nurses were unlawfully disciplined for our patient advocacy,” said Hillary Ferrell, former nurse at Olympia Fields Hospital in Illinois, another Prime hospital where six nurses were terminated during a unionization effort last month. “But we will never stop speaking up for our patients. Our patients and our community deserve safe staffing and safe patient care,” she said in the press release.
At Olympia Fields, four fired nurses had been re-instated by Monday night.
Nurses at Olympia Fields won their union election with 82% support on Sept. 23 and CMMC nurses won their union election with 91% on Sept. 24.
The announcement that a single CMMC nurse will return to work came from the National Nurses Organization, an affiliate of the National Nurses United union, at almost 8 p.m. Monday night.
The group said they are continuing to fight on behalf of the remaining nurses who were either suspended or fired.
“Prime needs to reinstate all nurses who were suspended or fired,” said Katie Grinnell, a former nurse at CMMC. “Also, Prime must stop challenging our overwhelming victory at the ballot box. We won our union election by a landslide.”

title: Maine's Biggest 2026 Pumpkin Was So Big It Nearly Cracked the All-Time Top 10
text:
Maine’s Biggest Pumpkin for 2026 Almost Landed in the Top 10 All Time
Someone tell Charlie Brown we've found the Great Pumpkin for 2026.
The Damariscotta Pumpkinfest is back once again, and with it, its weigh-off weekend.
According to the festival's Facebook page, Elroy Morgan took home the victory with his massive pumpkin, as well as landing a new Maine state record for his long gourd of 155.25 inches. And this isn't the first time Morgan has been a big winner.
The Biggest Pumpkin in Maine for 2026
Morgan has pulled off a back-to-back win for the biggest pumpkin in Maine.
In 2025, he secured the victory with his beast of a pumpkin that weighed 1,624.5. Now, for 2026, he delivered another monster, but one that was 200 pounds more.
The Damariscotta Pumpkinfest's website listed Morgan's latest grow at 1,847 pounds. That's about the weight of a large adult male polar bear. Don't let this pumpkin roll on you!
Unfortunately, it didn't make the top 10 for all-time biggest pumpkins, but it was very, very close.
Funnily enough, the No. 10 spot belongs to Morgan, who earned that place in 2021 with 1870.5 pounds. So close!
Wondering how the top 10 stack up?
READ MORE: Giant Pumpkins Take to the Water for Damariscotta’s One-of-a-Kind Regatta
Can you believe that No. 1 spot by WGME meteorologist Charlie Lopresti? That is one heck of a pumpkin.
The people who keep entering these weigh-offs year after year must love it, because you often see the same names pop up again and again. Honestly, that's the best thing. People who love what they do make the win that much sweeter.
Will Morgan make the top 10 next year? Maybe. We'll see. Either way, good grief, he's pulled off another big pumpkin for 2026.

title: Pedestrian dies after being hit by driver in Presque Isle
text:
A pedestrian walking along the Ginn Road in Presque Isle died after being hit by a motor vehicle over the weekend.
Shelby Sanborn, 67, died in the crash, which involved a vehicle driven by 18-year-old Silas Baser, Presque Isle Police Chief Chris Hayes said in a release Monday.
