The crash remains under investigation, and the police department has not determined fault or filed charges as of Monday.
The department will provide additional information “when appropriate,” Hayes said.

title: Maine’s volunteer libraries thrive with tight budgets. State rules could make that harder.
text:
STANDISH — Lynn Knowlton was ecstatic about a new furnace.
As president of the Richville Library, she waited eagerly on a recent Saturday morning for volunteers to help her install the contraption in the basement of the cozy, pale yellow building.
She bought the furnace with surprise cash donations from community members who wanted to help replace the outdated electric heating system that has strained the 103-year-old institution’s shoestring budget for years.
“I can’t stop happy dancing,” Knowlton said.
For all-volunteer-run libraries like this one, unexpected funding that helps serve their communities is a thrill.
What thrills them less is a proposed set of rules the Maine Library Commission is considering that would cut off their access to some state-provided services — internet, subsidized interlibrary loans, and the ability to receive grants through the Maine Public Library Fund — unless they pay their director, are open an average of 12 hours a week year-round, and participate in a specific number of professional development opportunities.
While the Richville Library serves Standish’s rural population of 11,000, other similar libraries in Maine are in more remote areas with even smaller communities, some of fewer than 1,000 people. They provide free internet, books, technology, regular programs and gathering spaces to small towns that otherwise don’t have them. Most run on annual budgets of less than $10,000, bolstered by fundraising, donations and grants. Some get annual help from their towns, usually $2,000 to $4,000.
Rural librarians say the measures would damage their libraries and communities. According to an impact assessment by the Maine State Library, 38 of approximately 257 public libraries in Maine do not currently meet the proposed standards.
The state commission began considering standards for libraries last November, but has eased its proposition over the past year in response to backlash. It voted to send its most recent draft for legal review in September.
Maine State Librarian Lori Stockman responded to requests for interviews sent to her and other state library leaders by explaining that they are “hesitant to say much” before the draft is finalized and public comment opens later this month.
Increasing costs and uncertain funding for the Maine State Library loom behind the rule’s efforts, said Chair Bryce Cundick at a commission meeting in January. The state agency laid off a third of its staff after federal funding cuts to the Institute of Museum and Library Services by the Trump administration in April 2025, but later regained some money and employees.
Money isn’t the only issue. Commission members and state librarians have also repeated that the requirements introduced would help ensure the quality of Maine’s libraries. Commission member Wynter Giddings said at the April meeting that paid staff leads to “sustainability” and “accountability” in libraries. Additional measures in the draft include requiring libraries to keep strategic plans.
Beyond Maine law stating a basic definition for public libraries, these standards would be the first set for libraries in Maine.
That has spurred frustration among volunteer librarians.
Dylan Johnston, head librarian and one of two volunteers at the East Millinocket Public Library, which serves a population of just over 1,500 from a town-owned building, said he thinks the push to disqualify them from state resources stems from a perception that their operations are not competent or valuable. Several other librarians have echoed that concern.
The process has raised questions about what it means to have a library and a librarian — many professional librarian roles require a master’s degree in library science.
“It’s very demeaning and deflating,” Johnston said. “This library has faced several challenges along the years, but I’ve kept it going. I’m an invaluable service.”
The library recently received a $50,000 grant from the Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation to purchase several pieces of furniture, a new sign and renovate the children’s area. Johnston said he helps people with technology issues and hosts a weekly group for older adults to give them a place to congregate.
Carol Wolf is the volunteer vice president of the Pembroke Library in Pembroke, one of the five libraries that would lose interlibrary loan services under the measures. She said it is not in the library’s budget to pay a director.
“Just because (libraries) don’t meet these direct criteria that the library commission wants to impose, does not seem to me to mean that they’re not effective libraries,” Wolf said. “This rule just doesn’t comport with reality in these small towns.”
Wolf is leading an effort to support small libraries, reverse the course of the rule, and try and get more representatives of rural libraries in northern Maine to apply for seats on the Maine Library Commission. Of the 26 seats, five are vacant, and no members are from north of Bangor. Members are appointed by the governor.
Losing internet access is the biggest threat for Johnston and other rural libraries, which could have to scramble to find the money to pay for it. Their current connectivity comes through NetworkMaine, which provides internet to most of Maine’s K-12 public schools and libraries. While NetworkMaine is state-provided, the federal service E-Rate covers roughly 70% of its costs.
One standard Maine already has in place mandates that libraries requesting subsidized interlibrary loan van delivery services must circulate more than 100 materials through the system per year to qualify.
According to a list compiled by Sarah Redfield, a lawyer in York who has voiced opposition to the rule, five libraries would be taken off the interlibrary loan route. Most rural libraries, including Richville and East Millinocket, don’t use the service.
Stockman, the state librarian, did not respond to requests for information about how much of the state library’s budget is used for NetworkMaine and interlibrary loan services for the potentially impacted libraries.
Karen MacGillivary is the volunteer director at the Laura E. Richards Library in Georgetown, a former one-room schoolhouse on a hill. The snowplow can’t reach the building and it lacks running water, forcing it to close in the winter months. It hosts what MacGillivary calls “Blizzard Books,” where patrons can sign out as many books as they want in October and exchange them with other community members until spring. She said circulation this past season increased by 200 books.
“It’s a happy place,” she said.
MacGillivary worries about the financial consequences of losing internet — many patrons come to the library just for that, and she does not know how the library would fund it alone.
The proposed rules are under review by the Office of the Maine Attorney General and the Department of the Secretary of State, and a 45-day public comment period is expected to open Thursday, with a public hearing on Oct. 29.
The commission will then respond to comments and decide whether to incorporate them at its January meeting. If the rules are implemented, libraries would have two years to start paying directors, with the option of requesting extensions.
Stockman emphasized that state law passed in 2011 mandates the commission to name minimum standards of library service, and the attorney general’s office advised it to create enforceable rules. However, the law does not specify what standards must be in place.
The current draft also does not specify how much libraries would need to pay directors. If the current draft were implemented as is, libraries could meet the requirement with a salary of as little as $1.
At a March commission meeting, Cundick said that the proposed measures should have been established much earlier. According to the state’s impact assessment, 44 states have established standards for libraries tied to eligibility for state resources.
Considering Maine’s long history of thriving small rural libraries that rely on state services, opponents say they believe the state should work to support them.
Six volunteers keep the Richville Library flourishing. Knowlton’s mother, Karen McNutt, is the director. Her father, David McNutt, is the treasurer, and her late grandmother was one of the young Standish girls in the Osmunda Club that began collecting books to create the library in the 1920s. Knowlton grew up in the house across the street, where her son now lives.
The library doubled its open hours to 13 a week in the past two years, and has expanded free programming to include American Sign Language classes, Red Cross trainings, a creative writer’s circle, multiple book clubs and more story times.
“There’s a lot of spirit still there in that place,” Karen McNutt said. “It’s pretty amazing.”
Knowlton and volunteers authored a laminated book of detailed biographical information about each of the Richville’s founders and its history. They work hard to make sure the library prospers.
“I’ve just gotten taken in by some of these stories and the commitments that people have, you know, for generations,” said Redfield, the lawyer pushing back on the proposed rules. “What I see is this direction to try to have all Maine libraries look alike, which is not what Maine is about.”

title: Cornell building is sprayed with graffiti blasting school's response to gang rape complaint
text:
ITHACA, New York (AP) — Cornell’s main administration building was splashed with graffiti and a glass door was broken overnight as student groups planned a protest Monday over the university’s handling of the alleged 2024 fraternity-house gang rape that has ignited a firestorm of anger on campus and beyond.
Holes were knocked into one of the administration hall’s glass doors, and the walls beside them were marked with red-painted messages condemning patriarchy and the Ivy League school’s handling of sexual assaults, news media photos showed.
Cornell spokesperson Kyle Kimball said in a statement that the university was investigating and that “damaging property is not the answer” to Cornellians’ “frustration and strong emotions.” A message seeking further details on the incident was sent to Kimball; campus police referred questions to his office.
Meanwhile, a roster of student organizations planned a late-afternoon “Justice for Survivors” demonstration to push for changes in the university’s process for handling sexual assault complaints and for more punishments connected to the one that followed a party at the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024.
A then-sophomore alleges that she was sexually assaulted there by multiple men after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.
The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, recently sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others. Her lawsuit said that she became fully incapacitated as fraternity members assaulted her, and that one man sent others a message inviting them to participate.
Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that some of the accused students, when interviewed by Cornell investigators, described the sexual activity as consensual.
The suit has drawn national attention to what Cornell, its police force and the local district attorney did after she told the campus police in November 2024 she “can say with 100% confidence I was raped.”
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others. In a statement last week, the administration bristled about the “false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case.”
Students, however, have demanded more accountability and transparency, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has said Jane Doe was “failed by people and institutions” including the Cornell police and local District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.
Hochul appointed the state attorney general last week to take over a criminal investigation that Van Houten had reopened days earlier, and the governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter.
After the week’s developments, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff released an apologetic video Saturday, saying that Jane Doe’s account “raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.”
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his support for an independent review of the university’s actions and vowed more transparency and a commitment to “finding the answers our community deserves.”

title: Gatorade recalls certain flavors nationwide. Here’s why
text:
(Gray News) - More than 122,000 cases of Gatorade have been recalled in 37 states, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
The recall affects 28-ounce bottles of Gatorade Lemon Lime, Gatorade Lemon Lime Zero, Gatorade Orange and Gatorade Orange Zero, according to the FDA. The products were recalled because they contain undeclared Yellow No. 5 and/or Yellow No. 6.
Affected Gatorade drinks were distributed to Alabama, Arkansas, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington and Wisconsin.
The recall received a Class II designation, which means the product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences, or that the probability of serious health consequences is remote.

title: Sass Jordan, 'Canadian Idol' judge and rock singer who toured with Aerosmith, Van Halen, has died
text:
Sass Jordan, 'Canadian Idol' judge and rock singer who toured with Aerosmith, Van Halen, has died
Sass Jordan, Canadian Idol judge and rock singer who had toured alongside Aerosmith and other artists like Van Halen at the start of her career, has died.
Video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
The singer's family said on Oct. 2 that she was surrounded by loved ones when she "peacefully crossed over to the other side."
"She remains in our hearts, an inimitable force of nature," her family said in a post on Instagram. "An irreplaceable being of light and joy!"
Jordan was born in England and moved to Montreal at three years old. There, she began playing guitar with her friends in Westmount Park as a young teen, her publicist Eric Alper shared after her death. By the time she was 16, Jordan was fronting bands in downtown Montreal clubs.
In a statement to People Magazine, Alper described Jordan as a "woman whose generosity and fire touched everyone who shared a stage, a studio or a kitchen table with her."
People Magazine said two years after she began her recording career as co-lead vocalist on “Come On (Baby Tonight)” from Bündock’s album Mauve, Jordan released her solo debut, Tell Somebody.
The title track rose to number 11 in Canada and she won the Juno Award for Most Promising Female Vocalist the following year. She was later nominated for Best Female Vocalist in 1990, 1993 and 1995.
Jordan then went on to tour alongside Aerosmith, The Rolling Stones, AC/DC, and Van Halen and joined "Canadian Idol" as a judge in 2003.
She was a judge on the show for all six seasons.
According to the Fort Frances Times, Jordan canceled her performances three months before her death, due to what her team described as a "serious medical condition."

title: Baltimore pastor to walk 40 miles through Maine calling for reparations
text:
A reverend will embark on a 40-mile journey from Brunswick to Augusta on Tuesday as part of a national campaign for reparations, symbolizing “40 acres and a mule,” an unfulfilled promise made to Black Americans after the Civil War.
The Rev. Robert Turner, the pastor of Empowerment Temple AME Church in Baltimore, will begin his walk in Brunswick early Tuesday morning and walk through Topsham, Bowdoinham, Richmond, Gardiner and Hallowell before arriving at the State House around 5:30 p.m.
Tuesday’s walk marks the 185th anniversary of Maine’s first Colored Convention, where Black Mainers gathered to demand equal citizenship.
Turner completed 40 40-mile walks from Baltimore to the White House before setting out to do reparations walks in all 50 states. Maine is his ninth.
“Now, my goal is to call on the nation to do repair,” he said Monday while preparing for his 49th trek.
Turner said he’s motivated by the people who fought for racial justice before him. When his body inevitably begins to ache and hurt, he said, he’ll be thinking of trailblazers like the late Gerald Talbot, Maine’s first Black legislator.
“You are much more mentally strong than you are physically strong,” Turner said, adding that he’s constantly wearing out gym clothes and sneakers.
Turner said he’s also commemorating the story of Malaga Island, which sits near the mouth of the New Meadows River in Phippsburg. The Casco Bay island was once home to a mixed-race community, until the state forcibly evicted its residents in 1912.
“(Maine) has a very rich history as it relates to race relations,” he said — including a long history of abolitionists.
Brunswick is a meaningful location to start the walk, being where Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” organizers said in a press release. It’s also home to Bowdoin College, where John Brown Russwurm became one of the first Black college graduates in the U.S. in 1826. Russwurm would go on to help found the nation’s first Black-owned newspaper.
Organizers said the public is invited to follow along with Turner as he makes his 40-mile trek, or greet him once he arrives in Augusta. He’ll begin at the corner of Maine and College Streets at 5 a.m.

title: Trump’s immigration crackdown divides rural voters as midterms approach, AP-KFF poll finds
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — More than a year into President Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown, a poll finds that voters in rural parts of the country are divided on whether those immigration policies have benefited or harmed their communities.
In The Associated Press-KFF survey of more than 2,000 rural voters in August, about a third said the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement had been positive for their community and about a third said it had been negative. The remaining 3 in 10, roughly, said it had no impact.
Trump promised tough enforcement on the campaign trail in 2024, and the survey highlights how a cornerstone of his base, rural supporters of his Make America Great Again movement, are especially likely to say they see a benefit where they live from the Republican president’s stringent immigration policies.
Yet many rural voters also say immigrants are a key part of their local economies, and some believe Trump’s immigration actions have gone too far.
Laura Leigh Taylor, a 37-year-old farmer who voted for Trump in 2024, said she disapproves of the wide-ranging scope of Trump’s immigration crackdown, which resulted in a friend’s hardworking father being deported.
“I understand getting rid of the rapists and the murderers,” she said. “But all the people that fell in between that really weren’t doing nothing but taking care of their family.”
Taylor now regrets her vote for Trump. As a resident of Smithville, Georgia, a town of about 600, Taylor thinks she will vote for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in November because, she said, the Democrats have been the ones talking about families being uprooted by Trump’s immigration enforcement.
“Just because of that simple fact, I’m going to go with him,” Taylor said.
Most rural voters want politicians to talk about immigration
Roughly three-quarters of rural voters say it’s “extremely” or “very” important for midterm candidates to talk about immigration, though that’s lower than the share who want them to address the cost of living, fraud in government programs or healthcare costs.
Rural voters don’t overwhelmingly think Trump’s immigration policies have helped their communities, but they are also less likely than the general public to say that Trump has overstepped in his efforts, which have involved mass deportations and rapid deportations of immigrants to countries where they have no ties.
Only about 4 in 10 rural voters say Trump has “gone too far” in restricting legal immigration or deporting immigrants living in the U.S. without authorization, below the 55% of U.S. adults overall who said the same in a September AP-NORC poll.
John Thomas, a 55-year-old from Liberty, Kentucky, supports Trump’s efforts to deport people without legal status. Thomas, who has just been approved for disability benefits after injuring his back in 2008, believes they put too much of a burden on the healthcare system. Regulating immigration, he said, is a means of providing better healthcare to Americans.
“They’ve been taking from everybody,” Thomas said of immigrants. “People that really need this stuff can’t get it because of them.”
David Grabowski, a professor of healthcare policy at Harvard Medical School, said that research suggests immigrants use less healthcare than native-born Americans. “It is hard to argue that they are placing an undue burden on the system,” he said, because many immigrants work in healthcare and pay taxes.
Most rural voters see the economic importance of immigrants
Immigrants often play key roles in sustaining local industries, including by filling jobs in manufacturing, healthcare and agriculture. The survey suggests the vast majority of rural voters see immigrants in the country legally as an important part of their local economies.
Shannon Monnat, director of the Center for Policy Research at Syracuse University and president of the Rural Sociological Society, said immigration has been a demographic lifeline for much of rural America. Rural areas have been losing young adults for years, she said.
“For a lot of small towns, immigrants are the reason the school and hospital stayed open and the county didn’t shrink,” Monnat said.
About 7 in 10 rural voters see immigrants who are in the country legally as “very” or “somewhat” important to their local economies, and a similar share say the same about temporary or seasonal agriculture workers. Hundreds of thousands of immigrants take seasonal jobs on U.S. farms each year, with most of them coming from Mexico, on H-2A visas.
Rural voters with a connection to agriculture and farming are more likely than those without one to say that temporary or seasonal workers are “very important” to their local economies, the poll found.
Jeff Miller, a 56-year-old Republican hydro blaster and vacuum technician, has mostly been pleased with Trump’s agenda, and he believes things are “heading in the right direction.” The one thing Miller has struggled with is Trump’s aggressive immigration policy, which he blames for the deportation of a “really good worker” and friend, who was removed from the U.S. when his work permit expired.
Miller, from Racine, Ohio, said he would support exceptions for hard workers, or just a less aggressive approach.
“There’s kind of an up-and-down thing because I lost a really good friend over that,” Miller said.
Rural voters are much less likely to say immigrants who are in the country illegally are beneficial, but 45% say they are at least “somewhat” important to local economies.
Albert Martinez, a 70-year-old Democrat from San Diego, Texas, voted for Trump in 2016, but he now believes the Trump administration has “gone amok.” The Army veteran said he is a proponent of getting criminals out of the country, but that is not what he is seeing happening with current immigration enforcement.
“They started doing everybody across the board,” Martinez said. “Innocent kids and women, people who work in restaurants, people who work in hotels, people who are building homes, people who are doing masonry work, and innocent, good, taxpaying people. Taxpayers. It’s insane.”
Rural MAGA voters support Trump’s immigration policies
Some of Trump’s most loyal supporters — rural Republicans who consider themselves MAGA supporters — are about twice as likely as rural, non-MAGA Republicans to see a benefit to Trump’s immigration policies where they live.
Roughly 4 in 10 rural voters identify as MAGA Republicans, while about 1 in 10 are Republicans but not MAGA supporters.
About two-thirds of rural MAGA Republicans say Trump’s immigration policies have had a positive impact where they live. Roughly half say the Trump administration has “not gone far enough” on deporting immigrants in the country illegally, while about half say his actions have been “about right.”
Katherine Reed, a 27-year-old Republican who supports the MAGA movement, has been pleased to see the Trump administration’s deportation policies play out. The resident of Mount Pleasant, Texas, believes her community has always been safe but that the administration’s policies have had a positive impact by reducing violent crime nationwide, saying, “It’s made life for people a lot safer.”
She believes if someone comes to America, they should “respect the law of the land” and “do it legally.”
“I want really amazing people to become Americans,” Reed said. “That’s the whole point of America.”
___
The poll of 2,241 U.S. adults registered to vote in rural areas of the country was conducted Aug. 12-24, 2026, using a sample drawn from the probability-based SSRS Opinion Panel. The margin of sampling error for the full sample is plus or minus 3 percentage points. In collaboration with AP, KFF researchers worked to design the survey sample and questionnaire, analyze and report findings.
___
This report is a collaboration between The Associated Press and KFF Health News. KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling and journalism.

title: Bangor man allegedly confessed to jailmate about Calais teen’s 1984 slaying
text:
The Bangor man accused of a 1984 Calais teenager’s murder allegedly told a jailmate he had suffocated the young woman by forcing her face into a bog and later dumped her naked body in the St. Croix River.
Raymond Brown, 67, is accused of the 1984 killing of Linda Maxwell, whose body was found Aug. 25, 1984, along the St. Croix’s shore in the small Washington County town of Robbinston.
During opening statements Monday in Brown’s long anticipated jury trial in Machias, prosecutors said the more than four decade investigation “ended where it began:” with Brown.
Brown’s trial is the latest twist in a cold case that went unsolved for more than 40 years. Brown, who appeared via Zoom during jury selection late last week, attended in-person, donning blue jeans, a salmon pink button up and white sneakers.
Brown, who had met Maxwell just weeks before her death, was one of several friends Maxwell was drinking with the night she was killed.
After a long night of partying, Brown was supposed to take Maxwell, whose friends said was visibly intoxicated, home that night. Instead, prosecutors say he killed her after she threatened to tell people he had raped her.
Brown first planned to dump her body in her driveway, but then decided to leave her in the water by Robbinston’s boat landing, according to the Assistant District Attorney Suzanne Russell. He later burned her clothes at his home, the prosecution said.
Brown allegedly recalled the night’s events to a Washington County jailmate in January 2026, following his arrest.
Brown told investigators a different story. Brown said he had dropped Maxwell off, alone, at a variety store in Milltown near a cemetery where her boyfriend was camping, roughly 14 miles by water from where she was later found dead.
Brown, who was 25 and married at the time, was seen flirting with Maxwell earlier that night, Russell said. Before the night of her death, Brown told another friend he wanted to have sex with Maxwell, according to the prosecution.
Brown later told investigators Maxwell wanted to swim that night, a claim refuted by those close to her who cited Maxwell’s fear of dark water. Maxwell was found floating in tidal waters about 20 feet offshore. Local police secured her body by tying a rope to her arm before state authorities arrived on scene, the prosecution said.
Brown’s boots were wet after he arrived home the night of the murder, his wife told detectives at the time, according to Russell.
Justine Berry, Brown’s attorney, conceded Brown was among the friends Maxwell was drinking with that night, but said the state still doesn’t know what happened to her. Berry, who said investigators “focused” on Brown, reminded jurors that the state’s medical examiner ruled Maxwell’s death a drowning.
In 2024, a detective with the state’s unsolved murder squad exhumed Maxwell’s embalmed body to perform a limited autopsy, Russell said. DNA found on her body could not be analyzed because of water damage and collection methods used in 1984, when DNA was not an accepted form of forensic science.
The prosecution displayed a map of the various places around Washington County where the teenagers were drinking that night. The jury went on a tour of those sites following opening statements Monday.
Justice Patrick Larson is presiding over the trial.
If convicted, Brown, formerly of Pembroke, faces 25 years to life in prison.
Brown’s defense attorney, Steve Smith, declined to comment on whether Brown would take the stand. The prosecution clarified some details but declined to comment on the pending case.
The Bangor man was arrested in May 2025 after a traffic stop on Broadway and later indicted by a grand jury.
Brown had five criminal convictions prior to the alleged slaying, including felony burglary and simple assault, according to the Bangor Daily News archives. He escaped from Washington County Jail in October 1977 shortly after his first felony burglary.
A local man discovered Maxwell’s naked body near a boat landing two days after she was last seen with friends in Calais, according to the BDN archives.
The Calais teenager was the daughter of the late Cleveland and Nancy Maxwell and sister to Patricia, Frank and Wayne Maxwell.
Maxwell was a member of the Woodland Baptist Church in Baileyville and ran track at the now-shuttered Robbinston Grade School, according to BDN archives. She was on the honor roll at Calais High School her freshman year and played on the school’s basketball team her junior year, according to the archives.
Maxwell would be 60 years old this year.

title: Old Port lingerie retailer adds Falmouth store
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Portland lingerie retailer picked Falmouth for its second location.
Aristelle leased a 1,180-square-foot space at the Shops at Falmouth Square at the Wyeth, a mixed-use residential and retail development at 267 U.S. Route 1. The store opened Sept. 25.
Josh Soley of CORE represented Aristelle in the lease transaction. Jack Baumann of Compass Commercial Brokers represented the Shops at Falmouth Square LLC.
Aristelle owner Ashley Tucci “delivers an impressive product and this expansion into Falmouth is only going to build on her success,” said Soley.
Instagram branding
Established in Portland’s Old Port in 2014, the bra and lingerie retailer, at 92 Exchange St., has served more than 20,000 women.
Tucci, a Maine native, acquired Aristelle in 2019 after working in software and financial-services sales across New England and New York, according to a news release.
During the pandemic, Tucci responded by showing up on Instagram, launching a weekly newsletter and building a community around the brand.
“Once we reopened the physical store, those first couple of years brought all this pent-up consumer demand,” Tucci said. “After that point, it was off to the races. We’ve just grown, grown, grown.”
The concept includes specialized fitting program that combines technical fit expertise with customer education.
“We’re not going to solve every challenge women face, but we can make a difference in how women feel about themselves, and that is something I take very seriously,” Tucci said. “We don’t go for size; we go for fit.”
The store has won top lingerie industry awards for marketing and concept.
The second location is in Falmouth’s Route 1 retail corridor, near food, wellness and specialty retail businesses. Tucci said other women-led businesses in and around the Shops at Falmouth Square include Café Luna, La Marchande, Josephine and Meg and Co.

title: Becoming windy and cold
text:
Becoming windy and cold
A strong cold front sweeps across Maine
Becoming windy and cold
A strong cold front sweeps across Maine
A strong cold front sweeps across Maine today. Early morning fog and low clouds will quickly give way to powerful westerly winds, with gusts reaching 25 to 35 mph this afternoon and a few hitting up to 40 mph. While a brief shower could pop up as the front crosses, most of the state will stay dry. Keep in mind that these strong wind gusts could snap a few tree limbs and trigger scattered power outages, so make sure outdoor items are secured before heading out.
The blustery conditions stay with us through Tuesday, keeping daytime temperatures feeling crisp despite plenty of sunshine. As high pressure builds overhead Tuesday night, the winds will finally drop off, setting the stage for the coldest night of the autumn season so far. Clear skies and calm conditions will let temperatures plummet, dropping into the 20s across northern valleys and the 30s everywhere else. Expect widespread frost south of the mountains by Wednesday morning, with a potential freeze for inland spots away from the immediate coast.
If you aren't a fan of the early preview of winter, hang in there. That high-pressure system slides east quickly on Wednesday, pulling warmer air back into the region. Afternoon highs will bounce right back into the 60s on Wednesday, with a few spots creeping close to 70 degrees by Thursday afternoon ahead of another weak front. That next system brings only light shower chances to northern areas late Thursday, followed by standard seasonable fall weather to carry us through the upcoming weekend.

title: A look inside the oldest bike company in America
text:
CONWAY, S.C. (InvestigateTV) — Sparks fly, tools turn, and workers assemble parts of made-to-order industrial-grade bicycles, recreational bikes, and trikes at the Worksman Cycles factory in Conway.
Wayne Sosin spent decades keeping the nation’s oldest bike maker rolling. He helped take over the more than 125-year-old family-owned company in 1987 before expanding operations from New York to Conway in 2015.
“We made a commitment to stay in America,” Sosin said.
Today, his bikes are mostly built in America with some necessary help from imported and domestic parts.
“We’re as close to made in America as you can get,” Sosin said. “We weld our frames, we powder coat our frames here, we assemble the bikes, we build the wheels, and that’s highly unusual because virtually every other bicycle sold in the United States is an imported bike in its complete form.”
Sosin gave a tour of the process, from powder-coating specialty frames to hand-building the wheels and assembling the bikes themselves.
Sosin said he enjoys making rides for everyone to enjoy.
“We make adult tricycles for seniors, and we also do tricycles for people with ability challenges,” Sosin said. “That’s been one of my favorite things to get involved in. It’s very gratifying.”
The company is also building opportunities so all groups can succeed.
“We tapped into a few different special communities like the deaf community and given those people a great opportunity, and they turned out to be wonderful workers for us, so that’s been very rewarding to us as well,” Sosin said.
Sosin takes pride in what they build and believes a bike is more than a machine.
“If we were manufacturing a product I didn’t believe in, or didn’t find fun or rewarding, I’d probably be retired at this point,” Sosin said. “It’s been a great ride.”
When asked about his favorite part of being on a bike, Sosin said, “It’s just freedom. It reminds me of being a kid again, the wind in your hair, whatever hair is left.”

title: Why Hannah Pingree has my vote
text:
I am in full support of Hannah Pingree for governor of Maine. I’ve known and admired Hannah for many years; I believe that she has the right combination of principled leadership skills, compassion, creativity and energy to enable our great state to realize its full potential over the next four and, hopefully, eight years.
As someone whose career included managing two Maine cities over a span of 30 years (first Calais and then 23 years in Augusta), I very much appreciate Hannah’s contributions as a legislator (including her time as speaker of the House) and more recently her leadership role in the Mills administration.
Her work championing, establishing and then leading the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future coordinated state agency efforts and important resources for Maine’s nearly 500 municipalities and 16 counties — something the prior administration had shortsightedly done away with when it abolished the State Planning Office.
Hannah is a native Mainer who’s done an admirable job of balancing the roles of spouse, mother, community leader and prominent public official. She’s warm, genuine and wicked smart. I hope folks will join me in voting for her on Nov. 3.
Rep. Bill Bridgeo
Augusta

title: UMaine will train rural K-12 teachers to bring more STEM into classrooms
text:
The University of Maine has received a $626,000 grant from the National Science Foundation to assist rural Maine teachers in bringing emerging science and technology into their classrooms.
The three-year project, which began Sept. 1, provides K-12 STEM teachers with research experiences in artificial intelligence, quantum computing and microelectronics, working alongside university scientists.
Nuri Emanetoglu, professor of electrical and computer engineering, is the project’s principal investigator. Susan McKay, professor emerita of physics and astronomy and a founder of the Maine Center for Research in STEM Education (RiSE Center) is co-principal investigator.
“There are two parts to it,” Emanetoglu said. “One is exposing the teachers to the research projects and the state of the art in these fields. The second is translating that into an educational experience for their students.”
Each year, six teachers will be selected to participate. The first cohort will spend four weeks at UMaine’s Orono campus in summer 2027, working with faculty education research specialists. They will have an additional three weeks to continue their research and develop classroom materials.
“The beauty of having teachers design these kinds of learning experiences is that they know their students,” McKay said. “They know what the students will know and what they’ll get excited about.”
Expanded opportunities
RiSE will support teachers throughout the school year as they refine their lessons and introduce new approaches in their classrooms.
The project focuses on teachers in rural, high-need Maine school districts, where students may have fewer opportunities to interact with scientists and engineers working in rapidly developing fields.
“This is where innovation is going to come from in our economy,” McKay said. “There’s no reason why these sites of innovation can’t be in rural areas with good connections all over the world.”
The program is also designed so its impact can extend beyond the initial 18 teachers. Participants will have opportunities to attend conferences and share the research and instructional materials with other educators.
“This is a real opportunity for them to emerge as leaders in the STEM teaching field,” McKay said. “That’s exciting because it helps sustain the work that they’ve started.”
For Emanetoglu, long-term success would mean seeing the impact move from UMaine laboratories into Maine classrooms and, eventually, the state’s workforce.
“From the students’ perspective, it’s being exposed to these high-tech, high-impact areas and new career opportunities,” Emanetoglu said. “Hopefully, we’ll get some of them to come to UMaine or another institution where they can further study these areas.”

title: The salmon paradox | Outdoors in Maine
text:
In all my years of fishing, two fly-fishing adventures stand out in my memory like no others: catching salmon that ran rivers from the sea. These rivers were far removed from each other; one was the fabled Kenai River in Alaska, and the other the equally fabled Upsalquitch River in New Brunswick.
For sport angling it was a heady time, the 1990s, before the sea-run salmon were in a seeming struggle for survival.

title: Starbucks mislabeled 8 ‘sugar-free’ protein drinks, lawsuit alleges
text:
(AP) - Starbucks is facing a consumer lawsuit over claims that the protein drinks labeled “sugar-free” on its cafe menus may actually contain more sugar than a Reese’s peanut butter cup.
The federal lawsuit filed late Friday in Seattle alleges that eight protein beverages Starbucks sells in the U.S. contain varying amounts of sugar even though the company lists them as sugarless.
On Monday, the menu on Starbucks’ U.S. website listed a 16-ounce (0.5-liter) Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Matcha with 16 grams of sugar and a 20-ounce (0.6-liter) version of the same drink with 21 grams of sugar. By comparison, one Reese’s cup has 11 grams of sugar.
Hagens Berman, a law firm that specializes in class action cases, filed the suit on behalf of three individual consumers who bought Starbucks’ sugar-free protein drinks in California, New York and Washington.
“Consumers avoid sugar for various reasons, whether that be general health, diabetes and blood glucose levels or other factors, and for many, a staunch mislabeling like this is significant,” said Steve Berman, a co-founder and managing partner of the Seattle-headquartered firm.
The plaintiffs contend that Starbucks’ naming and marketing of sugar-free products is “false, deceptive and unlawful” and that the company violated federal labeling regulations.
Seattle-based Starbucks said the sugar in its protein drinks comes from the protein-boosted milk it uses. The company said it doesn’t add sugar to the drinks and it uses sugar-free syrup for flavoring.
On Starbucks’ website Monday, the drinks were marketed as “sugar-free,” but the company also clearly stated the amount of sugar in each beverage and that they were made without added sugar.
“We believe these claims have no merit,” a Starbucks spokesperson said Monday. “Starbucks has consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices and nutritional content across product announcements, menus, marketing materials, Starbucks.com and the Starbucks app, and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves in this matter.”
Starbucks introduced its protein drinks in September 2025 to meet consumer demand for functional beverages and catch up to rivals like Dutch Bros, which launched protein-enhanced coffee drinks in 2024.
Dutch Bros also offers a lower-sugar version of its caramel-flavored Hopscotch Protein Latte, but it’s advertised as the Hopscotch Zero Sugar Added Protein Latte. The 16-ounce (0.5-liter) iced version has 7 grams of sugar and 11 grams of protein. By comparison, a 16-ounce (0.5-liter) iced Starbucks Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte has 9 grams of sugar and 29 grams of protein.
The lawsuit seeks damages on behalf of U.S. consumers who bought the drinks. It also wants the court to order Starbucks to stop using the label “sugar-free” on products that contain sugar.

title: 6 things to do in central Maine this week
text:
THE CONCERT
Don’t miss The Concert: A Tribute to ABBA set for 7:30 p.m. Thursday at Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., Waterville.
For well over a decade, the band has performed the most iconic hits from ABBA, including “Mamma Mia,” “S.O.S,” “Money, Money, Money,” “The Winner Takes All,” “Waterloo,” and “Dancing Queen.”
Come dance, come sing, having the time of your life at the ultimate tribute celebration!
Tickets: $56-$141; operahouse.org.
DAMARISCOTTA PUMPKINFEST & REGATTA
Pumpkins will take over downtown Damariscotta this weekend as the Damariscotta Pumpkinfest & Regatta returns for Indigenous Peoples’ Day weekend.
During the festival, set for Oct. 9-12, enormous pumpkins grown by local and regional growers are transformed into works of art and displayed throughout downtown and neighboring Newcastle. The volunteer-run festival is free and includes a pumpkin parade, pumpkin derby, children’s activities, food, street performers, contests and other events.
The signature event arrives Sunda when the Pumpkinboat Regatta takes to the Damariscotta River from noon to 2 p.m. Competitors climb inside hollowed-out giant pumpkins — some weighing hundreds of pounds — and race them in paddle and motorized divisions.
Other weekend highlights include the Pumpkin Parade from 2-4 p.m. Saturday; the Pumpkin Derby Sunday morning; and a pie-eating contest Sunday afternoon. The celebration continues Monday with the Tour de Gourd 5K, a children’s pumpkin hunt and the popular Pumpkin Drop, in which a giant pumpkin is hoisted high into the air before being dropped.
“THE GREAT GATSBY”
Be sure to see “The Great Gatsy” set for 7 p.m. Saturday through Monday at the Skowhegan Opera House, 225 Water St., Skowhegan.
Step into the dazzling Jazz Age with F. Scott Fitzgerald’s timeless tale of love, ambition and excess. The production brings roaring ’20s glamour to life as Jay Gatsby’s pursuit of the American dream collides with passion and betrayal.
Tickets cost $10-$15; lightsupskowhegan.org.
SWINE & STEIN BREWFEST
Gardiner Main Street is set to host brewfest from noon to 5 p.m. Saturday on Water Street in Gardiner.
The festival offers all-day samples from 20-plus of Maine’s best craft beverage makers in an open-air beer garden, food vendors, a full lineup of music, games and more.
Breweries, meaderies, cideries and distilleries will serve samples in the open air beer garden all day long. The options are different every year.
General admission begins at 1 p.m., VIP tasting hour starts at noon.
General admission is $40 in advance, VIP tickets cost $50, designated-driver admission is $10 and includes unlimited soft drinks and water; swineandsteinbrewfest.com.
MAINE MAPLE FALL FEST
Maple season may be associated with steaming sugarhouses and melting snow, but Maine maple producers are offering another chance to celebrate the state’s signature sweetener this fall during the annual Maine Maple Fall Fest.
The statewide event, organized by the Maine Maple Producers Association, is held Saturday and Sunday and offers visitors the opportunity to travel to participating sugarhouses for an autumn version of Maine’s popular spring maple weekend. Individual producers offer their own mix of activities, which can include sugarhouse tours, maple syrup tastings and demonstrations, along with maple candy, cotton candy, ice cream, baked goods and other maple products.
For more information visit mainemapleproducers.com.
TUSK
Tusk: The Classic Fleetwood Mac Tribute will take the stage at 8 p.m. Friday at the Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., Waterville.
The band is made up of five skilled professionals turned masters of their trade through decades of individual musical study, live performance, creative risk and devotion to the art
Tickets: $50-$60; operahouse.org.
Looking for more? Check out the online calendar listings for other entertainment offerings.

title: Monday Five and Five: County Champions and a Big Week Ahead
text:
The Monday Five and Five: PVC Champions, Top-10 Runs and Big Rematches Ahead
Another week of fall sports is in the books across Aroostook County, and this one had a little bit of everything.
We saw County champions crowned on the golf course, local runners compete against one of the largest cross country fields they will see all season, a goal scored with less than a second remaining, and plenty of offense on the soccer field.
Now, with the regular season moving deeper into October, some familiar County matchups are coming back around and the stakes continue to grow.
Here is this week's Monday Five and Five.
The Five Best From Last Week
5. Hailey Plant Beats The Clock For Presque Isle
This one was about as dramatic as a regular-season soccer game can get.
Presque Isle and Foxcroft Academy appeared headed toward a 2-2 finish Tuesday before Hailey Plant scored the game-winner with less than one second remaining, giving the Lady Wildcats a 3-2 victory.
Carrlyn Buck and Emily Collins also scored for Presque Isle, while Delanie Cyr added two assists.
4. Ava Ezell Puts Together A Six-Goal Week
Houlton's Ava Ezell had a big week offensively for the Lady Shires.
Ezell scored four goals and added an assist in Houlton's 6-1 victory over Van Buren on Tuesday.
She came back Saturday with two more goals as Houlton defeated Old Town 4-2.
That gave Ezell six goals and an assist across the two Houlton victories.
3. Katahdin Scores 16 In Saturday Sweep
Both Katahdin soccer teams filled the net Saturday against East Grand.
The Cougar boys earned a 7-0 shutout, led by three goals and an assist from Conor Schmidt. Leighton Rodgerson added a goal and two assists, while Gage Phillips recorded the shutout in net.
Katahdin's girls followed with a 9-1 victory.
Add it together and the two Cougar teams scored 16 goals in one afternoon.
2. County Runners Make Their Mark At Festival Of Champions
Aroostook County runners went to Belfast Saturday and held their own against a massive Festival of Champions field.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault finished seventh overall in the boys race with a time of 16:01.17, while Emma Graves placed eighth in the girls race at 19:06.96.
Houlton/GHCA put four runners inside the top 66 and finished ninth among 79 scoring boys teams.
Presque Isle had Lillian Johnson finish 19th and Aleah Rideout take 23rd, helping the Wildcats finish 12th in the girls team standings.
It was a strong showing for County cross country against competition from throughout Maine and New England.
1. Presque Isle Sweeps The PVC Golf Titles
Championship performances earn the top spot this week.
Patrick Collins shot a 74 at Hermon Meadows to capture the PVC boys individual championship, winning by two strokes.
Alice Korzekwa made it a Presque Isle sweep, shooting an 86 to win the girls championship.
Presque Isle also finished second in the team competition and qualified for the state championship.
Two individual champions and a state tournament berth made Thursday a big day for Wildcat golf.
Five Big Things To Watch This Week
5. Presque Isle Hits The Road
The Wildcats have a busy Class B North soccer week away from home.
The Presque Isle boys are scheduled to visit Orono Monday before the girls make the same trip Tuesday. The boys then head to Foxcroft Academy Thursday.
Saturday brings another road doubleheader, with Presque Isle scheduled to face Ellsworth in girls soccer at noon and boys soccer at 2 p.m.
With October underway, every one of those games becomes another opportunity to build momentum heading toward the postseason.
4. A Big Home Week For Caribou
Caribou also has plenty on the schedule.
The Vikings are set to host John Bapst in a makeup doubleheader Monday before Fort Kent comes to Caribou for Senior Night games later in the week.
The boys host Fort Kent Wednesday night, with the girls matchup following Thursday.
Then Hermon comes north Saturday for another Class B doubleheader, with the girls scheduled for noon and the boys at 2 p.m.
3. Fort Fairfield And Central Aroostook Meet Again
Thursday night should provide another good County doubleheader when Fort Fairfield visits Central Aroostook.
The girls are scheduled for 5 p.m., followed by the boys at 7.
Central Aroostook is coming off a sweep of Easton, while Fort Fairfield's girls beat Van Buren last week and the Tiger boys closed Saturday with a scoreless double-overtime tie against Bangor Christian.
It is another County rivalry worth keeping an eye on as the regular season moves toward its final weeks.
2. Presque Isle Golf Heads To States
After sweeping the PVC individual championships, Presque Isle now turns its attention toward the state tournament.
The Wildcats qualified as a team, while Patrick Collins and Alice Korzekwa are also among the individual qualifiers following their PVC championship rounds.
The MPA currently lists the Class B and Class C team and individual championships for Saturday, October 10, at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro.
After what Collins, Korzekwa and the Wildcats accomplished at Hermon Meadows, state championship weekend will be one of the biggest events involving a County team this week.
1. Two Big Rematches In Ashland
Tuesday may provide the most interesting night of County soccer this week.
Katahdin's boys return to Ashland after the Cougars won the first meeting 2-1 in double overtime earlier this season. Conor Schmidt scored both goals in that game, including the winner.
Then Central Aroostook and Ashland meet again in girls soccer.
Their first matchup was one of the best County games we have seen this fall, with Ashland edging Central Aroostook 3-2 in a meeting between two of the top teams we had been following in Class D North.
Two rematches, two established storylines and four familiar County programs make Ashland the place to watch Tuesday.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER DAY: Strong Winds Expected Tuesday, Isolated Power Outages Possible
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Monday. After an active afternoon with scattered showers and even a few reports of small hail across northern Maine, our attention quickly turns toward the wind heading into Tuesday. A tightening pressure gradient across the region will allow strong westerly winds to develop, prompting the National Weather Service to issue a Wind Advisory for Aroostook County from 8 AM through 5 PM Tuesday. With gusts potentially reaching 40 to 50 mph in spots, Tuesday has been designated a First Alert Weather Day.
Winds will already remain elevated overnight, but the strongest gusts are expected to develop Tuesday morning and continue through much of the afternoon. Westerly winds will generally run around 15 to 25 mph, with gusts frequently reaching 35 to 45 mph. The higher terrain across northern Maine could see gusts closer to 50 mph, with even stronger winds possible across the highest mountain summits.
These winds will be strong enough to bring down some smaller branches and could result in isolated power outages across the region. With portions of northern Maine currently at or near peak fall foliage, significant leaf loss will also be possible throughout the day Tuesday.
The Wind Advisory remains in effect from 8 AM through 5 PM Tuesday across Aroostook County. While the strongest winds are expected during the daytime hours, breezy conditions will continue into Tuesday evening before winds gradually begin to diminish overnight.
If you have any lightweight outdoor objects still outside, including decorations, trash cans or other loose items, it would be a good idea to secure them before Tuesday morning.
The latest computer model guidance shows widespread gusts around 35 to 45 mph developing across northern Maine by late Tuesday morning. Locations including Presque Isle, Caribou, Fort Kent and portions of western Aroostook County all have the potential to see gusts near or above 40 mph at times.
The combination of stronger winds and much cooler air will also create harsh conditions across the higher terrain. The National Weather Service notes that wind chills around Katahdin could remain in the teens even during the middle of the day Tuesday, meaning anyone heading into the mountains should be prepared for winter-like conditions.
Along with the wind comes a noticeably cooler feel. High temperatures Tuesday only look to reach the upper 40s and lower to mid 50s across much of northern Maine. Caribou looks to top out near 53 degrees, with Presque Isle and Houlton closer to 55 degrees. Fort Kent and several communities farther north and west may struggle to get much above 50 degrees.
Some sunshine will be possible through the day, but the gusty winds will make it feel considerably cooler than the thermometer suggests.
Winds begin to settle down Tuesday night, allowing temperatures to fall back into the lower 30s across much of Aroostook County. Patchy frost will be possible overnight, with some locations seeing frost into Wednesday morning. Our next chance for more widespread rain then arrives Wednesday night into Thursday.

Trump says he will pay for campaign-style ads with his PAC money after backlash over taxpayer funds
text:
Trump says he will pay for campaign-style ads with his PAC money after backlash over taxpayer funds
President Donald Trump said Monday he will no longer use taxpayer money to fund a series of promotional television ads, announcing that he will instead pay for them with funds raised for MAGA, Inc., the pro-Trump super PAC.
“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money. This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
The reversal follows criticism of the administration’s multimillion-dollar television advertising effort, which Republicans and Democrats alike have questioned. The White House has defended the spots as public service announcements.
As of Monday, at least an estimated $10.1 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent on the ads, according to a leading political ad-tracking firm, AdImpact.
As of last week, the administration had created at least 13 campaign-style ads promoting Trump and his policies. Spots that have yet to air include three ads highlighting the US military and operations in Iran and Venezuela, one titled “God Made Trump” and another recapping the UFC fight Trump hosted at the White House.
CNN obtained clips of 12 of the ads, ranging from 15 seconds to three minutes long, two of which have already aired. They appeared in a Dropbox account shared with CNN and run by LMD, the agency awarded the government contract for the ad buys. Each ad ends with the words “Paid for by the U.S. Government” at the bottom of the screen. Another ad, “Final Battle,” which is not in the Dropbox account, has also aired in recent weeks.
While each of the ads has a different theme, many of them include imagery of the president and audio with positive reviews from news reports. They also include patriotic images — including the cap toss at a military graduation, fireworks over Mount Rushmore and military flyovers.
Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and footage, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers said the ads were being produced in-house by the White House video team, part of the communications office responsible for the administration’s public messaging, though at least one was produced by a pro-Trump meme group.
Watchdog groups have said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications, but it’s not clear if outside groups have standing to file a lawsuit. Though the ads have received bipartisan criticism, Congress — which groups said had the clearest lane to provide some accountability — did not act to block the ads ahead of the midterms.
CNN’s Betsy Klein contributed to this report.

title: Falmouth rides depth to SMAA golf championship
text:
VASSALBORO — The Falmouth golf team fell one shot short of an SMAA championship last year.
The Navigators were eager to return to the top this season — and one of their newest players ensured they did.
Six Falmouth players broke 80, led by Dante Iannetta at 73 and senior transfer Sawyer Hebert at 75, and the Navigators shot 304 to hold off defending champion Cheverus (313) at the SMAA qualifier at Natanis Golf Course on Monday.
The Navigators and Stags, with Thornton Academy (325), Gorham (336), Deering (337) and South Portland (338), qualified for the Class A tournament Friday at Natanis. The Trojans were led by a 79 from Jacob Litwinetz, Gorham got a 79 from Charlie Sands, Deering had a 75 from Sam Carter and South Portland was led by Lucas Turkewitz’s 79.
Falmouth won the SMAA championship in 2024. The Navigators made it a goal to reclaim it.
“One hundred percent. We’ve got a lot of depth this year,” Iannetta said. “(Monday) showed it. We’ve got to do it one more time.”
On the Arrowhead side, Winthrop, which won the MVC title and automatically qualified for Saturday’s Class C championships last Thursday, nipped Maranacook for the top score at the conference qualifier. The Ramblers shot 331 while the Black Bears, paced by medalist Jack Fontaine’s 74 and Josh Herzing’s 84, were at 332. Madison, led by a 79 from Colton Pelletier, shot 345 to qualify as well.
“It’s very important (to score well), especially with me not playing well as our No. 1, it helps the team’s confidence a lot,” said Drew Mertzel, the 2025 Class C champion whose 83 was Winthrop’s second-best score behind Lincoln MacArthur’s 78, while Parker Dow (84) and Sam Corgan (86) also qualified. “(We know) if someone’s not having a good day, our team’s there to back us up.”
Cheverus, last year’s SMAA and Class A champion, got a 1-under 71 from medalist Sam Sirois and a 74 from Keane McGrath, but was taken down by Falmouth, which was in top form.
“They all got off to good, solid starts,” coach A.J. Simokaitis said. “In years past, whether it’s nerves or whatever it might be, you have one or two guys throw in a big number early in the round. … (This) gave them a little peace of mind, a little cushion.”
Iannetta notched three birdies to post the Navigators’ low score, and Victor Keefer (77), Alex Novick, Griffin Jacobsen and Anthony Graceffa (79 apiece) also shot under 80. The second-lowest score, though, went to Hebert, who led North Yarmouth Academy to the Class C title last year and had three birdies of his own Monday.
“I was just setting myself up, I wasn’t going for anything,” he said. “Falmouth is really competitive golf. … I was No. 7 at the beginning of the year and I needed to work really hard to get up there.”
The Navigators, however, weren’t rejoicing. Two years ago Falmouth won the SMAA qualifier but took fourth at states.
“Be happy with it but go through, find where you lost shots,” Iannetta said. “You can always make improvements.”
Back playing where he tied for second at states last year, Sirois made six birdies, including one on the 13th where he rolled in a bending 25-foot putt and gave a one-handed shrug after it fell.
“Hitting-wise, it wasn’t great, so the putter saved me a lot today,” he said. “(I made) a lot of 5- and 4-footers today, that’s big for me.”
The top score in the MVC event went to Fontaine, who excelled around the green. He birdied the opening hole, had birdies on two of the first three holes on the back, and notched his first eagle when he chipped in on the sixth.
“It was pretty nice,” he said. “I didn’t really believe it at first. And then I (looked) at the hole and there it was.”
In the MVC, individual qualifying spots went to players shooting 84 and under. That included Chris Johnson (78) and Dom Mangold (83) of Kents Hill, Vincent Chapman (80) and Jacob Irish (83) of Dirigo, Patrick Murphy (80) of Monmouth, and Maddox Foster-Grey (84) of Mt. Abram.
In the SMAA, Cheverus also took scores from Joe Stratman (81) and Mike Ray (87), while Thornton got an 80 from Henry Litwinetz, an 83 from Ryan Johnson and an 83 from Blake Goulet. Lukas Taafe shot 83, Payton Wilkins 84 and Andrew Cabral 90 for Gorham. Deering got an 82 from Liam Brunelle, an 89 from Cole Barringer and a 91 from Dominik Anthony, and South Portland got 86s from Jacob Robin and Noah Bates and an 87 from Gavin Schuster.
Qualifying individually were Portland’s Max Schaffer (Portland, 79), Jackson Humphrey (Bonny Eagle, 81), Jacob Willey (Noble, 81), Hunter Pulkkinen (Windham, 81), Caden Tito (Thornton, 81), Josh Albert (Scarborough, 82), Nolan Moore (Noble, 83), Graeme Thompson (Thornton, 83) and Luke Rice (Westbrook, 84).

A Third ‘Sicario’ Is Coming, With the Original Cast
text:
A Third ‘Sicario’ Is Coming With Emily Blunt, Benicio Del Toro, and Josh Brolin All Returning
Sicario did not look like franchise material. An ultra-dark, extremely violent thriller about the drug war? An ongoing film series? Apparently!
The first film had the benefit of a taut script by future Yellowstone creator Taylor Sheridan and superb direction from future Dune architect Denis Villeneuve. And it was a critical and commercial hit in 2015 So Lionsgate made a sequel, 2018’s Sicario: Day of the Soldado, written by Sheridan and directed by Stefano Sollima. Reviews for that one were a little weaker, but the sequel still made almost the exact same amount of money as the first film.
Now, per Deadline, Black Label Media and Thunder Road are preparing a third Sicario, which I hope will be called SicarThreeo. Padraic McKinley, who recently made the sharp period thriller The Weight will direct, from a screenplay by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight.
READ MORE: The 15 Best Movie Posters of the Year
Perhaps most importantly, the entire core original cast of Sicario — Emily Blunt, Benicio del Toro, and Josh Brolin — is reportedly expected to return for the film. Blunt played a FBI agent who joins a secret task force led by Brolin and del Toro’s characters, charged with taking down Mexican drug cartels. But she wasn’t in the sequel, which focused on just del Toro and Brolin’s characters as they try to start a war between the cartels in order to weaken all of their operations.
The first movie was very much about Blunt character’s education in this shady, shadowy world, an arc you can’t really repeat in a sequel. Then again, perhaps a decade or so later, you could show just how this system transformed her values and morality, the same way it did to Brolin and del Toro. That’s an idea that could easily have some legs.
Deadline says that “McKinley and Knight are currently working on the script with notes from stars and the plan is to shoot at the top of year.”

title: MaineCare will cover traditional Wabanaki healing practices
text:
Tribal health clinics soon will be able to bill MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, for traditional Wabanaki healing practices.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services announced Friday that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) granted the state a waiver to try new and expanded Medicaid coverage.
Tribal health clinics in Maine already provide traditional practices, including smudging, sweat lodges, talking circles and other ceremonies to patients. But they have to use other revenue sources to cover the costs.
That will change, likely by 2028, once tribal leaders and state officials work out the particulars of what will be covered under the waiver.
“I think this really gives merit and weight to what we always knew was good medicine for our people,” said Theresa Cochran, health director for the Mi’kmaq Nation.
The primary purpose of the waiver was to add MaineCare coverage for treatment of incarcerated people up to 60 days before they reenter society.
As Dr. Courtney Pladsen, MaineCare’s medical director, set out to draft the application, she was committed to maximizing the benefit. Tribal leaders in consultation meetings told Pladsen that other states had expanded Medicaid coverage in this way, and wondered if Maine might do the same.
“When I had read the other waivers and talked to other states about the opportunity, it just seemed like a no-brainer,” Pladsen said.
Maine joins Arizona, California, New Mexico and Oregon, which had similar waivers approved in 2024. It’s the first eastern state to take the step. CMS last week approved a similar request from Utah, bringing the total to six states nationwide.
The expansion must be budget neutral, under the terms of federal approval. The hope is that upstream interventions prevent downstream costs, Pladsen said, and any reimbursements under the program are billed to the federal agency, not the state.
“Our communities should never have to choose between the medicine of our ancestors and the coverage that makes care possible,” William Smith, board chairman of the National Indian Health Board, a national advocacy nonprofit, said in a statement. “(The) decision honors both, and it honors the trust and treaty obligations this country owes to Tribal Nations.”
Tribal members and their families seeking care from one of the five clinics operated by tribal governments in Maine, or from Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness, a statewide public health nonprofit, will be eligible. Over half of Wabanaki Public Health’s clients are on MaineCare, said the organization’s co-CEO Lisa Sockabasin, including 100% of those at its Bangor-based detox center.
Cochran’s department serves almost 600 people, while the statewide Wabanaki public health agency reaches over 7,000 people annually.
Sockabasin said the tribal health providers are looking to extend care beyond just treatment for substance use to fields including chronic disease and mental health as well.
“Tribal healing practices have been in our communities for thousands of years,” said Sockabasin, who is Passamaquoddy. “And those tribal ceremonies and practices and tradition provide immense healing for our community.”
Over the next year, leaders from healthcare providers will work with state Medicaid officials to determine exactly what practices will be covered by Medicaid, and how much clinics will be reimbursed for them.
Tribal knowledge-keepers have continued to use ceremonies to heal members of their communities even without a mechanism of government financial support, leaders emphasize. And they always will. Although there’s never a charge for those ceremonies, they do consume resources.
“Rather than having them adapt their cultural practices to our systems, we need to adapt our systems to their cultural practices,” Pladsen said.
It is an odd moment, Sockabasin acknowledged, in which traditional practices that are typically shared relationally within communities are to be assigned a dollar value.
But it’s also an opportunity for collaboration and for mutual growth, she said.
“We’re becoming more aware, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people, on what it takes to heal. We are both learning.”
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: From parents to former presidents: Who and what inspires the 2026 Mainebiz 40 Under 40 honorees
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
One of the best parts of honoring the Mainebiz 40 Under 40 honorees is getting to know everyone better through a profile questionnaire.
Proudest achievements
In keeping with their predecessors, the proudest accomplishments for this year’s cohort run the gamut from the personal to the professional. One honoree was the first in his family to go to college and earn a master’s degree. Another is celebrating a decade of recovery from substance use and has turned that experience into a purposeful career as a licensed alcohol and drug counselor helping others. Several are parents themselves, with one looking forward to fatherhood.
Hat tip to parents
When asked to name their personal heroes, several honorees paid tribute to their parents. “They taught me that showing up for your community isn’t something extraordinary, it’s simply what you do,” commented one. Another remarked on how her mom worked long hours while keeping the family grounded and well cared for.
Words that resonate
Favorite quotes can offer insight into a person’s personality and mindset.
This year’s selections come from a range of sources, from historic figures to past political leaders and pop culture icons, and span the humorous to the serious.
This year’s group draws inspiration from words by Nelson Mandela, Martin Luther King Jr., two former presidents named Roosevelt (Theodore and his distant cousin, Franklin Delano) as well as Helen Keller, musicians Billy Joel and Joan Baez, and humorists Erma Bombeck and Oscar Wilde.
Dinner party guests
One of the more intriguing questions we ask every year is: Which three guests, living or dead, would you invite to a dinner party — and why?
As always, the answers show plenty of thought and creativity, sparking the imagination about the dynamics and conversations that might unfold around the table if time travel were possible.
Some of the proposed combos this year: Stanley Tucci, Billy Crystal and John Candy; Eleanor Roosevelt, Fred Rogers and Martin Luther King Jr.; Paul McCartney, Dolly Parton and Michael Jackson; and Julia Child, Bonnie Raitt and Eleanor of Aquitaine.
Others on the dream guest list who would liven up any dinner party include: Prince, Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Steven Spielberg, Jesus Christ, Kelly Clarkson, Peyton Manning, Neil Armstrong, Oprah Winfrey, Golda Meier, Tom Brady and Muhammad Ali.
Several honorees named their late grandparents as preferred invitees and, for one 35-year-old, her mom at that same age.

title: No arrests announced in shootings that killed 2, left dozens injured at Georgia block party
text:
VIENNA, Ga. (AP) — Authorities in rural southern Georgia were still searching Monday for suspects in weekend shootings that killed two people and left nearly three dozen others injured when gunfire erupted during a sprawling block party to celebrate a homecoming football victory.
No arrests have been announced in Dooly County, where the sheriff says more than 50 shots were fired early Sunday in the small city of Vienna as more than 1,000 people were still outside celebrating long after midnight.
Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy identified the two people killed as Ja’Quavion Jackson, 21, of Cordele, and Macaleb Jackson, 23, of Hawkinsville. The two men don’t appear to be related, said Sara Lue, a spokesperson for the Georgia Bureau of Investigation.
An additional 35 people were injured — most of them by gunfire, though others were hurt in the chaotic scramble to flee, authorities told reporters at a Sunday news conference. The sheriff said an unspecified number were hospitalized with critical injuries.
Authorities haven’t said what may have motivated the shootings or precisely how many people were shot.
“At large parties with people from different places, not just your locals, sometimes problems come,” Peavy said Sunday.
Local officials say the block party wasn’t a school-sponsored event and didn’t have a city permit. Peavy said he had extra deputies working over the weekend in anticipation of homecoming drawing large numbers of alumni and other out-of-town visitors.
The sheriff did not immediately return a phone message Monday. Lue said no further updates were available from state investigators, who customarily assist Georgia’s rural communities in major cases.
The violence marred what Peavy said had been a large but otherwise peaceful celebration of Dooly County High School winning its homecoming football game in Vienna, a city of about 3,000 people located about 50 miles (80 kilometers) south of Macon.
Crowds of revelers gathered across an area covering four blocks, and Peavy said that he had deputies patrolling the area. When the first shots were fired and deputies rushed to the scene, he said, more gunfire sounded about a block away.
“It was so many people,” Peavy said. “And it was just hard to figure out what was going on.”
Among this weekend’s visitors was Antoria Felton of Jonesboro, who drove two hours to bring her daughter and six other girls to Vienna. She told WMAZ-TV that everything seemed peaceful when suddenly “bullets were going everywhere.”
Felton said she saw that “kids laying on the ground had been shot” as she scrambled to find her daughter and the other girls.
“The only thing I’m trying to do is find these girls,” Felton said. “Everybody scattered out everywhere, everybody running. It was terrifying.”

title: Why Hannah Pingree has my vote
