title: Black Mountain increases snowmaking capacity for upcoming winter season
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
RUMFORD — With more than $1.25 million dedicated to increase its snowmaking capacity, the small Black Mountain of Maine ski resort has worked to stretch those dollars in the wake of the ever-increasing cost of equipment.
Included in the work the resort did this summer with its employees and volunteers was building a new pumphouse and installing a new higher capacity pump system that will more than double snowmaking output, according to Roger Arsenault, chair of the Black Mountain board.
Arsenault, also a leading member of the Chisholm Ski Club, spoke at a Business After Hours event Sept. 30 at the ski resort.
He said the resort had four snowmaking guns in 2003, and “since then, we bought, bartered and stole 47 snow guns, 20 were purchased through the Northern Border Regional Commission grant for $388,000. We’re looking to get, maybe 10 more, and with a little luck on the cross-country course, we’ll have five.”
Besides the Northern Border grant in 2024, Black Mountain received $775,000 from a Congressionally Directed Spending. Community supporters contributed $102,555 in matching donations to secure the Northern Border grant.
Phase one of the project began in May 2025 with the purchase of five new mobile snow guns and 15 new tower guns. Throughout the summer, the tower guns were installed on the Upper Allagash and Saint John trails. A second transformer was also installed at the top of the triple chairlift to provide adequate power to the snowguns on those trails.
Building the new pumphouse and installing the new pump system was part of phase two, which is slated to be completed for the 2026-27 snowmaking season.
“Obviously, we don’t use it until we need the snow,” Arsenault said. “If Mother Nature doesn’t cooperate, we can make it happen. In the events that we run, we have to make a national commitment, and a guarantee.”
As part of the Business After Hours event, Black Mountain Outdoor Operations Manager Rob Wutzdorff gave a tour showing the work done over the summer.
“We’ve kept on some snowmakers year round and they’ve been helping us through this,” he said. “We’ve had some great volunteers, people that Roger (Arsenault) has known for a number of years and we appreciate their help.”
Their team, he said, is fewer than 10 people.
“I’m super proud of the guys for making this happen because none of us are professionals. I don’t want to sell us short, too. I’ve been in the construction trade somewhat since I was in my teens,” said Wutzdorff, who is in his 6th full year with the mountain. “I love it up here. My parents were a bunch of ski bums from New Hampshire and I found myself in the ski industry again after getting my feet wet years ago.”
Wutzdorff said phase two began in early June.
“We got the pumps in place and we’re just connecting some pipe right now,” he said. “We’ve been doing some welding out there, and that will connect us to the mountain from the new pumphouse. And we’re waiting for a transformer to be dropped and we can have power to those pumps down there.”
Arsenault estimated that in another two weeks they’ll be close to operational. Then, the manufacturer comes in and starts the pumps.
“And they give us the once over, because this is all new technology and computer programmed all variable frequency drives and a panel to run it,” Wutzdorff said. “So, we’ll be learning a bit as we get into this.”
Wutzdorff said the new system will allow them to start the system quicker and stay running in between the trails without having to shut down the whole line.
“We can send a crew up, shut the guns down first, and just switch lines in the pumphouse,” he said, “and that will save us hours, probably a good half day total from the start to finish of the process of shutting down and starting back up.”
Wutzdorff said snowmaking is the most expensive operation on the mountain.
“They’ll be some growing pains with the new system, I’m sure, but it’s a much more efficient system, pumping much more water,” he said. “You’ve got to have a good snowmaking system these days or you won’t make it. You’ve got to be efficient and can’t be wasting money out there.”
For the snowmaking reservoir, Wutzdorff said they excavated a hole of 150 by 250 feet that’s about 34 feet deep.
The pumphouse lines will run to five different areas of the mountain and will likely include the trails of Allagash, Summit, Upper Sunday, Novice and Nordic, supplying a thousand gallons per minute at 900 pounds of pressure out of the pumphouse.
“We were 500 gallons per minute and 645 pounds of pressure previously. So, we’ve doubled our volume going up the mountain and not quite doubled our pressure, which should help us at the top of the mountain because we’ve always been low on water pressure up there,” Wutzdorff said.
The pumphouse is also known as the mountain operations building, which Wutzdorff said will eventually be called the Skip MacFawn Building. MacFawn was a lifelong volunteer, ski patroller, patrol director and board member who dedicated more than 50 years to the ski resort.
The expansion project is slated to be complete for the 2027-28 snowmaking season with the final phase being to expand the snowmaking reservoir by more than 150%, increasing the water capacity to roughly 5 million gallons from the current 1.9 million gallons.

title: Penquis Good Neighbor Fund offers emergency heat aid to Maine families
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Last winter, the Penquis Good Neighbor Fund provided a vital lifeline to hundreds of local households facing home heating emergencies. Thanks to the generosity of community members, businesses, and partners, the fund helped deliver emergency fuel assistance to 582 households across Penobscot, Piscataquis, and Knox counties, providing a total of $255,131 in donated support to help families stay warm, safe, and dry during Maine’s coldest months.
The program is designed to assist households that may not qualify for federal heating programs such as HEAP or who are experiencing an urgent heating crisis and need immediate help.
The importance of the Good Neighbor Fund was especially evident during last season’s delay in the release of federal LIHEAP funding. When a government shutdown postponed HEAP assistance until December, the Good Neighbor Fund stepped in to help 191 households with emergency heating assistance totaling $71,586, ensuring families were not left without heat while waiting for their benefits. The program also supports individuals and families facing unexpected hardships, including those recovering from medical treatment, navigating a personal crisis, or living just above income eligibility guidelines for other assistance programs.
At its heart, the Good Neighbor Fund is a community helping community. Donations allow Penquis to provide emergency deliveries of approximately 100 to 125 gallons of heating oil or kerosene to eligible households throughout the region. This work is made possible not only by generous donors, but also by dedicated fuel vendors and delivery drivers who respond when neighbors need help most, often braving severe winter weather to ensure homes remain warm and safe. Every dollar donated makes a difference and helps provide emergency heating assistance to families at risk of going without heat. Donors may choose to support households in a specific town or county or allow their gift to be used wherever the need is greatest.
How to Donate: To help keep a neighbor warm this winter, visit penquis.org , click the “Donate” button at the top of the page, and select “Heat a Home.” Donations may also be made by check. Simply note “Good Neighbor Fund,” “Heat a Home,” or “Fuel Assistance” in the memo line. Every contribution, regardless of size, helps ensure local families have access to emergency heating assistance when they need it most.
HEAP
Here is a reminder about Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) program: HEAP provides support to income-eligible households in Penobscot, Piscataquis, and Knox counties facing high winter heating costs. Eligible homes heated by oil, kerosene, coal, pellets, wood, LP gas, or electricity may qualify for assistance.
HEAP has started taking applications for fuel assistance and will run through May 31, 2027, or until funding runs out. It may seem early to book an appointment, but there is a great need, and appointments are already booked until the end of the year. Statewide, HEAP applications were down from last year. Penquis was able to take a few more HEAP applications than the last HEAP season. All households that did apply and were found eligible were served.
How it works: The first applications are dedicated to “Priority Households” which includes a household member that pays for their heat but is also 60 years old and older, 72 months or younger, or someone who is disabled. Penquis appointments have been set up for anyone who applied in 2026 as a “Priority Household” which already includes 6,700 households. It is important to know that not everyone can be served on the first day and it may take a few days for someone to return your call. In fact, Penquis is already booked into December at this time. Once priority households are complete, the focus will switch to households that pay for their heat but do not fall under the “priority Household” status. Renters who have their heat included in their rent are next along with people who have “Room/Board”, and then finally those subsidized with heat included to keep them eligible for the Farm Bill or food stamps.
As of now, there has been no word from the federal government regarding funding for the 2027 Heating Season. Maine usually receives about $41 million. An average HEAP benefit for the Penquis area last season was about $570, higher than the previous year. It is important to know HEAP is an assistance program and is not designed to pay for the entire heating cost. Maine was very lucky to receive supplemental funding from the federal and state governments during the COVID-19 pandemic, but now that pandemic is over funding availability will likely be different this year.

title: Crowd of students protests Cornell’s response to gang rape complaint
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — Cornell students thronged a campus plaza to protest the university’s response to allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity house, and the school’s main administration building was splashed with graffiti and damaged overnight.
At a demonstration that overflowed the large space in front of the school’s student center, students, faculty members and others wore purple ribbons and held signs with such messages as “support survivors, expel rapists” and “Justice 4 every Jane Doe” — the name by which the woman who reported the assault is known in court papers. Other people watched from pathways, windows and a nearby hill.
“Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support,” student Athena Holloway told the crowd. “How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”
Hispanic studies professor Julia Chang added to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.”
Calls for Cornell president’s resignation
Speakers faulted fraternities, the university trustees and Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff, saying he and his administration have prioritized protecting the university’s reputation over students’ safety.
“Kotlikoff, resign!” demonstrators chanted, among other slogans, as they marched to the damaged administration building to present a list of demands. They included changes to how the student code of conduct defines sexual consent, an overhaul of the student discipline system and expulsions or degree revocations for all students involved in the alleged 2024 assault of the woman known as Jane Doe, among other things.
The woman’s account of being sexually assaulted by several fraternity brothers has made clear, on and beyond campus, that “for all the strong feelings about sexual assault, .... we do not do enough to prevent it, nor to support survivors after it happens,” student Madeline Gage said.
The group began disbanding with chants including “ban the frats!”
Graffiti and broken glass at an administration building
The Ivy League school has been trying to quell a firestorm over its handling of the alleged 2024 gang rape. Early Monday, the university found signs of the anger on the very walls of its administrative headquarters.
Holes were knocked into one of the building’s glass doors, and the walls beside them were marked with red-painted messages condemning patriarchy and the Ivy League school’s handling of sexual assaults, news media photos showed. Later Monday, the graffiti was removed and the door was boarded up.
Cornell spokesperson Kyle Kimball said in a statement that the university was investigating and that “damaging property is not the answer” to Cornellians’ “frustration and strong emotions.” Campus police referred questions to his office, which declined to provide more detail on the incident.
Jane Doe alleges that she was sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity members in October 2024 after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs. She was a Cornell student at the time.
The woman recently sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others. Her lawsuit said that she became fully incapacitated as fraternity members assaulted her, and that one man sent others a message inviting them to participate.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told Cornell investigators last year, according to records reviewed by The Associated Press.
Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that some of the accused students, when interviewed by Cornell investigators, described the sexual activity as consensual.
Shortly before she went to Cornell police in November 2024, Jane Doe recorded a phone call with one of the men she says raped her. ABC News broadcast portions of that call Monday, containing only what it said was his voice, and recounted other parts of the conversation in writing.
“What y’all did would be classified as gang rape,” she told him at one point, according to the network, which said she had provided the recording to the university.
Students are demanding transparency, accountability
The suit has drawn national attention to what Cornell, its police force and the local district attorney did after she told the campus police in November 2024 she “can say with 100% confidence I was raped.”
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others. In a statement last week, the administration bristled about the “false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case.”
Students, however, have demanded more accountability and transparency, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has said Jane Doe was “failed by people and institutions” including the Cornell police and local District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.
Hochul appointed the state attorney general last week to take over a criminal investigation that Van Houten had reopened days earlier, and the governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter.
After the week’s developments, Kotlikoff released an apologetic video Saturday, saying that Jane Doe’s account “raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.”
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his support for an independent review of the university’s actions and vowed more transparency and a commitment to “finding the answers our community deserves.”
___
Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz contributed from New York.

title: Former housemate of Biddeford ICE shooting victim tries to rebuild while struggling with loss
text:
Jhonathan Ramirez was at home in Biddeford on July 13 when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and killed his friend and housemate, Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, on the street outside. The shooting, he said, has turned his life upside down, and thrust his name into an unwanted spotlight. Now, he’s trying to rebuild his life while dealing with the lingering trauma of losing his friend.
Ramirez said he and Duran Guerrero had a lot in common. Both were from the same region of Colombia, had young kids and had come to the U.S. seeking a better life, eventually settling in Maine with their partners because they’d heard it was quiet and safe.
Ramirez said the two families had been splitting an apartment for the last couple years and were planning to make the most of summer.
“We had a lot of plans,” he said, in Spanish, “to go to the beach, to go to a lake, to do a cookout.”
All of those plans were abruptly snuffed out on the morning of July 13. Ramirez remembers hearing gunshots coming from the street outside.
He ran to the window and saw agents taking Duran Guerrero out of the car.
“When the ambulance came, they took out the stretcher, and they didn’t put anyone on it,” he said. “That’s when we realized he was no longer alive.”
Almost immediately, he said, journalists started knocking on his door nonstop. The car Duran Guerrero was driving was registered to Ramirez, and Ramirez’s name soon popped up in news articles.
Ramirez said he saw speculation online that he’d been the one ICE was actually looking for. But he said he’s done nothing to draw the attention of immigration enforcement.
“My family, we came here to get ahead, we’re good people,” he said. “I hope my name is cleared.”
The attorney handling his asylum case, Kerry Doyle, contests the idea that ICE even had a specific target when they stopped Duran Guerrero that day.
“From my experience with other people I’m representing here in Maine who were picked up off the street,” Doyle said, “it seemed pretty clear to me that they were just out looking for people who looked Hispanic.”
Doyle is also representing Ramirez in a process to secure a visa for victims of violent crime.
She said like Duran Guerrero, Ramirez has a work permit and no criminal record.
In addition to the unwanted attention, the shooting has drawn Ramirez into a growing circle of people across the country who’ve lost friends, family, and loved ones to ICE shootings.
Earlier this month, congressional Democrats heard testimony from some of those family members, including Ronaldo Salgado, whose father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, was shot and killed in Houston while driving his construction crew to work, just days before the Biddeford shooting.
“Our father’s last day started like so many days during his 35 years in this country, a country that he loved,” Salgado told lawmakers, imploring them to rein in the agency before someone else is killed.
“It is my motivation to continue fighting not just for my dad, but for everyone else’s dad and families like mine. I hope I’m doing the right thing every day, and I know my dad here is guiding me in the right direction,” he said.
Here in Maine, Ramirez is also searching for a way forward.
He and his family have since moved to a new home in Biddeford. They still meet up with Duran Guerrero’s partner at the park or at the mall from time to time so their daughters can play together, and, he said, hopefully distract themselves a bit from all they’ve been through.
But for Ramirez, there’s no avoiding his friend’s death.
“Everything has changed,” he said, “because there is an empty space in our lives.”
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Old Town temporarily bans data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Old Town became the second Greater Bangor community to pass a short-term ban on data centers Monday.
The six-month ban, which outlaws the development of data centers in the city’s industrial zones, is retroactive to Sept. 8, when the Old Town City Council first discussed the possibility of a ban.
Data center developments are already not allowed in other zones, according to the city’s land use ordinance.
Communities across Maine have passed moratoriums, or temporary bans, on data center developments this year due to the limited knowledge of how they will affect municipalities. The bans, which are generally set to last six months, give towns time to learn about the technology and draft laws to regulate its development.
The Old Town City Council passed the ban unanimously at its Monday meeting. Due to extensive conversation about a possible ban during a September meeting, discussion on the ban Monday lasted for about one minute.
“I think that our conversation last time was pretty substantial and overarching, and as previously stated, it gives us plenty of time to adequately assess the risks and benefits and pros and cons of all that this super complex, super new thing entails,” Councilor Zachary Wyles said.
Residents reached out to councilors before the ban was proposed to say they didn’t want a data center to come to Old Town.
Old Town could be a desirable location for a data center because of its history with businesses like Nine Dragons Paper and Old Town Canoe, and its industrial zones, Council President Christian Pushor said at the Sept. 8 meeting.
Councilors previously said a long-term ban in the form of zoning changes would be sent to a public referendum to allow voters to decide. The next possible election date would be June 2027. The six-month ban is set to expire in March, but an extension to June could be approved.
“I feel like this is such a hot topic that I would like it to go to the public instead of relying on people who have the time and energy to contact us,” Councilor Katrina Wynn said on Sept. 8.

title: ‘The Batman 2’ Production Paused For Matt Reeves’ ‘Family Matter’
text:
‘The Batman 2’ Production Paused So Matt Reeves Can Focus on ‘Family Matter’
The Batman Part II has not had the easiest time getting to theaters. It’s already been five years since the first The Batman was released in theaters, and the sequel — written and directed by Matt Reeves and starring Robert Pattinson as the latest iteration of the Dark Knight — was only just in production in the last few months. The film had originally been scheduled for release last week — October 2, 2026. Then it was pushed back to the fall of 2027, and then to the fall of 2028.
Don’t be shocked if the movie is pushed back again, because Warner Bros. announced that it was pausing production on the movie “while Matt Reeves focuses on a family matter.” Their statement added “Matt has the full support of DC Studios and we look forward to continuing the journey soon.” It’s unclear how long the delay may be.
READ MORE: Every Batman Actor, Ranked From Worst to Best
The sequel has taken so long to emerge that the whole premise of the previous Batman — a Caped Crusader in the early stages of his career, just a handful of years into his time as a costumed vigilante — will feel a bit moot by the time it’s released. (Pattinson will be almost 42 years old when Part II premieres.) On top of everything else, the franchise has had to contend with the end of the previous iteration of the DC Universe and the development of a new one, overseen by director James Gunn — one which The Batman is technically not even a part of.
Pattinson will be joined in The Batman Part II by returning stars Jeffrey Wright, Andy Serkis, and Colin Farrell, who will reprise their roles as Commissioner Gordon, Alfred, and the Penguin, respectively. The sequel’s new stars include Sebastian Stan as the new version of Two-Face and Scarlett Johansson as his wife Gilda.
The Batman Part II is currently scheduled for release on February 18, 2028. We’ll see if that date holds, or if the movie will be subject to further delays as a result of this production pause.

title: Getting started with weatherization in South Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As the seasons shift and the leaves exist on the cusp of change, you might sense the cooler air infiltrating your windows, walls, and doors. While putting on an extra layer or drinking some hot tea can increase your comfort for the meantime, weatherization is a long-term solution worth considering. A little can go a long way: It can help your home stay cooler in the summer, and warmer in the winter. From door sweeps to pipe insulation, weatherization seals up the air leaks and cracks around doors, windows, and insulates pipes: It is a permanent improvement to your home that can last for decades.
While getting started on your home energy efficiency journey might feel overwhelming, remember that you don’t need to do everything all at once. Small weatherization measures are a great first step that can reduce energy costs by up to $400 per year. Before the foliage fades, get started with some DIY weatherization to make your home a little more comfortable, energy efficient, and lower your energy costs this winter. We can help you. Through our new Home Energy Program, the Sustainability Department has been working with Age Friendly South Portland to assemble and give away weatherization kits at local events.
WEATHERIZATION KITS
On an early September morning, sustainability staff gathered with members of the Age Friendly South Portland committee to assemble weatherization kits, encompassing everything from door sweeps to window insulation kits. While singing along to music from a different era, the outlet gaskets and window caulk steadily dwindled as we compiled 250-plus bags. Although DIY efforts are not a be-all and end-all fix, they provide a way for people to get started. Check out our new tutorial video, which explains how to install the seven items in every kit: vimeo.com/1221856910.
South Portland residents can find us at the following upcoming events to receive a kit:
• Household Hazardous Waste Day on Saturday, Oct. 10, from 8 a.m. to noon at the South Portland Transfer Station
• Election Day from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. at various locations
Further, if you apply for the Home Energy Program, you won’t have to tackle these projects alone. You will receive a free one-hour home energy assessment and hands-on weatherization installation services. If you don’t get into the program (we only have funding this year to do home visits for 50 households), we encourage you to stop by our department’s office hours for free advice.
OFFICE HOURS
Do you want to get started with home energy upgrades, but have no idea where to begin? Or, did you receive multiple contractor quotes, and need some help picking one? Stop by the sustainability office to talk to an unbiased professional energy expert. At office hours, we can work with you to identify and explain options for clean energy upgrades, help connect you with qualified contractors, and highlight available rebates, tax credits, and incentives.
Office hours are Mondays from 4 to 5:30 p.m. at the sustainability office at 829 Sawyer St., South Portland. Call at 207-819-5477, or join online at tel.meet/ivt-cixj-ueg.
Robyn Landes is an AmeriCorps Resilience Fellow with the South Portland Sustainability Department.

Peyton Stewart, 11, received a life-saving bone marrow transplant from his older brother after being diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation causing an autoimmune deficiency.

title: Nolo changes from a hurricane to a typhoon after crossing the international date line
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Nolo has changed from a strong hurricane to a typhoon after it crossed the international date line.
Nolo was a Category 3 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kph) Sunday morning Hawaii time before it crossed the agreed-upon line in the Pacific Ocean that separates one day from the next. Names of tropical cyclones vary by the parts of the world where they occur.
Monday morning Japan time, Typhoon Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (162 kph) and was moving west at 19 mph (30 kph), according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.
“The good news is there’s a large, vast ocean, so even though it is still going to be strong, it’s not near any land,” said John Cangialosi, a senior hurricane specialist with the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami.
Tropical cyclones with winds over 74 mph (119 kph) are called hurricanes in the northern Atlantic Ocean and the central and eastern Pacific. They are typhoons in the North Pacific, while the South Pacific and Indian Ocean use just the generic term tropical cyclone no matter the strength of the storm.
Nolo is forecast to keep moving west and gradually weaken.
Nolo skirted Hawaii as a hurricane a week ago. It then lost some of its punch and became a tropical storm, before regaining hurricane strength on Friday.
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hurricane Rachel continued heading westward on a path away from Mexico.
As the storm moved further out to sea, it was sending dangerous waves and swells back to the coast of west-central Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula, according to the hurricane center.

title: 10th grader killed after school bus full of students rolls over in crash: ‘Terrible, tragic morning’
text:
(AP) — A Florida school bus carrying nearly 40 people overturned after being struck by an oncoming car on the way to a high school early Monday, killing a student and the driver of another vehicle that caught fire, authorities said.
A heavy presence of emergency responders rushed to the crash site in Winter Haven, south of Orlando, and 26 students were transported to a hospital, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said. At least one person was in critical condition.
EN ESPAÑOL | Mueren dos personas al volcar un autobús escolar en Florida
The crash left the bus upside-down on the side of the road. The front end was a mangled mess of metal and one of its four back tires appeared to be missing.
“It was a horrible crash,” Judd said. “It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life.”
The bus was headed to Winter Haven High School when an oncoming car crossed the center line and struck the side of the bus near the rear wheels, Judd said. The sheriff said the impact ripped the tire off the bus, which then crashed head-on into an oncoming Jeep that caught fire.
Most of the 39 people aboard the bus were high school students, along with the bus driver and the driver’s daughter. Judd said first responders spent the first several hours getting people to the hospital, identifying them and reuniting students with their parents.
“I think this is the most horrific bus tragedy we’ve had in decades, as far back as I can remember,” Judd said.
Officials didn’t immediately report the condition of the driver of the car that hit the bus, but Judd said that person had been heading to work and was cooperating with investigators. They were not arrested or charged with a crime.
Polk County Public Schools Superintendent Frederick Heid said students practice drills on how to leave a bus that is involved in an accident. Last month, another Polk County school bus was also involved in a crash but authorities said no students were on board at the time.
“This event could have been far worse. You can see the condition of the bus, you can see its current positioning,” Heid said.
Justin Sharpless, chairman of the Polk County school board, asked the community to come together to support the family of the girl who died, as well as the school and school staff.
“There are really no words that can take away the pain of losing a young person,” he said.

title: Coastal Rivers to offer guided hike on the River~Link Trail
text:
Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust will host a free, guided hike along the River~Link Trail from 2-5:30 p.m. Friday. This three-hour excursion offers community members an opportunity to explore one of the region’s largest remaining blocks of intact conserved land, which serves as a crucial habitat and corridor for native wildlife including moose, deer, bobcats and bears.
Led by Coastal Rivers naturalist Sarah Gladu, participants will trek along forest paths and historic farm roads, traverse the slopes of Edgecomb’s Mount Hunger and cross scenic woodland streams. Throughout the walk, hikers will learn about regional ecology, search for native plant species like rattlesnake plantain and look for active signs of local wildlife.
For this 5-mile, one-way walk, hikers will meet at the River~Link North trailhead on River Road in Newcastle, located just south of the Dodge Point parking area on the opposite side of the road, before carpooling to the McKay Road trailhead to begin the route.
The program is free and open to the public, though registration is required. Participants should wear sturdy walking shoes or boots and warm layers, and bring their own water and snacks. Tick precautions and post-hike checks are strongly encouraged.
To learn more or register for the event, visit coastalrivers.org/events.

title: White House blocks Politico from Air Force One amid press access lawsuit
text:
White House blocks Politico from Air Force One amid press access lawsuit
The White House is refusing to allow Politico on Air Force One on Monday, which means the news organization cannot fulfill its press corps pool responsibilities.
A Politico spokesperson confirmed that the publication was excluded from the out-of-town travel pool, a small group of reporters who travel with the president on trips.
President Donald Trump announced on Sept. 18 that he was “banning” Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House, a move that legal experts called unconstitutional.
The news outlets filed a lawsuit on Sept. 21 alleging the ban violates the First and Fifth Amendments. Judge Timothy J. Kelly sided with the plaintiffs and issued a temporary restraining order requiring the Trump administration to reinstate the journalists’ press badges.
Since then, however, the White House has repeatedly barred CNN from traveling on Air Force One on days when it has been CNN’s turn to be the TV pool representative. Now, on the day it was Politico’s turn to be the print pool representative, Politico has been barred as well.
The Trump administration appears to be justifying these new restrictions by saying that access to the White House complex is different than access to tight spaces like Air Force One. The Associated Press has an ongoing lawsuit over this distinction, since Trump tried to ban the wire service from certain spaces last year.
Monday’s action against Politico will likely be incorporated into the next legal filing by CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Judge Kelly is scheduled to hold a hearing on Thursday over the news outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction, which would protect press access to the White House for a longer period of time ahead of a potential trial.
“The law is absolutely clear. The harm to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound,” the attorney for the three news outlets, Ted Boutrous, said in a statement. “It is critical that the White House is enjoined to keep this unconstitutional ban on the free press out of commission.”
Last week, when reporters from TIME asked if Trump was ignoring the court order, Trump said no, and then communications director Steven Cheung piped in: “The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One.”
Cheung did not respond to a request for comment on Monday about the action against Politico.
Trump is slated to travel to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon.
With Politico barred from the trip, the White House offered the publication’s seat to other news organizations that routinely take turns in the out-of-town travel pool, and several publications declined, sources with knowledge of the matter told CNN.
Unusually, the White House’s Sunday night guidance email to the press corps did not list any news outlets traveling with the president at all — perhaps a sign that Politico’s seat was proving hard to fill.

title: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Dennis Hastert, whose congressional legacy as the longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.
Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007 and spent more than a year in prison later in life, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.
When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.
In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP’s poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job in 1999, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton’s impeachment trial.
After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush’s legislative agenda.
A post-congressional scandal lands Hastert in prison
In 2015 he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified “prior misconduct.” Nearly a year later, prosecutors said Hastert’s alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in Yorkville, a small town west of Chicago.
Prosecutors said Hastert sexually abused at least four team members during his coaching career, which lasted from 1965 to 1981.
The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them.
Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.
Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.
At the sentencing hearing, where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a “serial child molester.”
In a statement, Hastert said he was “deeply ashamed” and admitted that he “mistreated” some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.
He knew how hard being speaker would be
When he became House speaker, Hastert was aware of the pitfalls of holding the powerful position.
“You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn’t be,” Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. “But you come back home, and you’re home. You’re back where you’ve always been, and your feet are back on the ground.”
As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert’s aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.
“I really didn’t want to be president, temporary or otherwise,” Hastert wrote in a 2004 memoir.
Hastert’s journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.
In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.
Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.
In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995.
Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.
He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year.
Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor’s degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master’s in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.
In 2007, Wheaton named its new public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert’s indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.
Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago’s suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family’s feed business.
Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.

title: Corrections officer charged with sexual assault against an inmate
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - A Kennebec County corrections officer has been indicted by a grand jury for sexual assault after investigators say they uncovered an intimate relationship between him and an inmate.
Nicholas Fellows, 37, of Augusta was indicted for gross sexual assault and unlawful sexual contact.
According to court documents obtained by WABI, staff members at the Kennebec County Jail contacted investigators in July after discovering the relationship.
An inmate who witnessed the relationship told authorities they saw the female inmate writing explicit notes detailing their relationship and said the inmate had detailed how Fellows was able to get her into a room without cameras to perform sex acts.
Court records say video evidence from the jail showed the pair entering a room without recording devices as was reported, and Fellows and the inmate later admitted to the relationship.
Any sexual contact between a corrections officer and an incarcerated person under their authority is a crime under state law.
Kennebec County Sheriff Ken Mason told WABI that Fellows has been removed from his position.
“A report of an alleged violation of our S.O.P. and Maine State law by Officer Nicholas Fellows came to the attention of my command staff who brought it to my attention post haste,” Mason said. “Mr. Fellows was placed on administrative leave immediately and criminal investigation was conducted by my Detective Division. After our investigation, we had probable cause for an arrest and Mr. Fellows was arrested for the offense and terminated from employment with Kennebec County.”
Fellows was released from Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset on $10,000 bail in August.

title: Russian plague researcher dies of ‘unknown’ infection after suspected lab accident
text:
(CNN) - Authorities in Russia are investigating after a woman who worked at a plague research institute died following a suspected laboratory accident.
A 28-year-old woman has died after a suspected lab accident at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, Russian authorities say. She was diagnosed with pneumonia of “unknown” origin before her death.
Authorities are now investigating whether a dangerous infection, such as pneumonic plague, may have been released. They say the situation is stable at this time.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is monitoring the incident.
“We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” a U.S. State Department spokesperson told CNN. “Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”
What is pneumonic plague?
Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It is the only type of the disease that can be spread from person to person through infectious droplets coughed out by an affected patient, according to the CDC.
Symptoms of pneumonic plague include fever, headache, weakness and rapidly developing pneumonia.
The CDC says that while the plague is a potentially life-threatening disease, it is treatable with antibiotics.

title: Here’s where the country’s largest measles outbreak in 30+ years is
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials said Monday, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.
The U.S. is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 reported cases, according to the CDC. The nation has seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the past two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Since the beginning of last year, large outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest with 997 cases reported.
The governor of New York on Monday declared a disaster emergency because of measles cases in neighboring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extends the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and allows nurses to join doctors in ordering testing. The state has more than 100 cases this year.
Health officials say Pennsylvania’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia. There have been 1,004 cases, including 198 hospitalizations and five deaths, state officials said.
Health experts attribute such outbreaks to low vaccination rates.
It’s been decades since a U.S. state has seen an outbreak surpass 1,000 cases, stretching back to a multiyear outbreak in New York City in the early 1990s that infected more than 4,500 people.
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
Measles is highly contagious. It spreads when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, and through contaminated surfaces. It also can linger in the air for two hours. Up to 9 out of 10 people who are susceptible will get the virus if exposed, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
U.S. measles infections have been surging in recent years, as fewer kids get routine vaccines due to parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation.
Pennsylvania and New York are not the only states with a growing problem. Another is Ohio, with more than 200 cases this year. Like in Pennsylvania, some of the hardest-hit Ohio counties have significant Amish populations, which tend to have lower vaccination rates.
Meanwhile, CDC officials have quietly begun to acknowledge measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.
State officials in August announced that two unvaccinated residents died after being infected with measles.
The announcement quickly came under fire as a clash erupted between vaccine-promoting Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines.
Since then, Pennsylvania has reported three additional deaths.
But for weeks, the CDC — which Kennedy oversees — did not count any deaths on its measles data dashboard, instead saying it was seeking more information. That changed two weeks ago, when one death was finally counted, and again last week when a second was added to the agency’s tally.

title: My ancestors left Ireland for a better life. Ironically, now I’m looking back.
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Rob Glover is an associate professor of political science and honors at the University of Maine. These are his views and do not express those of the University of Maine System or UMaine. He is co-leader of the Maine Chapter of the Scholars Strategy Network, which brings together scholars across the country to address public challenges and their policy implications. Members’ columns appear regularly in the BDN.
Recently, my Irish passport arrived in the mail. It was the culmination of years of research, tracking down documents, and tangling with various bureaucracies to prove I was sufficiently Irish to be granted citizenship.
I expected to feel triumphant. Instead, given the state of our country, I found myself staring at it with a strange mixture of gratitude, sadness and an overwhelming sense of irony.
I am an American, born nearly 70 years after my grandmother departed Ireland for good. My eligibility for citizenship is a product of Irish policies that recognize that country’s unusual history of emigration, an attempt to maintain ties with the millions of Irish descendants flung all over the world. Ireland formalized citizenship by descent in the 1950s and has since cultivated a broader strategic relationship with its diaspora.
That history has given me an extraordinary gift. As an Irish citizen, I can now live and work indefinitely in Ireland or anywhere else in the European Union. At a moment when the future of my own country feels ominous and uncertain, I have sometimes jokingly referred to this process as seeking an “escape pod.”
The joke becomes considerably less funny when I think about how I got it.
My grandmother was two years old when she left Ireland with her mother and four siblings. They traveled first to Canada and in February 1913 by train to Boston, where someone was supposed to meet them and help them get settled.
No one showed.
I think about this a lot. My great-grandmother stood there in an unfamiliar city with five young children, no immediate place to live and no obvious way to support them. Whatever plan existed for a new life in America collapsed upon arrival. And somehow, she made it work. I wish I knew more about how.
Family history is frustrating that way. Moments that seem monumental in retrospect were simply days people had to figure out how to survive. There is no record of what my great-grandmother thought as she stood there, where they slept that night, or if she wondered whether crossing the Atlantic had been a colossal mistake.
Presumably, she was too busy figuring out what the hell to do next to record this for posterity.
What I do know is what followed. Her children grew up. Their children grew up. The opportunities accumulated across generations until, eventually, they reached me.
Out of a working-class upbringing, I was able to gain an education and become a professor. I have traveled, written, taught and built a life of extraordinary privilege compared with the woman who arrived in Boston with five young children and no one there to meet her. Her gamble paid dividends she could not have imagined.
And now comes the absurdity. Because my grandmother was born in Ireland, I have been given yet another opportunity: the legal right of national membership and return. My great-grandmother crossed an ocean with young children and zero safety net. I tracked down some documents and filled out a bunch of forms.
It’s humbling to think about how much of one’s life rests on the courage of strangers who you just happen to be related to.
My ancestors looked west across the Atlantic and saw possibility. More than 100 years later, I find myself looking back across that ocean with something resembling the same longing. They left amid economic insecurity, social and political conflict. Now, I have reclaimed that citizenship they left behind, wondering whether Ireland might someday offer me the same.
I never really knew the people who made these consequential decisions. But I have always possessed a sarcastic sense of humor and appreciation for the absurd. I imagine that I got some of it from them.
And if so, I suspect my great-grandmother would find this whole thing hilarious. She left Ireland so that her descendants might have choices she did not.
One hundred and fourteen years later, I am holding an Irish passport and discovering yet again just how many choices she left me.

Sen. Susan Collins responds to Gov. Janet Mills’ calls to approve increased LIHEAP funding
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Sen. Susan Collins is supporting Gov. Janet Mills’ calls to Congress to approve increased LIHEAP funding.
On Friday, Mills sent a letter to Maine’s Congressional Delegation saying current funding is not keeping up with heating oil costs and did not factor in the price increase caused by the war in Iran.
The DOER said Maine consumes more residential heating oil per capita than any other state and significantly more per capita than the five other states in New England. Approximately 50% of all Maine households rely on fuel oil as their primary heat source, although that has declined steadily from a mark of 70% in 2010, according to the DOER. Last year, Maine households received more than $42 million in LIHEAP funding last year.
Sen. Collins has asked the federal government to release the maximum amount of funding for LIHEAP. The Trump administration has proposed zeroing out funding for the program, but Collins has continued her push to increase it. The Senate appropriations committee has pushed to continue funding at more than $4 million this year.
Sen. Collins says Maine needs alternative options for home heating. “I have always thought that we should build a pipeline to bring Shale Gas from Pennsylvania into Maine. Natural gas is cleaner than home heating oil, it is cleaner, and it is a good supplement,” she said.
Gov. Mills has urged Mainers who need assistance to apply for the program. Applications opened in August and will stay open until funding is exhausted.

2 people killed, including a student, after Florida school bus rolls over in crash, sheriff says
A school bus flipped over onto its roof during a multivehicle crash in central Florida on Monday morning, killing two people — including a 10th-grade girl — and injuring several others, authorities said.
Nearly 40 people were on the school bus that was headed to Winter Haven High School in Winter Haven when an oncoming car crossed the center line and caused the crash, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said at a morning news conference.
“It was a horrible crash,” Judd said. “It was a terrible, tragic morning. "We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life.”
The bus had been traveling along a Winter Haven road shortly after 6 a.m. when an oncoming car crossed the center line and crashed into the side of the bus near the rear wheels, Judd said. The impact ripped the tire off the bus and caused it to crash head on into an oncoming Jeep, which caught on fire.
A person in the Jeep died. Judd said first responders spent the first several hours getting people to the hospital, identifying them and reuniting students with their parents.

title: Stroke survivor’s daily thumbs-up greeting has powerful effect on neighbors
text:
EATON RAPIDS, Mich. (Aging Untold) — For 10 years, George Doxtader has greeted passing drivers with a thumbs-up from a bench at the corner of State and Main.
“Ten years,” Doxtader said.
Doxtader, 78, spreads joy in the community with a thumbs-up that lifts the spirits of people passing by.
A daily routine
Kurt Norgaard, Doxtader’s friend and breakfast buddy, said Doxtader starts early.
“He gets up very early. He’s out here a lot of times at 4 a.m.,” Norgaard said. “And you’ll see a lot of waving and beeping — just how it is.”
Doxtader’s pastor said he is family and a blessing to the community.
“Aging Untold” host Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the greetings have an effect on the community.
“He’s found a way to connect to his community, and he’s found a way to make them see a bright light in the day … and that’s what we all need - purpose and meaning,” Cradduck said.
Recovering from strokes
Doxtader suffered two major strokes 35 years ago. He has paralysis on the right side of his body and has trouble speaking.
“Slow and gradual,” Doxtader said.
When he isn’t greeting passersby, Doxtader crochets blankets and pictures using his left hand.
Cradduck said Doxtader’s story shows what’s possible after setbacks.
“So he proved through his own resilience that no matter what life throws at you, you can make a way to still have a positive impact on the world around you and your community,” Cradduck said.
Doxtader can be found on Main Street in Eaton Rapids.

title: Patients’ shocking sexual assault claims lead to charges against former nurse
text:
MONROE, Wash. (KIRO) - A former nurse in Washington state is facing felony charges after several patients levied shocking claims of sexual assault against him.
Stephen Odingo, 61, faces four felony counts of indecent liberties after three women accused him of sexual assault. The women were all patients at EvergreenHealth Monroe, the hospital where Odingo worked as a nurse.
Charging documents from the Snohomish County Prosecutor’s office outline the case.
The first incident was reported in July 2024. A woman told police she checked into the medical center, and Odingo asked her to remove all her clothing. She said the nurse then “grabbed both [her] breasts and started to massage them” and “went down the front of her underwear with his hand,” according to the documents.
A second victim said that, in January 2025, Odingo repeatedly hugged her and held her hand then asked her to remove her bra. When she refused, the nurse reportedly tried to remove it himself, according to the documents.
Investigators said, in both cases, the women reported Odingo, and he was removed from their care teams.
A third victim reported Odingo just days after the second alleged incident. She told investigators she was nervous about her treatment and initially thought Odingo’s behavior was an attempt to comfort her, according to the documents.
She alleged Odingo gave her a back massage then told her, ‘Maybe you can take care of me sometime’ before kissing her on the mouth through his mask. She said the nurse later squeezed her breasts so hard she started crying after which he again tried to hug and kiss her before touching her genitals, according to the documents.
Following the third report, investigators say Odingo was suspended from work then resigned later that month.
Odingo is set to be arraigned Wednesday.
EvergreenHealth said patient safety is a priority and that it is cooperating fully with the investigation. The hospital would not comment further because this is an ongoing legal matter.

title: Patriots are back in the race after toppling Bills
text:
The New England Patriots’ early-season triumph at Buffalo last season was part of the 10-game winning streak that helped propel them on a Super Bowl run following a 1-2 start.
New England is hoping Sunday’s 29-26 victory over the Bills can provide a similar spark.
The Patriots are 2-2 on the season after handing their division rivals their first loss in the new Highmark Stadium.
Following a week of questions about quarterback Drake Maye’s struggles, poor offensive execution and a mounting number of injuries, their performance for the moment has brought a sense of confidence back to the defending AFC champions.
“Come on, man! We ain’t dead! We ain’t dead!” defensive tackle Cory Durden shouted as he embraced coach Mike Vrabel on his way to the locker room Sunday.
Vrabel was equally succinct in describing what the win meant for his team.
“Gets us back in the race,” he said.
What might be most encouraging was Maye’s play.
He wasn’t spotless, throwing his seventh interception of the season and losing a fumble. But he was poised with the game on the line, leading the Patriots on an eight-play, 73-yard drive that ended with Efton Chism III’s diving, one-handed, go-ahead catch in the end zone.
It capped a day that saw Maye throw for a season-high 269 yards and three TDs. It ended his two-game drought without a TD pass.
“Everybody understands how the quarterback has to perform in this league for the team to have success,” Vrabel said. “Everybody does have his back, starting with me and everybody all the way down.”
What’s working
Chism is the latest example of the Patriots’ history of finding success with undrafted free agents.
Signed after the 2025 NFL draft, he appeared in just eight games as a rookie, catching each of his three targets for 75 yards, with one touchdown.
He already has played in three of the four games this season, with seven targets and four catches for 41 yards.
What needs help
As excited as the Patriots were to see Chism come up big after Mack Hollins’ injury, there are mounting concerns at wide receiver.
Vrabel acknowledged Monday that Hollins likely would miss a couple of days of practice, putting his availability for Sunday’s game in jeopardy.
That would leave the Patriots down another top receiver, with A.J. Brown still on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain.
Signing another receiver is a possibility.
“Sure, anybody that could help us,” Vrabel said.
Stock up
Romeo Doubs. Following a rough debut in the season-opening loss to Seattle, Doubs is starting to show why the Patriots signed him to a four-year, $70 million deal this offseason. He had his first two touchdown catches of the season and is tied for second on the team with 12 receptions. Doubs’ 203 receiving yards are behind only Hollins (209).
Stock down
Vrabel. With the Bills trailing 14-7 and facing a third-and-goal on the New England 16, he received an unsportsmanlike conduct for arguing a defensive holding penalty on Marcus Jones.
Vrabel said he told the official it was a “terrible effing call.”
The penalty, along with Jones’ initial infraction, put the ball on the 6. The Bills tied the game following a TD run by Josh Allen two plays later.
“I’ve said that 87 times since I’ve been a head coach. It was nothing derogatory. You’d have to ask him. I think he was a little sensitive,” Vrabel said. “I apologized to him. Players responded, it was unfortunate. And I have to be better in those moments.”
Injuries
Cornerback Charles Woods left the game with a shoulder injury but was able to return. … Tight end Eli Raridon and fullback Reggie Gilliam also left the game with ankle injuries.
Key number
29 — In their first three games this season, the Patriots scored only 29 points in 30 drives. They had 29 points in their 12 drives against the Bills.
Next steps
The Patriots host the the Las Vegas Raiders (3-1) on Sunday.

text:

title: US Supreme Court does not take up case regarding lobster boat GPS tracking
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (WABI) - The US Supreme Court has declined to take up a case affecting the nation’s lobster industry.
The rule at issue lets fishery managers require electronic vessel trackers on federally permitted lobster boats, in the water and at the dock.
The First Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the rule last year.
Opponents called it “unconstitutional” in their appeal.
Supporters say tracking provides timely, accurate data for regulators as the New England lobster population declines.
Attorney Matthew Gillam from Pacific Law Group, who represents the Maine fisherman who challenged the rule said in a statement to WABI, ”While we are disappointed that the Supreme Court declined to hear Mr. Thompson’s cert petition, today’s decision does not diminish the importance of the issues presented. Forcing lobstermen to carry a GPS tracker on their private boats and submit to around-the-clock surveillance as a condition of keeping their license remains a serious constitutional concern. We are committed to fighting for Fourth Amendment protections from government overreach and we will continue to pursue every lawful avenue to protect individual rights."

title: Supreme Court begins new term with cases addressing climate change, immigration, and gun laws
text:
Supreme Court begins new term with cases addressing climate change, immigration, and gun laws
The Supreme Court's new term opens with cases addressing climate change lawsuits, immigration policies, and voting rights laws.
Supreme Court begins new term with cases addressing climate change, immigration, and gun laws
The Supreme Court's new term opens with cases addressing climate change lawsuits, immigration policies, and voting rights laws.
The Supreme Court begins its new term on Monday, addressing a packed docket that includes cases on climate change, immigration, and voting rights.
The justices are starting the term with a major climate change case involving energy companies seeking to block dozens of lawsuits that aim to hold them liable for damages related to climate change in Boulder, Colorado. Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in this case.
Several high-profile cases are scheduled through December, including one involving voting rights. The court will consider Arizona's push to enforce strict voting laws requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration. This follows President Donald Trump's unsuccessful attempt to pass a proof-of-citizenship bill through Congress.
The court will also hear two significant immigration cases. One focuses on the legality of the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to countries other than their own.
The other case examines the administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants living in the U.S. illegally, even if they have been in the country for years. The administration argues it can hold individuals without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have reviewed the issue disagree.
Later in the term, the justices will also hear cases involving religious rights and an assault weapons ban.

title: Bangor man on trial in 1984 killing of 18-year-old Calais woman Linda Maxwell
text:
MACHIAS, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor man accused of killing an 18-year-old Calais woman more than 40 years ago allegedly admitted the crime to a jailmate.
Opening statements were heard Monday in the murder trial of Raymond Brown, 67, for the 1984 killing of Linda Maxwell.
What prosecutors allege
Prosecutors say Brown told a jailmate he suffocated Maxwell in a bog and later dumped her body in the St. Croix River.
Assistant District Attorney Suzanne Russell told jurors Maxwell, her friends, and Brown had been drinking heavily the night Maxwell died.
Prosecutors say Brown, who was married at the time, wanted to have sex with Maxwell. They say Brown was supposed to take Maxwell home that night, but killed her after she threatened to tell people he raped her.
Russell said Brown planned to dump her body in her driveway but instead decided to leave her in the water.
Defense challenges murder claim
Brown’s attorneys questioned whether the state has proven Maxwell’s death was a murder after she was found in the river.
The medical examiner originally ruled her death a drowning.
The defense say Brown did not kill Maxwell, and the state decided to focus on him.
What’s next
Evidence in the trial will be presented to jurors Tuesday.

title: The Maine Marathon was not my day, but it wasn’t a loss
text:
This is not the story I was planning to write.
When I pitched this series to Sports Editor Bill Stewart, my goal was take readers through my training and then tell the triumphant story of my race at the Maine Marathon. I would write about all the miles I crushed during the race, fighting through the pain to get to the finish line, where I would ring the PR bell and then finally, after 12 years of trying, erase my goal time of 3:47 off the chalkboard that hangs in my apartment.
Unfortunately, I don’t get to tell that story.
I ran my sixth marathon Sunday morning and the day did not go as planned. I missed every one of my time goals, nearly dropped out multiple times, and was left wondering if I ever want to do this again.
I won’t bury the lead anymore than I already have: I finished the race in 4 hours, 13 minutes, 58 seconds. I missed my ‘A’ goal by 26 minutes, my ‘B’ goal by 23 minutes and my ‘C’ goal by nearly 14 minutes.
It was not the race I was hoping for, but there was way too much good to focus only on the bad.
It was a stellar day to run a marathon. It was right around 50 degrees when the race started, ideal weather for a marathon. I chatted up friends and hung out with folks from my run group until the race started, then I went my own way, to run my own race.
I was cruising between 8:45 and 9 minutes per mile for the first 6 miles, taking in all the signs and the ocean views, and shouting out friends and high-fiving my sister Melissa when I saw her just after mile 6. I stopped at the porta potty during mile 7 and choked down my second gel (I literally choked on it for a second, yuk), and picked the pace back up in mile 8.
The hills started at mile 10, but I was feeling good, keeping my effort relaxed, and dropped down to 8:36-8:43 per mile until the half marathon. I crossed the half in 1:57, a little slower than 3:47 pace, but right on target to give it a good effort on the way back to Portland.
My race took a turn in the 17th mile while climbing the hill at Tuttle Road in Cumberland. My right knee, the one that always gives me problems during marathons, started to really hurt as I approached that hill. Every swing of that leg, every time my foot hit the ground, my knee sang in agony. Before I started to limp, I told myself it was OK to walk to the top of that hill, then get back on pace at the top.
I never did get back on pace. The final 10-plus miles of the marathon was a slog. A slow, painful slow. I jogged when I could and walked when I felt I needed to. I considered dropping out every time I saw a medical tent, but didn’t allow myself to quit. That’s one thing I can take pride in.
I was about 2.5 miles from the finish line when I looked at my watch and saw 3:47 flip to 3:48. I knew long before that I wasn’t hitting that goal, but it still hurt to see the number pass so far from the end.
I jogged the final three-tenths of a mile, determined not to walk across the finish line. I shook hands with my colleagues, waited in line for pizza that never came, then left with my sister and brother-in-law for a well deserved lunch at Wilson County Barbecue. I celebrated the day, not necessarily the race.
Ten months after signing up for this race and after 18 weeks of training, I’m ready for a bit of a break. I’m looking forward to running again, but not right away. I’m going to recover, reflect and decide what’s next.
What won’t be next is another marathon. I don’t know if I’ll ever put myself through that again, but it’s too soon after the race to say, “No way.” After all, seven years ago after running the Chicago Marathon, I said that was it, yet here we are.
If I ever do decide to try again, I’ll remember how much fun I had this summer putting in the work, and do everything I can so it doesn’t physically feel the way it did on Sunday.
That will be a story I want to tell.

title: ‘This baby is gone’: 12-year-old girl killed in crossfire at youth football game
text:
BALTIMORE (WBAL) - A 12-year-old girl was killed and a woman was injured when gunfire erupted at a youth football game.
The shooting happened Saturday in Baltimore.
Police Commissioner Richard Worley said preliminary information indicated there were two shooters who were arguing over a parking space before gunfire erupted.
Officials said a 12-year-old girl, who was not immediately identified, was shot and killed in the crossfire. A woman was also injured with non-life-threatening injuries.
Authorities say two men also walked into hospitals seeking treatment from the incident.
Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said the shooting is one of the most “disgusting things” he’s ever seen in his life.
“We will find him. We will bring them here and bring them to justice for their family, but that’s not going to bring her back. That’s not going to stop these other kids from having the trauma of seeing somebody they know get shot and killed. That’s not gonna heal these folks. Two men got into a basic argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone,” he said.
“But two men — or so-called men — got into an argument, and now this baby is gone, never going to see her full potential. Her family is going to be hurting for this for the rest of their lives. Her classmates are going to be hurting. Her community is going to be hurting because people can’t handle their conflict in a different way,” Scott continued.
There was no information on potential suspects or arrests in the investigation.

title: Vehicle Explosion On Main Street In Readfield Traced To Improper Use Of Tannerite Target Practice Explosive
text:
Authorities Investigate A Vehicle That Was Blown Up With A Reactive Rifle Target In Readfield
The Maine Department of Public Safety says authorities are investigating a vehicle explosion in the Kennebec County town of Readfield.
Read More: Dexter Home Fire Shows Dangers Of Improper Cigarette Disposal
The State Fire Marshal's Office says Tannerite, an explosive usually used in rifle target practice, was the cause of the explosion at 846 Main Street on Sunday, September 27th. Multiple calls were made to first responders after the blast; the Readfield Fire Department was sent to the scene. Once they learned that an explosion had occurred, the State Fire Marshal's Office was tagged in to take over.
"State Fire Marshal Investigators responded and investigated the circumstances surrounding the event, which turned out to be a group of individuals shooting at the Tannerite that had been placed in the vehicle...The State Fire Office reminds people that state law governing the use of Tannerite allows up to 5 pounds of mixed product to be used for sport/target shooting only. Tannerite cannot be used to explode any item other than the packaging it is mixed in."
In fact, the safety instructions on the Tannerite.com website clearly state that putting the explosive on metal is a direct hazard.
"Follow all of the safety instructions. Elevate the target on a cardboard box and make sure the area is free of debris and dry grasses.
Do not use the target in locations where a general fire order is in effect, and do not use the target near combustible materials. Never place these targets inside, on top of, or under any metal, rock, or other surfaces that could produce flying debris or sparks, or within another object. This is dangerous and constitutes improper use of the product."
Read More: New Hampshire Man Charged In Death Of Wells Resident
Authorities say the investigation is still active, and the Fire Marshal's Office is now working in conjunction with the local D.A.'s Office to work out what charges will come of all of this.
