title: Online safety warnings shouldn’t scare older Mainers offline
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Jessica Perez is senior manager of digital opportunity at Maine Connectivity Authority, the quasi-governmental agency leading efforts to expand affordable, reliable internet access across Maine. Noël Bonam is state director of AARP Maine, which represents nearly 200,000 members 50 and older statewide.
“There is no electrician or milkman for the internet. There’s no one to help. You have to figure it out on your own or get help from your kids.” That is what an older woman told us this summer at the grand opening of the Encompass Education and Nutrition Center, SeniorsPlus’ new connectivity hub in Lewiston. She was talking about technology, but she put her finger on a much bigger problem.
We have spent years warning people about the dangers of being online. Watch out for scams. Do not click suspicious links. Protect your passwords. Be skeptical of what you see. Now, with artificial intelligence making it harder to distinguish what is real from what is not, those warnings have become even more urgent.
The warnings are justified. But at SeniorsPlus, we heard about an unintended consequence: some older Mainers are afraid of the internet at precisely the moment when they increasingly need it.
Healthcare is online. Job applications are online. Government services, banking, education and communication with family increasingly require digital participation. For people who did not grow up using the internet, opting out is becoming less realistic.
And yet, when something goes wrong, there often is no obvious — let alone trusted — person to call. People may not understand a medical portal, suspect an online scam, struggle to make their laptop work or simply not know how to accomplish something online. Too often, the answer is to figure it out themselves — or call their kids.
Maine has made enormous strides in expanding access to fast, reliable internet. More than 120,000 homes and businesses that once lacked reliable service are now connected, and tens of thousands more soon will be. But access is only the beginning. The real measure of these investments is whether they help Maine people live, learn, work and participate in their communities.
Maine’s next connectivity challenge is making sure the warnings meant to keep people safe online do not unintentionally deepen the very digital divide we have worked so hard to close.
AARP’s own survey shows that 1 in 5 Americans age 65 and older lacks confidence in
identifying online scams and fraud, and nearly a third report not having the skills to fully
participate online. But more than 70% say they would participate in technology
programs designed for them.
We cannot simply tell people to be more careful online — or hand them a device, connect their home and wish them luck. People need trusted, local places where they can ask questions, build skills and get help without feeling embarrassed or overwhelmed. That is exactly what the new connectivity hub at SeniorsPlus is designed to provide. With grant support from the Maine Connectivity Authority, people can use public computers, get one-on-one technology help, take computer skills classes and learn how to stay safe online.
Most importantly, it offers what the woman we met there said was missing: somewhere to turn when you cannot figure it out on your own.
Maine needs more places like SeniorsPlus: places where people of all ages can walk through the door, find someone they trust and ask for help. The good news is that Maine already has the infrastructure that matters most: trusted people in trusted places.
They are in our libraries, community centers, schools, municipal and tribal buildings, YWCAs and other local organizations — places where people already gather, learn, ask questions and look out for one another. Connectivity hubs build on that strength by bringing internet access, devices, digital skills and technical support into institutions that already anchor our communities.
As Maine enters its next chapter of connectivity, we should invest not only in the infrastructure that connects communities, but in the people and places that make those connections useful. The goal was never simply to build a network. It is to make sure Maine people can use connectivity safely and confidently to live, learn, work and participate.
We have spent years connecting Maine. The work ahead is making sure Maine people feel able to connect.

title: Tap ensemble in Myrtle Beach brings adults back to dance after decades
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A tap ensemble in South Carolina is made up of adults who are returning to tap dancing after stepping away for careers and family responsibilities.
Michele Selvanto-Kowalski spent more than 45 years teaching tap in New Jersey before moving to Myrtle Beach in 2014. She teaches all ages at Coastal Dance Center.
“I get chills when I teach it, I get chills when I talk about it,” Selvanto-Kowalski said.
Selvanto-Kowalski said the adults in her classes impress and inspire her the most.
“Their passion in the tap class, they just kept going and going… and that’s when I said, ‘You know what?’ Something clicked and said, ‘Let’s do this,’” Selvanto-Kowalski said.
Carolina Rhythm Tap Ensemble
Selvanto-Kowalski created a group for adults called the Carolina Rhythm Tap Ensemble.
“It gives them an opportunity to get out there and maybe pursue a dream that they always had but couldn’t do,” Selvanto-Kowalski said.
Aging Untold expert Katherine Ambrose said the ensemble is proof it’s not too late to return to a passion.
“When you pause a dream for work and family, it’s so great to be able to come back to it, and doing it with a group adds connection and belonging, which is important at every stage,” Ambrose said.
Some of the dancers in the ensemble grew up tap dancing but stopped to focus on careers, family and children.
Weekly practice and performances
The women practice choreography once a week and take tap classes to perfect their technique before performing in the community.
Ambrose said tap dancing also provides brain-and-body fitness.
“Tap is brain-and-body fitness at the same time. We’re talking balance, coordination, rhythm and memory all working together, and it can boost stability and confidence in everyday life,” Ambrose said.

title: Le Ronj’s London Fog: A Love Story
text:
Picture this: It’s 8 p.m. on a Wednesday. You’re a first year, doing more reading than you’ve ever done in your life, and you need a new study spot. It’s raining, and you wander your way into Le Ronj. In hopes of a small caffeine kick, not a big one, you know you need tea. Think back on your barista knowledge. In the collection of drinks chalked on the wall, you pick one you know will be okay: the London Fog.
On that rainy Wednesday evening, I discovered Le Ronj’s London Fog.
I was a barista in a past life. A small local place in Upstate New York that overcharged its customers and underpaid its employees. You know the type. Our espresso was good, maybe even great. Our London Fog was fine, reliable, and fine.
So when I walked into Le Ronj that evening, ordering a London Fog, I didn’t expect much more than fine. I assumed they were all just fine. The drink I was served, however, in that beautiful orange and white mug with butterflies painted on it, was better than I could have ever imagined. It exceeded fine by miles. The lavender powder on top, the perfectly steamed oat milk (it normally comes with whole milk, so the oat milk was a me thing, but it should be a you thing too: it makes all the difference). This was an all around amazing drink. Mind blowing, life changing. Just what I expect out of my New England liberal arts college.
Please, I’m begging you to try Le Ronj’s London Fog. If you’ve already tried Le Ronj’s London Fog, try another one. Live the liberal arts college life you’re meant to live.

title: Former news anchor sentenced for murdering her mother
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - A Kansas judge sentenced Angelynn Mock on Monday to life in prison without eligibility for parole for 25 years.
Mock, a former television news anchor in St. Louis, was suspected in the Oct. 31, 2025 death of her mother, 80-year-old Anita Avers, in south Wichita.
Mock pleaded guilty in August in the Sedgwick County case in which she was charged with one count of first-degree murder.
According to a probable cause affidavit, Mock’s stepfather told police that the 48-year-old Mock had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder. The diagnosis was later revised to schizoaffective disorder.
In July, a Sedgwick County District Court judge found Mock competent to stand trial and reversed an earlier ruling.
Mock’s guilty plea carries a presumptive sentence of life in prison without eligibility for parole for 25 years.

title: Tennessee Republicans consider more execution options after Christa Pike lethal injection fails
text:
Some of Tennessee’s top Republicans said Monday they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners after the failed execution of Christa Pike, which relied on a large dose of pentobarbital.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state’s Republican candidate for governor, said Pike’s unsuccessful execution last week “should not be grounds to halt carrying out the death penalty.” Rather, she said, Tennessee needs to reevaluate the way it does executions.
“If it’s lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully,” Blackburn told The Associated Press.
Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session.
“We want to broaden it, include more methods,” House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. “What those are as of today, I’m not sure. But I don’t think there’s any method that’s off the table at this point.”
Most U.S. states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary means, though South Carolina sets its default as electrocution and Idaho the firing squad, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Some states give prisoners a choice of execution methods. Death by electricity or gas is authorized in nine states, including five that specify nitrogen gas, the center said. Five states authorize a firing squad.
Florida, which leads the nation in executions this year, uses a three-drug lethal injection that includes a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart.
Tennessee’s execution procedures have been in the national spotlight since Wednesday, when prison officials gave Pike two doses of a barbiturate that were supposed to be lethal but didn’t ultimately kill her. Pike has remained hospitalized under guard, left unconscious and on a ventilator with blisters and burns on her arms from the drug, her lawyers have said.
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and slaying of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Pike was age 18 at the time and became one of the youngest women sent to death row.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee, whose term ends in January, halted the one remaining execution scheduled for this year and ordered an independent investigation into the state’s capital punishment system after Pike’s failed execution. He said Saturday the commissioner of the Department of Correction will step down.
Blackburn said comprehensive change is needed — “it is personnel, processes, procedures, protocols that are all going to need to be addressed.”
Tennessee law already allows electrocution if the department is unable to carry out a lethal injection despite reasonable efforts to do so. State law also gives people who committed crimes before 1999 the option of choosing electrocution.
Between 2018 and 2020, five Tennessee prisoners chose electrocution. That could remain an option for about two dozen of the 40 people on death row.
Sexton said the legislature could consider amending the law to give the state a choice of execution methods.
House Majority Leader William Lamberth said he is open to making electrocution the state’s primary means of execution. But no matter the method, Lamberth said he doesn’t want any changes to take too long to implement.
“We want these sentences to be carried out effectively, efficiently and humanely,” he said, adding: “Whatever we do, I do not want it to delay justice for these victims’ families.”
Republican state Sen. Todd Gardenhire, chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said he expects a deliberate review of what went wrong and what can be done to improve the execution process.
“I think the electric chair is the quickest and simplest way to do it,” he said.

title: 4 teens charged in murder of 16-year-old shot after high school football game, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Police in Tennessee say four teenagers have been charged after a 16-year-old boy was killed in a drive-by shooting after a high school football game.
Cameron Frierson, 16, was killed in a drive-by shooting Aug. 21 after he went to a football game at Pearl-Cohn High School, according to Nashville police. It was around 10:30 p.m. when police say someone in a white sedan drove by and began shooting, hitting Cameron multiple times as his brother stood close by.
Now, police say four teenagers — ages 16, 17, 17 and 18 — have been arrested in connection with the killing. All four are charged with criminal homicide and engaging in a criminal conspiracy.
Police say all of the suspects were inside the white sedan when the shots that hit Cameron were fired. The investigation into a motive for the gunfire is ongoing.
‘I miss him so much’
Cameron’s parents spoke with WSMV after his death, describing their son as a teenager who was “truly being a kid” on the night he was killed.
Cameron was a student at Hunters Lane High School and the oldest of seven siblings. His mother, Brittany Frierson, said he loved football, cars and fashion. He had a dream of getting an HVAC degree and owning his own business.
“I miss him so much. I miss the laugh and his smile,” Frierson said.
Cameron’s mother said he worked two jobs but had the night off Aug. 21. He had been looking forward to going to the football game with his friends all week. She said no mother should ever have to worry about their child not coming home from a school football game.
“It could have been anybody’s child. It’s not right for us to live in the city and not enjoy the city. He was 16, just like any other 16-year-old,” Frierson said. “They weren’t doing anything wrong. Gun violence and these kids is serious.”

title: ‘Diamond in the rough’: Plans for Lewiston’s Red Shop discussed
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON — The city’s so-called Red Shop has been a lot of things over the years, but if current plans come to fruition, it may find itself in its biggest role yet.
Built in 1938, the Red Shop on Water Street served as a machine shop for the Bates Mill complex and later to control water flow in the canal system. The city building most recently has been used as storage for local group Lewiston Rowing’s boats.
Portland developer Christopher Thompson sees the park and its surroundings as the city’s next opportunity for a year-round destination that could include entertainment, recreation, hospitality and public gathering.
He sees seasonal concert series and other events that may spill over into Simard-Payne Memorial Park and it all starts with that humble red structure that came to be known as the Red Shop.
“Simply put, I think that building is extraordinary,” Thompson said Monday night. “It’s a diamond in the rough. It’s got incredible character.”
John Blais, the city’s developer of economic and community development, likewise feels like the potential of the Red Shop meshes beautifully with the larger plans the city has to revitalize the riverfront.
“We want to strengthen the relationships between the building, the park and the riverfront,” Blais said on Monday. “We want to celebrate the riverfront. It’s just a beautiful place.”
Planners and developers already have their ideas about what the Red Shop and surrounding area might become, sure enough. But the purpose of a public meeting at the Hampton Inn on Monday night was to hear what regular Lewiston folks would like to see at the historic building.
Roughly four dozen people attended the meeting. They were asked to fill out cards explaining, in fine detail, how they would like to see the future of the Red Shop unfold.
They were asked what types of events they would like to see; what they imagined the outside of the building looking like after renovations and what they would prefer to see for the interior.
Themes emerged. It turns out people do like the idea of summer concerts and live performances in and around that storied red building. They have notions about what it should look like, both inside and out.
Although not everybody agrees on what plans for the Red Shop should look like — some would like to see plans scaled down to keep the site mainly for community access — planners say this was the kind of information they were after.
“We plan to take this feedback and hopefully, incorporate some of it into a joint development agreement,” City Manager Bryan Kaenrath said.
The city acquired the Red Shop and the canals around it in 2018.
Last year, the city completed its Simard-Payne Memorial Park Master Plan, which calls for a redesign featuring improved river access and trails, public art, a new pavilion and expanded amphitheater, playground, splashpad and space designed for festivals, concerts and general use.
“Development of the red shop will help support large-scale events in Simard-Payne park, which follows the goals outlined in the Riverfront Master Plan,” Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline said Monday night. “I’m excited about the economic activity that this will generate.”
Earlier in the summer, Thompson, who also helped develop the Hampton Inn on Lincoln Street, presented a proposal to the city nearly two decades in the making.
Those plans call for the sale of 39 Lincoln St., the sale or lease of the Red Shop and the creation of a 30-year tax increment financing agreement.
Thompson said the vision for the Red Shop is to preserve the timber-frame building and equip it with a small kitchen, new bathrooms and to generally bring the building up to code, open it toward the park and to open it seasonally at first, and then, eventually, year-round.
But he admits that his visions, though richly detailed, are still in the nascent stage. He imagines getting the Red Shop going as a venue for seasonal events for starters and letting it grow from there.
“We’re still in the very early stages of figuring out,” Thompson said. “Exactly what would a build-out look like and what would the program be? That’s part of the reason for being here tonight.”

title: Popular Rockland restaurant to end nearly 2 decade-long run
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — The Home Kitchen Cafe, a restaurant where lines of customers are often seen waiting to enjoy an early or midday meal, will be closing on Oct. 18, the owners announced Saturday.
James Hatch and Susan Schiro announced the news on the restaurant’s Facebook page.
“After 18 unforgettable years, we’ve made the difficult decision to close Home Kitchen Cafe & Bakery and begin a new chapter in retirement,” they said.
“This place has always been about more than food. It’s been about doing things the right way, every single day. From scratch cooking to genuine hospitality, we set a standard for ourselves and worked hard to live up to it. This is not a post we ever thought we would make, but in today’s world, maintaining our level of quality has become increasingly challenging. Like many in our industry, we’ve faced a growing struggle to find and keep the skilled, dedicated team needed to consistently deliver the experience our customers expect and deserve. Rather than compromise what Home Kitchen Cafe stands for, we feel it’s the right time to step away,” the couple said.
“To our incredible employees, past and present, you are the heart of this story. Your commitment, resilience, and pride in your work carried us through every busy morning and every demanding season. Quite simply, we would not have made it this far without you.
“And to our loyal customers and community, thank you for your unwavering support over the years. You filled our dining room, shared your lives with us, and made this journey deeply meaningful.
“We leave with gratitude, pride, and a lifetime of memories, confident that what was built here, in Rockland’s North End, will always be something unique and special.
“Please stop by in the next two weeks as the Cafe and Bakery will remain open through Oct. 18,” the restaurant owners stated.
In July 2024, the couple announced they were hoping to sell the business and building and real estate at 650 Main St. in the heart of Rockland overlooking the harbor. Hatch and Schiro said they would only sell if they found new owners who would uphold their values and traditions.
The restaurant was born during the Great Recession and weathered the COVID-19 pandemic.
The couple opened the business in February 2009. They initially leased the property from the Fish family but purchased the property in May 2011. The cafe underwent major renovations in late 2012 and reopened in February 2013.
In a 2013 interview when they reopened, the couple noted that everyone said they were crazy to open a restaurant in 2009, the worst of economic times. That opening occurred during the Great Recession.
“But we had a vision,” Hatch said in that interview.
That vision has led to Home Kitchen being a popular spot for locals and tourists to enjoy breakfast and lunch.
In that 2013 interview, the couple said they carefully planned going into the restaurant business. Hatch and Schiro operated a graphics business for 16 years. During that time, however, the plans were developed for that ultimate goal.
Hatch said the first job he had was as a teen working at a Mexican restaurant in Damariscotta where he worked his way up from dishwasher to head cook.
“This is the culmination of everything we have done in business,” he said. “People have said we were an overnight success but it has taken 22 years.”
Schiro — a Bangor native — said the experience of running their graphics business, which they sold a few years before opening Home Kitchen, helped them operate Home Kitchen Cafe in terms of finances and customer service. The year before they opened the restaurant, the couple hired another person to work at their graphics business to do the work that Hatch did in producing the screen print design T-shirts so that he could transition to the restaurant.
Hatch said his favorite item on the menu is huevos rancheros. He said the success of that offering and the rest of the menu is that all the ingredients are made fresh at the restaurant including the corn tortillas. Those homemade corn tortillas also are used in his fish tacos.
“Everything is made from scratch,” Hatch said.

title: ‘No better time than now’: Couple gets engaged during massive I-95 pileup
text:
LAKE MARION, S.C. (Gray News) - A couple traveling from Philadelphia turned chaos into a lifelong memory during a massive crash involving more than 60 vehicles.
Kevin Cossa and Meghan Quinn were traveling for vacation when they were caught in the crash on the Santee Bridge over Lake Marion.
“We just crashed, and then we got out and made sure everybody was safe. And they were telling us we needed to leave the bridge...,” Quinn said.
With traffic stopped and uncertainty all around them, Cossa decided there was no reason to wait for the perfect moment.
“I just figured that I wouldn’t find another moment as unique as that one,” Cossa said.
Right there on the bridge, he asked Quinn to marry him — and she said yes.
“He was like, ‘I was gonna do this tomorrow but no better time than now,’” Quinn said.
“I honestly, at that point in time, with so much confusion and everything going on, didn’t even know what tomorrow meant,” Cossa said.
The couple was later treated at MUSC Health Orangeburg.
“We’re grateful Kevin and Meghan are doing well and wish them safe travels, a happy engagement and many years of happiness together,” MUSC Health said on Facebook.

title: MaineCare will cover traditional Wabanaki healing practices
text:
Tribal health clinics soon will be able to bill MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, for traditional Wabanaki healing practices.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services announced Friday that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) granted the state a waiver to try new and expanded Medicaid coverage.
Tribal health clinics in Maine already provide traditional practices, including smudging, sweat lodges, talking circles and other ceremonies to patients. But they have to use other revenue sources to cover the costs.
That will change, likely by 2028, once tribal leaders and state officials work out the particulars of what will be covered under the waiver.
“I think this really gives merit and weight to what we always knew was good medicine for our people,” said Theresa Cochran, health director for the Mi’kmaq Nation.
The primary purpose of the waiver was to add MaineCare coverage for treatment of incarcerated people up to 60 days before they reenter society.
As Dr. Courtney Pladsen, MaineCare’s medical director, set out to draft the application, she was committed to maximizing the benefit. Tribal leaders in consultation meetings told Pladsen that other states had expanded Medicaid coverage in this way, and wondered if Maine might do the same.
“When I had read the other waivers and talked to other states about the opportunity, it just seemed like a no-brainer,” Pladsen said.
Maine joins Arizona, California, New Mexico and Oregon, which had similar waivers approved in 2024. It’s the first eastern state to take the step. CMS last week approved a similar request from Utah, bringing the total to six states nationwide.
The expansion must be budget neutral, under the terms of federal approval. The hope is that upstream interventions prevent downstream costs, Pladsen said, and any reimbursements under the program are billed to the federal agency, not the state.
“Our communities should never have to choose between the medicine of our ancestors and the coverage that makes care possible,” William Smith, board chairman of the National Indian Health Board, a national advocacy nonprofit, said in a statement. “(The) decision honors both, and it honors the trust and treaty obligations this country owes to Tribal Nations.”
Tribal members and their families seeking care from one of the five clinics operated by tribal governments in Maine, or from Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness, a statewide public health nonprofit, will be eligible. Over half of Wabanaki Public Health’s clients are on MaineCare, said the organization’s co-CEO Lisa Sockabasin, including 100% of those at its Bangor-based detox center.
Cochran’s department serves almost 600 people, while the statewide Wabanaki public health agency reaches over 7,000 people annually.
Sockabasin said the tribal health providers are looking to extend care beyond just treatment for substance use to fields including chronic disease and mental health as well.
“Tribal healing practices have been in our communities for thousands of years,” said Sockabasin, who is Passamaquoddy. “And those tribal ceremonies and practices and tradition provide immense healing for our community.”
Over the next year, leaders from healthcare providers will work with state Medicaid officials to determine exactly what practices will be covered by Medicaid, and how much clinics will be reimbursed for them.
Tribal knowledge-keepers have continued to use ceremonies to heal members of their communities even without a mechanism of government financial support, leaders emphasize. And they always will. Although there’s never a charge for those ceremonies, they do consume resources.
“Rather than having them adapt their cultural practices to our systems, we need to adapt our systems to their cultural practices,” Pladsen said.
It is an odd moment, Sockabasin acknowledged, in which traditional practices that are typically shared relationally within communities are to be assigned a dollar value.
But it’s also an opportunity for collaboration and for mutual growth, she said.
“We’re becoming more aware, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people, on what it takes to heal. We are both learning.”

title: FBI Director Kash Patel gets engaged to longtime girlfriend, country singer Alexis Wilkins
text:
FBI Director Kash Patel gets engaged to longtime girlfriend, country singer Alexis Wilkins
FBI Director Kash Patel is engaged to his country singer girlfriend, Alexis Wilkins; the pair announced in a post to X on Sunday evening.
Wilkins, 27, posted a black-and-white photo of herself standing with Patel, 46, flashing her hand in front of them to show off her ring with the caption, "Went and got the law involved." The two have been dating since before Patel took over as head of the FBI in 2025, when she attended his swearing-in.
The country singer and political commentator released her debut album in 2023. Wilkins has been affiliated with conservative groups and writes on her website that she "honors country tradition while adding relevance and current commentary."
Patel, who reposted Wilkins' photo, has faced criticism for traveling on government aircraft on trips that have no known or apparent law enforcement purpose, including using an FBI jet to fly to State College, Pennsylvania, for a pro wrestling event where Wilkins performed the national anthem. Photos posted to social media by Wilkins afterward showed the couple smiling while she held an oversized golden championship belt.
Wilkins also made headlines as a performer at President Donald Trump's Great American State Fair on the National Mall as part of America 250, as other artists pulled out of the event after finding out it was not a non-partisan celebration.

title: Weakened fuel efficiency goals will cause lasting damage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Trump administration recently lowered goals for fuel efficiency in many gas-powered vehicles. The previous goal, set by the Biden administration, was for 50.4 miles per gallon in 2031. This change brings that down to 30.1 mpg. This reduction will increase emissions and accelerate climate change when we need to slow it down.
There’s another aspect of this, which is that continued reliance on fossil fuels puts us all at risk. As we’ve seen in the war with Iran, relying on fossil fuel shipments from other countries leaves us economically vulnerable.
Those of us in Maine, as well as elsewhere, are already feeling this. A recent news report (“Rising gas prices eating into profits of Mainers who drive their cars for a living,” Sept. 28) pointed out how those who drive as part of their jobs — such as with Lyft, Uber, and DoorDash — are having to make changes to their jobs now that they spend so much on gas. That will also impact their customers.
I know how much of a difference it makes to get 50 mpg, since that’s about what I get with my hybrid. Yes, I still need to buy gas, but the rising prices have had much less of an impact on me. Not everyone can afford a hybrid, but if the previous fuel standards were kept, even those without a hybrid would benefit.
As it is, this change is short-sighted, environmentally harmful, and will have lasting negative impacts on all of us. I encourage everyone to keep this in mind when voting this November.
Erica Bartlett
Portland

title: How the Trump administration's revamped healthcare price transparency rules could impact patients
text:
How the Trump administration's revamped healthcare price transparency rules could impact patients
Consumer advocates say the rules are an important step, but stress there's more work today to ensure full transparency.
How the Trump administration's revamped healthcare price transparency rules could impact patients
Consumer advocates say the rules are an important step, but stress there's more work today to ensure full transparency.
The Trump administration is rolling out revamped rules intended to improve healthcare price transparency.
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said Monday that the goal is to give patients "the clearest picture yet" of their costs before receiving care, as one Gallup poll suggests that the majority of Americans are in the dark.
The rules finalized on Monday build on transparency requirements established during President Donald Trump's first term by strengthening what health insurers must disclose about the prices that they negotiate with doctors and hospitals.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the industry responded to the initial rules by flooding the zone with confusing and redundant data.
"The information was impossible to decipher, and even the employers who have hundreds of attorneys working for them could not figure out the differentiation in prices," Kennedy said. "When President Trump returned to office, he saw these evasive tactics that the industry had taken, and he directed us to build on that foundation."
The updated rules aim to streamline and simplify that data, while strengthening accountability around data accuracy. The rules also require group health plans and health insurance issuers to provide consumers with personalized cost-sharing information by phone, in addition to existing online tools.
The Trump administration says the changes will help employers make better-informed decisions on health coverage and empower technology developers to build helpful consumer tools.
Sophia Tripoli, managing director of health policy for the consumer advocacy group Families USA, said the updated rules are a positive step, but she stressed that there is more work to do to ensure that the average consumer can easily access and compare pricing data.
"There is not easily accessible pricing data at a consumer's fingertips so that they can, today or tomorrow, meaningfully shop for health care. We are just not there yet," Tripoli said.
Even under the new rules, Tripoli is concerned that there are loopholes that could discourage full price transparency.
"It is why it's so important to get a federal law passed in Congress this session to address some of these issues that the regulations don't quite capture," Tripoli said.
A bipartisan bill, called the "Patients Deserve Price Tags Act," advanced out of the Senate Health Committee this summer. It remains to be seen if it will pass following the midterm elections before new lawmakers are sworn in next year.
In a news release, Hassan's office said the bill would go further than federal regulations by requiring the disclosure of cash prices and patient-specific cost-sharing estimates, as opposed to payer-negotiated minimum and maximum prices.
The American Hospital Association has pushed back on the bill, arguing it would impose unnecessary administrative burdens that would be particularly difficult for small and rural hospitals to implement.

title: Peaks Island cafe will host ‘Widow’s Bay’ watch parties
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In the mood for something to send a shiver down your spine this October — and also make you fall down laughing? Look no further than Baba’s Cafe on Peaks Island.
Every Thursday night in October, Baba’s Cafe will be hosting “Widow’s Bay” watch parties as a way of engaging with the community and encouraging offseason tourism to the island. They’ll watch two episodes of the Emmy-winning Apple TV+ series a week, culminating in the show’s season finale just in time for Halloween weekend.
“(‘Widow’s Bay’) is a really fun show, and it’s been striking a chord with a lot of people in Maine seeking togetherness, community and a little bit of spookiness in October,” said Millie Hillman, winter manager and director of community engagement for Baba’s Cafe.
While the exact location of Widow’s Bay isn’t explicitly stated (although the island is implied to be located somewhere off the New England coast), Hillman chose the show because she sees similarities between the titular town, which exists under a centuries-old curse, and Peaks Island, including their shared “island quirk,” the spookiness of Peaks’ abandoned Battery Steele Fort, and even a few ghosts (Peaks Island offers a ghost tour in the fall).
Hillman originally conceived of the event as a neighborhood watch party, but a post on social media gained more traction than she expected. While she has some mild concerns over the cafe’s 40-person seating capacity, Hillman said that anyone is welcome to join the party.
2026 marks the first year that Baba’s Cafe has been open past Labor Day, and Hillman was brought on in part to coordinate events for the upcoming winter season. The cafe expects to be open year-round with limited hours from 8 a.m.-2 p.m. Thursday through Sunday. In addition to the watch parties, the cafe also offers acoustic music on Sunday afternoons and Spanish conversation hours on Friday afternoons.
Hillman hopes that events such as the “Widow’s Bay” watch parties will draw greater attention to the cafe and entice visitors to stay on Peaks Island for more than just a night.
“We want to show people that Peaks and the Casco Bay islands don’t just need to be a summer activity,” said Hillman. “There’s something really magical about coming out here in the fall and the winter, and experiencing all that Maine has to offer.”
IF YOU GO
“Widow’s Bay” watch party, 6-7:30 p.m. Thursdays in October, Baba’s Cafe, 79 Island Ave., Peaks Island, free to the public. Hillman advises visitors take the 5:35 p.m. Casco Bay Ferry to Peaks Island.

title: Former ‘American Idol’ singer Caleb Flynn awaits sentencing for wife's murder
text:
A former Ohio music pastor who once appeared on “American Idol” was set to be sentenced Monday after a jury convicted him of murdering his wife while he was having an affair.
Prosecutors said Caleb Flynn, 40, staged a home invasion in February after shooting his wife, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old schoolteacher and volleyball coach. Flynn claimed she was killed by a burglar at their home in Tipp City, a suburb north of Dayton.
He sent a text message to his lover the night before the shooting, saying, “I choose you. I’m free. Actions will come tomorrow,” prosecutors said.
Flynn faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole after the jury found him guilty last week of murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence.
Flynn appeared briefly on “American Idol” in 2013, telling TV viewers about how his wife had encouraged him to chase his dreams on the singing competition. He sang before judges Mariah Carey, Randy Jackson and Nicki Minaj but did not advance to the main competition in Hollywood.
During closing arguments, prosecutors told jurors that Flynn wanted out of his marriage when he shot his wife. The couple’s two daughters were home with their father when police arrived.
During the trial, Alleigha Botner testified she met Flynn in 2022 while she was a 20-year-old intern at his church and had an affair with him for more than a year. She told jurors that Flynn said he hated his wife and had thoughts of killing her.
Jurors also heard AI-generated love songs that prosecutors say he made for Botner. Flynn didn’t testify on his own behalf, nor did anybody else.
The gun used to kill Ashley Flynn was not found at the scene, and his attorney told jurors that investigators found no evidence that Caleb Flynn fired a gun that day. Prosecutors said his fingerprints and DNA were at the scene and that his devices showed him moving about the house, even though he claimed he was asleep at the time of the shooting.

title: The New York Times shortchanged Troy Jackson
text:
On Sept. 20, the New York Times ran a profile on Troy Jackson, “A Progressive Brawler Tries to Flip a Senate Seat in Maine.”
Progressive races this cycle have two issues which play large: the treatment of Palestinians and AIPAC attempting to influence races. Despite the primacy of these issues, the Times never mentioned Jackson’s views on the treatment of Palestinians or the millions of dollars from AIPAC and AIPAC-adjacent donors going to Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign.
The article did find room for the 1988 alleged pushing incident between Jackson and his partner. As the Times reported, both Jackson and his partner deny the incident.
The Times’ Israel coverage has drawn criticism, including reported internal guidance for reporters to avoid terms like “genocide” and “occupied territory.” We saw how the Times was dogged in taking down Graham Platner; a pattern.
Maine deserves fair elections free of outside influence. We must remain vigilant as Election Day approaches.
Eric Vos
Rockland

title: Characters of the County: For Robert DeWitt, The Devil Is In The Details
text:
Some people say don’t sweat the small stuff. Damariscotta resident Robert DeWitt isn’t one of them.
The 82-year-old retired orthodontist is meticulous down to the smallest detail for his hobbies, which comes in handy since several of them involve creating miniature models.
DeWitt’s projects have included a notoriously challenging ship model, a thoroughly decked out dollhouse, and a to-scale model village. His current passion project involves his lifelong love affair with motorcycles, which has grown into a restoration hobby in his retirement.
The most personal of these projects is his model village, which is populated with houses DeWitt has lived in and even includes a cemetery with his loved ones who have passed.
The village started with DeWitt’s former home in Richmond. In 2011, after living in Damariscotta for 10 years, DeWitt decided to make a miniature of his former home.
“I spent a lot of time on that house, so I wanted to make a model of the house,” he said.
DeWitt knew the current owners, and contacted them with the idea.
The couple told DeWitt he would never be able to build it. DeWitt took that as a personal challenge.
He did not have any experience making models, so it took some trial and error and his final method was pretty different from how other hobbyists made models. First DeWitt constructed the exterior frame of the house from plywood. Then he uploaded photos of the building to his computer and used Photoshop and Microsoft Word to flatten the images and scale them to the correct size for the model village.
Finally, he printed the images on heavy-duty cardstock, cut them out, and glued them to the model building frame.
Once he built that first model, DeWitt knew he wanted to build more. He decided to build a whole village, and knew right away it would include a working model train.
He built models of his house in Boothbay Harbor, his family camp in Boothbay Harbor, and his current house in Damariscotta.
DeWitt also added models of the historic Newcastle train station on Depot Street, the Bayville Post Office in Boothbay Harbor, and the Newcastle office building his orthodontics practice used.
He constructed a family cemetery in the model village, enclosed within a stone wall. The cemetery was constructed like the houses, made from plywood and then covered with printed cardstock. The tombstone are all inscribed with the names of family members who have died.
When DeWitt decided to add a swing set at one house in the village, he contacted the CedarWorks Playsets in Rockport, got a set of plans from them, and constructed an exact swing set model to scale.
He has added trees, people, and animals throughout the model village. He even wired up a working model train, complete with lights and sounds.
DeWitt worked continuously on the project until about 2016, when he began working on motorcycles.
He had always been interested in motorcycles, and worked at repair shops in Ohio as a young man and in Maine after his retirement in 2013. He said his interest in them likely stemmed from his childhood.
“When I was a kid in Akron, Ohio, everybody who rode a motorcycle was a hoodlum,” he said.
So, of course, he wanted one, and he has owned a motorcycle most of his life. He didn’t start restoring vintage motorcycles until 2016. The first one was a BMW R50 from 1964, sold to him by a friend.
Immediately, DeWitt started working on the restoration of that bike and has averaged about one per year since then. He built out a community of resources as he restored the bikes, as well.
“I met some people along the way,” he said. “I know who to go to for just about everything now.”
DeWitt has “a guy” for anything he would need, he said.
Last winter he started mentoring a 23-year-old young man in South Bristol to pass on his knowledge of the vintage bikes.
DeWitt now has a collection of nine motorcycles and seven are ones he has restored. They are displayed like a museum exhibit in his garage, each one perfectly put back together and lovingly restored to like-new conditions.
The one he is most proud of is the 1968 BMW that he purchased brand new in 1968 at the age of 25.
“I’m the only one who’s ever owned it,” he said.
He said there are likely not many bikes that age with just one owner.

title: Kennebec County Jail correctional officer indicted on sexual assault charges
text:
A corrections officer at the Kennebec County Jail in Augusta is accused of having a sexual relationship with an inmate earlier this year.
Nicholas Fellows, who was employed as a Kennebec County corrections officer at the time of the alleged incident, was indicted in late September on charges of gross sexual assault and unlawful sexual contact, both of which are felonies.
Under state law, it’s a crime for any sexual contact between a corrections officer with supervisory authority over an incarcerated person. An indictment is not a determination of guilt but indicates enough evidence exists for a case to move forward to trial.
Fellows’ coworkers reportedly discovered the inmate relationship in late July and that a brief internal investigation revealed the relationship was likely sexual.
In an interview, an inmate told Detective John Bourque that they had seen Fellows pass notes with the inmate he’s charged with having a relationship with, some of which described sexual acts. The inmate said they’d seen Fellows’ relationship with the other inmate progress.
The inmate who allegedly had a relationship with Fellows confirmed the sexual acts detailed in the notes occurred. In an interview with Bourque, she described her sexual contact with Fellows and said Fellows had orchestrated a situation in which the two could be unsupervised.
The Morning Sentinel’s policy is not to name victims of alleged sexual assault without their explicit consent.
In an affidavit in support of probable cause, Bourque wrote that Fellows was arrested Aug. 10 for gross sexual assault.
Fellows was held at Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset, where he was released Aug. 21 on $10,000 bail. The conditions of his bail state that Fellows can have no indirect or direct contact with the inmate or staff of Kennebec County jail or the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office.
On Tuesday, Chris Read, chief deputy at the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office, confirmed Fellows was fired from his position as a corrections officer at the time of his arrest.
Fellows is set to appear at the Capital Judicial Center in Augusta for his arraignment at 8:30 a.m. Oct. 27, following a dispositional conference. A dispositional conference is a nontestimonial hearing where the involved parties discuss the merits of the evidence, defense and motions with a judge.
HOW TO GET HELP
IF YOU or someone you know has experienced sexual violence, you can call the statewide Sexual Assault Crisis and Support Line at 1-800-871-7741 for free and confidential help 24 hours a day.
TO LEARN more about sexual violence prevention and response in Maine, visit the Maine Coalition Against Sexual Assault website at mecasa.org.

title: Judge weighs what evidence jurors will hear in Maine sisters murder case
text:
SKOWHEGAN, Maine (WABI) - A judge will decide what evidence jurors can hear in the murder trial of a Garland woman accused of killing her sister.
Bonnie Coombs, 69, is charged with intentional or knowing murder in the April 2025 shooting death of her sister, Velma Withee, 78.
Prosecutors and defense attorneys appeared in a Somerset County courtroom Monday for a hearing on pretrial motions over admissible evidence.
Both sides agreed to exclude footage of Coombs’ arrest, calling it irrelevant to the case.
They remain divided on several other key issues, including:
- Prior arguments between Coombs and her sister and theft records
- Cell tower data prosecutors say contradicts Coombs’ account of her whereabouts. Defense attorneys argued the data missed discovery deadlines and requires expert analysis
- Gunshot residue evidence from the vehicle where Withee is believed to have been shot, with both sides seeking to challenge crime lab findings
The judge ordered both sides to submit supporting case law by the end of the week and then will issue a ruling after reviewing those filings.

title: Letter to the Editor: Your health is on the line
Former news anchor sentenced for murdering her mother
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - A Kansas judge sentenced Angelynn Mock on Monday to life in prison without eligibility for parole for 25 years.
Mock, a former television news anchor in St. Louis, was suspected in the Oct. 31, 2025 death of her mother, 80-year-old Anita Avers, in south Wichita.
Mock pleaded guilty in August in the Sedgwick County case in which she was charged with one count of first-degree murder.
According to a probable cause affidavit, Mock’s stepfather told police that the 48-year-old Mock had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder. The diagnosis was later revised to schizoaffective disorder.
In July, a Sedgwick County District Court judge found Mock competent to stand trial and reversed an earlier ruling.
Mock’s guilty plea carries a presumptive sentence of life in prison without eligibility for parole for 25 years.

title: Falmouth rides depth to SMAA golf championship
text:
VASSALBORO — The Falmouth golf team fell one shot short of an SMAA championship last year.
The Navigators were eager to return to the top this season — and one of their newest players ensured they did.
Six Falmouth players broke 80, led by Dante Iannetta at 73 and senior transfer Sawyer Hebert at 75, and the Navigators shot 304 to hold off defending champion Cheverus (313) at the SMAA qualifier at Natanis Golf Course on Monday.
The Navigators and Stags, with Thornton Academy (325), Gorham (336), Deering (337) and South Portland (338), qualified for the Class A tournament Friday at Natanis. The Trojans were led by a 79 from Jacob Litwinetz, Gorham got a 79 from Charlie Sands, Deering had a 75 from Sam Carter and South Portland was led by Lucas Turkewitz’s 79.
Falmouth won the SMAA championship in 2024. The Navigators made it a goal to reclaim it.
“One hundred percent. We’ve got a lot of depth this year,” Iannetta said. “(Monday) showed it. We’ve got to do it one more time.”
On the Arrowhead side, Winthrop, which won the MVC title and automatically qualified for Saturday’s Class C championships last Thursday, nipped Maranacook for the top score at the conference qualifier. The Ramblers shot 331 while the Black Bears, paced by medalist Jack Fontaine’s 74 and Josh Herzing’s 84, were at 332. Madison, led by a 79 from Colton Pelletier, shot 345 to qualify as well.
“It’s very important (to score well), especially with me not playing well as our No. 1, it helps the team’s confidence a lot,” said Drew Mertzel, the 2025 Class C champion whose 83 was Winthrop’s second-best score behind Lincoln MacArthur’s 78, while Parker Dow (84) and Sam Corgan (86) also qualified. “(We know) if someone’s not having a good day, our team’s there to back us up.”
Cheverus, last year’s SMAA and Class A champion, got a 1-under 71 from medalist Sam Sirois and a 74 from Keane McGrath, but was taken down by Falmouth, which was in top form.
“They all got off to good, solid starts,” coach A.J. Simokaitis said. “In years past, whether it’s nerves or whatever it might be, you have one or two guys throw in a big number early in the round. … (This) gave them a little peace of mind, a little cushion.”
Iannetta notched three birdies to post the Navigators’ low score, and Victor Keefer (77), Alex Novick, Griffin Jacobsen and Anthony Graceffa (79 apiece) also shot under 80. The second-lowest score, though, went to Hebert, who led North Yarmouth Academy to the Class C title last year and had three birdies of his own Monday.
“I was just setting myself up, I wasn’t going for anything,” he said. “Falmouth is really competitive golf. … I was No. 7 at the beginning of the year and I needed to work really hard to get up there.”
The Navigators, however, weren’t rejoicing. Two years ago Falmouth won the SMAA qualifier but took fourth at states.
“Be happy with it but go through, find where you lost shots,” Iannetta said. “You can always make improvements.”
Back playing where he tied for second at states last year, Sirois made six birdies, including one on the 13th where he rolled in a bending 25-foot putt and gave a one-handed shrug after it fell.
“Hitting-wise, it wasn’t great, so the putter saved me a lot today,” he said. “(I made) a lot of 5- and 4-footers today, that’s big for me.”
The top score in the MVC event went to Fontaine, who excelled around the green. He birdied the opening hole, had birdies on two of the first three holes on the back, and notched his first eagle when he chipped in on the sixth.
“It was pretty nice,” he said. “I didn’t really believe it at first. And then I (looked) at the hole and there it was.”
In the MVC, individual qualifying spots went to players shooting 84 and under. That included Chris Johnson (78) and Dom Mangold (83) of Kents Hill, Vincent Chapman (80) and Jacob Irish (83) of Dirigo, Patrick Murphy (80) of Monmouth, and Maddox Foster-Grey (84) of Mt. Abram.
In the SMAA, Cheverus also took scores from Joe Stratman (81) and Mike Ray (87), while Thornton got an 80 from Henry Litwinetz, an 83 from Ryan Johnson and an 83 from Blake Goulet. Lukas Taafe shot 83, Payton Wilkins 84 and Andrew Cabral 90 for Gorham. Deering got an 82 from Liam Brunelle, an 89 from Cole Barringer and a 91 from Dominik Anthony, and South Portland got 86s from Jacob Robin and Noah Bates and an 87 from Gavin Schuster.
Qualifying individually were Portland’s Max Schaffer (Portland, 79), Jackson Humphrey (Bonny Eagle, 81), Jacob Willey (Noble, 81), Hunter Pulkkinen (Windham, 81), Caden Tito (Thornton, 81), Josh Albert (Scarborough, 82), Nolan Moore (Noble, 83), Graeme Thompson (Thornton, 83) and Luke Rice (Westbrook, 84).

title: Supreme Court declines to take up Maine lobster boat tracking appeal
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear a Maine lobsterman’s legal challenge to an electronic vessel tracker requirement, putting an end to the multiyear lawsuit.
The court denied a request to take up the appeal by Frank Thompson, a Vinalhaven lobsterman, Maine Morningstar reported.
In a statement, Maine Department of Marine Resources Commissioner Carl Wilson said the department believes the tracking data is critically important to the long-term sustainability of the lobster fishery.
“It will inform the lobster stock assessment, enhance offshore enforcement and support better decision-making in a range of federal management contexts,” Wilson said.
Thompson’s attorney, Matthew Gilliam with Pacific Legal Foundation, said in a statement that the denial does not diminish the importance of the issues in the suit.
“Forcing lobstermen to carry a GPS tracker on their private boats and submit to around-the-clock surveillance as a condition of keeping their license remains a serious constitutional concern,” Gilliam said. “We are committed to fighting for Fourth Amendment protections from government overreach and we will continue to pursue every lawful avenue to protect individual rights.”
At the center of the case is a 2023 requirement that all federally licensed lobster vessels must operate GPS trackers. The rule was passed by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, and implemented by the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
Thompson sued Wilson, the Marine Resources commissioner, in federal court when the rule went into effect in 2024, arguing that the tracking constituted an unreasonable search and seizure and violated his constitutional rights.
But federal judges were not persuaded. The lawsuit was dismissed by the district court, and that ruling was upheld by the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last year. With the Supreme Court declining to intervene, the 1st Circuit ruling is the final order in the suit.
The Conservation Law Foundation previously filed an amicus brief in the case, supporting the regulations and arguing that it is legal and vital to track lobster boats to ensure effective management of the industry.
“New England’s lobster population has declined dangerously,” Conservation Law Foundation Associate Attorney Sarah Shahabi said in a statement. “Tracking lobster boats provides the timely and accurate data that regulators need. This decision is a valuable step toward appropriately managing this iconic species.”
This story was published by Maine Morningstar.

title: Long-term care insurance: What it covers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Long-term care can get expensive fast, and long-term care insurance may help.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down how long-term care insurance works and what it pays for.
What long-term care insurance actually pays for
“Long-term care insurance is an insurance that pays for care,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “And what do I mean by care? Hands-on care. Bathing, dressing, going to the bathroom.”
The first step for anyone considering a policy is understanding the real cost of care, she said.
“The first thing I would suggest is, look at how much care costs. Look at your budget,” O’Rourke said.
When to buy — and why age matters
O’Rourke said there’s a window where buying in makes the most financial sense.
“You ideally would get it between 50 and 70 — 50 years old, 70 years old,” O’Rourke said. “The younger you are, the less you’re going to pay. If you’re a woman, you’re going to pay more than a guy. And the longer you wait, the higher the premium goes up.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said rising rates of chronic illness among younger adults are a factor in making the decision as well.
“Why are people in their 40s, 45, having these health issues?” Rogers said. “The state of health of the country and all of us right now is people are getting sicker at earlier ages, and we know it’s metabolic disease and metabolic disorders ... people are having insulin resistance and that’s affecting a lot of the different diseases that are showing up early. So, a lot of people who have these medical conditions are now under the age of 50. So they have to make a decision, do I pay a little bit more longer to get what I need or do I wait ‘til later and pay more.”
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck agreed that paying in earlier can pay off.
“If you can budget for it earlier and you can get it and you can pay into it longer, your benefit will end up being — there’ll be more in the account,” Cradduck said.
Understanding the elimination period
O’Rourke explained that most policies include a waiting period before benefits kick in.
“You can have an elimination period of 30 days, 60 days, 90 days, no days,” O’Rourke said. “Elimination period is, you have to pay for the care over a period of time to prove that you’re going to need it long term. Then after you’ve proved that you need that care ... you can start the clock and start putting in the claims to get paid for the care that you’re paying for.”
Cradduck said one benefit kicks in once a claim is approved.
“The beauty once you invoke the policy and once you get it started, you don’t have to pay the premium any longer,” Cradduck said.
Hybrid policies and reading the fine print
Cradduck said hybrid long-term care policies are among her preferred options because they offer more flexibility.
“There are hybrid models, and those are the ones that I really like, because if you don’t use it, then it can go into a life insurance,” Cradduck said. “Some of them are use-it-or-lose-it policies.”
Cradduck said no two policies are alike, so find out what you have.
“I’ve billed this stuff for years. I’ve seen all kinds of companies and different policies, and I’ve never seen two that are the same, never. So find out what you have, always,” Cradduck said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose urges planning in advance.
“Planning creates options. If you don’t plan in advance, you’re going to lose options. You’re going to lose having a choice, and maybe lose out on all the money that you’ve paid in,” Ambrose said.
Ambrose recommended policyholders review their paperwork with a professional.
“Pull that policy out right now and get with a local professional that can help explain exactly what you have,” she said.
How benefits are paid out
O’Rourke said policies typically set a maximum lifetime benefit and a daily payout cap.
“You have a maximum lifetime benefit and that might be unlimited. It might be a certain amount — $200,000, $300,000. And then they pay by the day,” O’Rourke said.
Cradduck described two clients with very different outcomes.
“I had one gentleman who truly needed full-time care. His policy would only pay $200 a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year,” Cradduck said. “And then I had a gentleman who was 24/7 care, 168 hours a week. So we’re talking almost $30 grand a month, and for four years, $360,000 a year. Now, the policy didn’t cover every penny, but it covered over $200,000 a year. And he could do that for 10 more years and not maximize out.”
Cradduck said the lesson is about flexibility, not guaranteed coverage.
“What people have to realize is you’re not buying care here. You’re buying the choices for the care that you’re going to need,” she said.
O’Rourke said that decision should start with a budget and a family health history.
“You have to look at, what is your budget. Do you have the money to do it? Do you have enough liquid income to be able to afford it?” O’Rourke said. “If you do have the money to afford it, do you have a family history of long-term chronic diseases — like is there Parkinson’s or Alzheimer’s or something that you’re maybe at a higher risk for needing long-term care?”
Resources
Key takeaways
- Care can be expensive — long-term care insurance may help cover some of the cost.
- Know caps and limits — know your policy, waiting periods and daily caps to understand what you will get.
- Budget for long-term premiums — check your budget to see if it’s something that you can afford and sustain.

title: Mother and son from Bermuda named as passengers on missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
text:
The two people aboard an air ambulance that crashed in the waters off Massachusetts over the weekend while flying from Bermuda to Boston were identified Monday as a mother from Bermuda and her son.
Bermuda police said Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41, both Bermudian nationals, were aboard a Gulfstream G100 with four crew members when it went missing off Nantucket around 1 a.m. Saturday.
Searchers later found a “debris field” off the coast of the island, but with no sign of the six people on board after a 66-hour search that spanned more than 4,400 miles (7,081 kilometers), the U.S. Coast Guard suspended rescue efforts Sunday.
The names of the plane’s crew have not been released, but Latitude Air Ambulance, the Ontario-based company that owned the plane, said Sunday that its staff faces the “heartbreaking reality” that all aboard the plane are now presumed dead.
“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family,” the company said in a statement. “They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred. We are grieving their loss deeply.”
Peter Byl, president of Latitude Air Ambulance, said Monday the company’s immediate focus was on supporting the victims’ families and cooperating fully with authorities.
“We will not speculate about the circumstances or cause of the accident while that work is underway,” he wrote in an email.
The Canadian-registered jet had departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport on a nighttime flight to Massachusetts. Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been “coming in blind” as a storm loomed. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.
It’s not clear if or when the search for the victims will resume. The Coast Guard in Boston didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment.
Bermuda police, in its statement posted on Facebook, said the investigation into the crash is being conducted by the U.S. National Transportation and Safety Board in conjunction with Canada’s Transport Safety Board.
The NTSB said Monday that more information is expected to be released soon as the “appropriate investigative jurisdiction is currently being determined.”

title: Are self-driving cars legal for public use in Maine?
text:
No.
Maine has not enacted legislation allowing for broad use of autonomous vehicles on public roads, though it has established a regulatory framework authorizing their use in approved pilot programs.
Staffing and recruiting firm Elevation Proving Grounds, using data from the National Conference of State Legislatures, reported in July that autonomous driving was fully legal in 21 states.
Another 11 states only allowed testing or limited pilot programs, the firm found, while a few others have imposed explicit safety restrictions.
In 2018, then-Gov. Paul LePage signed an executive order to form an advisory committee on “highly automated vehicles.” The Maine Legislature also passed a resolve to allow their testing, demonstration and deployment. The state has since established rules for pilot program evaluation and approval.
In 2019, Maine lawmakers rejected broader legislation that would have established rules for registering autonomous vehicles, licensing operators and assigning liability; the bill died in committee.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: Weakened fuel efficiency goals will cause lasting damage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Trump administration recently lowered goals for fuel efficiency in many gas-powered vehicles. The previous goal, set by the Biden administration, was for 50.4 miles per gallon in 2031. This change brings that down to 30.1 mpg. This reduction will increase emissions and accelerate climate change when we need to slow it down.
There’s another aspect of this, which is that continued reliance on fossil fuels puts us all at risk. As we’ve seen in the war with Iran, relying on fossil fuel shipments from other countries leaves us economically vulnerable.
Those of us in Maine, as well as elsewhere, are already feeling this. A recent news report (“Rising gas prices eating into profits of Mainers who drive their cars for a living,” Sept. 28) pointed out how those who drive as part of their jobs — such as with Lyft, Uber, and DoorDash — are having to make changes to their jobs now that they spend so much on gas. That will also impact their customers.
I know how much of a difference it makes to get 50 mpg, since that’s about what I get with my hybrid. Yes, I still need to buy gas, but the rising prices have had much less of an impact on me. Not everyone can afford a hybrid, but if the previous fuel standards were kept, even those without a hybrid would benefit.
As it is, this change is short-sighted, environmentally harmful, and will have lasting negative impacts on all of us. I encourage everyone to keep this in mind when voting this November.
Erica Bartlett
Portland

title: How hazard trees stand in the way of wildfire cleanup
text:
ROWENA Ore. (InvestigateTV) - In the blink of an eye lives can be upended by a natural disaster, and recovering from one can last long after the danger is gone.
Many residents remain unable to rebuild. The fire tore through the community on June 11, leaving behind not just loss, but a new and unexpected barrier to recovery.
What didn’t burn is now what’s holding people back.
Charred trees, weakened and unstable, still stand across properties throughout the community. Known as hazard trees, they are dangerous enough to halt any rebuilding efforts. Until they are removed, construction cannot begin.
For many residents, the obstacle is not a lack of will or resources to rebuild, but the remnants of the fire itself.
Clearing the first path forward
On property after property, volunteers are stepping in to help.
Teams from Team Rubicon, a veteran-led disaster response organization, are working to remove trees and clear debris at no cost to homeowners. It is the kind of work that must happen before anything else can.
“What they’re doing is they’re actually giving us hope,” said Shane Wolfe, who helped start a nonprofit supporting the Rowena community after his father lost his home in the fire.
That hope comes in a place still grappling with trauma.
“We’re still in trauma,” Wolfe said. “Our entire lives changed, everything changed for people living here. And then also all of their families, overnight, and we’re just still in the recovery, the disaster.”
Just down the road, Wylesha Wilcox walks through what remains of her property, still taking in the scale of what was lost.
“We used to have a triplex here. So we had a mixture of like cabins and manufactured homes here. And then as you keep going, we lost 10 properties,” Wilcox said.
She plans to rebuild, but for now, the trees remain in the way.
“Until these come down, we can’t start anything,” Wilcox said.
The danger left behind
Fire-damaged trees can appear intact but are often structurally compromised, capable of falling without warning. Removing them requires skill, equipment, and money that many property owners simply do not have.
That is where volunteers step in.
Krystal Samsel, a Navy veteran and teacher, drove six hours from Washington to spend her spring break helping in Rowena.
“I live by the motto of whatever’s needed,” Samsel said. “It is great to see humanity and in the worst times humanity comes together and it’s so good. It’s so good to be part of that.”
Leading the effort on the ground is Joe Goodenough, a saw boss responsible for training and coordinating volunteer sawyers. Like many in the group, he traveled a long distance to be there. He lives in Alaska, where he drives trucks on ice roads and fights forest fires.
But Rowena is not just another deployment.
“I grew up here. I was born in The Dalles. Rowena, specifically where we’re sitting. My grandfather had a house. He lived in this neighborhood that we’re sitting in for about 45 years,” Goodenough said.
Among the trees he has helped remove was an old maple with branches that he used to swing from as a kid.
“It’s awful to come back under these circumstances. But it’s neat to be able to be a part of that whole building process. Because I know these people and they know me,” he said.
A mission that hits close to home
Goodenough has spent about a decade deploying with Team Rubicon to disaster zones across the country. The work has shown him the full scope of what fire can erase.
“Every single thing that a human being put on that site is lost,” he said. “It would be easier to rebuild on a piece of dirt out in the forest than it would at a site where a home once stood.”
But in Rowena, the work carries a different weight.
“I’ve been doing this a long time with TR and it’s always somebody else’s world, right? It’s always, you know, we’re the folks coming in to instill hope. But like, we’re instilling hope for me,” he said. “These guys are bringing my family peace, directly, you know. It’s freakin’ incredible thing to be a part of that.”
Recovery, one tree at a time
As volunteers continue their work, the community is slowly finding its footing. Progress comes incrementally, measured not in rebuilt homes yet, but in cleared lots and safer ground.
At the same time, another fire season looms.
With record low snowpack in the mountains, anxiety is building even as recovery continues. Residents are trying to prepare for what may come next while still processing what happened last summer.
For now, the work continues, one tree at a time, each one bringing the possibility of rebuilding a little closer.
