title: Washington Capitals captain Alex Ovechkin says his 22nd NHL season will be his last
text:
Washington Capitals captain Alex Ovechkin says his 22nd NHL season will be his last
Alex Ovechkin said Monday that his 22nd season in the NHL will be his last, beginning the farewell tour for the longtime Washington Capitals captain who holds the league's career goal-scoring record.
Ovechkin addressed teammates to deliver the news before the team posted a message from him on social media.
"It's sad, but it is what it is," Ovechkin said in his locker room address. "It's hard, but let's enjoy it and let's do some special things this year."
Ovechkin signed a one-year contract this past summer and turned 41 on Sept. 17. All signs pointed to this being the end, and he said he and his family decided as much in recent months.
"I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it's the right decision," the Russian star said in a statement released before the Capitals' home opener Wednesday night.
Ovechkin broke Wayne Gretzky's goals record in April 2025 and entered this season at 929. The front office acquired Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch in trades and signed fellow forward Boone Jenner and defenseman Vincent Desharnais in free agency to add around a young core in the hopes of making another long playoff run and contending for the Stanley Cup.
"Let's make the playoffs, let's have fun and enjoy the moment because times fly," Ovechkin told the team. "For young guys who are first year or experienced guys, I remember that moment, and enjoy the time. Because times fly. It seems like yesterday I was here my first year."
Speaking to reporters later Monday, Ovechkin said this was the right time to announce his decision, two days before the home opener.
"I'm not 20 years old," he said. "I want to play with my kids when they're growing up. Play hockey, play soccer, play basketball. I want to be healthy enough to do that kind of stuff."
Ovechkin has spent his entire career with Washington, winning the Calder Trophy as rookie of the year in 2005-06, the Hart Trophy as MVP three times and leading the NHL in scoring nine times. He was playoff MVP in 2018 when he led the Caps to the first Stanley Cup championship in franchise history.
There's been speculation Ovechkin could receive an unfriendly reception on the road after he appeared in an ad for a party aligned with Vladimir Putin during the offseason. But there wasn't much sign of that during the first two games of the season — at Carolina and at Tampa Bay.
When addressing the fallout from that last month, Ovechkin confirmed he'd be going back to live in Russia when he retired from the NHL.
In Washington's season-opening win over the Hurricanes, Ovechkin had 12 minutes, 46 seconds of ice time, the lowest of his career in a game when he wasn't injured or ejected.
Monday was 21 years to the day after Ovechkin made his debut with the Capitals.
"It's been pretty good career, pretty good 22 seasons," he said. "Obviously the goal that we have, to bring a Stanley Cup to D.C., we did it."
Although the Capitals have designs on making the playoffs this season, within a couple hours of Ovechkin's announcement, tickets for Washington's regular-season home finale against Pittsburgh on April 4 were going for a minimum of $825 on StubHub. With D.C. hosting college hockey's Frozen Four next year, the Capitals finish the regular season with three straight road games, wrapping up April 10 at Philadelphia.
The Capitals missed the playoffs in 2025-26, but Ovechkin played all 82 games and scored 32 goals. He's reached 30 in every season of his career except 2020-21, when he played only 45 games.
Long before he broke through during the Capitals' Stanley Cup run, Ovechkin had rejuvenated hockey in Washington, and he'll retire as one of the city's most accomplished athletes in any sport. The Capitals drafted him No. 1 overall in 2004, and he and Pittsburgh's Sidney Crosby became stars almost immediately in 2005 when the league emerged from missing a season because of a lockout.
"Before we even met, we were kind of built up against each other: It's kind of a natural thing to happen," Crosby said. "Over the years developed a friendship with him. Have a ton of respect for him, and you play against someone that long, you're compared and see each other enough I think that's something that builds over time."
Ovechkin's combination of goal-scoring skill, physicality and boundless energy made him an instant hit, and he scored a career-high 65 goals in his third season, which earned him the first of his MVP honors.
"He's done everything," said Penguins center Evgeni Malkin, a fellow countryman who was picked second after Ovechkin in the 2004 draft. "He do everything for team, for league. I hope he plays good this year, no injury, he just stay healthy, score goals and enjoy the game."
Washington's penchant for postseason heartache, which existed long before Ovechkin showed up, followed him for a while as well. The Capitals won the Presidents' Trophy three times with the league's best regular-season record, falling short in the playoffs each time before a Washington team that merely won its division finally went all the way in the playoffs.
In four postseason meetings between Crosby and Ovechkin — in 2009, 2016, 2017, 2018 — the winner won the Stanley Cup each time. Washington's home opener Wednesday is against Pittsburgh.
"Definitely have had some great battles over the years," Crosby said. "Obviously when you get to our age, that's something that you have to make decisions on and for him, as long as he's happy and enjoying it, that's the biggest thing."
___
Whyno reported from New York.
___
AP freelance writer Sammi Silber in Arlington, Virginia, and AP Sports Writer Will Graves in Pittsburgh contributed to this report.

title: Greenville man shot a 196-pound deer on opening day of Maine archery hunt
text:
Greenville resident Jim Plourde had never seen the 196-pound deer that walked into his shooting lane on opening morning of Maine’s regular archery season.
He shot the 9-point with a crossbow around 7:45 a.m. Saturday from a treestand in Wildlife Management District 9.
The buck came through a thicket but turned around just before reaching the shooting lane. It stood behind the trees for nearly 10 minutes before turning back and stepping into the opening.
When it entered the lane, Plourde stopped it with a bleat call and took the shot from about 30 yards away.
Because the deer didn’t have an exit wound, tracking was difficult, he said. When he found it about an hour later, he was surprised by its size and rack.
Although he has two trail cameras in the area, neither had captured a picture of the buck.
The successful hunt marked the second consecutive year when Plourde has taken a buck with a crossbow. Last year, he shot a six-pointer.
Hunters can take one antlered deer per year with their big game license. A second antlered deer can only be taken in designated expanded archery areas.

title: Ex-pastor, 'American Idol' contestant Caleb Flynn sentenced for wife's murder
text:
Ex-pastor, 'American Idol' contestant Caleb Flynn sentenced to life in prison for wife's murder
Caleb Flynn, the former pastor and "American Idol" contestant convicted of murdering his wife, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole Monday.
The judge called Flynn's actions "impossible to fathom," saying he poses "extreme risk of harm to the public — in fact, the highest risk."
Video above: Caleb Flynn sentenced to life in prison
He was found guilty last week of shooting and killing his wife, Ashley, in their Ohio home, then staging the scene to look like a break-in.
"Your actions were abhorrent," the judge said while handing down sentencing. "You could've walked away, you could've separated from her and let her walk on this Earth."
"You shattered their sense of security, you shattered their innocence. You took something from them they will never get back, their mother," the judge continued, speaking about Flynn's two daughters.
Prosecutors said Flynn staged a home invasion in February and claimed a burglar killed his wife, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old schoolteacher and volleyball coach. In his 2013 appearance on “American Idol,” Flynn credited his wife with encouraging him to chase his dreams on the singing contest. He did not advance to the main competition in Hollywood.
With tears rolling down his cheeks, Flynn apologized to his family just before being sentenced, starting with his two young daughters, who were home when he shot his wife in her sleep. He called their births the “greatest joy in this life.”
Although he said he accepted responsibility for his words and decisions, Flynn remained adamant that he was innocent.
“As I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife,” he said.
Ashley's family and daughters also provided statements that were read aloud in court.
"We trusted you, we believed in you, we honestly would've laid down our lives for you. And because of that, one of my greatest fears was that people will look at you and what you have done and begin questioning whether any of this, Christianity, faith, Jesus was real," Ashley's sister, Kayla Keyt, said.
"Caleb's decision created permanent loss that has created permanent consequences," Ashley's brother-in-law, Matt Keyt, said in his statement, asking for the maximum sentence for Caleb.
Ashley's mother Jill and Matt Keyt also read statements from Caleb Flynn's daughters as he broke down in tears.
"I don't even know where to start. How could you do such a thing? I looked up to you, I loved you with all my heart, and then you lied to everyone. Mommy was the person perfect, the absolute perfect person. What did she ever do to make you hate her so much?" Matt Keyt read from one of the daughter's statements. "You chose to kill the only mother I ever had."
"You had the best life ever, and you decided to throw it away forever for a girl who was half your age," Ashley Flynn's mother shared in a statement from one of his daughters.
The daughter's statement ended saying she does not plan to come visit Caleb Flynn.
Video below: Letters from Caleb Flynn's children read during sentencing
During closing arguments, prosecutors told jurors that Flynn wanted out of his marriage when he shot his wife at their house in Tipp City, a suburb north of Dayton. He sent a text message to his lover the night before the shooting, saying, “I choose you. I’m free. Actions will come tomorrow,” prosecutors said.
During the trial, Alleigha Botner testified she met Flynn in 2022 while she was a 20-year-old intern at his church and had an affair with him for more than a year. She told jurors that Flynn said he hated his wife and had thoughts of killing her.
The gun used to kill Ashley Flynn was not found at the scene, and his attorney told jurors that investigators found no evidence that Caleb Flynn fired a gun that day. Prosecutors said his fingerprints and DNA were at the scene and that his devices showed him moving around the house, even though he claimed he was asleep at the time of the shooting.
The jury deliberated for less than three hours before delivering the guilty verdict last Tuesday.
Flynn was found guilty on all charges and gun specifications: aggravated murder, three counts of murder, two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence.
Video below: Ashley Flynn's parents speak at sentencing of Caleb Flynn
The Associated Press' Julie Carr Smith and Patrick Aftoora-Orsagos contributed.

title: Why Hannah Pingree has my vote
text:
I am in full support of Hannah Pingree for governor of Maine. I’ve known and admired Hannah for many years; I believe that she has the right combination of principled leadership skills, compassion, creativity and energy to enable our great state to realize its full potential over the next four and, hopefully, eight years.
As someone whose career included managing two Maine cities over a span of 30 years (first Calais and then 23 years in Augusta), I very much appreciate Hannah’s contributions as a legislator (including her time as speaker of the House) and more recently her leadership role in the Mills administration.
Her work championing, establishing and then leading the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future coordinated state agency efforts and important resources for Maine’s nearly 500 municipalities and 16 counties — something the prior administration had shortsightedly done away with when it abolished the State Planning Office.
Hannah is a native Mainer who’s done an admirable job of balancing the roles of spouse, mother, community leader and prominent public official. She’s warm, genuine and wicked smart. I hope folks will join me in voting for her on Nov. 3.
Rep. Bill Bridgeo
Augusta

title: Simple settings changes that could protect you from AI hackers
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Artificial intelligence is making it easier than ever for criminals to hack into personal devices, according to Kara Sprague, CEO of cybersecurity firm HackerOne, which works with some of the world’s biggest companies to find security flaws before hackers do.
Sprague said the shift is driven by how much software is now part of daily life. That software carries more vulnerabilities than ever, and hackers are increasingly relying on sophisticated AI systems to carry out attacks.
Sprague said one of the simplest ways to protect personal information is being cautious about what gets typed into an AI chatbot.
“What you end up typing into an AI chatbot doesn’t simply disappear when you’re done using it,” Sprague said. “And so you need to think about these chatbots almost like strangers that you might encounter on the street. You wouldn’t hand them your street, your home address, or your phone number or your bank details. So don’t hand those things to these models either.”
Sprague said a useful rule of thumb is to avoid typing anything into a chatbot that wouldn’t be said out loud to a stranger.
Sprague also recommends reviewing privacy settings within AI tools.
“You can go into the privacy settings of whichever AI tool you are using and turn off the model training and memory retention,” Sprague said. “Most people don’t realize that their conversations might be used to improve the model for the next person, and that might also sound fine until you consider what you’ve been typing into these models.”
Sprague said users should always verify and critically evaluate information AI tools provide. She also noted that ethical hackers work to test software systems for vulnerabilities, aiming to fix weaknesses before bad actors can exploit them.

title: Online safety warnings shouldn’t scare older Mainers offline
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Jessica Perez is senior manager of digital opportunity at Maine Connectivity Authority, the quasi-governmental agency leading efforts to expand affordable, reliable internet access across Maine. Noël Bonam is state director of AARP Maine, which represents nearly 200,000 members 50 and older statewide.
“There is no electrician or milkman for the internet. There’s no one to help. You have to figure it out on your own or get help from your kids.” That is what an older woman told us this summer at the grand opening of the Encompass Education and Nutrition Center, SeniorsPlus’ new connectivity hub in Lewiston. She was talking about technology, but she put her finger on a much bigger problem.
We have spent years warning people about the dangers of being online. Watch out for scams. Do not click suspicious links. Protect your passwords. Be skeptical of what you see. Now, with artificial intelligence making it harder to distinguish what is real from what is not, those warnings have become even more urgent.
The warnings are justified. But at SeniorsPlus, we heard about an unintended consequence: some older Mainers are afraid of the internet at precisely the moment when they increasingly need it.
Healthcare is online. Job applications are online. Government services, banking, education and communication with family increasingly require digital participation. For people who did not grow up using the internet, opting out is becoming less realistic.
And yet, when something goes wrong, there often is no obvious — let alone trusted — person to call. People may not understand a medical portal, suspect an online scam, struggle to make their laptop work or simply not know how to accomplish something online. Too often, the answer is to figure it out themselves — or call their kids.
Maine has made enormous strides in expanding access to fast, reliable internet. More than 120,000 homes and businesses that once lacked reliable service are now connected, and tens of thousands more soon will be. But access is only the beginning. The real measure of these investments is whether they help Maine people live, learn, work and participate in their communities.
Maine’s next connectivity challenge is making sure the warnings meant to keep people safe online do not unintentionally deepen the very digital divide we have worked so hard to close.
AARP’s own survey shows that 1 in 5 Americans age 65 and older lacks confidence in
identifying online scams and fraud, and nearly a third report not having the skills to fully
participate online. But more than 70% say they would participate in technology
programs designed for them.
We cannot simply tell people to be more careful online — or hand them a device, connect their home and wish them luck. People need trusted, local places where they can ask questions, build skills and get help without feeling embarrassed or overwhelmed. That is exactly what the new connectivity hub at SeniorsPlus is designed to provide. With grant support from the Maine Connectivity Authority, people can use public computers, get one-on-one technology help, take computer skills classes and learn how to stay safe online.
Most importantly, it offers what the woman we met there said was missing: somewhere to turn when you cannot figure it out on your own.
Maine needs more places like SeniorsPlus: places where people of all ages can walk through the door, find someone they trust and ask for help. The good news is that Maine already has the infrastructure that matters most: trusted people in trusted places.
They are in our libraries, community centers, schools, municipal and tribal buildings, YWCAs and other local organizations — places where people already gather, learn, ask questions and look out for one another. Connectivity hubs build on that strength by bringing internet access, devices, digital skills and technical support into institutions that already anchor our communities.
As Maine enters its next chapter of connectivity, we should invest not only in the infrastructure that connects communities, but in the people and places that make those connections useful. The goal was never simply to build a network. It is to make sure Maine people can use connectivity safely and confidently to live, learn, work and participate.
We have spent years connecting Maine. The work ahead is making sure Maine people feel able to connect.

title: Timeline of Maine's Senate race: How we arrived at Collins vs. Jackson
text:
Timeline of Maine's Senate race: A look at how we arrived at Collins vs. Jackson
The U.S. Senate race in Maine is one of the most watched in the country and has taken a number of twists and turns ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, is looking to secure her sixth term in the Senate, something no senator from Maine has done before.
She faces a challenge from former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, a Democrat who has only been in the U.S. Senate race for just over two months.
Graham Platner, an oyster farmer from Sullivan, won the June 9 Democratic primary despite dealing with several controversies throughout his campaign. But less than a month later, Platner dropped out of the Senate race following allegations of sexual assault.
The Maine Democratic Party then scrambled to find a new candidate before a July 27 deadline. Jackson, who started the 2026 election cycle as a gubernatorial candidate, was chosen as the Democratic Senate nominee at a special nominating convention held July 25.
Maine's Senate race also saw outgoing Gov. Janet Mills suspend her campaign after six months in the running, and another Democratic candidate switch to an entirely different race.
Maine's Total Coverage created a timeline of events surrounding major candidates in the U.S. Senate race.

title: Why this law could leave adult children paying parents’ medical debt
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Would you ever pay a bill that wasn’t yours? Depending on which state you live in, you could be forced to pay for your parents’ debts.
It’s called filial responsibility, and you could be legally liable for unpaid bills. The laws vary state to state and historically are rarely enforced, but legal experts are concerned that could change.
Sarah Daro had no contact with her father for nearly two decades because of his addiction to drugs. When he died a few years ago, she received a call from a cremation business informing her that she was responsible for his burial.
“They said it was our responsibility to bury him. And that if we had the means, we had to pay for the burial,” Daro said.
She was told that if she refused to pay, she could face jail time or a fine. Daro, who was 28 and pregnant at the time, opted to pay the $3,000 fee.
What is filial responsibility
California, where Daro’s father died, has a filial responsibility law. The law makes adult children responsible for the care and support of their parents if the parents cannot care for themselves.
Nearly half of U.S. states have a version of the law. In Indiana, South Dakota and Louisiana, an adult child could have to pay for a parent’s food, shelter and medication. Seven states, including Kentucky, Massachusetts and Virginia, threaten jail or prison time if an adult child doesn’t pay.
Almost all of the states with the law could require financially stable adult children to support an indigent parent medically, which could include nursing home care and hospital bills.
Carla Sigler is an estate planning attorney in Louisiana, which has filial responsibility.
“Most people today are floored when they find out that they as adult children still have a responsibility to honor, respect and even provide for their parents,” Sigler said.
Sigler said the laws date back more than 100 years, to a time before Medicaid existed.
“Before you had Medicaid, you had state governments that were going broke trying to take care of these needy, aging people,” she said. “So these laws were originally enacted so nobody had to be a burden to the state budget, basically.”
Sigler said the need for filial responsibility dropped once Medicaid, Medicare and Social Security were in place, but many states kept the laws on the books.
Medicaid cuts raise concern
Attorneys say the laws have rarely been enforced for decades, but Sigler said that could change because of Medicaid cuts.
The federal government is set to cut $1 trillion from Medicaid spending by 2034 as part of the Big Beautiful Bill. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office projects millions of people will lose coverage.
If a parent is on Medicaid while in a facility, Sigler warns that adult children will need to worry about filial responsibility laws.
“It’s the gap periods people need to worry about. Before I get the Medicaid coverage, and what if it stops,” Sigler said. “When there’s no coverage, who’s gonna pay? If it’s not Medicaid, it could be you.”
Eric Carlson, with the group Justice in Aging, said the number of filial responsibility cases nationwide is currently in the “low double digits” per year. Carlson said there is no way of knowing how often the law is used to recoup money, and he suspects cases are more common than they appear because most don’t go to trial or become public.
When adult children are pursued for unpaid medical bills, Carlson said the amount could cost thousands of dollars.
A North Dakota man had to pay over $100,000 after a court ruling. And in Pennsylvania, one man paid $93,000 while another woman was sued for $300,000 — all for their parents’ unpaid nursing home bills.
Efforts to repeal the law
Pennsylvania is known for enforcing filial responsibility. State Rep. Tarik Khan (D-Philadelphia) has worked on legislation to repeal it.
Khan thinks it’s wrong for adult children to pay a debt that isn’t theirs. Pennsylvania lawmakers have made at least six other attempts to repeal or reform filial responsibility. All of them failed.
“You know corporations hate being told what to do,” Khan said. “And then you are leaving fewer options for these hospitals and nursing homes to get what they need. Now, I think we all agree in Pennsylvania that should not mean that they should be able to go after families and sue families and sick collection agencies on families.”
Idaho, Montana, Utah and Iowa have repealed filial responsibility laws, but Sigler said that’s not the norm.
“The reason you haven’t seen them repealed is because there’s lobbyists on the other side that are saying, don’t repeal that,” she said. “If you cut Medicaid, how am I gonna pay for this facility? Where’s my source of funding? They want those laws to stay on the books.”
The American Health Care Association and National Center for Assisted Living, advocacy groups for skilled nursing and assisted living facilities, said they could not comment because it is a “state-by-state issue.”
What to do if you’re contacted
Daro lives in Nevada, another filial responsibility state. She feels ready to handle the issue if it comes up again.
“I think it’s so scary because most people don’t know,” Daro said, describing her reaction to learning about filial responsibility laws. “This happened to me, it could happen to anybody.”
Those interviewed agreed nursing homes and hospitals should get paid for their services, but they said the burden should not fall to a patient’s child.
Sigler recommends contacting an attorney immediately if you receive a demand for payment of a parent’s bill. The Pennsylvania woman sued for $300,000 ended up not having to pay after her attorneys proved she didn’t have the means to do so.
If you don’t live in a filial responsibility state but your parents do, and you are sued for their bills, Sigler said to get a lawyer immediately. You may not be subject to another state’s laws, but legal guidance can help navigate the issue.
If you live in a filial responsibility state and want the law repealed, you can contact your state legislators.

title: Sterility concerns lead FDA to recall thousands of eye drop products
text:
Sterility concerns lead FDA to recall thousands of eye drop products
More than 500,000 eye drop products have been recalled from store brands including Walgreens due to a "lack of assurance of sterility."
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said Sterling Pharmaceutical Services LLC initiated the recall for the eye drops, which were sold under several brand names, including Walgreens, on Aug. 20.
According to the FDA, the Class II recall covers nine products and nearly 750,000 units.
Walgreens is said to account for a significant portion of the recalled products.
According to the FDA's website, a Class II recall is a "situation in which use of or exposure to a violative product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote."
More than 300,000 bottles of Walgreens Lubricant Eye Drops (0.5 fluid ounces) and 199,600 packs of the twin pack of the product sold and distributed by Walgreens have been recalled.
Also part of the recall are more than 12,800 packs of AvKare Carboxymethylcellulose Sodium Ophthalmic Solution 0.5%, Lubricant Eye Drops (0.5 fluid ounces); 107,377 packs of the two-count twin packs distributed by AvKare; 19,284 bottles of Cameron Pharmaceuticals’ Carboxymethylcellulose Sodium 0.5% Lubricant Eye Drops (0.5 fluid ounces); and 14,538 bottles of TRP The Relief Products Gentle Eyes Lubricant Eye Drops, Carboxymethylcellulose sodium 0.5%, and 34,368 tubes of Major LubriFresh P.M. Nighttime Ointment (0.125 ounces).
To see all recalled products, you can visit the FDA's website.
More than 39,000 bottles of Clear Eyes Maximum Itchy Eye Relief were recalled in August, with 2.5 million bottles of Lupin Pharmaceuticals prescription eye drops recalled the month prior due to contamination concerns.
Consumers with the affected products should immediately stop using them and speak with their doctors, the FDA says.

title: Russian plague researcher dies of ‘unknown’ infection after suspected lab accident
text:
(CNN) - Authorities in Russia are investigating after a woman who worked at a plague research institute died following a suspected laboratory accident.
A 28-year-old woman has died after a suspected lab accident at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, Russian authorities say. She was diagnosed with pneumonia of “unknown” origin before her death.
Authorities are now investigating whether a dangerous infection, such as pneumonic plague, may have been released. They say the situation is stable at this time.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is monitoring the incident.
“We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” a U.S. State Department spokesperson told CNN. “Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”
What is pneumonic plague?
Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It is the only type of the disease that can be spread from person to person through infectious droplets coughed out by an affected patient, according to the CDC.
Symptoms of pneumonic plague include fever, headache, weakness and rapidly developing pneumonia.
The CDC says that while the plague is a potentially life-threatening disease, it is treatable with antibiotics.

title: Corrections Officer charged with sexual assault against an inmate
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - A Kennebec County Corrections Officer has been indicted by a grand jury for sexual assault after investigators say they uncovered an intimate relationship between him and an inmate.
Nicholas Fellows, 37, of Augusta was indicted for gross sexual assault and unlawful sexual contact.
According to court documents obtained by WABI, staff members at the Kennebec County Jail contacted investigators in July after discovering the relationship.
An inmate who witnessed the relationship told authorities they saw the female inmate writing explicit notes detailing their relationship and said the inmate had detailed how Fellows was able to get her into a room without cameras to perform sex acts.
Court records say video evidence from the jail showed the pair entering a room without recording devices as was reported, and Fellows and the inmate later admitted to the relationship.
Any sexual contact between a corrections officer and an incarcerated person under their authority is a crime under state law.
Kennebec County Sheriff Ken Mason told WABI that Fellows has been removed from his position.
“A report of an alleged violation of our S.O.P. and Maine State law by Officer Nicholas Fellows came to the attention of my command staff who brought it to my attention post haste,” Mason said. “Mr. Fellows was placed on administrative leave immediately and criminal investigation was conducted by my Detective Division. After our investigation, we had probable cause for an arrest and Mr. Fellows was arrested for the offense and terminated from employment with Kennebec County.”
Fellows was released from Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset on $10,000 bail in August.

title: Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at 84
text:
Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at 84
Dennis Hastert, the nation’s longest-serving Republican House speaker, who helped turn much of President George W. Bush’s agenda into law before his own political legacy was forever fouled by allegations that he molested high school athletes when he was a wrestling coach, died over the weekend, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.
Video above: Former Asst. US Attorney Reacts to Hastert Case in 2016
Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007, died of natural causes at his home, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.
When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.
In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP’s poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted Bill Clinton’s impeachment trial.
After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert took much of what Bush proposed and steered it to passage, including massive tax cuts and a measure that amounted to a huge expansion of prescription drug benefits — the biggest change in Medicare in decades.
His legacy was suddenly thrown into doubt in 2015, when he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors filed papers that described what media reports had suggested for months: Hastert’s misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in the small town of Yorkville, west of Chicago.
During a 16-year coaching career, he led his team to a state championship and was named national coach of the year in 1976. But behind the accolades, prosecutors said, Hastert sexually abused at least four team members from 1965 to 1981.
The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sex acts on them.
Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.
Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.
At the sentencing hearing where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a “serial child molester.” A former wrestler struggled with his emotions as he told the court about his “dark secret” from adolescence.
In his own statement, Hastert said he was “deeply ashamed” and admitted that he "mistreated” some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.
The public knew nothing about Hastert’s past when Republicans lost seats in the 1998 midterm elections. Hastert confronted Gingrich about dissatisfaction in the GOP ranks, saying it was unlikely Gingrich could hold his post, Hastert wrote in "Speaker: Lessons from 40 Years in Coaching and Politics."
"Well, I'll make them support me," he quoted Gingrich saying of the GOP rebels. Told that was unlikely, Gingrich asked Hastert what to do.
"Do what you have to do," he replied. The next day, Gingrich stepped down as speaker and left the House.
Hastert’s path to the speaker’s office was cleared when Louisiana Rep. Bob Livingston, who was considered a lock to replace Gingrich as speaker, resigned after acknowledging several extramarital affairs.
In January 1999, Hastert broke with tradition by delivering his acceptance speech from the House floor and by allowing Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, a Missouri Democrat, to briefly preside over the day's proceedings.
"Solutions to problems cannot be found in a pool of bitterness," Hastert said in his speech. "They can be found in an environment in which we trust one another's word, where we generate heat and passion, but where we recognize that each member is equally important to our overall mission of improving the life of the American people."
Hastert was aware of the personal pitfalls of holding the powerful position.
"You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. "But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground."
He was generally viewed as a friendly, even-tempered lawmaker. His wrestling experience followed him to Washington, with GOP colleagues often calling him "coach.”
Hastert said he lacked the appetite for higher office.
As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert’s aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.
"I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," he wrote in his book. But he decided that he would not pass the office to the constitutional officer next in line if an Electoral College deadlock extended beyond Inauguration Day. In the end, the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling ended the recount, and Bush moved into the White House.
Hastert’s journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.
In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.
Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986, when local Republican leaders put him on the primary ballot, replacing freshman Rep. John Grotberg, who was battling cancer. Hastert went on to beat the Democrat with 52 percent of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.
In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995. Several years later, DeLay was the force driving Clinton’s impeachment and was simply too toxic to seek the speaker’s chair.
Hastert’s tenure was marked by a shift of power from committee chairmen to GOP leaders, fealty to the Bush administration and an explosion of congressional pet projects known as earmarks. Democrats fumed that he weakened the ethics process that ensnared DeLay, who left Congress under a cloud of criminal charges in 2006.
Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.
He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year. In 2008, he joined the Washington lobbying firm of Dickstein Shapiro as a senior adviser, specializing in government law and strategy.
Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master’s in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.
In 2007, Wheaton named its newly created public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert’s indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.
Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family feed business.
Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.

title: Haunted trails and trunk-or-treats: Western Maine readies for Halloween fun
text:
Western Maine communities are filling the October calendar with harvest celebrations, Halloween parties, trunk-or-treats and other seasonal activities. Here is a guide to some of the events announced so far.
Oct. 10
Haunted Chandler Farm, 31 Chandler Road in Strong, will hold its annual Trunk or Treat from 4 to 5:30 p.m. Oct. 10. Vehicle setup begins at 2 p.m. Organizers are inviting participants to decorate their trunks and are hoping to have 35 vehicles take part in the free event.

title: The New York Times shortchanged Troy Jackson
text:
On Sept. 20, the New York Times ran a profile on Troy Jackson, “A Progressive Brawler Tries to Flip a Senate Seat in Maine.”
Progressive races this cycle have two issues which play large: the treatment of Palestinians and AIPAC attempting to influence races. Despite the primacy of these issues, the Times never mentioned Jackson’s views on the treatment of Palestinians or the millions of dollars from AIPAC and AIPAC-adjacent donors going to Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign.
The article did find room for the 1988 alleged pushing incident between Jackson and his partner. As the Times reported, both Jackson and his partner deny the incident.
The Times’ Israel coverage has drawn criticism, including reported internal guidance for reporters to avoid terms like “genocide” and “occupied territory.” We saw how the Times was dogged in taking down Graham Platner; a pattern.
Maine deserves fair elections free of outside influence. We must remain vigilant as Election Day approaches.
Eric Vos
Rockland

title: What Bangor City Council candidates say they’d do to limit drug use and syringe litter
text:
Public drug use and syringe litter are frequent subjects of complaints at Bangor City Council meetings and on social media, and many voters say they’re key factors in determining who they’ll support in this year’s election.
The Bangor Daily News asked each candidate the following question: We’ve heard from a lot of residents who are concerned about public drug use and syringe litter. What policy changes, if any, would you pursue to address these issues, and what evidence do you have to support them?
Many candidates proposed restrictions on the city’s syringe service programs, which are generally funded by the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention but can be limited or banned within a municipality. Although research shows that these programs reduce HIV spread and do not increase syringe litter, they are often unpopular, and some community members see them as enabling drug addiction.

title: Oversize load arrives in South Portland after weeklong journey from Jay
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A “super oversize” load, as some public safety departments have dubbed it, that has been crawling south across Maine over the past week reached its destination in South Portland on Tuesday morning.
The nearly 220-foot-long and roughly 20-foot-wide load is a heat recovery steam generator that was trucked from the former Androscoggin Mill in Jay over the course of several nights. It weighs more than 683,000 pounds.
The oversize load was originally expected to make it to South Portland within two days of its Sept. 29 departure. However, after night one of its journey, officials said it would take days longer than anticipated.
The convoy spurred road closures and attracted onlookers as it slowly wove its way through portions of Franklin, Androscoggin, Oxford, York and Cumberland counties.
For the last leg of the journey Monday night into Tuesday, the transport truck, escorted by utility crews and law enforcement personnel, was expected to depart Buxton at about 9 p.m. Monday, Maine State Police said in a news release.
The convoy crossed a Maine Turnpike bridge early Tuesday morning, a few hours after crews set up a jumper bridge — essentially steel beams put across the bridge to spread out the weight of the load.
From there, it traveled along U.S. Route 1 in Scarborough to Broadway and Elm Street in South Portland, its final destination in Maine.
At 8 a.m. Tuesday, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Transportation confirmed that the load had arrived in South Portland.
It’s the first of nine oversize loads planned for the route. Maine DOT said last week that the schedule for the eight remaining transports will be released following the completion of the first.
JGT2 Redevelopment purchased the Jay mill site from Pixelle Specialty Solutions in 2023. Tony McDonald, a JGT2 partner, said in an email that the heat recovery steam generator is among a dozen pieces of old mill equipment that the company sold to Packaging Corporation of America.
In addition to two more heat recovery steam generators, the remaining planned transports will carry three gas turbines and three gas turbine-driven electric generators, McDonald said. Some other pieces of equipment have already been removed from the site, he added.
McDonald said his company is not involved in the transport of the equipment, and a spokesperson for Packaging Corporation of America did not respond to a request for further details on Monday.
Headquartered in Illinois, Packaging Corporation of America is one of the largest producers of containerboard in the United States. It operates over 120 facilities across the country, including nine mills and dozens of plants.
This story was updated on Oct. 6 after authorities confirmed that the load had reached its destination.
Staff Writer Morgan Womack contributed to this report.

Fire destroys second-floor bedroom in Dexter home; dog dies
A woman escaped a house fire in Dexter Saturday afternoon that killed a dog and caused smoke damage throughout the residence, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office.
The Dexter Fire Department was dispatched around 2:37 p.m. to a fire at 249 Line Road. Firefighters found the fire in a second-floor bedroom and were able to contain the flames to that room.
The home's only occupant was a 40-year-old woman who managed to escape the fire. She was taken to Northern Light Sebasticook Valley Hospital in Pittsfield for smoke inhalation and other unspecified injuries that officials said were not life-threatening.

Officials say a dog was killed in the fire.
Investigators with the Maine State Fire Marshal determined that the fire started in the second-floor bedroom and was caused by the improper disposal of smoking materials.
Officials ruled the fire as accidental.

title: Law firm warns Ogunquit officials of legal fallout over family’s tin roosters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A national nonprofit claims the town of Ogunquit is violating the First Amendment and risking “costly litigation” by repeatedly fining a family for its giant tin rooster sculptures.
In a letter sent on Monday morning from the Institute of Justice to Town Manager Matthew Buttrick and Code Enforcement Officer Tyler McOsker, Texas attorney Daniel Woislaw demanded that the town stop enforcing the sign code on the roosters and rescind several fines issued to the LeBlanc family.
The dispute started earlier this year when the LeBlancs received a $150 fine and an order to remove dozens of 6-foot-tall rooster statues they had placed in front of their home along Route 1. Since then the family has been fined nearly $2,000 and the issue has become national news.
The LeBlancs say the roosters comfort their 6-year-old daughter, Pyper, who has autism. Town officials say it’s illegal signage for their restaurant The Omelette Factory, which is connected to the family’s home.
Woislaw wrote that Ogunquit officials’ concerns over the roosters stem from a misinterpretation of the colorful statues. He referenced part of the town’s code that states that no business or residential signage can be changed or moved without a permit from the code enforcement officer, and that this framework applies to “any object the town decides communicates something to the public.”
“And that is precisely how the town has treated the LeBlancs’ roosters: not as the whimsical yard sculptures they resemble, but as regulated signage, simply because the town has decided that the roosters say something it doesn’t like,” Woislaw wrote.
Dave LeBlanc told the Portland Press Herald in June that The Omelette Factory does use a rooster as its logo, but that Pyper’s roosters aren’t connected to the restaurant. Both he and Woislaw noted that because roosters don’t lay eggs, the sculptures have nothing to do with the egg-based restaurant.
“It appears that the town considers the LeBlancs’ roosters to be signs because they are roosters, instead of tigers, bears or some other animal,” Woislaw wrote. “And the town has come to associate roosters with the LeBlancs’ business, The Omelette Factory, which prepares and sells eggs (notwithstanding that roosters don’t lay eggs).”
The dispute has prompted several neighbors in Ogunquit to place roosters on their own lawns in solidarity. Woislaw noted that the town officials seem to be bypassing a handful of identical roosters in town, in front of both businesses and private residences.
“A few tin roosters do not implicate traffic safety or any aesthetic interest that countless other unregulated lawn decorations in Ogunquit do not implicate equally, some of which are identical to the LeBlancs’ roosters,” Woislaw wrote.
McOsker and Buttrick did not immediately respond to requests for comment Monday.
Sara LeBlanc, co-owner of The Omelette Factory, said in an email Monday afternoon that the family is working directly with the Institute for Justice.
“Whether it escalates to court depends on the town’s response,” she said.

title: Pennsylvania's measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the US
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials said Monday, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.
The U.S. is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 reported cases, according to the CDC. The nation has seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the past two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Since the beginning of last year, large outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest with 997 cases reported.
Health officials say Pennsylvania’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia. There have been 1,004 cases, including 198 hospitalizations and five deaths, state officials said.
Health experts attribute such outbreaks to low vaccination rates.
It’s been decades since a U.S. state has seen an outbreak surpass 1,000 cases, stretching back to a multiyear outbreak in New York City in the early 1990s that infected more than 4,500 people.
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
Measles is highly contagious. It spreads when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, and through contaminated surfaces. It also can linger in the air for two hours. Up to 9 out of 10 people who are susceptible will get the virus if exposed, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
U.S. measles infections have been surging in recent years, as fewer kids get routine vaccines due to parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation.
Pennsylvania is not the only state with a growing problem. Neighboring Ohio has reported more than 200 cases this year. Like in Pennsylvania, some of the hardest-hit Ohio counties have significant Amish populations, which tend to have lower vaccination rates.
Meanwhile, CDC officials have quietly begun to acknowledge measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.
State officials in August announced that two unvaccinated residents died after being infected with measles.
The announcement quickly came under fire as a clash erupted between vaccine-promoting Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines.
Since then, Pennsylvania has reported three additional deaths.
But for weeks, the CDC — which Kennedy oversees — did not count any deaths on its measles data dashboard, instead saying it was seeking more information. That changed two weeks ago, when one death was finally counted, and again last week when a second was added to the agency’s tally.

title: Flu cases are rising earlier this year — here's what that means
text:
Flu cases are rising earlier this year — here's the best time to get your shot
The sooner you get it, the sooner you are protected.
Flu cases are rising earlier this year — here's the best time to get your shot
The sooner you get it, the sooner you are protected.
If you’ve been debating whether it’s worth it to get a flu shot this year, experts have a resounding answer: yes, ASAP.
Flu season typically runs from October to May, but flu activity is already “rearing its head early,” says Deborah Plate, D.O., a family physician at Cleveland Clinic. While an early uptrend in flu cases is not ideal, the good news is that an annual flu shot helps protect you (and those around you) from a severe case of the flu.
Why you need an annual flu shot
Every year, experts take data from the Southern Hemisphere (where the winter flu season has already hit) to optimize the next annual vaccine, according to Dr. Plate. These updates are why you need to get a flu shot every year.
“Some patients might say, ‘Gee, I got it last year, why do I need it again this year?’ But what we know is that it evolves every year differently. It mutates, and it changes, like a lot of the other viruses that we deal with that are respiratory viruses,” she says.
During last year’s particularly active flu season, the cumulative hospitalization rate for the flu in children 5 to 17 years old was the highest since the 2009–2010 season. However, there is a lot of evidence to show that getting your annual flu shot protects you and others around you from a severe case of the flu, which can lead to hospitalization or death. In fact, getting the shot can lower a person’s chance of a flu-related doctor visit by 40% to 60%.
“In addition to the benefits of minimizing the risk for severe disease in our own children, the flu shot helps protect the community around us, including immunocompromised classmates or children with chronic medical conditions,” says Ashanti Woods, M.D., a Baltimore-based pediatrician.
If you’re over 65, your risk for flu complications rises, so the CDC and ACIP recommend receiving a higher-dose flu vaccine rather than a standard one if you’re over 65. If you’re over 65 and develop flu symptoms, call your doctor right away. You may be eligible for antiviral treatment.
When is the best time to get a flu shot?
With this year’s flu season already in full swing, now is the time to get a vaccine, according to experts. “This vaccine typically takes about two weeks to really settle into our systems to protect us,” Dr. Plate says. “So the sooner, the better this year.”
You can get a flu shot at many convenient locations, including your doctor’s office, pharmacies, health clinics, and some workplaces and schools. The vaccine is free with most health insurance plans, and people without insurance may be able to get a free or low-cost vaccine through community health programs.
The bottom line
Flu shots help protect you and those around you from getting sick with the flu. While they don’t fully shut out your chances of illness, they are highly effective at preventing a severe case that could lead to hospitalization or death. Doctors are already starting to see flu cases, so get your vaccine as soon as possible to help yourself stay healthy this winter.

title: Home affordability gap for first-time buyers widens as costs rise
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Home affordability gap for first-time buyers widens as costs rise
As the rise in home prices outpaces income, many first-time buyers don't earn enough to afford a starter home.
The latest data from the National Association of Realtors showed that the monthly mortgage payment for a typical starter home in the U.S. was $2,158. That would require a first-time buyer to earn an income of at least $103,584, factoring in interest rates and down payment.
But nationally, the median income for first-time buyers is short of that at about $72,100.
A starter home is often described as a smaller home purchased by a first-time buyer with the goal of getting into the market, but defining it with data is more complex.
The National Association of Realtors defines it as homes that are 85% of the median home value. But first-time home buyers are actually only able to afford homes that are about 60% of the median home sale price.
“There is a pretty big gap between what we traditionally call a starter home and what many first-time buyers can actually afford,” Nadia Evangelou, a principal economist and director of real estate research for the National Association of Realtors, said.
The National Association of Realtors calculates a home affordability index for first-time buyers using the 85% data point and income data.
When the index is above 100, it means starter homes are affordable for a family earning the median income. It's been below 100 since around 2021.
The recent trend of low affordability for first-time buyers, isn't because there's a shortage of starter homes, Evangelou said. There's more starter homes today than there were 20 years ago.
The high cost of rent prevents people from saving. Plus interest rates have also risen to 7.28%.
Evangelou also pointed to the age of the typical owner of starter homes, which is 59.
"For many people, their starter home became their long-term home," Evangelou said.
The difficulties reflect consumer sentiment as well. About 9 in 10 young adults say it's more difficult for young people to buy a home than it was for their parents, according to the Pew Research Center.
Affordability at the national level looks a lot different from the local level.
The Get the Facts Data Team analyzed data from the National Association of Realtors on first-time buyer housing affordability by metro area. The data includes an analysis of 177 metropolitan areas in the U.S.
About 80% of the metro areas had affordability scores for first-time buyers below 100, meaning people made a median income less than qualifying income needed to buy a starter home.

title: Online safety warnings shouldn’t scare older Mainers offline
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Jessica Perez is senior manager of digital opportunity at Maine Connectivity Authority, the quasi-governmental agency leading efforts to expand affordable, reliable internet access across Maine. Noël Bonam is state director of AARP Maine, which represents nearly 200,000 members 50 and older statewide.
“There is no electrician or milkman for the internet. There’s no one to help. You have to figure it out on your own or get help from your kids.” That is what an older woman told us this summer at the grand opening of the Encompass Education and Nutrition Center, SeniorsPlus’ new connectivity hub in Lewiston. She was talking about technology, but she put her finger on a much bigger problem.
We have spent years warning people about the dangers of being online. Watch out for scams. Do not click suspicious links. Protect your passwords. Be skeptical of what you see. Now, with artificial intelligence making it harder to distinguish what is real from what is not, those warnings have become even more urgent.
The warnings are justified. But at SeniorsPlus, we heard about an unintended consequence: some older Mainers are afraid of the internet at precisely the moment when they increasingly need it.
Healthcare is online. Job applications are online. Government services, banking, education and communication with family increasingly require digital participation. For people who did not grow up using the internet, opting out is becoming less realistic.
And yet, when something goes wrong, there often is no obvious — let alone trusted — person to call. People may not understand a medical portal, suspect an online scam, struggle to make their laptop work or simply not know how to accomplish something online. Too often, the answer is to figure it out themselves — or call their kids.
Maine has made enormous strides in expanding access to fast, reliable internet. More than 120,000 homes and businesses that once lacked reliable service are now connected, and tens of thousands more soon will be. But access is only the beginning. The real measure of these investments is whether they help Maine people live, learn, work and participate in their communities.
Maine’s next connectivity challenge is making sure the warnings meant to keep people safe online do not unintentionally deepen the very digital divide we have worked so hard to close.
AARP’s own survey shows that 1 in 5 Americans age 65 and older lacks confidence in
identifying online scams and fraud, and nearly a third report not having the skills to fully
participate online. But more than 70% say they would participate in technology
programs designed for them.
We cannot simply tell people to be more careful online — or hand them a device, connect their home and wish them luck. People need trusted, local places where they can ask questions, build skills and get help without feeling embarrassed or overwhelmed. That is exactly what the new connectivity hub at SeniorsPlus is designed to provide. With grant support from the Maine Connectivity Authority, people can use public computers, get one-on-one technology help, take computer skills classes and learn how to stay safe online.
Most importantly, it offers what the woman we met there said was missing: somewhere to turn when you cannot figure it out on your own.
Maine needs more places like SeniorsPlus: places where people of all ages can walk through the door, find someone they trust and ask for help. The good news is that Maine already has the infrastructure that matters most: trusted people in trusted places.
They are in our libraries, community centers, schools, municipal and tribal buildings, YWCAs and other local organizations — places where people already gather, learn, ask questions and look out for one another. Connectivity hubs build on that strength by bringing internet access, devices, digital skills and technical support into institutions that already anchor our communities.
As Maine enters its next chapter of connectivity, we should invest not only in the infrastructure that connects communities, but in the people and places that make those connections useful. The goal was never simply to build a network. It is to make sure Maine people can use connectivity safely and confidently to live, learn, work and participate.
We have spent years connecting Maine. The work ahead is making sure Maine people feel able to connect.

title: The cost of Susan Collins outweighs the benefit
text:
How many federal dollars does it take to offset the rollback of constitutionally guaranteed rights of more than a half century? How many federal dollars is sufficient to offset the cost of previously defeated diseases like polio and measles to return to Maine families?
How about the cost to Mainers of legally dubious tariffs or war? And what about the cost to Mainers who stand to lose their health benefits through Medicaid, or lost food assistance?
Yes, Sen. Collins has brought home some “bacon” to Maine’s seniors, rural hospitals and first responders, but at what cost? Sen. Collins has let Maine down. It’s long past time for “Susie from The County” to return to her status in The County.
Bob Riley
Saco

title: Patriots are back in the race after toppling Bills
text:
The New England Patriots’ early-season triumph at Buffalo last season was part of the 10-game winning streak that helped propel them on a Super Bowl run following a 1-2 start.
New England is hoping Sunday’s 29-26 victory over the Bills can provide a similar spark.
The Patriots are 2-2 on the season after handing their division rivals their first loss in the new Highmark Stadium.
Following a week of questions about quarterback Drake Maye’s struggles, poor offensive execution and a mounting number of injuries, their performance for the moment has brought a sense of confidence back to the defending AFC champions.
“Come on, man! We ain’t dead! We ain’t dead!” defensive tackle Cory Durden shouted as he embraced coach Mike Vrabel on his way to the locker room Sunday.
Vrabel was equally succinct in describing what the win meant for his team.
“Gets us back in the race,” he said.
What might be most encouraging was Maye’s play.
He wasn’t spotless, throwing his seventh interception of the season and losing a fumble. But he was poised with the game on the line, leading the Patriots on an eight-play, 73-yard drive that ended with Efton Chism III’s diving, one-handed, go-ahead catch in the end zone.
It capped a day that saw Maye throw for a season-high 269 yards and three TDs. It ended his two-game drought without a TD pass.
“Everybody understands how the quarterback has to perform in this league for the team to have success,” Vrabel said. “Everybody does have his back, starting with me and everybody all the way down.”
What’s working
Chism is the latest example of the Patriots’ history of finding success with undrafted free agents.
Signed after the 2025 NFL draft, he appeared in just eight games as a rookie, catching each of his three targets for 75 yards, with one touchdown.
He already has played in three of the four games this season, with seven targets and four catches for 41 yards.
What needs help
As excited as the Patriots were to see Chism come up big after Mack Hollins’ injury, there are mounting concerns at wide receiver.
Vrabel acknowledged Monday that Hollins likely would miss a couple of days of practice, putting his availability for Sunday’s game in jeopardy.
That would leave the Patriots down another top receiver, with A.J. Brown still on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain.
Signing another receiver is a possibility.
“Sure, anybody that could help us,” Vrabel said.
Stock up
Romeo Doubs. Following a rough debut in the season-opening loss to Seattle, Doubs is starting to show why the Patriots signed him to a four-year, $70 million deal this offseason. He had his first two touchdown catches of the season and is tied for second on the team with 12 receptions. Doubs’ 203 receiving yards are behind only Hollins (209).
Stock down
Vrabel. With the Bills trailing 14-7 and facing a third-and-goal on the New England 16, he received an unsportsmanlike conduct for arguing a defensive holding penalty on Marcus Jones.
Vrabel said he told the official it was a “terrible effing call.”
The penalty, along with Jones’ initial infraction, put the ball on the 6. The Bills tied the game following a TD run by Josh Allen two plays later.
“I’ve said that 87 times since I’ve been a head coach. It was nothing derogatory. You’d have to ask him. I think he was a little sensitive,” Vrabel said. “I apologized to him. Players responded, it was unfortunate. And I have to be better in those moments.”
Injuries
Cornerback Charles Woods left the game with a shoulder injury but was able to return. … Tight end Eli Raridon and fullback Reggie Gilliam also left the game with ankle injuries.
Key number
29 — In their first three games this season, the Patriots scored only 29 points in 30 drives. They had 29 points in their 12 drives against the Bills.
Next steps
The Patriots host the the Las Vegas Raiders (3-1) on Sunday.

title: Acclaimed Maine author Ron Currie visits Ellsworth Public Library
text:
ELLSWORTH — The Ellsworth Public Library will host award-winning Maine author Ron Currie this Thursday, Oct. 8 at 6 p.m. for a conversation about his latest novel “We Will See You Bleed” (2025) — a book with strong Maine roots.
The novel, the second in Currie’s Waterville trilogy, is currently being adapted for Netflix by “Stranger Things” creators Matt and Ross Duffer.
“We love bringing local audiences into conversation with writers whose work connects our community to bigger national and global conversations — and Ron’s work is a great example of that,” EPL Assistant Director Renee McManus said.
Currie will discuss his writing and the Maine history behind the novel, including the 1987 paper mill strike in Jay, and how those events shaped the story. He also weaves the experiences of the Franco-American community in Maine into his storytelling.
Free and open to the public. Event page: https://ellsworth.libcal.com/calendar/EPL-Events/author-talk-with-ron-currie.
Currie is the award-winning author of five novels. He has won the New York Public Library’s Young Lions Award, the Addison M. Metcalf Award, the Alex Award and the Pushcart Prize. His books have been translated into 15 languages, and his short fiction and nonfiction have received recognition in Best American anthologies. He lives in Portland and teaches in the University of Southern Maine Stonecoast MFA program.

title: Trump tried to make an ally out of fishermen. Some have started to turn on him
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — John Evich, a commercial fisherman in Washington and Alaska, has voted for President Donald Trump three times, viewing him as someone who would fight for his industry.
But these days, Evich is weary of the high cost of doing business at sea, with fuel prices rising and trade hostilities with Canada jeopardizing markets for the crabs that he pulls off the ocean floor.
“If somebody came along that was going to do a better job, I would vote for them in a heartbeat,” he said.
Evich’s sentiment, echoed throughout the U.S. seafood industry, is another piece of a political puzzle that is working against Trump in the midterm elections. Dissatisfaction among commercial fishermen could cause collateral damage for Republicans in competitive races in Washington, Alaska and Maine.
“Having those costs be so much higher this year has really undermined the viability of some of our fisheries,” Alaska fisherman Linda Behnken said.
Trump sought to make an ally out of fishermen during his first term with expanded fishing territory, aggressive trade moves and cutting down regulations on the water. He did so again after his second election.
But one of Trump’s government cutback efforts, cuts to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which regulates fisheries, has left the agency slower to respond to the industry’s needs, fishermen said. Staff cutbacks also resulted in the agency reducing weather balloons used to gather data fishermen rely on.
Fuel costs have also crept up during the war with Iran, pushing diesel fuel into the $6-per-gallon range when it was less than $4 per gallon a year ago — a major burden for a diesel-dependent industry. And the trade war with Canada has complicated the American seafood industry’s relationship with a country it has long been interconnected with, fishermen said.
The Trump administration has continued trying to win the hearts of fishermen with industry-friendly moves, including an early September promise to reduce more regulatory burdens in response to a 2025 executive order. And some of the industry’s key states, such as Alaska, Washington and Maine, are important to Trump politically this year because of competitive House and Senate races. But support on the water could be waning.
“I’m for whatever has to happen for the greater good in the long run for my family and my country,” Evich said.
Trump has cozied up to the fishing industry for years
Trump has positioned himself as a pro-fishing president since his first term, when one of his major moves to impact the fishing industry was the rollback of Obama-era fishing restrictions for Northeast Canyons and Seamounts National Monument off the New England coast. Biden later restored the protections, and then Trump removed them again.
The fishing industry is potentially a natural ally for Trump. A 2026 NOAA survey of commercial fishing crews found that 70% thought fishing rules were too restrictive, and Trump has fashioned himself as an enemy of bureaucracy and red tape.
But in recent months, Trump has brought disruption to the fishing industry in a time when it can ill afford it, said John Sackton, founder of SeafoodNews.com and a longtime industry analyst. He said he sees an industry that is eager to “turn the page” on the Trump administration.
“Now what’s happened is that there has been this unbelievable wave of disruption from everything — targeting NOAA and fisheries, science and even weather reporting that people rely on,” said Sackton, who also cited tariffs and the rising cost of doing business as problems Trump brought to the industry.
Fuel costs and tariffs are huge concerns for fishermen
The high price of fuel is “one of the most immediate pressures on us as commercial fishermen,” said Bonnie Brady, executive director of the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association in New York.
Nearly all of the U.S.’s commercial fishing fleet uses marine diesel fuel, which makes soaring fuel costs a burden they can’t avoid. Fuel prices are so high right now that fishermen sometimes can’t afford to leave the dock at all, she said.
“Actual dockside marine-fuel prices vary, but the magnitude of the increase is undeniable. It determines whether a trip is economically viable, what the crew earns and whether necessary vessel maintenance can be performed,” Brady said.
In Rhode Island, fisherman Chris Brown, who targets species such as fluke and squid out of Point Judith, puts it more bluntly.
“It’s huge. It’s crazy. Thank you, Donald Trump,” he said sarcastically.
Trump’s trade war with Canada is a more complicated matter because Canada exempted U.S. fish and seafood products from its counter-tariffs that followed the U.S. placing tariffs on Canadian goods. Prior to the exemption, Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, said U.S. lobstermen risked becoming “collateral damage in a broader trade dispute.”
But unease among fishermen remains, in part because Canada is the U.S.’s largest seafood trading partner. The U.S. also relies on Canada for seafood processing and manufacturing of fishing gear. For some species, such as lobster and salmon, American and Canadian fishermen fish very close to each other or even in the same waters.
A trade war with such a key partner could have negative consequences for the fishing industry, said Steve Train, a lobster fisherman from Long Island, Maine, who described himself as a “right-leaning centrist” who has voted Republican more than Democrat.
“I get the standing up to a bully concept, but too many people will be caught in the middle of this,” Train said. “Both sides need to reconsider these tariffs, and they need to reconsider soon.”
Cuts to NOAA are troubling to fishermen
NOAA Fisheries, the arm of NOAA tasked with overseeing commercial fishing, is facing a budget cut of more than 40% in the fiscal 2027 budget proposal. That would result in cuts to science programs, fisheries management and data collection.
Those cutbacks trickle down to the fishermen and result in a lack of fishing opportunities, Sackton said. Some in the fishery also have the impression NOAA is too understaffed to regulate fisheries in a timely fashion, he said.
In Sitka, Alaska, Behnken said the Trump administration’s cutbacks at NOAA have made it more difficult for her and others who rely on the agency. She said she has a lot of empathy for the workers left at the agency, who she said are “doing the work of three people, particularly at the weather service,” but it is still frustrating for fishermen.
“It’s hard to retain good people when their future at the organization is that uncertain,” said Behnken, who is executive director of the Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association.
