title: All in all, the best season is fall in the Brunswick area
text:
OK, I’ll admit it. I’m a sucker for all things pumpkin-flavored. Pumpkin spice coffee. Or pumpkin eggnog. Or ice cream. Or even cheesecake. Have you ever tried the pumpkin pie gelato at Gelato Fiasco? But that’s not the only reason my favorite season is fall. Here are some others.
Schools and colleges are in full swing. Early jitters have eased; routines have begun to set; friendships have been forged. It’s a new start, brimming with possibilities.
The World Series captivates the nation’s attention. Despite the popularity of college and professional football, I remain partial to baseball, truly America’s pastime. Sorry, all you soccer aficionados. Given a choice between watching soccer or baseball, be it shutout or slugfest, I’ll take baseball every time. And I’ll never understand the appeal of NASCAR.
Halloween sparks creativity. Children spend hours answering the crucial question, “What am I going to be this year?” Back when I was a kid, boys usually opted to be a cowboy or a Native American. Girls often chose to be a princess or an angel. Then again, those were the 1950s when conformity took precedence over self-expression. Vanilla ruled. And father knew best.
When it comes to Halloween, times have changed for the better. I always enjoy Brunswick’s spirited parade on the town mall where kids and parents dress in costumes that run the gamut. Such community gatherings cut way down on trick-or-treating from house to house, not a bad thing.
Veterans Day, which originated from Armistice Day, always evokes memories of marching in a parade with the Boy Scouts in Parkersburg, West Virginia. And Tina and I were delighted to purchase bricks to honor our fathers in the Veterans Plaza on the town mall. Her father fought in the Pacific during World War II, while my dad was working on the Manhattan Project in Hanford, Washington. I’m sorry that I didn’t buy a brick to honor my great grandfather, George B. Kenniston, who fought for the Union in the Civil War.
My birthday is in the fall, Nov. 13 to exact. In fact, I was born on a Friday the 13th, so I’ve always considered 13 my lucky number and Friday my favorite day. That said, I’m not a big fan of Black Friday sales. You won’t see me lined up for hours in front of a big box store to purchase anything, no matter how tempting the deal.
Thanksgiving, on the other hand, has special meaning. There’s the celebratory meal, of course, although I prefer mince or apple or pecan pie over pumpkin pie. Most important, we have the chance to express our gratitude for many blessings and many people. That’s especially important during these chaotic times.
Let’s not forget the magnificent autumn leaves. Remember the lyrics of that old Nat King Cole song? “The falling leaves drift by the window, the autumn leaves of red and gold. I see your lips, the summer kisses, the sun-burned hands I used to hold.” People who leave New England often say they miss the change of seasons. There’s just something magical about witnessing the changing of the leaves, the emergence of all those reds and golds slowly replacing the greens.
To be sure, the changing of the leaves serves as a metaphor for us older folks. While we may fondly remember Frank Sinatra singing “The September of My Years,” we’re entering the November or, perhaps, December of our years.
But still and all it’s good to be alive. In the fall. Or any other season for that matter. And a spoonful of ice cream, pumpkin or any other flavor, can help the medicine go down.
David Treadwell, a Brunswick writer, welcomes commentary and suggestions for future “Just a Little Old” columns at [email protected].

title: The New York Times shortchanged Troy Jackson
text:
On Sept. 20, the New York Times ran a profile on Troy Jackson, “A Progressive Brawler Tries to Flip a Senate Seat in Maine.”
Progressive races this cycle have two issues which play large: the treatment of Palestinians and AIPAC attempting to influence races. Despite the primacy of these issues, the Times never mentioned Jackson’s views on the treatment of Palestinians or the millions of dollars from AIPAC and AIPAC-adjacent donors going to Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign.
The article did find room for the 1988 alleged pushing incident between Jackson and his partner. As the Times reported, both Jackson and his partner deny the incident.
The Times’ Israel coverage has drawn criticism, including reported internal guidance for reporters to avoid terms like “genocide” and “occupied territory.” We saw how the Times was dogged in taking down Graham Platner; a pattern.
Maine deserves fair elections free of outside influence. We must remain vigilant as Election Day approaches.
Eric Vos
Rockland

title: Former ‘American Idol’ singer Caleb Flynn sentenced for wife’s murder
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — A former music pastor in Ohio who appeared briefly on “American Idol” was sentenced Monday to life in prison without the possibility of parole, after a jury convicted him last week of murdering his wife while he was having an affair.
The judge said Caleb Flynn, 40, used his Christian faith to manipulate others and showed no remorse for actions marked by “layers of deceit, manipulation and cruelty.”
With tears rolling down his cheeks, Flynn apologized to his family just before being sentenced, starting with his two young daughters, who were home when he shot his wife in her sleep. He called their births the “greatest joy in this life.”
Although he said he accepted responsibility for his words and decisions, Flynn remained adamant that he was innocent.
“As I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife,” he said.
Prosecutors said Flynn staged a home invasion in February and claimed a burglar killed his wife, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old schoolteacher and volleyball coach. In his 2013 appearance on “American Idol,” Flynn credited his wife with encouraging him to chase his dreams on the singing contest. He did not advance to the main competition in Hollywood.
During the trial, Flynn didn’t testify on his own behalf, nor did anybody else.
Family members, including Ashley’s parents, spoke in favor of the harsh sentence Monday, while saying they had forgiven Flynn because they didn’t want her legacy to be hatred.
Her sister, Kayla Keyt, said Flynn’s actions have scarred their entire church community, prompting children to run into their parents’ bedrooms to make sure their fathers haven’t killed their mothers.
As a family member read a statement written by his daughter Ava, Flynn sobbed uncontrollably as a pile of tissues grew on the defense table in front of him. At one point, it appeared he might fall over.
“Mommy was the perfect person,” her statement said. “The absolute perfect person. What did she ever do to you to make you hate her so much?” In her statement, his daughter Alyssa said she wouldn’t visit him in prison.
During closing arguments, prosecutors told jurors that Flynn wanted out of his marriage when he shot his wife at their house in Tipp City, a suburb north of Dayton. He sent a text message to his lover the night before the shooting, saying, “I choose you. I’m free. Actions will come tomorrow,” prosecutors said.
During the trial, Alleigha Botner testified she met Flynn in 2022 while she was a 20-year-old intern at his church and had an affair with him for more than a year. She told jurors that Flynn said he hated his wife and had thoughts of killing her.
The gun used to kill Ashley Flynn was not found at the scene, and his attorney told jurors that investigators found no evidence that Caleb Flynn fired a gun that day. Prosecutors said his fingerprints and DNA were at the scene and that his devices showed him moving around the house, even though he claimed he was asleep at the time of the shooting.
The jury found him guilty of multiple counts, including murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence.

title: Simple settings changes that could protect you from AI hackers
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Artificial intelligence is making it easier than ever for criminals to hack into personal devices, according to Kara Sprague, CEO of cybersecurity firm HackerOne, which works with some of the world’s biggest companies to find security flaws before hackers do.
Sprague said the shift is driven by how much software is now part of daily life. That software carries more vulnerabilities than ever, and hackers are increasingly relying on sophisticated AI systems to carry out attacks.
Sprague said one of the simplest ways to protect personal information is being cautious about what gets typed into an AI chatbot.
“What you end up typing into an AI chatbot doesn’t simply disappear when you’re done using it,” Sprague said. “And so you need to think about these chatbots almost like strangers that you might encounter on the street. You wouldn’t hand them your street, your home address, or your phone number or your bank details. So don’t hand those things to these models either.”
Sprague said a useful rule of thumb is to avoid typing anything into a chatbot that wouldn’t be said out loud to a stranger.
Sprague also recommends reviewing privacy settings within AI tools.
“You can go into the privacy settings of whichever AI tool you are using and turn off the model training and memory retention,” Sprague said. “Most people don’t realize that their conversations might be used to improve the model for the next person, and that might also sound fine until you consider what you’ve been typing into these models.”
Sprague said users should always verify and critically evaluate information AI tools provide. She also noted that ethical hackers work to test software systems for vulnerabilities, aiming to fix weaknesses before bad actors can exploit them.

title: Stroke survivor’s daily thumbs-up greeting has powerful effect on neighbors
text:
EATON RAPIDS, Mich. (Aging Untold) — For 10 years, George Doxtader has greeted passing drivers with a thumbs-up from a bench at the corner of State and Main.
“Ten years,” Doxtader said.
Doxtader, 78, spreads joy in the community with a thumbs-up that lifts the spirits of people passing by.
A daily routine
Kurt Norgaard, Doxtader’s friend and breakfast buddy, said Doxtader starts early.
“He gets up very early. He’s out here a lot of times at 4 a.m.,” Norgaard said. “And you’ll see a lot of waving and beeping — just how it is.”
Doxtader’s pastor said he is family and a blessing to the community.
“Aging Untold” host Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the greetings have an effect on the community.
“He’s found a way to connect to his community, and he’s found a way to make them see a bright light in the day … and that’s what we all need - purpose and meaning,” Cradduck said.
Recovering from strokes
Doxtader suffered two major strokes 35 years ago. He has paralysis on the right side of his body and has trouble speaking.
“Slow and gradual,” Doxtader said.
When he isn’t greeting passersby, Doxtader crochets blankets and pictures using his left hand.
Cradduck said Doxtader’s story shows what’s possible after setbacks.
“So he proved through his own resilience that no matter what life throws at you, you can make a way to still have a positive impact on the world around you and your community,” Cradduck said.
Doxtader can be found on Main Street in Eaton Rapids.

title: Musician Julia Keefe brings the rich history of Indigenous big bands to Maine
text:
Jazz has been a part of Julia Keefe’s life since she was 4 years old, listening to the “beautiful melody” of Billie Holiday’s “No More” as her mom cleaned up around the living room.
After she grew up and moved away from Kamiah, Idaho, to Spokane, Washington, Keefe, a member of the Nez Perce tribe, discovered and fell in love with jazz musicians like Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan and Louis Armstrong. But it wasn’t until high school, when she discovered the pioneering Coeur d’Alene jazz singer Mildred Bailey, that Keefe felt herself reflected in the art form.
“By being able to tie Indigeneity back to a historical and influential jazz figure, it sort of allowed me to exist in this space,” said Keefe. “I remember thinking in high school, it’s important that I talk about being Native because there might just be another Native person who loves jazz and wants to pursue this music, and they won’t, and they’ll feel very isolated without that outspokenness of my cultural identity.”
In the years since, Keefe has made Indigenous identity and cultural connectivity centerpieces of her musical career, both as a solo artist and as the vocalist and director for the Julia Keefe Indigenous Big Band.
The big band, which released its debut album “Incarnadine” in May, is composed of 16 Indigenous musicians from across the Americas. The band was created to “celebrate the diversity and vitality of Indigenous people in jazz.”
On Oct. 15 the Julia Keefe Indigenous Big Band comes to the State Theatre for a performance Keefe hopes will “empower people to support Indigenous artists” and leave them “feeling uplifted by the music.”
“The band is one part celebration, one part protest, but all parts love,” said Keefe.
While the program will feature some songs from Indigenous jazz pioneers, many of the songs were composed and arranged by the band’s members.
“For a lot of these more contemporary songs, it’s sort of the reimagining and reframing of Indigenous melodies into this big band soundscape, and it works so beautifully,” said Keefe.
THE HISTORY BEHIND THE MUSICIANS
As jazz grew in popularity throughout the United States in the early 20th century, Indigenous big bands and small ensembles began to appear on reservations across the country, according to Keefe. Notable Indigenous jazz musicians of the era include Mildred Bailey, “Big Chief” Russell Moore, Oscar Pettiford and Charlie Parker.
This “overlooked part of music history,” Keefe said, ties back to the legacy of Indian boarding schools and their traumatic and, in many cases, fatal practices centered around forcing Indigenous children to conform to Western culture.
“There were marching bands and choirs at these boarding schools,” Keefe explained. “And for those fortunate enough to survive that education, they went back to their homelands with this knowledge of Western music and instruments.”
This history is part of what Keefe hopes audiences and other Indigenous peoples will rediscover via the Big Band. She described some of her bandmates returning home and asking around about the music ensembles that existed during this period, or finding old family photos and playbills of relatives who were in a jazz band.
“It’s very sort of family lore,” said Keefe. “But also a really crucial part of Indigenous family history.”
HOW THE BIG BAND GOT ITS START
Keefe had never considered directing a big band until she met Delbert Anderson, a Diné (Navajo) trumpet player and co-founder of the Big Band. Following a conversation about Indigenous big bands, Anderson called and encouraged her to apply for the South Arts Creative Residency Grant to fund her own Indigenous big band.
Keefe was granted $40,000 in funding, and in May 2022, the Julia Keefe Indigenous Big Band premiered at the Washington Center for Performing Arts for a four-day residency.
After social media call-outs and reaching out to institutions with large Indigenous populations, Keefe held virtual auditions, eventually assembling 16 musicians from across the continent – even attracting Indigenous performers from as far away as Hawaii and Alaska.
“Immediately it felt like a big group of cousins getting together and making music,” said Keefe.
At the end of the residency, Keefe remembers band members asking, “This isn’t a one-off, right?”
“It really has become my life’s calling, my mission, my purpose,” Keefe said.
Before starting the Big Band, Keefe said she knew only two other contemporary Indigenous musicians – Anderson and Mali Obomsawin, an Odanak Abenaki bassist and vocalist – but in the ensuing four years has connected with over 80 Indigenous musicians.
“Hopefully, one day we can all get together for an Indigenous jazz summit and just learn from each other, build community, and collaborate,” said Keefe.
The Julia Keefe Indigenous Big Band, presented by Portland Ovations. 7 p.m. Oct. 15. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $35-55. portlandovations.org.

title: The ego has invaded American politics
text:
Ron Snyder lives in Dexter.
Our church, like many churches, is experiencing an attendance decline that is causing financial challenges. This week I encountered a church leader who was, in my opinion, disrespectful to me and our pastor. For reference, there was nothing done that I would consider illegal, only disrespectful.
However, this caused me to decide that I needed to review the church leader’s and the church’s performance as if I were doing a business turnaround. In so doing, one must always look at the product being marketed and with whom the business is competing and then determine why the poor performer is not keeping pace.
This analysis led me to a conclusion I had previously given little thought or consideration: A church is really a business that markets behavioral laws. They may also provide shelter and lease instructors, but they also employ managers and have a management structure to manage and control their operation.
But with whom are they really competing? The clue came when my pastor said she was not allowed to talk about politics.
Who, besides churches, provides moral and behavioral rules that humans must follow? The answer was geographical leaders or government and political leaders.
In some countries, religious leaders take over governing the country’s inhabitants. In others, political leaders take control and provide laws that take precedence over religious leaders. The answer became even clearer when one looks at how they are funded. One collects tithes, the other taxes and each’s leaders decide how they are redistributed.
This turned me to the U.S. Constitution and prompted the question of, “How are we prepared?”
Surprisingly, our founders prepared us very well if we use the tools they included in our Constitution 250 years ago. First, they recognized the power struggle between religious leaders and territorial government leaders. They solved this by including freedom of religion. All church leaders were welcomed to participate in America’s leadership.
But the second part of their planning and analysis displays even more foresight. They included a plan and provision to address leaders’ egos. They provided set terms: representatives, two years; presidents, four years; senators, six years. Additionally, they provided a procedure to impeach an unsatisfactory leader during his or her elected term. And more importantly, they left administration in the hands of the inhabitants of the territory being represented: voters.
Our founders did not provide for political parties. Political parties were a method devised by egotistical government leaders to divide voters and disperse money collected in taxes. However, the Constitution’s writers did also plan for this and point us in the direction our representatives and we, the voters, need to go to make America great again.
Whether in church or state, we need to remove the egotistical leaders who want to collect our tithes and taxes and distribute them as they see fit and replace them with ones who will work for all of us and distribute our labor for the benefit of all mankind. In America, as long as political parties and churches exist, this means voters must register independent and insist on implementing ranked-choice voting.
I urge you, the voter, to truly make America great again.
Be respectful of your neighbors and insist that your representative represent you and address the ego issues that have invaded and overtaken our leadership. If they don’t, you have the choice in November. And for you Christians who believe the U.S. is a Christian country, remember Jesus was not a member of a Christian church. He was a Jewish rebel in the Jewish synagogue who took offense to the way church leaders treated mankind.
Good luck, America, and regardless of your church affiliation, God will prevail.

title: Patriots are back in the race after toppling Bills
text:
The New England Patriots’ early-season triumph at Buffalo last season was part of the 10-game winning streak that helped propel them on a Super Bowl run following a 1-2 start.
New England is hoping Sunday’s 29-26 victory over the Bills can provide a similar spark.
The Patriots are 2-2 on the season after handing their division rivals their first loss in the new Highmark Stadium.
Following a week of questions about quarterback Drake Maye’s struggles, poor offensive execution and a mounting number of injuries, their performance for the moment has brought a sense of confidence back to the defending AFC champions.
“Come on, man! We ain’t dead! We ain’t dead!” defensive tackle Cory Durden shouted as he embraced coach Mike Vrabel on his way to the locker room Sunday.
Vrabel was equally succinct in describing what the win meant for his team.
“Gets us back in the race,” he said.
What might be most encouraging was Maye’s play.
He wasn’t spotless, throwing his seventh interception of the season and losing a fumble. But he was poised with the game on the line, leading the Patriots on an eight-play, 73-yard drive that ended with Efton Chism III’s diving, one-handed, go-ahead catch in the end zone.
It capped a day that saw Maye throw for a season-high 269 yards and three TDs. It ended his two-game drought without a TD pass.
“Everybody understands how the quarterback has to perform in this league for the team to have success,” Vrabel said. “Everybody does have his back, starting with me and everybody all the way down.”
What’s working
Chism is the latest example of the Patriots’ history of finding success with undrafted free agents.
Signed after the 2025 NFL draft, he appeared in just eight games as a rookie, catching each of his three targets for 75 yards, with one touchdown.
He already has played in three of the four games this season, with seven targets and four catches for 41 yards.
What needs help
As excited as the Patriots were to see Chism come up big after Mack Hollins’ injury, there are mounting concerns at wide receiver.
Vrabel acknowledged Monday that Hollins likely would miss a couple of days of practice, putting his availability for Sunday’s game in jeopardy.
That would leave the Patriots down another top receiver, with A.J. Brown still on injured reserve with a high ankle sprain.
Signing another receiver is a possibility.
“Sure, anybody that could help us,” Vrabel said.
Stock up
Romeo Doubs. Following a rough debut in the season-opening loss to Seattle, Doubs is starting to show why the Patriots signed him to a four-year, $70 million deal this offseason. He had his first two touchdown catches of the season and is tied for second on the team with 12 receptions. Doubs’ 203 receiving yards are behind only Hollins (209).
Stock down
Vrabel. With the Bills trailing 14-7 and facing a third-and-goal on the New England 16, he received an unsportsmanlike conduct for arguing a defensive holding penalty on Marcus Jones.
Vrabel said he told the official it was a “terrible effing call.”
The penalty, along with Jones’ initial infraction, put the ball on the 6. The Bills tied the game following a TD run by Josh Allen two plays later.
“I’ve said that 87 times since I’ve been a head coach. It was nothing derogatory. You’d have to ask him. I think he was a little sensitive,” Vrabel said. “I apologized to him. Players responded, it was unfortunate. And I have to be better in those moments.”
Injuries
Cornerback Charles Woods left the game with a shoulder injury but was able to return. … Tight end Eli Raridon and fullback Reggie Gilliam also left the game with ankle injuries.
Key number
29 — In their first three games this season, the Patriots scored only 29 points in 30 drives. They had 29 points in their 12 drives against the Bills.
Next steps
The Patriots host the the Las Vegas Raiders (3-1) on Sunday.

title: Pennsylvania measles cases reach more than 1,000. Track outbreaks in your state
text:
Pennsylvania measles cases reach more than 1,000. Track outbreaks in your state
The Pennsylvania Department of Health reported more than 1,000 measles cases confirmed so far in 2026 Monday.
The 1,004 cases have been reported in 39 out of Pennsylvania's 67 counties. More than a third of the measles cases were in Lancaster County with 391 cases, according to the latest data. The county with the second-largest number of cases was Mifflin with 118 cases.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health has reported 198 hospitalizations and five deaths associated with measles as of Monday. Just four of the confirmed 1,004 cases were people who were vaccinated.
The two deaths are the first reported in 2026. Three deaths were reported in 2025, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Measles cases across the U.S. have surged in 2026. In August, the total number of confirmed cases for 2026 surpassed the number in all of 2025, making it the worst year since 1991. As of the most recent CDC data available, released Oct. 2, 3,887 cases of measles had been reported.
The Get the Facts Data Team is tracking measles cases collected by the CDC and updated weekly. The data may not include the most recent data from a state due to the reporting frequency. For example, Pennsylvania's most recent cases are not included.

title: California scientist wins a Nobel Prize, then makes school lunches for his kids
text:
STANFORD, California (AP) — Dr. Karl Deisseroth spent hours fielding congratulatory calls after learning early Monday that he had won a Nobel Prize for medicine for helping to open a new field of brain science called optogenetics.
But it wasn’t long before the California scientist asked for a break from all the attention for a more ordinary task: He needed to make school lunches for his children, who were asleep in the family home in Stanford, where their father had been speaking in the middle of the night with journalists and well-wishers.
Deisseroth, 54, shared this year’s medicine prize with two researchers in Germany for their work in optogenetics, a field that combines light with genes to switch on and off neurons in living brains.
A self-described night owl, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator and Stanford University professor often works past midnight. After reviewing papers and emailing his students, he said he had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly in Stockholm.
“I almost felt as if I’d lost the power of forming words,” he told The Associated Press, “but I recovered after a minute or two.”
He regained speech quickly enough for remote interviews with AP science reporters. Speedy emails with the Stanford communications staff had helped put them in touch.
“No real sleep was achieved,” he said an hour after the announcement.
As the science reporters chatted with Deisseroth over the phone and Zoom, an AP photographer and videographer raced to his home in Stanford.
The photographer arrived around 3:30 a.m. to find Halloween decorations outside the home but just one light on inside. He was worried he had the wrong house before mustering the courage to knock on the door.
Dr. Michelle Monje-Deisseroth, the scientist’s wife, answered and ushered the photographer into their home, where the Nobel winner was taking calls from the couch.
Monje-Deisseroth, an HHMI investigator and Stanford pediatric neuro-oncologist, was at his side when she wasn’t making coffee for the Stanford communications staff who had joined the celebration. Deisseroth was surprised to hear his work had been honored with a Nobel Prize, he told the AP, but his wife was not.
Deisseroth recounted the research he conducted with fellow Nobel winners Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, and its real-world impact.
“For me, I’m a physician-scientist. I am a psychiatrist. I care about patients and my patients who have autism, who have depression,” he said. “I care about the hope that this brings. But I’m also a basic scientist, and I care about understanding this amazing organ, the brain, and how it works and how it integrates and computes and delivers all the things that make us human.”
As Deisseroth wrapped up the interviews, he told the Stanford staff he needed an hourlong break beginning at 6:30 a.m. His kids would be waking up, he said, and they would need lunches before leaving for school.
When one of the Stanford representatives wondered if the neighbors would mind all the late-night commotion, Monje-Deisseroth shrugged it off.
They live in faculty housing, she said. There are a lot of Nobels in the neighborhood.
__
Ramakrishnan reported from New York. Associated Press writers Stefanie Dazio in Berlin and Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report.
___

title: Gatorade issues major recall across more than 30 states
text:
Gatorade issues major recall across more than 30 states
Gatorade is recalling thousands of cases of its sports drink over food dye that wasn't declared on the packaging.
The recall covers 28 oz. Gatorade Lemon Lime, Gatorade Lemon Lime Zero, Gatorade Orange, and Gatorade Orange Zero with expiration dates from April to June 2027. The Food and Drug Administration says there was undeclared Yellow No. 6 or Yellow No. 5 or both.
Allergies and adverse reactions to food dyes are rare but do happen, according to the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology. For instance, Yellow No. 5 may cause itching and hives in some people, the FDA says.
The issue in this recall was that they were not listed on product labels.
The FDA has classified the recall as Class II, meaning "use of or exposure" to the product could cause "temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences," or where "the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote."
The recalled product was distributed to these states: Alaska, Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington and Wisconsin.
These lot numbers are covered:
Lot 091026 DL — June 7, 2027; Lot 091126 DL — June 8, 2027; Lot 072226 DT — April 18, 2027; Lot 072426 TL — April 20, 2027; Lot 073126 TL — April 27, 2027; Lot 072926 TL — April 25, 2027; Lot 073026 TL — April 25, 2027; Lot 081026 TL — May 7, 2027; Lot 082126 OA — April 18, 2027; Lot 080126 DL — April 28, 2027; Lot 082026 DL — May 17, 2027; Lot 083126 DT — June 7, 2027; Lot 082526 KM — May 22, 2027; Lot 090426 KM — June 1, 2027; Lot 072726 TL — April 23, 2027.

title: Vehicle Explosion On Main Street In Readfield Traced To Improper Use Of Tannerite Target Practice Explosive
text:
Authorities Investigate A Vehicle That Was Blown Up With A Reactive Rifle Target In Readfield
The Maine Department of Public Safety says authorities are investigating a vehicle explosion in the Kennebec County town of Readfield.
Read More: Dexter Home Fire Shows Dangers Of Improper Cigarette Disposal
The State Fire Marshal's Office says Tannerite, an explosive usually used in rifle target practice, was the cause of the explosion at 846 Main Street on Sunday, September 27th. Multiple calls were made to first responders after the blast; the Readfield Fire Department was sent to the scene. Once they learned that an explosion had occurred, the State Fire Marshal's Office was tagged in to take over.
"State Fire Marshal Investigators responded and investigated the circumstances surrounding the event, which turned out to be a group of individuals shooting at the Tannerite that had been placed in the vehicle...The State Fire Office reminds people that state law governing the use of Tannerite allows up to 5 pounds of mixed product to be used for sport/target shooting only. Tannerite cannot be used to explode any item other than the packaging it is mixed in."
In fact, the safety instructions on the Tannerite.com website clearly state that putting the explosive on metal is a direct hazard.
"Follow all of the safety instructions. Elevate the target on a cardboard box and make sure the area is free of debris and dry grasses.
Do not use the target in locations where a general fire order is in effect, and do not use the target near combustible materials. Never place these targets inside, on top of, or under any metal, rock, or other surfaces that could produce flying debris or sparks, or within another object. This is dangerous and constitutes improper use of the product."

Authorities say the investigation is still active, and the Fire Marshal's Office is now working in conjunction with the local D.A.'s Office to work out what charges will come of all of this.

title: Bates Historical Society Panel Celebrates Hispanic Heritage Month
text:
On Sept. 25, the Bates Historical Society held a panel to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month and discuss Hispanic identity and U.S. history. Catered by Chipotle, the event was the Bates Historical Society’s first of the year.
On the panel were Assistant Professor of History and Latin American and Latinx Studies Erik Bernardino, Politics Professor Clarisa Pérez-Armendáriz and Hispanic Studies Associate Professor Stephanie M. Pridgeon.
The professors discussed what Professor Bernardino called the “constant struggle over what to call this group of people,” talking about the terms Hispanic, Latino and Latinx. The professors pointed out that our conception of a “pan-Latinidad” is very modern.
Professor Pérez-Armendáriz furthered the discussion, linking modern Spanish-speaking identity to the rise of Spanish-language mass media, with large channels such as Univision and Telemundo offering news, politics, and cultural content to Spanish-speaking Americans.
On non-Hispanic authors writing books about Hispanic characters, the panel appeared to reach consensus that the nature of the representation matters far more than who is creating the work. Specifically, they noted that good representation comes from real knowledge of the cultures the author writes about.
Professor Pridgeon described a healthy author-subject relationship as dialectical, with both sides exchanging and attempting to empathize. In a similar vein, the professors recommended some Hispanic media and filmmakers such as “Our America” by José Martí and Patricio Guzmán.
Professor Pridgeon pointed out that most of the world uses the term “American” to refer exclusively to the United States. However, many Latinos use the Spanish equivalent of “América” to refer to themselves, sometimes including the United States and Canada, and sometimes deliberately excluding them. In addition to the Hispanic communities’ self-understanding, Professor Pridgeon noted that the term “América” is used by anti-colonial authors such as José Martí to refer to Latino countries oppressed and colonized by the United States.
ICE loomed large over the discussion: Professor Pérez-Armendáriz detailed how raids continue to have a large influence on Latino life and culture in the United States. Professor Pérez-Armendáriz noted that it has pushed some people to try to make themselves closer to whiteness, while for others it has encouraged them to express themselves openly as an act of resistance.
Regarding ongoing Hispanic historiography, Professor Bernardino mentioned recent political interference, including the cancellation of an exhibit on the Young Lords political movement after the far-right Heritage Foundation criticized it for featuring the Marxist political organization.
The panel brought together students from different backgrounds, including many Hispanic students and students taught by the featured professors, to explore the changing identity of Hispanic Americans in the Americas.

title: Ukraine claims its attacks have taken out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity
text:
Ukraine claims its attacks have taken out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity
Ukraine said that its long-range strikes have neutralized more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow's ability to supply its forces during its 4 1/2-year-old invasion.
Related video: Trump touts G7 plan to release oil and diesel reserves to address high prices
The Defense Ministry said Sunday that recent strikes on refineries in cities including Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov and Syzran had put 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity out of action. The claim could not be independently verified.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their aerial assaults as progress along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line has largely ground to a halt.
Ukrainian forces have repeatedly attacked refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict gasoline sales.
President Vladimir Putin said in a rare admission Thursday that the strikes had caused Russia to lose roughly 1% of its gross domestic product.
“They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” Putin said at a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts.
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that analysts from Ukraine’s intelligence services, the General Staff, and the Defense Ministry itself had assessed the effects of the strikes.
“Fifty-one percent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings. Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory,” he said.

title: Portland City Council votes to remove Jewel Box bus shelter from public art collection
text:
PORTLAND — The City Council voted unanimously Monday to remove the Jewel Box bus shelter on Congress Street from its public art collection, clearing the way for the 22-year-old structure to be replaced with a new transit shelter.
The Jewel Box — with its bending glass walls, aluminum canopy and cast iron base — was installed in 2004 and has been a visible landmark near Monument Square since. More recently, it’s fallen victim to vandalism and raised safety concerns, and has been increasingly expensive for the Public Art Committee to maintain.
The vote Monday came after the Public Art Committee recommended last month to deaccession the art installation, which will allow the city and Greater Portland Metro to coordinate on replacing it.
Kat Zagaria Buckley, the committee chair, previously said the structure is “by far” the most expensive piece to maintain among the city’s collection, averaging about $5,000 a year.
According to a council memo, the committee has spent $35,000 to maintain it since 2004, including $8,700 since 2023 due to vandalism. A recent estimate put future renovations at another $32,000.
The ongoing problems have included graffiti, broken glass, drug activity, public health concerns and more. Public comment submitted ahead of Monday’s meeting highlighted the issues.
Christian Saucedo, a Brown Street resident for the past decade, said he’s watched the shelter degrade “from a beautiful art piece citizens could use to wait for the bus into a gathering place for drug dealers and drug users.”
He said he’s called the police several times after watching overdoses or violence occur, and that most of the time, those waiting for the bus can’t use the shelter.
“As an artist myself, it pains me to ask you to dismantle the shelter, but it’s the only solution for our block,” he said.
Another resident of the Arts District, Mary Ames, said she often sees the Portland Downtown ambassador team arrive early in the morning to “spray vomit from the benches, pick
up needles, remove human waste and other drug-related paraphernalia.” She said she stopped walking her dog nearby because it once stepped on a needle.
When supporting the recommendation to remove the shelter last month, Zagaria Buckley said members of the committee didn’t feel that relocating the structure was appropriate, and that changing its design would not allow the artists’ original concept to stay intact.

title: 10th grader killed after school bus full of students rolls over in crash: ‘Terrible, tragic morning’
text:
(AP) — A Florida school bus carrying nearly 40 people overturned after being struck by an oncoming car on the way to a high school early Monday, killing a student and the driver of another vehicle that caught fire, authorities said.
A heavy presence of emergency responders rushed to the crash site in Winter Haven, south of Orlando, and 26 students were transported to a hospital, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said. At least one person was in critical condition.
EN ESPAÑOL | Mueren dos personas al volcar un autobús escolar en Florida
The crash left the bus upside-down on the side of the road. The front end was a mangled mess of metal and one of its four back tires appeared to be missing.
“It was a horrible crash,” Judd said. “It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life.”
The bus was headed to Winter Haven High School when an oncoming car crossed the center line and struck the side of the bus near the rear wheels, Judd said. The sheriff said the impact ripped the tire off the bus, which then crashed head-on into an oncoming Jeep that caught fire.
Most of the 39 people aboard the bus were high school students, along with the bus driver and the driver’s daughter. Judd said first responders spent the first several hours getting people to the hospital, identifying them and reuniting students with their parents.
“I think this is the most horrific bus tragedy we’ve had in decades, as far back as I can remember,” Judd said.
Officials didn’t immediately report the condition of the driver of the car that hit the bus, but Judd said that person had been heading to work and was cooperating with investigators. They were not arrested or charged with a crime.
Polk County Public Schools Superintendent Frederick Heid said students practice drills on how to leave a bus that is involved in an accident. Last month, another Polk County school bus was also involved in a crash but authorities said no students were on board at the time.
“This event could have been far worse. You can see the condition of the bus, you can see its current positioning,” Heid said.
Justin Sharpless, chairman of the Polk County school board, asked the community to come together to support the family of the girl who died, as well as the school and school staff.
“There are really no words that can take away the pain of losing a young person,” he said.

text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - During his stop in Bangor Sunday for a canvass launch event statewide, Democratic U.S. Senate Candidate Troy Jackson replied to questions regarding his tight Senate Race with Maine Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins.
A NYT poll updated on October 2nd shows both Jackson and Collins are tied at 50%.
Collins had criticized Jackson for spreading “baseless lies” amid allegations following a report by ProPublica last month.
The report said that Collins was allegedly at the center of an FBI probe involved in “pay-to-play” scheme with Naval Defense Company Navatek.
Collins denies the claims, saying they are the allegations are “categorically false.”
Jackson said that Collins needs to stand up and take accountability.
“She should worry about who she takes money from. I don’t take corporate money. I don’t trade votes for things like that. That’s on her. I don’t know what else to say about it, but I’m sure she is very concerned about it,” said Jackson,
Ahead of the first televised debate Thursday, Jackson also spoke about how he is preparing ahead of time.
“Your record is always something I felt very strongly about. I am very excited to be able to be on the debate stage and talk about the things that I’ve done compared to the things that she’s done. She can defend her, and. I’ll defend mine. I’m proud of what I fought for.”
A full statement sent to WABI from Susan Collins campaign can be found below:
“Troy Jackson took hundreds of thousands of dollars of corporate money when he was Maine Senate President. Tobacco money, pharmaceutical companies, electric companies — you name it. It is the height of hypocrisy for him to lecture anyone on campaign money. These are seven year old allegations and the Biden led FBI and the FEC both said there was no indication that Senator Collins had done anything wrong. Troy just doesn’t know what he is talking about.”
WABI and WAGM will be hosting a debate between Jackson and Collins on Tuesday, October 13th at 7 p.m.
It will be streamed on-air and online.

text:
PORTLAND, Maine — Over 5,500 runners signed up to run in the Maine Marathon on Sunday in Portland, an all-time high in the history of the race.
The winner in the women’s division was Betsy Burke, who finished with a time of 2:54:08. The Rye, New York, native said she didn’t come into Sunday morning expecting the win.
“I know the bike came up to me sometime in the teens and said something, and I was like ‘What?’ He said ‘You’re in the lead.’ That’s weird,” recalled Burke.
Burke said that she had won races in the past, but it has been a while, and the training leading up to this year’s race had a bit of a speed bump.
“I ran a lot less,” said Burke. “I had foot surgery in January. So I do a lot of it on the Peloton now, but, you know, I still work hard.”
The male winner was Dylan Stoltzfus, who came in at 2:23:59, a personal record, according to Stoltzfus.
For him, this year was a revenge tale. In last year’s race, Stoltzfus came in fifth, and he was determined to get a better result in this year’s race.
“Anyone who knows me knows I haven’t shut up about this for like two months,” answered Stoltzfus. “You never know who’s going to show up. Just nightmares of someone who I have no chance against, but traditionally 2:25ish gets it done.”
When he crossed the finish line, he was met by cheers and roars, some coming from those closest to him, including his roommates and his girlfriend.
“She puts up with so much. She makes me feel like a superhero,” commented Stoltzfus. “Getting back to see her was all I could think about for the last five miles.”
“He has spent the last year running,” recalled his roommate Cole. “Even when he was watching a movie in the living room, he’s on the foam roller just stretching out. Just saying ‘I’m going to win the marathon, I’m going to win it.’”
According to race organizers, the marathon has a financial impact on the city of $3 million. They said that 54% of the runners come from out of state not only to run the course, but also to explore the city and state.
“When I first took over, we worked on our brand and our purpose, and we decided to be a destination race,” stated Race Director Bob Dunfey. “And so we market throughout the country and the world.”
According to Dunfey, the race also brought in an estimated $700,000 to $900,000 for around 100 charities, including the marathon’s beneficiaries and individual nonprofits chosen by the runners.

title: Bangor golf fights thunder, lightning and hail to repeat as KVAC A champion
text:
ROCKPORT — After some key graduations a year ago, Chris Junkins wasn’t sure what type of season Bangor would have in 2026.
On Monday, the young Rams showed their potential.
Battling through hail, thunder and lightning, Bangor (160) repeated as Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference Class A champions, holding off Messalonskee (164) and Camden Hills (174) on the Par-34 front nine of Samoset Resort Golf Course.
“We lost a lot of seniors last year, so (this year) kind of felt like a rebuild after that,” said Junkins, Bangor’s head coach. “But as the year started and we started playing, you could see that our team was good, with some good young players who are helping us out.”
Junior Jacoby Harvey led the way for Bangor, shooting a 2-over 36, followed by junior Carter Catell (38) and freshman Mason Webb (42).
Play began at 3 p.m., but after only two holes, a quick but powerful hail storm hit the course, along with thunder and lightning. Each player left their golf balls on the course, hopped into their golf carts and headed back to the clubhouse.
Play resumed at 4:45 p.m., leaving players less than two hours to finish their round before dark. Playing quickly, the final group finished play at 6:30.
“The upperclassmen, we’ve been here before, but we were telling the younger players, ‘Stay patient, keep your head and don’t lose sight of what we’re looking for,'” Harvey said. “Every shot, each kid is dealing with the same thing. You just have to be mentally stronger than the other kids and we’ll do what we need to do.”
Junkins said the Rams’ experiences this season help them secure Monday’s win.
‘We were here Saturday and played two rounds on the front (nine),” Junkins said. “They were able to see the course twice. We played in wind at home. A week ago, we played in a lot of wind at Penobscot Valley (Country Club in Orono) for our pod championship. We played in the rain this year. I think all of that plays in the results at the end (of the year), learning different golf courses, giving them different opportunities to play and learn.”
Messalonskee had a strong outing from their No. 2 player, junior Greyson Dooley, who shot a 3-over 37. Junior Trent Bell shot 42, while senior Evan Hayes shot 43.
Freshman Ryan Irish (5-over 39) had the top score for Camden Hills, while senior Lila Dailey and junior Landon Reynolds each shot 45.
The postseason continues Tuesday with the KVAC Qualifier at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro. The Class A championships are scheduled for Friday, while the Class B and Class C championships will be on Saturday. All three rounds will be held at Natanis.
“That’s a big win over two big teams (today), that’s a big momentum swing,” Harvey said. “We’re not going to take (Tuesday) lightly, we’re going to try to set a new low (score), hopefully, and keep that momentum going into Friday and just do the same thing and maybe get a state championship.”

title: AI industry insiders voice alarms to NYC council as local governments take up safety concerns
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Artificial intelligence insiders warned New York City’s leaders about the dangers of the emerging technology on Monday, calling for greater oversight as local governments move to respond to mounting concerns that the systems could endanger humanity.
At a hearing of the New York City Council, recently departed employees of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind described a reckless culture at the firms, saying the biggest tech companies are racing to create technology they do not understand how to control.
“The companies run on a startup mindset: Move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photo sharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built,” said Jacob Coxon, a former engineer at Anthropic who has become a leading voice for regulation.
State and city governments have been considering ways to regulate AI as the Trump administration has taken a passive approach and Congress has proven inactive. President Donald Trump has dismissed AI fears as a “hoax” and signed an agreement late last month that largely allows the companies to self-police.
Coxon was a little-known engineer at Anthropic until he announced his departure through a series of social media posts that caught global attention. He told the Council that AI could have tremendous upsides, but without transparency and safeguards, it’s more likely that things will spiral out of control.
“On the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs and it could end in human extinction,” Coxon said.
A panel of AI company staffers — representing tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta — also testified at the hearing in Manhattan on Monday, telling officials that their systems are already improving people’s daily lives and stressing that they are laser-focused on safety.
“I share your commitment to ensuring that technology is developed safely and that its benefits are widely shared,” said Morgan Dwyer of OpenAI.
At one point during the hearing, Julie Menin, the speaker of the City Council, asked each company representatives to “quantify the risk posed by AI in the worst case catastrophic scenario.”
Dwyer answered: “I don’t know — I also don’t think it matters whether it’s 1% or 10% or 20% chance that something catastrophic will go wrong. None of these levels is remotely acceptable. We should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we can keep under human control.”
Menin slammed the response as “flippant at best.”
“I would say that the percentage chance doesn’t matter. What matters is the commitment to safety, and that is what OpenAI is committed to doing,” Dwyer said.
The City Council is considering several AI regulations, including proposals to require companies to disclose information about AI tools, require third-party approval for AI systems in the city and allow whistleblowers to receive a portion of fines from AI companies that violate laws.
Separately, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has moved to impose reporting and transparency standards around AI, as have governors elsewhere, though their power is somewhat limited since AI technology can reach across state lines, as well as the globe.

title: Aroostook County's next jail will not be in Presque Isle
text:
The Bangor Daily News was the first to report this story. What you’re reading here would likely not be made public without the efforts of professional journalists asking questions, interviewing sources and obtaining documents.
Aroostook County is in the midst of a search for land to locate a new jail, but that jail will not be built on municipal land in its biggest city.
The Presque Isle City Council declined to submit any city-owned land for consideration in response to a request from the county last month, according to an undated letter sent by City Manager Sonja Eyler to county leaders that the Bangor Daily News obtained.
“Following substantial discussion, the Council determined that the City does not have a suitable parcel capable of accommodating the proposed jail facility,” Eyler wrote in the letter.
The council’s decision has not previously been made public. It was made following a Sept. 21 executive session. The council met in mid-September to discuss the possibility of locating the jail in Presque Isle.
The jail could still be built on privately-owned land in the city. The owner of a 54.43 acre former mobile home park along Route 1 near the Caribou town line made the property available to the county for $1.3 million. The lot has been on the market since late June and is currently listed for $1.95 million.
Aroostook County has been evaluating how to replace its current jail for several years. The existing facility, situated in downtown Houlton, was built in 1889 and last renovated more than 40 years ago. Federal corrections experts called the building overcrowded and unsafe during a visit in 2024, and a jail commission has been studying options for the facility since 2023.
A 2025 needs assessment compiled by a consulting group recommended two potential locations for the new jail: in Houlton or in the vicinity of Presque Isle and Caribou, more central to The County’s population centers.
The report concluded that population shifts have made the existing jail’s location “less than ideal.” The jail was originally built in Houlton because of a former statutory requirement for the facilities to be in the county seat, but that puts it at least a two-hour drive away from many towns in the St. John Valley.
“There were indications from some agencies located to the north that a number of arrests are regularly not made in an effort to reduce trips to the current jail,” the report noted.
While Presque Isle will not house the next jail on city property, its City Council “unanimously supports locating the jail in central Aroostook. We urge the County to give substantial weight to the operational and logistical value of a central location as it evaluates proposals,” Eyler wrote.
“This is not simply a question of convenience or community preference. It is a practical public safety and service delivery consideration,” Eyler added. “A central Aroostook location has the potential to reduce transportation time and expense, improve law enforcement capacity across a large rural county, and create a facility that is more accessible to the people and systems it must serve.
The council is “prepared” to support another central Aroostook community that has a suitable location for the jail, Eyler said.
The consultant who conducted the needs assessment estimated last summer that the price tag to construct the jail could range from $91 million to $112 million, depending on its size, but construction costs have risen since.
A bond referendum to fund construction of the facility could come before voters as early as next year. If the selected land is outside of Houlton, that will also have to be approved at referendum.
Correction: An earlier version of the story incorrectly ruled out Presque Isle as a possible location for the new jail.

title: Researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of 'unknown' infection, reports say
text:
US State Department, CDC monitoring after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
Dozens of people were reported to be in isolation after a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and other infectious diseases died of an undisclosed illness.
VIDEO: CNN's Fred Pleitgen on quarantine in Russia after researcher dies from 'unknown' infection
The researcher, a 28-year-old female laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, died after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of “unknown” origin, according to Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease.
Rospotrebnadzor has played down the link between the death of the researcher — named in local media as Darya Shipilova — and her work.
“No micro-organisms associated with the employee’s professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient,” it asserted, adding that the “epidemiological situation” in the region was stable.
Nevertheless, the agency’s head, Anna Popova, traveled to Irkutsk on Friday, according to the local governor, Igor Kobzev, for what he described as an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission.
The meeting was in connection with a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region,” Kobzev said on Telegram.
Reached by phone on Monday, the institute where the researcher worked told CNN it was not commenting on the incident.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration was watching the situation closely. “I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it,” Rubio said.
Speaking later on Monday, President Donald Trump said the US would be willing to help. “Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help,” Trump told reporters before departing the White House for Nebraska. “I hate to see them having it,” Trump added. “It’s a rough disease.”
Anti-epidemic measures
Regional authorities are implementing a “comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures,” according to Maxim Modin, the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district in eastern Russia, near the Mongolian border.
The inpatient facility at the hospital where the worker was treated has been placed under quarantine, and several departments have stopped discharging or admitting patients, Modin said. Other hospitals in the region have also been closed, according to local media reports.
Irkutsk authorities also cancelled the annual community clean-up event that was scheduled for the weekend — a decision local media linked to the incident.
The woman’s death was confirmed by officials last week.
Ekaterina, a resident of Shekelov, told CNN on Monday that there were no visible changes in the city, but locals were anxious. “My acquaintances are slightly panicking,” she said.
Another resident, who wished to remain anonymous, said he was “shocked” by the news.
Unofficial reports, including by the independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala, have said that nearly 200 people are under observation.
Several people who had made contact with the researcher have been diagnosed with Covid-19 and rhinovirus, the most frequent cause of the common cold, Rospotrebnadzor said, state news agency TASS reported on Monday.
In its only comment on the incident, the Kremlin said people should only trust updates coming from the official agency.
“One should rely on official statements from Rospotrebnadzor rather than listening to various rumors and speculation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday.
WHO says public health risk “low”
The World Health Organization told CNN it was in contact with the Russian health authorities to “verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway, and their results.”
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” it said.
Despite such reassurances, several countries in the region have put in place safeguarding measures.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Health said that while the risk was “very low”, the situation was being monitored and “sanitary and quarantine controls were implemented at state border crossing points.”
Uzbekistan said it “increased the readiness” of relevant authorities to deal with highly infectious diseases. Kyrgyzstan, which does not share a land border with Russia is some 1,500 miles from Irkutsk, announced Monday it was introducing quarantine controls at state border crossing points.
A virologist in Siberia, Alexander Chepurnov, told CNN that the strict protocols being followed were designed to prevent onward spread.
“After any suspected exposure, staff are instructed to immediately report it, decontaminate, undergo medical assessment and be isolated in a separate dedicated facility for however long they might be infectious,” Chepirnov said.
Deadly but not easily transmitted
Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization, told CNN that while pneumonic plague is deadly, it is not very transmissible and one would have to be exposed to a high bacterial load to become sick.
In that sense, it is unlike respiratory illnesses such as COVID, she said.
There is endemic plague among wildlife in parts of Siberia, Rassmussen added.
According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute employs around 95 researchers and is a major public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russia’s Far East.
The head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, said earlier that the employee died “possibly from the plague,” but noted there had been no outbreak of the disease in his region.
Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plagues that are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
The other two types typically spread from contact with infected fleas, animals or infected tissues.
An aluminum plant near the laboratory instructed staff to wear masks as a precautionary measure. The director of Irkutsk Aluminum Plant, Artem Fominikh, noted “conflicting reports” were circulating and called for calm.
The infection in the Irkutsk region is “most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease,” a former head of Rospotrebnadzor, Gennady Onishchenko, said on Friday.
Onishchenko told TASS that the onset of cold weather would likely prevent transmission.
A US State Department spokesperson told CNN Sunday that it was aware of the possible death due to pneumonic plague in Russia.
“We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” the spokesperson said. “Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”
Patients with pneumonic plague develop fever, headache, weakness and and “a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucous,” according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The World Health Organization notes that the plague has a high fatality rate, but is also easily treated with antibiotics if caught early.

title: Workshop maps next steps for outdoor recreation in Jay region
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — More year-round, outdoor events throughout Jay, Livermore and Livermore Falls was the priority for the more than 40 people who participated in a two-day regional workshop Sept. 30 and Oct. 1.
The Recreation Economy for Rural Communities workshop at Spruce Mountain Ski Slope brought together residents and local, state, regional and federal partners to review recreation assets, assess work already underway and identify resources and next steps for future projects.
Participants worked systematically from reviewing outdoor recreation assets and community progress to identifying current priorities and resources that could support specific strategies, according to Shelley Kruszewski, regional planner with the Androscoggin Valley Council of Governments.
Examples of work already underway included upgrades at Spruce Mountain Ski Slope and the Androscoggin Land Trust’s regional wayfinding project.
The resulting action-plan priorities are organized around three broad areas: growing local capacity, developing outdoor and downtown events and experiences, and continuing to improve year-round access to outdoor recreation amenities across the three-town region.
The workshop was built on the 2025 Recreation and Facilities Master Plan for Jay, Livermore and Livermore Falls, which identified opportunities to improve recreation facilities, strengthen connections among destinations and use outdoor recreation as part of a broader regional economic development strategy.
Before the workshop, Kruszewski said the workshop process was intended to move that planning into more detailed action steps, including timelines, milestones, financial and staffing needs, responsibilities and other work needed to advance projects.
“Emphasis will be on near term and implementable next steps needed to move forward,” Kruszewski said.
Participants also examined how individual recreation sites could complement one another as part of a connected regional network rather than operate as isolated facilities.
Projects and destinations previously identified for discussion included the Livermore Falls Recreation Area, French Falls, Area Youth Sports, Spruce Mountain Ski Slope and Spruce Mountain Conservation Area.
The workshop included a community tour during which members of the workshop steering committee and federal, regional and state partners examined recreation and downtown connections firsthand.
In Livermore Falls, participants discussed ways outdoor recreation could connect with the downtown. At the Jay Recreation Area, they discussed trail connections and opportunities for outdoor programming.
Those discussions reflected a broader goal of the workshop: connecting recreation assets with town centers and creating opportunities for residents and visitors to move between trails, recreation areas, businesses and downtown destinations.
“The workshop will also provide the opportunity to focus attention on placemaking and how outdoor recreation connects to the town centers,” Kruszewski said before the event.
The workshop also gave community members an opportunity to speak directly with agencies and organizations that may be able to help identify technical assistance, partnerships and potential funding sources.
“The value of having these partners at the table is that they can hear directly from the communities about their priorities and help identify technical assistance, funding programs, partnerships or other resources that may align with those goals,” Kruszewski said.
The Recreation Economy for Rural Communities program does not directly provide project funding. Participation, however, connects communities with government agencies, technical resources, other communities pursuing similar projects and potential funding programs. Kruszewski previously said some funding opportunities are limited to communities participating in the program.
The federal planning assistance program focuses on helping rural communities strengthen outdoor recreation economies while supporting Main Street revitalization.
The program involves the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, USDA Forest Service, Northern Border Regional Commission, Appalachian Regional Commission and Denali Commission. Holly Fowler of Northbound Ventures Consulting is facilitating the local process, while Androscoggin Valley Council of Governments is coordinating with the three towns and the local steering committee.
The work also overlaps with a Tri-Town recreation branding and wayfinding project that grew out of the 2025 master plan.
Members of the Tri-Town Recreation Committee and steering committee previously supported a successful Rural Investment Project Grant application to create cohesive regional branding and wayfinding signs for recreation destinations. The Androscoggin Land Trust is leading that project.
The master plan identified promotion of key recreation areas, improved signs, co-branding and wayfinding as priorities.
The workshop’s action planning will continue beyond the two-day session. Organizers previously said the draft action plan would be refined through three post-workshop calls that will also be open to participants.
“The community’s input during the workshop becomes the centerpiece of the final deliverable of the planning process,” Kruszewski said.
She had also stressed before the workshop that local participation would be central to the process.
“This is a community-driven process,” Kruszewski said. “It only works if the community comes and shares their input.”

title: Dexter house fire caused by improperly disposed smoking materials
text:
DEXTER, Maine (WABI) - Improper disposal of smoking materials caused a house fire in Dexter over the weekend and has been ruled accidental, according to the State Fire Marshal’s Office.
The fire happened just after 2:30 p.m. Saturday on Line Road.
Firefighters arrived to find fire in a second-floor bedroom and quickly put it out. The remainder of the home sustained smoke damage.
The State Fire Marshal’s Office says the homeowner, a 40-year-old woman, escaped the home. She was taken to a local hospital for smoke inhalation and other injuries.
Officials say a dog died in the fire.
The Corinna, Garland, Hartland, St. Albans, and Newport Fire Departments provided mutual aid to the Dexter Fire Department.
No other injuries were reported.

title: Pres. Trump promises checks for seniors
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is promising government payments to senior citizens, with just a month to go until the midterm elections.
It’s a move aimed at helping those on Medicare, so the president is promising $90 checks to more than 20 million seniors.
The White House said the $90 payments for seniors will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund. Medicare Part B enrollees can expect to receive a one-time payment sometime this month - either by direct deposit - or by a check in the mail.
To be eligible, seniors must be living in the U.S. and not be already receiving premium assistance from Medicaid.
In addition, seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage are also not eligible for the payment.
Senator Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) accused the president of trying to bribe the electorate. He issued a statement:
“This year, Trump handed seniors a $200 monthly Medicare premium for the first time ever, and he also shoveled $20 billion in extra payments to insurance companies selling private Medicare plans, This is another desperate attempt by a failed president to escape Americans’ revulsion with his failed agenda, amounting to one tank of Trump-inflated gas.”
President Trump has also promised to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. That payment - which would cost more than $1 trillion - would need approval from Congress, although the president has indicated he thinks he might be able to issue those checks without lawmakers approval.

title: Augusta Schools propose closing Hussey Elementary, expanding Farrington
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Augusta superintendent’s office has formally announced plans to close Hussey Elementary and expand Farrington Elementary, but the decision is ultimately up to local voters on election day.
The proposal calls for additions to Farrington Elementary and the closure of the Lillian Hussey School. The planned additions to Farrington include a universal pre-k model, 19 new classrooms and a designated STEM space.
The total cost of the project is about $53.5 million, to be reimbursed by the state. Superintendent Mike Tracy, of Augusta Schools, said construction would not be paid for by Augusta taxpayers.
Tracy said the project was approved under the state’s prior district funding model, making it the last project in Maine to qualify for full state reimbursement.
“I think it’s a once in a lifetime opportunity, especially with the law that just changed where local towns will have to have a local share for any future building projects,” Tracy said. “So, the fact that we’re on the last project at 100% state funded is a really big deal.”
The new state rule requiring a local contribution started July 1.
If approved, the district says construction would begin in summer 2028 and finish in summer 2030.

title: This program promotes reading for kids before they get into kindergarten
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - A Missouri six-year-old is reading more books than many people read in a lifetime.
Pew Research in the past found that the average American reads about 12 books a year. An elementary student outside of St. Louis crushed this number by reading 1,000 books before he entered kindergarten.
Malachi Henderson, 6, started kindergarten in the fall, shortly after completing the 1,000 Books Before Kindergarten program at the St. Louis County Library.
The program is designed to encourage childhood literacy through reading amongst caregivers and children.
The program encourages reading by allowing families to track each and every book. And the more books you read, the better the prizes get.
“If we can get children excited about reading and thinking it’s something fun that they want to do when they’re young, they’ll keep striving as they are learning, even when it is a little bit difficult,” said Laura Polak, who helps run the program for the library system. “By third grade, they’re learning by reading, so building this foundation early on really sets children up for future success.”
Childhood literacy is a critical predictor of long-term academic and life success.
Studies have shown that third graders not reading at grade level are four times more likely to drop out of high school. Lower proficiency in reading can also lead to lower income, poor health outcomes, and even higher incarceration rates.
Malachi’s mom, Angel Dallas, said as a child she often observed her own mother reading around the house.
“I grew up in a home where we had books and things to read and we were always at the library and I always saw my mom reading and it was just very inspiring to me at a young age,” said Dallas.
So, when Dallas was pregnant with Malachi, she began reading to him. Once he was born, she discovered the library’s program and slowly began crossing books off the list.
When Malachi was three-years-old, he was reading on his own, she said.
“Reading is the foundation for every other subject possible and that’s why it was always important for me for Malachi to know how to read, to recognize words to know different words,” she said. “His language is also advanced and teachers are telling me that he’s on track to be in the gifted program when he gets into elementary school.”
Malachi and his mother now share the same passion for reading, always making room for a new book on the shelf.
Hundreds of libraries nationwide participate in the program and you can find a list of branches in your state as well as resource to start the journey at home on 1000booksbeforekindergarten.org.
