title: New Supreme Court term begins with cases on climate change, immigration and gun rights
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court’s new term begins Monday with cases on climate change, religious rights and President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration high on the agenda.
Here’s a look at what’s in store:
Climate change
The high court is starting its term with a major climate change case. The justices will hear an appeal from energy companies trying to block dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold them liable in court for damage related to climate change.
Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in a case out of Boulder, Colorado, where local officials say the industry should help shoulder the escalating costs of disasters linked to climate change.
The companies, Suncor and ExxonMobil, say lawsuits aren’t the way to deal with the global issue. They have the backing of the Trump administration, which argues the litigation is a power grab intended to impose regulations on emissions.
Assault weapons bans
About a dozen states have banned semiautomatic rifles like AR-15s, which are often called assault weapons. They say the guns are disproportionately used in mass shootings, and banning them helps reduce gun violence.
Challengers say those laws violate the Second Amendment. They argue that AR-15s and other similar weapons are among the most popular and commonly owned guns in the country.
The conservative-majority court has expanded gun rights in recent years, and four justices had signaled that it was only a matter of time before the court took up the issue. The case will be considered in December.
Immigration
The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump’s wide-reaching crackdown.
One is about deportations of migrants who can’t be quickly sent back to their home countries. The Trump administration has been sending thousands to other countries where they have no ties, under a series of often-secret agreements.
The Supreme Court will consider overturning lower court orders allowing them a chance to object. The justices have allowed the flights to continue in the meantime.
The other case is over the administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants who have been living in the U.S. illegally, even if they’ve been in the country for years.
The administration argues it can hold people without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have considered the issue disagree.
Voting
A Republican push to enforce strict Arizona voting laws will also come before the justices this term.
One measure requires people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form, and another calls for regular purges of the voter rolls to remove people if their citizenship could not be confirmed.
It comes as Trump has failed to get legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for registering to vote through Congress. Arguments are set for December.
Religious rights
Catholic preschools that can’t take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November. It’s the justices’ latest case involving religious rights.
St. Mary Catholic Parish says it’s been left out of the state’s universal preschool program over its faith-based admissions policies, which exclude kids from LGBTQ+ families.
Colorado says religious schools are welcome to participate but have to follow nondiscrimination laws. The program was created by a 2020 ballot measure and provides public funding for preschool at schools selected by parents.

title: Woman dies after stopping to help driver of flipped car on interstate
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A New Orleans woman died after she stopped to pull a trapped driver from a flipped car on Interstate 10 and was struck by another vehicle, according to her family.
Ka’Sheena Daniels, 31, died Sept. 25 on westbound I-10 near Elysian Fields Avenue after helping free a driver she recognized as her neighbor, said Franchon Williams, a friend who was with her.
New Orleans police said the crash began when a speeding car made a sudden lane change and flipped, prompting several drivers to stop and help the trapped driver.
Police said another vehicle then struck one of the stopped cars, pushing it into the crowd of people who had gathered to help. Multiple people were hurt, but Daniels was the only person who died.
Daniels was born and raised in New Orleans, had just celebrated a birthday and was raising her adopted son, Noah, while working in accounting, according to her mother, O’Sheenana Daniels.
“She just was that girl,” O’Sheenana Daniels said in an interview Friday. “If you needed help...and she could do it, it was done.”
Daniels left New Orleans East last Friday night to go out with close friends. The group saw a flipped car on the interstate, and Williams said Daniels recognized the driver as her neighbor.
“We see the lady. We try to help her out. My friend KK jumped out,” Williams said, referring to Daniels.
Williams said her friend pulled the woman out of the car and that only a few moments passed before Daniels was struck, causing her to fall from the interstate.
“(We’re) looking for my friend. (We’re) looking up under the cars, everywhere, and then they told me, like, ‘Well, y’all, somebody went over,’” Williams said. “They put their flashlight down there. It’s my friend. She’s just down there.”
O’Sheenana Daniels said she helped authorities locate her daughter after the crash.
“I started screaming my (baby’s) name, and she said, ‘Ma,” O’Sheenana Daniels said. “When they heard her say that, they ran where...she was calling from.”
O’Sheenana Daniels said she can’t believe her daughter’s death and struggles with the circumstances surrounding it.
“It’s sad to say, but I wish she just never would have helped (anybody),” O’Sheenana Daniels said. “I just wish she would have just kept on going about her business.”
Williams said she and Daniels had planned to start paramedic school next week. Williams said she will pursue that goal in her friend’s honor.
New Orleans police said the investigation is ongoing. Daniels’ family has set up a GoFundMe to pay for her funeral.

Obama to appear with El-Sayed in Detroit as the ex-president gets more involved in the midterms
text:
Obama to appear with El-Sayed in Detroit as the ex-president gets more involved in the midterms
Former President Barack Obama will campaign alongside Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit later this month, lending his support to the progressive nominee after a bruising Democratic primary exposed divisions within the party.
Obama will appear with El-Sayed at an Oct. 24 rally that will also feature other top Democratic candidates in Michigan, including Jocelyn Benson, the party's nominee for governor. Obama is getting significantly more involved in the midterm elections, with additional campaign stops and advertisements expected to come in the closing weeks, according to plans shared first with The Associated Press.
The Detroit event is a notable show of support for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in an August primary and has since worked to consolidate Democratic support in his race against Republican Mike Rogers. The open seat is expected to be among a handful that will decide which party controls the majority next year.
Obama taped two dozen ads last week for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate that will be released in the coming days and weeks, in addition to more campaign stops soon to be announced.
He appeared earlier this year in a campaign ad with Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek and campaigned in Texas with Senate candidate James Talarico and the candidate for governor, Gina Hinojosa. This week, he will headline a Washington fundraiser supporting Democratic Senate candidates.
Obama aims to help El-Sayed shore up support in a key area
El-Sayed defeated Stevens by less than a percentage point in a primary that became a national test of the Democratic Party's ideological direction. El-Sayed drew support from leading progressives, including Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders and Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Stevens was backed by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.
Some ads that supported Stevens showed Obama praising her, and she outperformed El-Sayed in Wayne County, winning about 51% of the Democratic primary vote compared with 45% for El-Sayed. The county includes Detroit, where more than three-quarters of residents are Black.
Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian person to serve as vice president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month.
Now the Oct. 24 rally with Obama, the first Black president, could give El-Sayed a boost on the first day of Michigan's required early in-person voting period. Obama spoke with El-Sayed by phone following his primary victory.
It will also be a boost for the other candidates in what is one of the most consequential elections in recent Michigan history. There are open races for governor, secretary of state and attorney general, in addition to control of the state legislature being at play.
Benson, who will also appear with Obama, is facing Republican Rep. John James in the race for governor.
Benson and James are set to debate for the first time on Tuesday, and El-Sayed and Rogers are scheduled to debate for the first time on Oct. 8.
Obama returns to the campaign trail for the closing stretch
Obama has been selective in his involvement in the midterms so far, but his planned ramp-up in the final weeks follows a pattern from recent elections. He campaigned in Detroit on Oct. 22 during the 2024 presidential election and was in the city Oct. 29 during the 2022 midterms.
His campaign appearances can draw large crowds and prominent guests. Rapper Eminem introduced Obama at his Detroit rally in 2024.
This week, he will headline an event with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee that will include a conversation with Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester. That follows a September event with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

title: Portland man sentenced for killing roommate
text:
Portland man sentenced for killing roommate
Domingus Nobrega pleaded guilty to killing his roommate Matthew Merrick in November 2024
Portland man sentenced for killing roommate
Domingus Nobrega pleaded guilty to killing his roommate Matthew Merrick in November 2024
Domingus Nobrega has been sentenced to 16 years in prison for killing his roommate Matthew Merrick in November 2024.
"I’m glad it’s done and he is going to jail," Merrick’s mother, Debra Kelly, said following the sentencing hearing in Cumberland County Court on Monday.
Prosecutors initially charged Nobrega with murder but agreed to drop the charge as part of a plea deal that was reached in August. Nobrega pleaded guilty to manslaughter instead. Prosecutors said a key witness in the case died, limiting the state’s ability to take it to trial.
In Maine, murder carries a minimum sentence of 25 years with the possibility of life in prison. Manslaughter carries a maximum sentence of 30 years.
Nobrega’s defense attorneys and Kelly were pleased with the outcome.
"He won't be hurting anybody else," Kelly said. "It took so long to get to this point, but I'm really glad it did and really thankful for the people that helped me."
During the hearing, the prosecutor asked the judge to require Nobrega to make a payment to the Victims’ Compensation Fund. The state hadn't discussed restitution during the plea agreement because the deal came together quickly. As a result, the judge denied the request.
The fund helps victims and their family members manage unexpected costs that arise as a result of a crime. In this case, it reimbursed Kelly for Merrick’s funeral expenses.
"You don't expect to pay to have your son or daughter be buried before you," Kelly said.
Kelly said she was grateful for the financial assistance and support from the court’s victim advocate, who helped her navigate the process.
"It’s like she’s part of my family now," Kelly said. "I could sit there and cry by myself, but she was there to help me stand up."
According to Maine law, the distinction between murder and manslaughter involves a defendant’s state of mind, whether the killing was intentional and whether the defendant was provoked. Those factors can make a murder charge more difficult to prove in court.

title: Unusual arrival. Why a transatlantic flight made a rare landing in Portland, Maine
text:
Unusual arrival. A transatlantic flight made a rare landing in Portland, Maine
Traffic at the Portland International Jetport continues to increase, but Sunday brought an unusual arrival - an international passenger flight with an unusually large plane for Portland.
A United Airlines flight from Edinburgh, Scotland, was headed to Washington Dulles International Airport, but dealt with stronger headwinds crossing the Atlantic Ocean than anticipated, causing the plane to use more fuel than expected.
The Boeing 757-200 had to divert to Portland to get more fuel, landing at about 4:15 p.m.
While FedEx does use 757s in Portland, the Airbus A321 is typically the largest passenger aircraft to serve Portland. The 757-200 is nine feet longer than the A321, though both have similar seating capacity and the 757 has a slightly wider cabin.
The 757 is also about six feet taller than the A321. Because of the aircraft’s additional height, a scissor lift was needed for refueling. Crews added about 5,000 gallons of fuel to the plane while the passengers remained on board.
Because the plane was refueled while passengers were on board, the Portland Fire Department Red Units from the Jetport stood by.
Once refueling was complete, Flight 979 left the Jetport and continued on to Washington Dulles.
The plane was on the ground in Portland for just over an hour.
There has not been regularly scheduled international service to the Portland International Jetport since 2013, when Air Canada ended its service between Portland and Toronto.

title: Maine’s volunteer libraries thrive with tight budgets. State rules could make that harder.
text:
STANDISH — Lynn Knowlton was ecstatic about a new furnace.
As president of the Richville Library, she waited eagerly on a recent Saturday morning for volunteers to help her install the contraption in the basement of the cozy, pale yellow building.
She bought the furnace with surprise cash donations from community members who wanted to help replace the outdated electric heating system that has strained the 103-year-old institution’s shoestring budget for years.
“I can’t stop happy dancing,” Knowlton said.
For all-volunteer-run libraries like this one, unexpected funding that helps serve their communities is a thrill.
What thrills them less is a proposed set of rules the Maine Library Commission is considering that would cut off their access to some state-provided services — internet, subsidized interlibrary loans, and the ability to receive grants through the Maine Public Library Fund — unless they pay their director, are open an average of 12 hours a week year-round, and participate in a specific number of professional development opportunities.
While the Richville Library serves Standish’s rural population of 11,000, other similar libraries in Maine are in more remote areas with even smaller communities, some of fewer than 1,000 people. They provide free internet, books, technology, regular programs and gathering spaces to small towns that otherwise don’t have them. Most run on annual budgets of less than $10,000, bolstered by fundraising, donations and grants. Some get annual help from their towns, usually $2,000 to $4,000.
Rural librarians say the measures would damage their libraries and communities. According to an impact assessment by the Maine State Library, 38 of approximately 257 public libraries in Maine do not currently meet the proposed standards.
The state commission began considering standards for libraries last November, but has eased its proposition over the past year in response to backlash. It voted to send its most recent draft for legal review in September.
Maine State Librarian Lori Stockman responded to requests for interviews sent to her and other state library leaders by explaining that they are “hesitant to say much” before the draft is finalized and public comment opens later this month.
Increasing costs and uncertain funding for the Maine State Library loom behind the rule’s efforts, said Chair Bryce Cundick at a commission meeting in January. The state agency laid off a third of its staff after federal funding cuts to the Institute of Museum and Library Services by the Trump administration in April 2025, but later regained some money and employees.
Money isn’t the only issue. Commission members and state librarians have also repeated that the requirements introduced would help ensure the quality of Maine’s libraries. Commission member Wynter Giddings said at the April meeting that paid staff leads to “sustainability” and “accountability” in libraries. Additional measures in the draft include requiring libraries to keep strategic plans.
Beyond Maine law stating a basic definition for public libraries, these standards would be the first set for libraries in Maine.
That has spurred frustration among volunteer librarians.
Dylan Johnston, head librarian and one of two volunteers at the East Millinocket Public Library, which serves a population of just over 1,500 from a town-owned building, said he thinks the push to disqualify them from state resources stems from a perception that their operations are not competent or valuable. Several other librarians have echoed that concern.
The process has raised questions about what it means to have a library and a librarian — many professional librarian roles require a master’s degree in library science.
“It’s very demeaning and deflating,” Johnston said. “This library has faced several challenges along the years, but I’ve kept it going. I’m an invaluable service.”
The library recently received a $50,000 grant from the Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation to purchase several pieces of furniture, a new sign and renovate the children’s area. Johnston said he helps people with technology issues and hosts a weekly group for older adults to give them a place to congregate.
Carol Wolf is the volunteer vice president of the Pembroke Library in Pembroke, one of the five libraries that would lose interlibrary loan services under the measures. She said it is not in the library’s budget to pay a director.
“Just because (libraries) don’t meet these direct criteria that the library commission wants to impose, does not seem to me to mean that they’re not effective libraries,” Wolf said. “This rule just doesn’t comport with reality in these small towns.”
Wolf is leading an effort to support small libraries, reverse the course of the rule, and try and get more representatives of rural libraries in northern Maine to apply for seats on the Maine Library Commission. Of the 26 seats, five are vacant, and no members are from north of Bangor. Members are appointed by the governor.
Losing internet access is the biggest threat for Johnston and other rural libraries, which could have to scramble to find the money to pay for it. Their current connectivity comes through NetworkMaine, which provides internet to most of Maine’s K-12 public schools and libraries. While NetworkMaine is state-provided, the federal service E-Rate covers roughly 70% of its costs.
One standard Maine already has in place mandates that libraries requesting subsidized interlibrary loan van delivery services must circulate more than 100 materials through the system per year to qualify.
According to a list compiled by Sarah Redfield, a lawyer in York who has voiced opposition to the rule, five libraries would be taken off the interlibrary loan route. Most rural libraries, including Richville and East Millinocket, don’t use the service.
Stockman, the state librarian, did not respond to requests for information about how much of the state library’s budget is used for NetworkMaine and interlibrary loan services for the potentially impacted libraries.
Karen MacGillivary is the volunteer director at the Laura E. Richards Library in Georgetown, a former one-room schoolhouse on a hill. The snowplow can’t reach the building and it lacks running water, forcing it to close in the winter months. It hosts what MacGillivary calls “Blizzard Books,” where patrons can sign out as many books as they want in October and exchange them with other community members until spring. She said circulation this past season increased by 200 books.
“It’s a happy place,” she said.
MacGillivary worries about the financial consequences of losing internet — many patrons come to the library just for that, and she does not know how the library would fund it alone.
The proposed rules are under review by the Office of the Maine Attorney General and the Department of the Secretary of State, and a 45-day public comment period is expected to open Thursday, with a public hearing on Oct. 29.
The commission will then respond to comments and decide whether to incorporate them at its January meeting. If the rules are implemented, libraries would have two years to start paying directors, with the option of requesting extensions.
Stockman emphasized that state law passed in 2011 mandates the commission to name minimum standards of library service, and the attorney general’s office advised it to create enforceable rules. However, the law does not specify what standards must be in place.
The current draft also does not specify how much libraries would need to pay directors. If the current draft were implemented as is, libraries could meet the requirement with a salary of as little as $1.
At a March commission meeting, Cundick said that the proposed measures should have been established much earlier. According to the state’s impact assessment, 44 states have established standards for libraries tied to eligibility for state resources.
Considering Maine’s long history of thriving small rural libraries that rely on state services, opponents say they believe the state should work to support them.
Six volunteers keep the Richville Library flourishing. Knowlton’s mother, Karen McNutt, is the director. Her father, David McNutt, is the treasurer, and her late grandmother was one of the young Standish girls in the Osmunda Club that began collecting books to create the library in the 1920s. Knowlton grew up in the house across the street, where her son now lives.
The library doubled its open hours to 13 a week in the past two years, and has expanded free programming to include American Sign Language classes, Red Cross trainings, a creative writer’s circle, multiple book clubs and more story times.
“There’s a lot of spirit still there in that place,” Karen McNutt said. “It’s pretty amazing.”
Knowlton and volunteers authored a laminated book of detailed biographical information about each of the Richville’s founders and its history. They work hard to make sure the library prospers.
“I’ve just gotten taken in by some of these stories and the commitments that people have, you know, for generations,” said Redfield, the lawyer pushing back on the proposed rules. “What I see is this direction to try to have all Maine libraries look alike, which is not what Maine is about.”

title: FBI arrests woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader's family for China
text:
FBI arrests woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader's family for China
The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport as she was leaving the country, and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president's family for China.
Related video: Thousands of US troops heading to the Mideast amid uncertainty about war's direction
Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI.
Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges of working for China as an unregistered agent, Assistant U.S. State Attorney Bill Essayli announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said.
Zhang was arrested as she was departing for China. Her nationality was not clear, and an attorney who represents her could not be determined. She was due to appear Monday in federal court in Los Angeles.
Taiwan’s Presidential Office confirmed President Lai Ching-te’s relatives were the targets, without specifying if it was the president’s son or other family members, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression.”
“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts — which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families — as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday, and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing was closed for the holidays.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, but Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory. Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and Beijing do not belong to each other and that the “People's Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan.”
China considers him a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace.”
While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan, notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.

title: When the university talks about a $19 million deficit, students deserve to know what comes next
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OPINION: The University of Maine is facing a projected $19 million structural budget gap, and faculty retrenchments and staff layoffs are expected to be part of the university’s response.
What does this mean for us students?
In their Sept. 17 letter to faculty and staff, the Office of the President said that operating costs have grown faster than appropriations and tuition revenue. The letter also discussed enrollment pressures, changes in federal funding, financial aid and international student enrollment, as well as the costs associated with addressing deferred maintenance. These are the main ways our university’s budget deficit got to $19 million.
A faculty position is a professor who teaches a class. A staff position can be an academic adviser, an administrator, someone who supports student organizations or a person who keeps a campus service running. When those positions disappear, students experience the consequences. The university still has yet to announce the number of faculty or staff positions that will ultimately be eliminated, nor has it determined when the affected employees will receive notice.
That uncertainty is why students deserve more information.
UMaine has said it will continue developing the FY28 budget through the fall, submit a draft to the University of Maine System (UMS) in January and hold a budget town hall in October. Students should show up.
Most of us don’t need to understand every line of a university budget, but we do need to understand that we are directly affected by the decisions being made. Students pay tuition. We choose where to live, what program to study and where to spend four or more years of our lives based partly on what a university promises to provide.
If the university is considering closing programs, changing course availability or reducing personnel, students deserve to understand how those decisions will affect the education we are paying for. We deserve transparency.
Students should be asking what assumptions produced the projected deficit. We should be asking how different areas of the university will be evaluated. We should be asking what criteria will determine whether a program is considered underenrolled. We should be asking what alternatives were considered before positions are eliminated. Most importantly, we should be asking how the university plans to protect the quality of a student’s education while reducing its workforce. A university is made up of people. That support is part of what we’re paying for.
As UMaine moves toward its FY28 budget, students should not have to wait until a class disappears from their schedule or a familiar professor is suddenly gone to find out what the university’s financial decisions mean for them. The $19 million figure may be the headline, but for students the most important part is what comes after it. We deserve to know what comes next.

title: Kayaker catches shark, gets bitten twice while trying to release it

title: Bangor considering a new rebate program that could reduce home energy costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangor City Council may implement a new climate rebate program that would help households save money on their energy bills by adding heat pumps, solar power and weatherization features to homes.
That could provide needed assistance as Mainers’ concerns around energy costs are more intense than ever going into the winter. Heating oil prices in the state are 80% higher than last year and hit a record $6.02 per gallon two weeks ago as the Iran War rages on.
The proposed climate rebate program would be part of the Penobscot Climate Action Plan, a regional plan approved by Bangor and ten other communities two years ago with the goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and improving resilience to the effects of climate change.
It would do so by allocating $50,000 in climate action plan funds for rebates. Households could apply to receive roughly $2,000, Planning Officer Anja Collette reported at a Monday night meeting of the Bangor council’s business and economic development committee.
Helping those residents retrofit their homes would help reduce emissions and “also has a very high potential to help residents be more resilient to power outages and things like that, and also high fuel costs,” Collette said.
Heat pumps would be most helpful for households using heating oil, and solar power would be most helpful to those using electric heating, according to a memo from the city’s planning division. Weatherization would help save costs for all households.
The city has access to about $200,000 in climate action plan funds through the federal government, Collette said in response to a question from Councilor Wayne Mallar.
If approved, the climate rebates would build on existing assistance programs offered through the quasi-state agency Efficiency Maine and the city’s community development block grant program by providing “gap financing” for costs not covered by those other programs, according to the memo.
The proposal suggests offering a tiered rebate system based on income that would give higher rebates to lower income residents.
City councilors seemed supportive of the proposal. City staff plan to determine more details of the proposed program in the next month.
The city might also consider using some of the funding to help residents buy plug-in solar panels, which could also help renters, Collette told the committee.

title: Supreme Court declines to take up Maine lobster boat tracking appeal
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a Maine lobsterman’s legal challenge to an electronic vessel tracker requirement, putting an end to the multi-year lawsuit.
In an order Monday, the court denied a request to take up the appeal by Frank Thompson, a Vinalhaven lobsterman.
In a statement, Maine Department of Marine Resources Commissioner Carl Wilson said the department believes the tracking data is critically important to the long-term sustainability of the lobster fishery.
“It will inform the lobster stock assessment, enhance offshore enforcement and support better decision-making in a range of federal management contexts,” Wilson said.
Thompson’s attorney, Matthew Gilliam with Pacific Legal Foundation, said in a statement that the denial does not diminish the importance of the issues in the suit.
“Forcing lobstermen to carry a GPS tracker on their private boats and submit to around-the-clock surveillance as a condition of keeping their license remains a serious constitutional concern,” Gilliam said. “We are committed to fighting for Fourth Amendment protections from government overreach and we will continue to pursue every lawful avenue to protect individual rights.”
At the center of the case is a 2023 requirement that all federally licensed lobster vessels must operate GPS trackers. The rule was passed by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, and implemented by the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
Thompson sued DMR Commissioner Carl Wilson in federal court when the rule went into effect in 2024, arguing that the tracking constituted an unreasonable search and seizure and violated his constitutional rights.
But federal judges were not persuaded. The lawsuit was dismissed by the district court, and that ruling was upheld by the First Circuit Court of Appeals last year. With the Supreme Court declining to intervene, the First Circuit ruling is the final order in the suit.
The Conservation Law Foundation previously filed an amicus brief in the case, supporting the regulations and arguing that it is legal and vital to track lobster boats to ensure effective management of the industry.
“New England’s lobster population has declined dangerously,” Conservation Law Foundation Associate Attorney Sarah Shahabi said in a statement. “Tracking lobster boats provides the timely and accurate data that regulators need. This decision is a valuable step toward appropriately managing this iconic species.”

title: Autumn is ideal for observing the natural world
text:
Fall is in the air. As Earth makes its annual pilgrimage around the sun, our 23.5-degree tilt relative to the plane of orbit contributes to our days getting shorter.
This lower-angle, low-intensity light is beloved by photographers and artists. Gone is the harsh, overhead, summer light that flattens landscape details; instead, this increasingly horizontal, directional light travels through the atmosphere, scattering much of the blue wavelength light, allowing the richer amber, gold, and red hues to dominate. Elongated autumnal shades offer more nuanced contrast, adding a vivid edge to colors, affording a dramatic, dimensional quality to the landscape.
This changing light also triggers changes in the natural world.
For example, decreasing daylight affects hormone production in mammals, signaling them to prepare for winter. Squirrels exemplify this as they furiously cache food for the coming winter. Black Bears gorge to build extensive fat stores to see them through their winter’s hibernation. Most local terrestrial mammals grow a thicker fur to insulate against plunging temperatures.
Decreasing daylight triggers multiple responses in birds. First, they undergo prebasic molt. Over a course of time ranging from weeks to months, they replace every worn-out, frayed, or broken feather with new plumage. This provides fresh insulation and, more importantly, enhances flight efficiency, directly making possible fall migration.
Migration takes incredible reserves of energy. Migratory birds feed during the day, some adding 50% to their body weight, only to burn through all of that energy to fuel their night’s migration. Songbirds take to the skies as the sun sets, average 100-250 miles, then, as the sun rises, land to forage once again.
Songbirds evolved the habit of night migration to take advantage of the lack of thermals, those rising columns of warm air favored by daytime migrants, especially raptors. An absence of thermals means less turbulence and smoother long-distance flight. Cooler night air helps prevent those small-bodied fliers from overheating during the continuous exertion required of long-distance flight. And then there is the fact that nearly all winged predators are raptors that fly almost exclusively during the day.
Night migration is something we can directly witness. Although there is some level of migration nearly year-round, it peaks in September and October. Nearly 10 million birds cross our state during a single night at the peak of migration. Such concentrations of birds in flight readily shows up on weather radar.
When radar came into practical use during World War II, British operators saw mysterious, unexplainable blobs on their screens, nicknaming them “angels.” In a 1945 issue of the journal “Nature,” David Lack and George Varley published a foundational article identifying the “angels” as birds. Today, Cornell Laboratory of Ornithology’s BirdCast.org is a data-based website that analyzes and presents bird migration data derived from the U.S. National Weather Service’s network of Doppler weather radar in near real time. If you are curious about the phenomenon of bird migration, spend some time checking out the website.
These days, the landscape being awash in color. Everywhere we look, the colorful canopy of our maple and birch and beech forests is the direct result of shortening daylength.
During the growing season, leaves make large amounts of chlorophyll to capture sunlight for energy. Chlorophyll is a naturally green pigment. This time of year, the shortened days and cooler temperatures break down chlorophyll. Another pigment, carotenoids, expresses in yellows and oranges. These pigments, always present, are masked by chlorophyll. As chlorophyll breaks down, the carotenoid pigments are expressed. Reds and purples are the color of anthocyanins, which are made in the fall as remaining sugars, trapped by cool air inside the leaves, reacts with sunlight. And then there are the tannins, which impart a brown color to leaves (especially oaks) after the other pigments fade.
On a sunny day, walking through a glade of birch and beech is to be treated to a golden glow, the effect of which is only enhanced by the low-angle ambient lighting. This is especially true where the newly refurbished Hemlock Trail skirts the northwest corner of Great Meadow — what is today a glorious hedgerow was initially created under the direction of George B. Dorr as a road to improve access to Sieur de Monts Spring.
The last few weeks, any walk in the woods (or in your dooryard, for that matter) reveals a panoply of fungi, with mushrooms most evident. Although found throughout the growing season, the cooler temperatures, morning fog, and soaking rains of autumn trigger the emergence of diverse fungi (the “rain rule” posits that most wild funguses begin to pop up 2-10 days after a soaking rain).
Fungi belong to their own Kingdom: Fungi. Mushrooms are merely the most visible form of fungi; specifically, they are the fruiting bodies of the otherwise mostly subterranean mycelial network.
The question of whether fungi are primitive or not is complex. Single-celled, thread-like fungal organisms are ancient. Mushrooms are a relatively modern evolutionary development, more closely related to animals than plants, with highly specialized communication networks.
These networks are expressed in the form of a complex underground network of mycelium. This root-like network of thready filaments partners with most plants across Maine, seamlessly intertwining with the plant’s roots in symbiotic relationships. Tiny threads of fungi wrap around tree roots in a mycorrhizal network. These mycorrhizal networks are the www of the plant and fungus world; that is, “wood wide web.” This network facilitates nutrient transfers and communicates important information to trees and plants about stressors such as changes in chemistry or attacks by pests and pathogens, among other things.
Fungi also serve a significant role as decomposers, breaking down fallen logs, dead twigs, and decaying leaves, ultimately recycling nutrients back into the soil.
Mushrooms can be as delectable as they can be deadly. Never eat a mushroom unless you are absolutely certain of its identification: many edible mushrooms closely resemble toxic ones. If you have eaten a mushroom and feel sick, call 911 or call poison control at 800-222-1222.
Fall is a wonderful time to explore the natural world.

title: Struggling UMaine football team fires offensive coordinator/quarterbacks coach
text:
The struggling University of Maine’s football team, which has one of the worst offenses among the 124 schools in the Football Championship Subdivision, has fired offensive coordinator/quarterbacks coach Mikahael Waters according to WFVX Fox 22/WVII ABC 7 sports director Jack Webb.
He is being replaced by running backs coach Sean Green, the former state championship-winning head coach at Portland and Cape Elizabeth High Schools.
He has also been the quarterbacks coach and involved in play-calling at the University of New England in Biddeford.
Head coach Jordan Stevens’ Black Bears are mired in a five-game losing streak and are 1-5 overall, 1-2 in the Coastal Athletic Conference.
Waters was in his eighth season on the UMaine staff, joining the staff in July of 2019 as the tight ends coach.
He spent four years in that capacity before moving on to coach the wide receivers.
He was elevated to the position of assistant special teams coordinator and pro liaison in the summer of 2022.
He became the special teams coordinator a year later and, in March of 2024, he was named the offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach.
In 2025, the Black Bears averaged 54 rushing yards per game more than in 2024 and they averaged 29.5 points per game in the CAA, the most by a UMaine offense in 10 years.
This season has been an offensive nightmare even though the Black Bears returned four starters in the interior offensive line, a tight end and running backs Rashawn Marshall, a Phil Steele Freshman All-American in 2025, and Nick Laughlin.
However, UMaine does have two inexperienced quarterbacks in Eddie Buehler and Caden Drezek and both have been inconsistent while also being victimized by several drops by their receivers and the inability to establish a consistent running game.
Buehler has seen the vast majority of playing time, starting the first five games before the two split Saturday’s game, a 24-16 loss to CAA newcomer Sacred Heart (Connecticut).
The Black Bears are currently 109th or worse in six offensive categories: points per game (14.5, 118th), total yards per game (270.2, 115th), passing completion percentage (52%, 113th), rushing yards per game (96, 110th), fourth down conversion rate (26.7%, 109th) and passing yards per completion (10.25, 109th).
UMaine is also ranked 97th in time of possession (28 minutes per game), 93rd in passing yards per contest (174.2), 90th in third down conversions (33%) and tied for 85th in first downs with 89.
UMaine has next weekend off and will return to action on Saturday, Oct. 17 when it hosts CAA rival Bryant (RI) at 1 p.m. at Morse Field in Alfond Stadium.

title: Tannerite was used to blow up vehicle in Readfield, officials say
text:
Tannerite was used to blow up vehicle in Readfield; Maine State Fire Marshal's Office investigating
The Maine State Fire Marshal's Office announced it is investigating an incident in Readfield, where Tannerite was used to blow up a vehicle.
The Readfield Fire Department responded to multiple reports of an explosion at 846 Main St. on Sept. 27, and found that a vehicle had been blown up with Tannerite.
Maine State Fire Marshal's Office investigators responded to Readfield and determined that a group of people had been shooting at Tannerite that had been placed in the vehicle.
Fire Marshal's Office investigators are working with the Kennebec County District Attorney's Office on any possible charges in connection with the incident.
In a news release about the explosion, the Fire Marshal's Office said it wanted to remind people that state law governing the use of Tannerite allows for up to 5 pounds of mixed product to be used for sport/target shooting only, and that Tannerite cannot be used to explode any item other than the packaging it is mixed in.
The investigation remains ongoing.

title: Sen. Susan Collins responds to Gov. Janet Mills’ calls to approve increased LIHEAP funding
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Sen. Susan Collins is supporting Gov. Janet Mills’ calls to Congress to approve increased LIHEAP funding.
On Friday, Mills sent a letter to Maine’s Congressional Delegation saying current funding is not keeping up with heating oil costs and did not factor in the price increase caused by the war in Iran.
The DOER said Maine consumes more residential heating oil per capita than any other state and significantly more per capita than the five other states in New England. Approximately 50% of all Maine households rely on fuel oil as their primary heat source, although that has declined steadily from a mark of 70% in 2010, according to the DOER. Last year, Maine households received more than $42 million in LIHEAP funding last year.
Sen. Collins has asked the federal government to release the maximum amount of funding for LIHEAP. The Trump administration has proposed zeroing out funding for the program, but Collins has continued her push to increase it. The Senate appropriations committee has pushed to continue funding at more than $4 million this year.
Sen. Collins says Maine needs alternative options for home heating. “I have always thought that we should build a pipeline to bring Shale Gas from Pennsylvania into Maine. Natural gas is cleaner than home heating oil, it is cleaner, and it is a good supplement,” she said.
Gov. Mills has urged Mainers who need assistance to apply for the program. Applications opened in August and will stay open until funding is exhausted.

title: Judge weighs what evidence jurors will hear in Maine sisters murder case
text:
SKOWHEGAN, Maine (WABI) - A judge will decide what evidence jurors can hear in the murder trial of a Garland woman accused of killing her sister.
Bonnie Coombs, 69, is charged with intentional or knowing murder in the April 2025 shooting death of her sister, Velma Withee, 78.
Prosecutors and defense attorneys appeared in a Somerset County courtroom Monday for a hearing on pretrial motions over admissible evidence.
Both sides agreed to exclude footage of Coombs’ arrest, calling it irrelevant to the case.
They remain divided on several other key issues, including:
- Prior arguments between Coombs and her sister and theft records
- Cell tower data prosecutors say contradicts Coombs’ account of her whereabouts. Defense attorneys argued the data missed discovery deadlines and requires expert analysis
- Gunshot residue evidence from the vehicle where Withee is believed to have been shot, with both sides seeking to challenge crime lab findings
The judge ordered both sides to submit supporting case law by the end of the week and then will issue a ruling after reviewing those filings.

title: Forest Service Receives Concerns Over LDA Landfill
text:
LIMESTONE, Maine (WAGM) - A complaint filed with the Maine Forest Service is bringing attention to a quarry burn site at Loring.
According to the Maine Forst Service, on Sept. 9th Limestone resident Robert Fico reported concerns about a burn pile at a quarry on Loring Air Force Base. Fico claimed the pile contained prohibited materials, including construction debris, fiberglass, mattresses, glass, and possibly engine parts. The Maine Forest Service says they have previously had issues with improper burning at that location. On Sept. 10th, Ranger Connor Hrynuk spoke with Fico, who claimed some debris may have come from contractors working on nearby housing.
Ranger Hrynuk instructed the Loring Development Authority’s CEO Jonathan Judkins to separate non-wood materials before any future burning and to conduct burns only at the designated location. Documents say Judkins told the ranger a roll-off dumpster would collect material that could not be burned and agreed to notify them before future burns. On Sept. 18Ranger Keith Draper reported that Judkins said the pile was ready for inspection. Draper later checked and confirmed that the pile had been separated.
In a statement Judkins said quote: “LDA owns a regulated Construction and Demolition Debris landfill. It is separate from the former Air Force/Superfund landfill areas at Loring and is not a public or municipal landfill. Household garbage and hazardous waste are not authorized for disposal there. LDA and our engineering consultant are working directly with Maine DEP regarding the landfill and the planned Manser Drive demolition project. That process includes regulatory controls governing demolition material, asbestos-containing material, transportation, documentation, placement, and covering of material. We are not aware of any authorized disposal of household garbage or hazardous waste at the LDA CDD landfill. If someone has specific information regarding suspected unauthorized dumping, we welcome that information so it can be investigated promptly.”
If you have information about unauthorized dumping on Loring, contact the LDA at 560-9496.

title: A $30 painting, found in ‘dark corner’ of estate sale, has fetched $1.35M at auction. Here's why
text:
$30 estate sale painting sells for $1.35M after being identified as lost Gertrude Abercrombie piece
An enigmatic oil painting bought for just $30 at an estate sale fetched more than $1.35 million at auction after it was confirmed to be the work of celebrated surrealist Gertrude Abercrombie.
The 8-by-11-inch still-life was discovered in a “dark corner” of a Michigan home in July, according to Freeman’s, the auction house that brought the painting to market this month. An expert has identified it as Abercrombie’s “Alderman Merriam’s Shells,” which had been unseen in public for almost 75 years.
Completed in 1951, the painting depicts a collection of ten seashells — a common motif used by Abercrombie, who is often described as American art’s “Bohemian Queen.” Over the next two years, it was exhibited at six of the painter’s solo exhibitions, then priced between $50 and $150.
But the artist never sold the work, instead gifting it to a doctor in Kalamazoo, Michigan in exchange for medical services. The mysterious painting was then passed down through the doctor’s estate following his death, before eventually appearing at July’s estate sale.
The lucky buyer, who has remained anonymous, is described by the auctioneer as “a longtime hunter of record albums and mid-century furniture.” Detailing the find, Freeman’s said the painting had been discovered “tucked in a dark corner of a hallway leading to the garage — overlooked by every other buyer that day.”
Upon seeing the signature (reading “Abercrombie, ‘51”), barely visible against the dark background, the buyer took a $30 gamble. According to Freeman’s, they then diverted a family vacation to visit Milwaukee Art Museum, where an Abercrombie exhibition was on show. There, in an exhibition catalog, a 1952 news clipping showed a photo of the painting next to the real-life shells it depicts.
The bargain hunter then took the artwork to Freeman’s auction house, which was one of the exhibition sponsors. Abercrombie expert Susan Weininger, an art history professor at Roosevelt University, later authenticated the work as genuine — and still in its original frame. The painting was subsequently cleaned by art restorer Julian Baumgartner, who, in a video documenting his work, described it as being in “perfect condition,” aside from some grime and clouded varnish on its surface.
“It was drab, missing its life, but now cleaned, retouched, and revarnished, it’s alive and radiant,” he said.
The painting had been valued by Freeman’s at $150,000 to $250,000, though bids at last Thursday’s sale far surpassed estimates, setting a new auction record for Abercrombie’s work. In 2025, Sotheby’s sold another of Abercrombie’s paintings, “Message for Mercy” for a then-record of $1.02 million, more than triple its high estimate.
A largely self-taught artist, Abercrombie, who died in 1977, was renowned for her otherworldly, dream-like compositions. She was also known for hosting legendary salons at her home, in Chicago’s Hyde Park, where jazz stars like Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker often performed.
Snail shells and seashells (along with owls, cats, mysterious doorways and, in her own words, “simple things that are a little strange”) were recurring themes of her work. They often appeared cracked or marked with holes and set against Abercrombie’s signature sparse backdrops, whether barren moonlit landscapes or deep black voids. Some of her other uncanny compositions placed shells beside cryptic flags and dominoes or, in cases like 1967’s “Snail Woman,” birthing abstracted female figures.
Objects in Abercrombie’s highly autobiographical works usually symbolized parts of her own experiences and identity, rather than abstract ideas. “I always paint myself,” she once said. Freeman’s auction listing meanwhile suggests that shells “served as a talisman of friendship, typically gifted to those closest to her.”
In a press release prior to Thursday’s sale, the auction house’s senior vice president Zachary Wirsum described the painting’s rediscovery as “magnificent.” He recalled telling visitors at the Milwaukee exhibition that Abercrombie’s paintings do, occasionally, crop up at estate sales. “Little did I know that one of those ‘once in a while’s would occur less than a month later,” Wirsum is quoted as saying.

title: Setting the record straight: A response to recent claims about the Sheriff’s race
text:
I respect Rep. Milliken, Sen. Grohoski and Rep. Friedmann’s right to support whichever candidate they believe is best suited to serve Hancock County.
However, when an opinion includes questionable assertions, voters deserve complete context. My intention is not to tell anyone who to support, but to provide information so voters can decide for themselves.
Last spring, I met with these three legislators for approximately 90 minutes to discuss my background, vision for the Sheriff’s Office, and their questions. I answered openly and honestly and later offered to meet individually to address any concerns. None accepted. Many issues raised in their letter never came up during our meeting, nor was I contacted beforehand. An opportunity to provide context could have prevented errors of fact and assumption.
Experience and administrative responsibility
Years of service alone do not establish what responsibilities someone held, decisions they made, or what they accomplished.
Corey Bagley spent approximately five years combined as lieutenant and chief deputy. I have approximately three years in an administrative role as lieutenant. However, these positions carried substantially different responsibilities.
The Sheriff’s Office structure changed after Corey’s tenure. His role was primarily a road supervisor, while today, patrol sergeants directly supervise deputies on the road, leaving the lieutenant with significantly greater administrative responsibilities.
As a lieutenant, I have been responsible for budgeting, personnel management, training, equipment, grants, policies, operations, representing the Sheriff’s Office before the County Commissioners, and other organizational responsibilities.
Corey has repeatedly stated that experience matters and separates us. I agree. However, experience should be evaluated in the context of the responsibilities actually held in those positions. His tenure in the same position involved fewer administrative responsibilities than the role carries today.
Voters should consider what each candidate was responsible for, the decisions each made, and what each accomplished.
Budget and equipment
The letter’s characterization of the budget requires context.
During Corey’s involvement in the budget process, the Sheriff’s Office exceeded its budget by approximately $94,000 in 2022 and more than $207,000 in 2023.
When I was promoted in early 2024, the budget was already established. That year ended $117,000 over budget, in part due to four retirements generating more than $118,000 in contractual accrued-leave payouts beyond my control.
In 2025, the first budget I helped develop from the outset, overspending fell to approximately $14,000. This was accomplished despite roughly $50,000 in unanticipated contractual expenses, including compensatory-time payouts and state retirement system changes. At the Commissioners’ request to retain higher-mileage vehicles, the Sheriff’s Office exceeded its vehicle maintenance budget by $37,000.
The legislators also incorrectly cited a budget increase of more than $700,000 from 2024 to 2025. Records available to the public show the 2025 increase was approximately $430,000, of which roughly $278,000 involved wages and fringe benefits controlled by the County Commissioners, not the Sheriff’s Office. These figures were readily available to Rep. Milliken, who serves on the County Budget Advisory Board.
The letter characterizes Taser and vehicle purchases as “frivolous” and unnecessary. Many Tasers purchased during Corey’s tenure had reached or exceeded their service life, some were nonfunctional, and the discontinued model could no longer be repaired. Replacement was necessary to ensure deputies had a reliable less-lethal option, and the purchase was approved by the County Commissioners.
Regarding vehicles, the Chevrolet Tahoes proposed cost approximately $3,000 less per vehicle than the passenger trucks suggested by Commissioner Bill Clark. The Tahoes were also Police Pursuit Vehicle (PPV) models specifically designed for law enforcement, with upgraded brakes, suspension, and wiring to accommodate police equipment. People may reasonably disagree about vehicle selection, but this was the less expensive option.
Promotion and eligibility
The letter questions my promotion directly from patrol deputy to lieutenant without first serving as sergeant. This was the same career progression Corey followed. Moving directly from patrol to lieutenant is not unprecedented, nor has it previously been characterized as an experience shortcut.
ICE information
The letter understandably questions a link about ICE information under the Sheriff’s section of the Hancock County website.
The Sheriff’s Office does not control the website, it is managed by the County Administrator’s Office. I do not have administrative access, did not create or request the page, and was unaware of the link. That context matters before drawing conclusions about my actions or positions based on the webpage. After learning about the link, I requested its removal, and it has since been taken down.
Sheriff Kane and my own record
Sheriff Scott Kane’s support is another recurring theme. Sheriff Kane and I are two different people.
I respect him and appreciate his support, but that does not mean I agree with every decision or policy during his tenure. His support reflects his assessment of my ability to lead the Sheriff's Office. I have my own leadership style, priorities, and vision. I believe the Sheriff’s Office can and must continue to improve.
Public safety and the future
I believe in strong law enforcement, but law enforcement cannot solve every public-safety problem alone. Mental health services, substance-use treatment, domestic-violence resources, and community partnerships are all important.
I have worked with organizations including AMHC, Healthy Acadia, NAMI Maine, and Next Step Domestic Violence Project. I have advocated for a Behavioral Health Coordinator, worked to reestablish the Sheriff’s Office’s participation in drug treatment court, and focused on building meaningful relationships between deputies and the communities they serve.
Ultimately, Hancock County voters will decide who they believe is qualified to serve as Sheriff.
I ask voters to examine the entire record: the responsibilities each candidate held, decisions made, programs implemented, personnel led, budgets managed, and changes accomplished.
Hancock County voters deserve complete context and the opportunity to evaluate both candidates’ records for themselves.

title: InvestigateTV+: Potential medical breakthrough for sepsis
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ explores how sepsis attacks the body and the medical breakthrough one doctor says could potentially save lives.
Then, we take an in-depth look at how burnt trees stand in the way of rebuilding after wildfires and meet the volunteers doing dangerous work to help families move forward.
Plus, how experts say reading 1,000 books before kindergarten is not only doable but can set up a child for success.
A potential treatment to reduce sepsis deaths
Sepsis kills more than 350,000 adults and 1,800 children in the United States each year, according to the CDC. One in three adults who die in the hospital have sepsis.
A doctor in Kansas City, Missouri, has made a discovery that could drastically reduce that statistic.
Burnt trees standing in the way
In June 2025, a wildfire tore through the community of Rowena, Oregon. It forced 8,000 people to evacuate and destroyed more than 56 homes.
Many residents remain unable to rebuild. What didn’t burn is now what’s holding people back.
Charred trees, weakened and unstable, still stand across properties throughout the community. Known as hazard trees, they are dangerous enough to halt any rebuilding efforts.
Oldest bicycle factory in the nation
Wayne Sosin spent decades keeping the nation’s oldest bike maker rolling. He helped take over the more than 125-year-old family-owned company in 1987 before expanding operations from New York to Conway in 2015.
“We made a commitment to stay in America,” Sosin said.
1,000 books and counting
A Missouri six-year-old is reading more books than many people read in a lifetime.
Pew Research in the past found that the average American reads about 12 books a year. An elementary student outside of St. Louis crushed this number by reading 1,000 books before he entered kindergarten.
Malachi Henderson, 6, started kindergarten in the fall, shortly after completing the 1,000 Books Before Kindergarten program at the St. Louis County Library.

title: Woman killed in Plymouth collision has been identified
text:
The woman who died after a Wednesday evening collision in Plymouth has been identified.
Kendall Thompson, 67, of Dixmont was driving a Chrysler sedan east on Moosehead Trail about 6:39 p.m. when a Hyundai Santa Cruz driven by 69-year-old Timothy Malo of Newport crossed the centerline and the two vehicles collided, according to the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
The crash sent both vehicles off the road and into Plymouth Pond, the sheriff’s office said.
Thompson was taken to the hospital with serious but not life-threatening injuries. His passenger, a 68-year-old Patricia Thompson of Dixmont, succumbed to her injuries at the hospital.
Malo was taken to the hospital with injuries not considered life-threatening.

title: Penquis Good Neighbor Fund offers emergency heat aid to Maine families
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Last winter, the Penquis Good Neighbor Fund provided a vital lifeline to hundreds of local households facing home heating emergencies. Thanks to the generosity of community members, businesses, and partners, the fund helped deliver emergency fuel assistance to 582 households across Penobscot, Piscataquis, and Knox counties, providing a total of $255,131 in donated support to help families stay warm, safe, and dry during Maine’s coldest months.
The program is designed to assist households that may not qualify for federal heating programs such as HEAP or who are experiencing an urgent heating crisis and need immediate help.
The importance of the Good Neighbor Fund was especially evident during last season’s delay in the release of federal LIHEAP funding. When a government shutdown postponed HEAP assistance until December, the Good Neighbor Fund stepped in to help 191 households with emergency heating assistance totaling $71,586, ensuring families were not left without heat while waiting for their benefits. The program also supports individuals and families facing unexpected hardships, including those recovering from medical treatment, navigating a personal crisis, or living just above income eligibility guidelines for other assistance programs.
At its heart, the Good Neighbor Fund is a community helping community. Donations allow Penquis to provide emergency deliveries of approximately 100 to 125 gallons of heating oil or kerosene to eligible households throughout the region. This work is made possible not only by generous donors, but also by dedicated fuel vendors and delivery drivers who respond when neighbors need help most, often braving severe winter weather to ensure homes remain warm and safe. Every dollar donated makes a difference and helps provide emergency heating assistance to families at risk of going without heat. Donors may choose to support households in a specific town or county or allow their gift to be used wherever the need is greatest.
How to Donate: To help keep a neighbor warm this winter, visit penquis.org , click the “Donate” button at the top of the page, and select “Heat a Home.” Donations may also be made by check. Simply note “Good Neighbor Fund,” “Heat a Home,” or “Fuel Assistance” in the memo line. Every contribution, regardless of size, helps ensure local families have access to emergency heating assistance when they need it most.
HEAP
Here is a reminder about Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) program: HEAP provides support to income-eligible households in Penobscot, Piscataquis, and Knox counties facing high winter heating costs. Eligible homes heated by oil, kerosene, coal, pellets, wood, LP gas, or electricity may qualify for assistance.
HEAP has started taking applications for fuel assistance and will run through May 31, 2027, or until funding runs out. It may seem early to book an appointment, but there is a great need, and appointments are already booked until the end of the year. Statewide, HEAP applications were down from last year. Penquis was able to take a few more HEAP applications than the last HEAP season. All households that did apply and were found eligible were served.
How it works: The first applications are dedicated to “Priority Households” which includes a household member that pays for their heat but is also 60 years old and older, 72 months or younger, or someone who is disabled. Penquis appointments have been set up for anyone who applied in 2026 as a “Priority Household” which already includes 6,700 households. It is important to know that not everyone can be served on the first day and it may take a few days for someone to return your call. In fact, Penquis is already booked into December at this time. Once priority households are complete, the focus will switch to households that pay for their heat but do not fall under the “priority Household” status. Renters who have their heat included in their rent are next along with people who have “Room/Board”, and then finally those subsidized with heat included to keep them eligible for the Farm Bill or food stamps.
As of now, there has been no word from the federal government regarding funding for the 2027 Heating Season. Maine usually receives about $41 million. An average HEAP benefit for the Penquis area last season was about $570, higher than the previous year. It is important to know HEAP is an assistance program and is not designed to pay for the entire heating cost. Maine was very lucky to receive supplemental funding from the federal and state governments during the COVID-19 pandemic, but now that pandemic is over funding availability will likely be different this year.
2027 Income Guidelines
For one month’s income:
- Family Size of 1: $3,173

If you would like to learn more about HEAP or the Good Neighbor Fund programs and would like to set up an appointment or to check to see if you have an appointment already scheduled, please call the Penquis team at 973-3500. You may also make an appointment by visiting the Penquis or MaineHousing websites. To do an online HEAP application go to MaineHousing.org .

title: Volunteer musicians bring live music to hospital patients
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (Aging Untold) — A group of volunteer musicians in Nashville is bringing live music to hospital rooms for patients, families and staff.
Alex King takes the music from room to room at TriStar Centennial. She has performed for patients, including Penn Pennington, for whom she first played several years ago while he was battling leukemia.
A video of their song went viral.
The performances are part of Musicians on Call, an organization that sends volunteer artists to play for patients.
Volunteers visit patients monthly
Allie Lamb takes her guitar on rounds a couple of days every month. She said seeing a kid’s face light up is rewarding.
“Give my voice in a way that matters,” she said.
Lamb encourages patients to sing along, clap and get involved during performances.
“It helps me stay positive,” Mayra Martinez, a patient, said.
The group performs more than 3,000 times a year for patients in Nashville.

title: Clouds arrive overnight, some showers tomorrow and gusty winds Tuesday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - It will not be as cold tonight with lows mainly around 50. A front will march its way across the state tomorrow and bring some showers with it. It will also bring some gusty winds behind it into Tuesday as the pressure gradient tightens because of a low to our north. Then yet another comfortable fall week.
Tonight: Clouds arrive ahead of next system
It will cloud up and stay relatively warm on Sunday night ahead of our next system which will arrive on Monday, some light showers may also work their way in. Winds will also pick up out of the SW at 10-15 mph overnight.
Monday: Rain crosses state west to east, then gusty winds
Rain may arrive in the early morning on Monday especially in western regions. It will quickly move across the state with less than a quarter of an inch for most. It will be clear by the evening hours more than likely.
Tuesday and beyond: Windy Tuesday then another nice fall week
Following the rain it will likely get gusty Tuesday. It may gust over 40 mph for places up in the county with gusts over 35 across much of the rest of the region. This will knock a large number of leaves off the trees and being some colder temps as well.
Sunday: Mainly sunny. Highs near 60. Winds NW at 5-10 mph
Sunday night: Not as cold and clouds arrive. Lows near 50. Winds SW at 10-15 mph
Monday: Showers arrive with general cloudiness. Highs near 60. Winds SW at 10-15 mph.
Monday night: Mainly clear. Lows in the 30s and 40s. Windy with winds W at 15-20 mph.
Tuesday: Sun all around but chillier with highs in the 50s. Winds W15-25 mph with gusts to 35-40 mph.

title: Falmouth rides depth to SMAA golf championship
text:
VASSALBORO — The Falmouth golf team fell one shot short of an SMAA championship last year.
The Navigators were eager to return to the top this season — and one of their newest players ensured they did.
Six Falmouth players broke 80, led by Dante Iannetta at 73 and senior transfer Sawyer Hebert at 75, and the Navigators shot 304 to hold off defending champion Cheverus (313) at the SMAA qualifier at Natanis Golf Course on Monday.
The Navigators and Stags, with Thornton Academy (325), Gorham (336), Deering (337) and South Portland (338), qualified for the Class A tournament Friday at Natanis. The Trojans were led by a 79 from Jacob Litwinetz, Gorham got a 79 from Charlie Sands, Deering had a 75 from Sam Carter and South Portland was led by Lucas Turkewitz’s 79.
Falmouth won the SMAA championship in 2024. The Navigators made it a goal to reclaim it.
“One hundred percent. We’ve got a lot of depth this year,” Iannetta said. “(Monday) showed it. We’ve got to do it one more time.”
On the Arrowhead side, Winthrop, which won the MVC title and automatically qualified for Saturday’s Class C championships last Thursday, nipped Maranacook for the top score at the conference qualifier. The Ramblers shot 331 while the Black Bears, paced by medalist Jack Fontaine’s 74 and Josh Herzing’s 84, were at 332. Madison, led by a 79 from Colton Pelletier, shot 345 to qualify as well.
“It’s very important (to score well), especially with me not playing well as our No. 1, it helps the team’s confidence a lot,” said Drew Mertzel, the 2025 Class C champion whose 83 was Winthrop’s second-best score behind Lincoln MacArthur’s 78, while Parker Dow (84) and Sam Corgan (86) also qualified. “(We know) if someone’s not having a good day, our team’s there to back us up.”
Cheverus, last year’s SMAA and Class A champion, got a 1-under 71 from medalist Sam Sirois and a 74 from Keane McGrath, but was taken down by Falmouth, which was in top form.
“They all got off to good, solid starts,” coach A.J. Simokaitis said. “In years past, whether it’s nerves or whatever it might be, you have one or two guys throw in a big number early in the round. … (This) gave them a little peace of mind, a little cushion.”
Iannetta notched three birdies to post the Navigators’ low score, and Victor Keefer (77), Alex Novick, Griffin Jacobsen and Anthony Graceffa (79 apiece) also shot under 80. The second-lowest score, though, went to Hebert, who led North Yarmouth Academy to the Class C title last year and had three birdies of his own Monday.
“I was just setting myself up, I wasn’t going for anything,” he said. “Falmouth is really competitive golf. … I was No. 7 at the beginning of the year and I needed to work really hard to get up there.”
The Navigators, however, weren’t rejoicing. Two years ago Falmouth won the SMAA qualifier but took fourth at states.
“Be happy with it but go through, find where you lost shots,” Iannetta said. “You can always make improvements.”
Back playing where he tied for second at states last year, Sirois made six birdies, including one on the 13th where he rolled in a bending 25-foot putt and gave a one-handed shrug after it fell.
“Hitting-wise, it wasn’t great, so the putter saved me a lot today,” he said. “(I made) a lot of 5- and 4-footers today, that’s big for me.”
The top score in the MVC event went to Fontaine, who excelled around the green. He birdied the opening hole, had birdies on two of the first three holes on the back, and notched his first eagle when he chipped in on the sixth.
“It was pretty nice,” he said. “I didn’t really believe it at first. And then I (looked) at the hole and there it was.”
In the MVC, individual qualifying spots went to players shooting 84 and under. That included Chris Johnson (78) and Dom Mangold (83) of Kents Hill, Vincent Chapman (80) and Jacob Irish (83) of Dirigo, Patrick Murphy (80) of Monmouth, and Maddox Foster-Grey (84) of Mt. Abram.
In the SMAA, Cheverus also took scores from Joe Stratman (81) and Mike Ray (87), while Thornton got an 80 from Henry Litwinetz, an 83 from Ryan Johnson and an 83 from Blake Goulet. Lukas Taafe shot 83, Payton Wilkins 84 and Andrew Cabral 90 for Gorham. Deering got an 82 from Liam Brunelle, an 89 from Cole Barringer and a 91 from Dominik Anthony, and South Portland got 86s from Jacob Robin and Noah Bates and an 87 from Gavin Schuster.
Qualifying individually were Portland’s Max Schaffer (Portland, 79), Jackson Humphrey (Bonny Eagle, 81), Jacob Willey (Noble, 81), Hunter Pulkkinen (Windham, 81), Caden Tito (Thornton, 81), Josh Albert (Scarborough, 82), Nolan Moore (Noble, 83), Graeme Thompson (Thornton, 83) and Luke Rice (Westbrook, 84).

title: Family mourns 7-year-old girl stabbed to death while walking with sister; suspect charged
text:
CHICAGO (WLS) - A Chicago family is mourning a 7-year-old girl who was stabbed to death while walking with her older sister as police say the suspect faces a murder charge.
A vigil was held Sunday to honor 7-year-old Eddimar Paola Hernandez, a day after she was stabbed to death in Chicago’s Chatham neighborhood. Family members were immediately brought to their knees the moment they returned to the spot where the little girl was attacked.
“She was happy,” said Eddimar’s stepfather, Pedro Izqueirdo, in Spanish. “She had dreams, to be big.”
Eddimar was out with her older sister Saturday morning when Chicago police say 48-year-old Shavon Gayden stabbed her in the back multiple times. The 7-year-old died at the hospital.
Security video shows bystanders rushing in, helping to detain Gayden until police arrived.
At a community vigil Sunday, Alderwoman Michelle Harris of the 8th Ward said Gayden had allegedly gotten into an altercation with staff at a nearby wireless store before allegedly attacking and killing Eddimar.
Police say Gayden is facing a first-degree murder charge.
“You send your baby out. It’s a beautiful Saturday morning, and then, they don’t come back home,” Harris said.
Eddimar’s family remembers her as a bright little girl who loved to draw, play with her siblings and wait by the window for her parents to come home from work. Her mother, Estefany Hernandez, is calling for justice.
“My daughter’s death should not be left like this,” Hernandez said in Spanish. “There must be justice for my little girl. She wasn’t bothering anyone.”
Gayden is scheduled to appear in court Monday.
Investigators have not released a motive in Eddimar’s murder.

title: Trump vows: ‘We will pass the death penalty’ for drug dealers, traffickers, law enforcement killers

Pike was set to be executed for her role in the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, 19. It would have been Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in 200 years.
