title: Former ‘American Idol’ singer Caleb Flynn sentenced for wife’s murder
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — A former music pastor in Ohio who appeared briefly on “American Idol” was sentenced Monday to life in prison without the possibility of parole, after a jury convicted him last week of murdering his wife while he was having an affair.
The judge said Caleb Flynn, 40, used his Christian faith to manipulate others and showed no remorse for actions marked by “layers of deceit, manipulation and cruelty.”
With tears rolling down his cheeks, Flynn apologized to his family just before being sentenced, starting with his two young daughters, who were home when he shot his wife in her sleep. He called their births the “greatest joy in this life.”
Although he said he accepted responsibility for his words and decisions, Flynn remained adamant that he was innocent.
“As I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife,” he said.
Prosecutors said Flynn staged a home invasion in February and claimed a burglar killed his wife, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old schoolteacher and volleyball coach. In his 2013 appearance on “American Idol,” Flynn credited his wife with encouraging him to chase his dreams on the singing contest. He did not advance to the main competition in Hollywood.
During the trial, Flynn didn’t testify on his own behalf, nor did anybody else.
Family members, including Ashley’s parents, spoke in favor of the harsh sentence Monday, while saying they had forgiven Flynn because they didn’t want her legacy to be hatred.
Her sister, Kayla Keyt, said Flynn’s actions have scarred their entire church community, prompting children to run into their parents’ bedrooms to make sure their fathers haven’t killed their mothers.
As a family member read a statement written by his daughter Ava, Flynn sobbed uncontrollably as a pile of tissues grew on the defense table in front of him. At one point, it appeared he might fall over.
“Mommy was the perfect person,” her statement said. “The absolute perfect person. What did she ever do to you to make you hate her so much?” In her statement, his daughter Alyssa said she wouldn’t visit him in prison.
During closing arguments, prosecutors told jurors that Flynn wanted out of his marriage when he shot his wife at their house in Tipp City, a suburb north of Dayton. He sent a text message to his lover the night before the shooting, saying, “I choose you. I’m free. Actions will come tomorrow,” prosecutors said.
During the trial, Alleigha Botner testified she met Flynn in 2022 while she was a 20-year-old intern at his church and had an affair with him for more than a year. She told jurors that Flynn said he hated his wife and had thoughts of killing her.
The gun used to kill Ashley Flynn was not found at the scene, and his attorney told jurors that investigators found no evidence that Caleb Flynn fired a gun that day. Prosecutors said his fingerprints and DNA were at the scene and that his devices showed him moving around the house, even though he claimed he was asleep at the time of the shooting.
The jury found him guilty of multiple counts, including murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence.

title: Mother, godmother charged in death of 4-year-old

title: Maine ICE observers added to DHS database, unsealed court records say
text:
A federal immigration agent added eight Maine residents to a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database in January, including several observers of immigration enforcement activity, according to newly unsealed court records.
One woman, Caryln Williams, was held by U.S. Customs and Border Protection while returning from a trip to Quebec as a result of being in the Department of Homeland Security’s Investigative Case Management (ICM) system. An agent testified that he added her to it after her car was observed at a location where multiple people were recording federal agents on Jan. 20, according to court records in a lawsuit against DHS.
But Williams wasn’t driving her car that morning, her spouse was.
Williams was “not physically present, or in any other way present, at the scene of the Jan. 20 encounter with this ICE agent,” Williams’ attorney JoAnna Suriani said on Monday.
Williams, her partner Polyxenia Pantos, and two other Maine residents are suing DHS, accusing the agency of violating their First Amendment rights. The federal lawsuit alleges that agents threatened to add observers in Maine to a database for “domestic terrorists.” A motion from the plaintiffs filed last week, citing depositions and other evidence that remains sealed, states that an agent added Williams to the ICM system, an existing database used by DHS to document cases by Homeland Security Investigations.
Attorneys for DHS stated in a motion to dismiss the case that the agent — an HSI Boston officer, identified as “J.C.” — added eight people to ICM who “he believed posted potential threats to law enforcement.”
The plaintiffs say in their filings that six of those people were observers.
DHS has denied any allegations of wrongdoing, including the existence of a database for domestic terrorists.
A spokesperson for DHS did not address questions from a reporter about the case Monday, but maintained the agency does not run a database for domestic terrorists. Attorneys for DHS did not respond to a request for comment.
The plaintiffs asked the court in the motion to issue an injunction before trial, barring agents from retaliating against observers with threats of a database and other tactics, like driving by protesters’ homes or calling them.
“Once you are in that database, or a database like it … the reach of where that data goes, including who has access to it, and what it can be used for in the future, is, in my opinion, very chilling,” said Suriani, an attorney with the nonprofit Protect Democracy, which is representing the plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs are also asking that Williams’ classification in the ICM database be modified, so she can travel internationally without being automatically detained or subject to a second inspection by border officials.
Attorneys for DHS have said in hearings and court filings that the government has a policy to protect observers and protesters who engage in First Amendment activity, and that agents receive relevant training. In March, the government also argued that only a few agents in Maine were recorded by observers talking about a database for domestic terrorists, and that those agents violated DHS policy.
No agents were disciplined, the plaintiffs argued in court records, citing depositions that remain under seal at the government’s request. Suriani also disagreed with characterizations that the agents were “rogue.”
According to a motion filed by Williams’ attorneys, the agent identified as J.C. testified during a deposition that he added Williams to the ICM database as an “aggressive woman (who) interject(ed) herself into an arrest.” The motion alleges that he also called Williams hours after Pantos was seen recording ICE agents, identifying himself only as someone from DHS and encouraging her to tell Pantos “not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist.”
Documents filed last month by the government identify J.C. as “Mr. Coleman.” Attempts to reach Coleman through social media, email and DHS were unsuccessful.
The plaintiffs’ motion also states that agents have continued driving by the homes of people who film and protest them. One agent said in his deposition that this was meant to “show them that we knew who they were” and “have them stop following us,” according to the plaintiffs’ filing.
This is the plaintiffs’ second time asking for pretrial relief. U.S. District Judge John Woodcock denied their request for a temporary restraining order against DHS in March, ruling that he didn’t have enough evidence to merit such an emergency measure.
In their latest filing, the plaintiffs said most of the agents whom they deposed said they considered the Maine observers to be interfering with immigration arrests. Plaintiffs have denied interfering with arrests.
“The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that’s what we’re asking the court to stop,” Suriani said.
Both sides are still responding to the government’s motion to dismiss, and the plaintiffs’ motion for preliminary injunction. A hearing for either request has not yet been scheduled.
The ICM database is hosted by software company Palantir, according to a statement the company released in 2022 and recent reporting by Wired. A spokesperson for Palantir declined to comment Monday.

title: Maine’s volunteer libraries thrive with tight budgets. State rules could make that harder.
text:
STANDISH — Lynn Knowlton was ecstatic about a new furnace.
As president of the Richville Library, she waited eagerly on a recent Saturday morning for volunteers to help her install the contraption in the basement of the cozy, pale yellow building.
She bought the furnace with surprise cash donations from community members who wanted to help replace the outdated electric heating system that has strained the 103-year-old institution’s shoestring budget for years.
“I can’t stop happy dancing,” Knowlton said.
For all-volunteer-run libraries like this one, unexpected funding that helps serve their communities is a thrill.
What thrills them less is a proposed set of rules the Maine Library Commission is considering that would cut off their access to some state-provided services — internet, subsidized interlibrary loans, and the ability to receive grants through the Maine Public Library Fund — unless they pay their director, are open an average of 12 hours a week year-round, and participate in a specific number of professional development opportunities.
While the Richville Library serves Standish’s rural population of 11,000, other similar libraries in Maine are in more remote areas with even smaller communities, some of fewer than 1,000 people. They provide free internet, books, technology, regular programs and gathering spaces to small towns that otherwise don’t have them. Most run on annual budgets of less than $10,000, bolstered by fundraising, donations and grants. Some get annual help from their towns, usually $2,000 to $4,000.
Rural librarians say the measures would damage their libraries and communities. According to an impact assessment by the Maine State Library, 38 of approximately 257 public libraries in Maine do not currently meet the proposed standards.
The state commission began considering standards for libraries last November, but has eased its proposition over the past year in response to backlash. It voted to send its most recent draft for legal review in September.
Maine State Librarian Lori Stockman responded to requests for interviews sent to her and other state library leaders by explaining that they are “hesitant to say much” before the draft is finalized and public comment opens later this month.
Increasing costs and uncertain funding for the Maine State Library loom behind the rule’s efforts, said Chair Bryce Cundick at a commission meeting in January. The state agency laid off a third of its staff after federal funding cuts to the Institute of Museum and Library Services by the Trump administration in April 2025, but later regained some money and employees.
Money isn’t the only issue. Commission members and state librarians have also repeated that the requirements introduced would help ensure the quality of Maine’s libraries. Commission member Wynter Giddings said at the April meeting that paid staff leads to “sustainability” and “accountability” in libraries. Additional measures in the draft include requiring libraries to keep strategic plans.
Beyond Maine law stating a basic definition for public libraries, these standards would be the first set for libraries in Maine.
That has spurred frustration among volunteer librarians.
Dylan Johnston, head librarian and one of two volunteers at the East Millinocket Public Library, which serves a population of just over 1,500 from a town-owned building, said he thinks the push to disqualify them from state resources stems from a perception that their operations are not competent or valuable. Several other librarians have echoed that concern.
The process has raised questions about what it means to have a library and a librarian — many professional librarian roles require a master’s degree in library science.
“It’s very demeaning and deflating,” Johnston said. “This library has faced several challenges along the years, but I’ve kept it going. I’m an invaluable service.”
The library recently received a $50,000 grant from the Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation to purchase several pieces of furniture, a new sign and renovate the children’s area. Johnston said he helps people with technology issues and hosts a weekly group for older adults to give them a place to congregate.
Carol Wolf is the volunteer vice president of the Pembroke Library in Pembroke, one of the five libraries that would lose interlibrary loan services under the measures. She said it is not in the library’s budget to pay a director.
“Just because (libraries) don’t meet these direct criteria that the library commission wants to impose, does not seem to me to mean that they’re not effective libraries,” Wolf said. “This rule just doesn’t comport with reality in these small towns.”
Wolf is leading an effort to support small libraries, reverse the course of the rule, and try and get more representatives of rural libraries in northern Maine to apply for seats on the Maine Library Commission. Of the 26 seats, five are vacant, and no members are from north of Bangor. Members are appointed by the governor.
Losing internet access is the biggest threat for Johnston and other rural libraries, which could have to scramble to find the money to pay for it. Their current connectivity comes through NetworkMaine, which provides internet to most of Maine’s K-12 public schools and libraries. While NetworkMaine is state-provided, the federal service E-Rate covers roughly 70% of its costs.
One standard Maine already has in place mandates that libraries requesting subsidized interlibrary loan van delivery services must circulate more than 100 materials through the system per year to qualify.
According to a list compiled by Sarah Redfield, a lawyer in York who has voiced opposition to the rule, five libraries would be taken off the interlibrary loan route. Most rural libraries, including Richville and East Millinocket, don’t use the service.
Stockman, the state librarian, did not respond to requests for information about how much of the state library’s budget is used for NetworkMaine and interlibrary loan services for the potentially impacted libraries.
Karen MacGillivary is the volunteer director at the Laura E. Richards Library in Georgetown, a former one-room schoolhouse on a hill. The snowplow can’t reach the building and it lacks running water, forcing it to close in the winter months. It hosts what MacGillivary calls “Blizzard Books,” where patrons can sign out as many books as they want in October and exchange them with other community members until spring. She said circulation this past season increased by 200 books.
“It’s a happy place,” she said.
MacGillivary worries about the financial consequences of losing internet — many patrons come to the library just for that, and she does not know how the library would fund it alone.
The proposed rules are under review by the Office of the Maine Attorney General and the Department of the Secretary of State, and a 45-day public comment period is expected to open Thursday, with a public hearing on Oct. 29.
The commission will then respond to comments and decide whether to incorporate them at its January meeting. If the rules are implemented, libraries would have two years to start paying directors, with the option of requesting extensions.
Stockman emphasized that state law passed in 2011 mandates the commission to name minimum standards of library service, and the attorney general’s office advised it to create enforceable rules. However, the law does not specify what standards must be in place.
The current draft also does not specify how much libraries would need to pay directors. If the current draft were implemented as is, libraries could meet the requirement with a salary of as little as $1.
At a March commission meeting, Cundick said that the proposed measures should have been established much earlier. According to the state’s impact assessment, 44 states have established standards for libraries tied to eligibility for state resources.
Considering Maine’s long history of thriving small rural libraries that rely on state services, opponents say they believe the state should work to support them.
Six volunteers keep the Richville Library flourishing. Knowlton’s mother, Karen McNutt, is the director. Her father, David McNutt, is the treasurer, and her late grandmother was one of the young Standish girls in the Osmunda Club that began collecting books to create the library in the 1920s. Knowlton grew up in the house across the street, where her son now lives.
The library doubled its open hours to 13 a week in the past two years, and has expanded free programming to include American Sign Language classes, Red Cross trainings, a creative writer’s circle, multiple book clubs and more story times.
“There’s a lot of spirit still there in that place,” Karen McNutt said. “It’s pretty amazing.”
Knowlton and volunteers authored a laminated book of detailed biographical information about each of the Richville’s founders and its history. They work hard to make sure the library prospers.
“I’ve just gotten taken in by some of these stories and the commitments that people have, you know, for generations,” said Redfield, the lawyer pushing back on the proposed rules. “What I see is this direction to try to have all Maine libraries look alike, which is not what Maine is about.”

title: Matt Dunlap is the type of person Maine’s 2nd District needs
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Jeff McCabe is a former majority leader of the Maine House of Representatives with a long career in natural resources and outdoor recreation. A registered Maine Guide for more than 20 years, he lives in Skowhegan with his wife and their three children.
You don’t often get the chance to know a true statesman, outdoorsman, and genuinely good person. I’ve been fortunate enough to know Matt Dunlap.
When I was newly elected, Matt and I were sitting together during orientation and started talking about hunting season. I mentioned that my lever-action .30-30 was being repaired. Matt didn’t hesitate. He simply said, “No problem. I’ll let you borrow one of my rifles.”
That might sound like a small thing, but to me it wasn’t. It was Matt being Matt — generous, welcoming and willing to help without making a big deal about it.
I’ve always admired Matt’s commitment to Maine’s outdoors. He understands that our sporting heritage is about more than hunting or fishing. It’s about conservation, stewardship, passing traditions down and making sure the next generation has the opportunity to experience Maine the way so many of us have. His commitment to conservation and hunter education is something I deeply respect. He understands that if we want Maine’s outdoor traditions to continue, we have to teach and invest in the next generation.
Throughout my time in elected office, I reached out to Matt directly when constituents needed help. I knew I could call him and he would listen. One weekend, I contacted him when he was secretary of state about a local business owner and several employees who had their licenses stolen while they were in Hawaii. Matt didn’t say, “That’s not my problem.” He worked to help them.
Later, when I worked for a state employee union, I saw another side of Matt. Workers would come to the State House, and Matt would actually sit down and talk with them. He listened. He asked questions. He wanted to understand what they were going through. He treated people with dignity, regardless of their position or politics.
Those experiences stand in stark contrast to what I personally witnessed during my eight years in the Legislature and two years working with a labor union when it came to Paul LePage.
I remember the closure of the Madison paper mill — more than 200 good jobs gone — and how, when leaders from both parties sat down with Gov. LePage to find a way forward, he used the meeting to rant about his political grievances instead of offering solutions, while families in Somerset County wondered how they’d pay their bills. I remember that frustration and anger in the State House.
And I remember the workers at the Downeast Correctional Facility, who arrived one February morning to find their prison being emptied by armed officers on the governor’s orders — their jobs gone with no notice, in a part of Washington County that could least afford it. Those experiences left a lasting impression on me about what leadership should — and should not — look like.
For me, this isn’t about political slogans. It’s personal.
I’ve seen Matt Dunlap treat people with respect when nobody was watching. I’ve seen him help people who needed someone to answer the phone. I’ve seen his commitment to Maine’s land, wildlife and sporting traditions. And I’ve seen him sit down with people who disagree with him and actually listen.
That’s the kind of person I believe Maine’s 2nd Congressional District deserves representing them.
Someone who knows Maine. Someone who cares about Maine. Someone who will work with people instead of simply working against them.
That person, in my experience, is Matt Dunlap.

title: The cost of Susan Collins outweighs the benefit
text:
How many federal dollars does it take to offset the rollback of constitutionally guaranteed rights of more than a half century? How many federal dollars is sufficient to offset the cost of previously defeated diseases like polio and measles to return to Maine families?
How about the cost to Mainers of legally dubious tariffs or war? And what about the cost to Mainers who stand to lose their health benefits through Medicaid, or lost food assistance?
Yes, Sen. Collins has brought home some “bacon” to Maine’s seniors, rural hospitals and first responders, but at what cost? Sen. Collins has let Maine down. It’s long past time for “Susie from The County” to return to her status in The County.
Bob Riley
Saco

title: Acadia Senior College hosts rural healthcare discussion
text:
BAR HARBOR — The elimination of maternity care in rural Maine has an impact more far-reaching than it seems. Aside from the risks to families associated with traveling long distances for healthcare, there is an economic risk to eliminating women’s health services in rural towns. Linda Robinson will outline the progression of how the decision to close rural health services evolved, the effect these decisions have on Maine’s population, and the economic impact they present for rural communities.
Linda Robinson was a founding member of the Women’s Health Center in 1993 and practiced there for 23 years. She has worked internationally in several capacities and most recently completed a Fulbright Scholarship in Malawi. She has taught The History of Women’s Health Care at College of the Atlantic. Her next project will be collecting and writing women’s stories about access to maternity care in rural Maine.

title: Firefighter had to ‘gnaw’ his way free after being handcuffed by girlfriend, 911 call reveals
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG/Gray News) - An Ohio firefighter appeared in court Monday, three days after her arrest for allegedly refusing to remove a man from handcuffs, stealing his car and phone, and breaking into his home.
The alleged victim is a fellow Toledo firefighter and a captain within the department.
Kenasia Guilford, 33, faces multiple charges, including abduction. The two firefighters were in a relationship, according to a 911 call.
Guilford’s attorney, Richard Mitchell, spoke in court earlier this week.
“This series of incidents stems from a paramour situation, where some information was learned by the defendant that would make anyone have substantial concern and was traumatic,” Mitchell said.
In a 911 call from the captain’s friend, the victim’s friend detailed a call for help at four in the morning.
“I had a friend call me. He showed up at my house at four, saying his girlfriend handcuffed him,” the caller said.
Police say Guilford handcuffed the man to a staircase, with his consent, but affidavits say she later refused to let him go. The caller described how his friend broke free.
“And he said he had to gnaw — she handcuffed him to some railing or something. He said he had to fight his way off of there, so he might be injured, I don’t know,” the caller said.
The caller also told dispatchers he picked up his friend and drove him home.
Investigators say Guilford stole the man’s car, broke into his house, and was later found hiding inside.
“He told me to hover around so he could go and get his keys, and I can take him to go get his truck. But as I was waiting, I see her walking down the street in the pitch dark, running toward his house. I was on the phone with my wife, and she was like, ‘You might need to call 911,’ but I don’t even know what to say,” the caller said.
The alleged victim was walking down the street still in handcuffs, according to the 911 call. Police later had to cut the handcuffs off. It’s not clear how the alleged victim was able to contact his friend in the first place.
“You said he has no phone on him?” a dispatcher asked.
“No, I got his bag. He had a bookbag on him, but she had the phone. I think that’s why he was — why she handcuffed him — to get to his phone or something like that. And that’s why he didn’t have his phone on him,” the caller said.
Monday, a judge set Guilford’s bond at $10,000, with a no-contact order, and ruled she must wear an ankle monitor while the case is pending.

title: Court bailiff accused of selling fake CPR certifications to daycares
text:
THOMSON, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) - A Georgia man is accused of selling invalid CPR certifications to employees at daycare and adult care facilities.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigation arrested and charged James Ed Lewis, 66, of Thomson, with three counts of filing false documents and one count of theft by taking.
Kakika Eubanks, who runs Lil Bo Peep Learning Center, said the children at her daycare are like her own.
“They’re like my little ones. They’re like my own children. So I would tend to them and treat them and love them just like my own kids,” Eubanks said.
Eubanks said CPR certification is required by the state for her workers.
“CPR is required by the state. For all of my workers,” she said.
To teach the class, Eubanks called Lewis, a first responder she had known for years. Lewis provided state certificates along with training logs.
The GBI said the cards were fake and that Lewis was not certified to issue them.
“I was devastated. I was shocked. I was in disbelief. I just couldn’t believe that it wasn’t, you know, that this had happened,” Eubanks said.
Lewis turned himself in Wednesday and was booked into the McDuffie County Jail.
Law enforcement sources said the fake cards were handed out at as many as three daycares, including at Thomson’s First Methodist Church.
According to the GBI, Lewis was not certified as a CPR instructor at the time the course was provided to the businesses.
To clarify, being certified as a CPR instructor isn’t the same as being certified in CPR. Lewis is certified in CPR, according to documents.
“I was mad. I was very upset. Very upset,” Eubanks said.
Lewis was a longtime firefighter and former lieutenant. He was employed by the McDuffie County Sheriff’s Office, working security as a bailiff at the McDuffie County Government Complex, a job he retired from after he was bonded out of jail.
He informed the county Wednesday morning that he would be retiring immediately, McDuffie County Manager Brandon Burton said.
Eubanks said she had known Lewis for years.
“I’ve been knowing him for years, actually since I was little, but I found him doing a fire and safety training years ago, and he started doing our CPR and first aid training since. So he’s been doing our CPR training for years,” she said.
Eubanks said no one at her daycare had to use the CPR skills listed on the certificates.
“Thank God that we didn’t need CPR or anything during this time frame because I mean, we didn’t have the proper CPR training that we thought that we had that we trusted in him to give us,” she said.
The Thomson Police Department asked the GBI to investigate the allegations on March 24.
Preliminary information indicates several daycare businesses and adult care facilities in Thomson paid Lewis to provide CPR certification courses to their employees.
Those businesses were later told by the Georgia Department of Early Care and Learning that the courses Lewis taught, and the CPR certification cards he provided to attendees, were invalid, according to the GBI.
We have reached out to Lewis for a comment.
The investigation remains active and ongoing.
Anyone with information is asked to contact the GBI Regional Investigative Office in Thomson at 706-595-2575.
Anonymous tips can also be submitted by calling 1-800-597-TIPS (8477), online, or through the “See Something, Send Something” mobile app.

title: Appeals court weighs judge's authority to restore Trump administration funding cuts to Harvard
text:
BOSTON (AP) — A federal appeals court heard opposing arguments Monday over whether a judge had the authority to restore billions of dollars in funding that the Trump administration cut from Harvard University.
U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs ruled last year that the cuts amounted to illegal retaliation for Harvard’s rejection of the administration’s demands for changes to Harvard’s governance and policies.
The government had tied the move to Harvard’s delays in dealing with antisemitism, but the judge said the university’s federally backed research had little connection to discrimination against Jews.
The ruling restored more than $2.6 billion in research funding for the wealthy Ivy League school.
Though the money has resumed flowing, a Justice Department attorney told a three-judge panel of the First U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday that Burroughs lacked the legal power to require the administration to pay it.
The fight over the money was a contractual dispute that rightly belonged in a different court: the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, DOJ attorney Michael Velchik said. That court, which traces its origins to the mid-1800s, handles lawsuits by citizens seeking money from the federal government.
“The problem is that the district court lacked jurisdiction to order specific performance,” Velchik told the First Circuit. “That is the only thing that we’re complaining about here.”
Velchik cited recent U.S. Supreme Court rulings in support of his argument.
Paul Clement, an attorney for Harvard, said the case was not a straightforward contractual dispute, but raised broader issues of retaliation and discrimination. The district court’s decision restoring the funding was the “perfect remedy” for the violations it found, he said.
“These are not claims that really depend on the contract in any particular way,” he said.
First Circuit Judge Joshua Dunlap, a nominee of President Donald Trump, pressed Clement on whether Burroughs had in effect issued an order requiring payment and whether Harvard could make its broader legal claims without a contract.
The other judges on the panel, Sandra Lynch and Gustavo Gelpi, were nominated by Democratic presidents. The judges did not immediately rule.
Harvard’s lawsuit accused the Trump administration of waging a retaliation campaign against the university after it rejected a series of demands in a letter from a federal antisemitism task force.
The letter demanded sweeping changes related to campus protests, academics and admissions. It was meant to address government accusations that the university had become a hotbed of liberalism and tolerated anti-Jewish harassment on campus.
The administration also has sought to prevent Harvard from hosting foreign students and threatened to revoke its tax-exempt status in a clash watched widely across higher education.
During Monday’s arguments, Lynch expressed skepticism of the administration’s claim that Harvard had been indifferent to antisemitism.
“There are no findings. There was no investigation. There was simply an announcement, ‘We’re terminating against that backdrop,’” she said.
It appeared the administration “didn’t want to have to cope with what the law and the facts of this case presented,” the judge added.
___
Thanawala reported from Atlanta.

title: California woman arrested for allegedly spying for China
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The FBI arrested a California real estate agent as she prepared to fly to China, accusing her of secretly working for Beijing to surveil the president of Taiwan’s family in the U.S., federal officials said.
The case comes at a fraught moment for U.S.-China relations, with Taiwan persistently at the center of their military and diplomatic rivalry. Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory.
The FBI and federal prosecutors allege Wanying Zhang surveilled the house of the president’s son and sent photos, videos and license plate information for his vehicles to a Chinese government official. The federal criminal complaint does not name the alleged target, but the FBI’s rapid response account on the social media platform X said it was the president’s son. Ting-Yu Lai, the president’s elder son, lives and works in the Seattle area as an engineer.
Zhang, a 34-year-old real estate agent from Irvine who also went by the name Heather, was arrested Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport and charged with working for China as an unregistered agent, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. Zhang is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Shawn Lewis, a spokesperson for the U.S. attorney’s office.
Zhang appeared in downtown Los Angeles federal court Monday for an initial hearing to confirm she understood her rights. She has not yet been formally indicted.
Judge Steve Kim told her she was not financially eligible for a public defender and would need to hire a private attorney as soon as possible. A hearing to determine bail or whether she would be detained was scheduled for Wednesday afternoon.
Her husband, Edric Ding, was at the courthouse but declined to comment.
California records show Zhang has been a licensed real estate agent since 2016. A Zillow page shows she has sold seven homes in the last year around Orange County.
Justice Department has been arresting alleged Chinese agents
The case is the latest in a series of Justice Department prosecutions aimed at rooting out alleged covert agents advancing Beijing’s interests on American soil.
Many of the cases have centered on what the Justice Department says is China’s aggressive effort to locate and harass pro-democracy activists living in the U.S. and suppress their speech. The Justice Department also says Beijing is determined to sway American public opinion in its favor by cultivating relationships with political figures seen as having access to the levers of power.
The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.
Taiwan’s Presidential Office confirmed President Lai Ching-te’s relatives were the targets, without specifying if it was the president’s son, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression.”
“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts — which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families — as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
Federal officials say surveillance happened in September 2025
At the direction of Chinese officials, Zhang and another person flew to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, and conducted surveillance outside the target’s home, according to an affidavit with the criminal complaint. A home security camera near the target’s home recorded the pair filming the target and their family from a vehicle, the affidavit said.
Zhang then allegedly sent a Chinese official information related to the surveillance, including photos, videos and license plate information from the target’s vehicles. The affidavit said that photos like that and the location of close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese official could be useful to China if officials wished to “obtain leverage” over Taiwan’s president “during any potential conflict.”
According to the affidavit, Zhang attended the University of International Relations in Beijing, which the FBI agent writing the affidavit said is known to be affiliated closely with China’s intelligence apparatus. Many of the university’s graduates go on to work for ministries in Beijing, including the country’s intelligence apparatus.
The affidavit said Zhang and a classmate who became a Chinese government official had kept in contact since graduating around 2014, and he introduced her to another government official, and she was in contact with both in 2025.
In a post dated Sept. 2, 2025, on the Chinese language app Xiaohongshu, Zhang complained about the long wait at the Seattle airport’s security check, wondering aloud if it was the “least efficient international airport” in the U.S.
She regularly shared photos of her travels around the world and dining at high-end restaurants.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, but Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory. Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and Beijing do not belong to each other and that the “People’s Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan.”
China considers him a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace.”
While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan, notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.
In May, a Southern California mayor agreed to plead guilty to acting as an illegal agent for the Chinese government, and resigned from her city position. Eileen Wang, the mayor of Arcadia, had been charged with one count of acting in the U.S. as an illegal agent of a foreign government. She was accused of doing the bidding of Chinese officials, such as sharing articles favorable to Beijing, without prior notification to the U.S. government as required by law.
___
Wu contributed to this report from Bangkok and Stengle contributed from Dallas. Reporters Eric Tucker and Didi Tang contributed to this report from Washington.

title: What Troy Jackson and Susan Collins need from their high-stakes debates
text:
After weeks of squaring off over ads, social media and the press, Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson are just a few days away from facing each other on the debate stage.
Debate prep has been underway in recent days, according to Democratic and Republican sources. Neither campaign wanted to discuss preparations in detail. Coming as both candidates have held events across the state and after Collins wrapped up the Senate session in Washington until after the midterms, the pair is poised for the first two of four in-studio debates starting Tuesday on CBS News 13 and Thursday on WMTW.
The first televised clashes will give Mainers a fresh take on a five-term incumbent with a record of defying polls and winning crucial moderates, and a progressive former Maine Senate president and logger from Allagash, who admittedly lacks polish but has a record of winning over voters in conservative regions, including in and around Collins’ hometown of Caribou.
Experts this week said the debate marked an opportunity for both candidates to re-introduce themselves beyond the tens of millions of dollars in advertising dominating the airwaves. Another key goal is to bring thousands of undecided and unenrolled voters into the fold.
Both campaigns are likely practicing with stand-ins for their opponents, and campaign teams and surrogates are poised to capture and share clips of “debate moments that can live forever” for better or worse, Emily Cain, a Democratic strategist, said.
“You don’t want to say anything that’s going to upset your base too much, and at the same time you want to find a way to reach those people, who may or may not be watching, who haven’t made up their minds yet,” she said.
Cain, who has participated in several congressional debates, including against Jackson in 2014, said the average debate isn’t a game-changer. But it’s an opportunity “to have a really big moment or a really bad moment,” she said.
She added that the race largely hinged on whether voters think Collins should serve a historic sixth term. Collins must use the debates to explain “why she deserves and is ready to continue,” while Jackson’s challenge is convincing voters she shouldn’t and that he’s a solid replacement, Cain said.
Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist and former Collins staffer, said the senator and Jackson are “both tough in their own ways.” He said it’s likely the candidates have a few “solid sessions” before each debate, but not as many as there would be if fewer than four debates were scheduled.
Dutson expects a firm yet polite tone from both candidates as opposed to an exchange as testy or negative as some of the ads from the outside groups backing the campaigns.
“They’ve both been in public service for a long time, and have had high intensity with people from time to time,” he said. “But the debate is like a job interview for a very serious position. Neither of these [candidates] are built for that Trumpesque political performance.”
Debates can often let down candidates’ bases on both sides of the aisle, Dutson said. And with progressives hungry to target Trump “and so amped up from former Democratic nominee Graham Platner’s rhetoric,” they may be left wanting if Jackson seeks to appeal to more middle-ground voters without a “knockout punch,” he said.
“Susan Collins doesn’t get knocked off balance,” he said. “I don’t see a scenario where anybody would really trip her up.”
This year’s debates are head to head. The pair will be able to focus on their own track records and each other without other candidates, whereas in 2020 Collins and Democratic former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon also contended with independents Max Linn and Lisa Savage. Linn derailed two debates, once by deliberately not responding to moderator questions and another time by cutting up face masks with a pair of scissors. He died in 2021.
Jackson, who has hammered Collins for not holding public town halls, unsuccessfully pressed for at least two of the debates to be town-hall style with unscreened questions from the audience.
The pair’s contrasting styles could make for an interesting debate, Dutson said. With Collins, there are fewer concerns “that there’s a gaffe or viral moment of the day” because “she’s so disciplined and has a strong grasp of the facts,” he argued.
Cain said there’s “no question” Collins has “an extensive vocabulary and experiences to bring” to the debate stage. But Jackson, who just this week apologized for remarks on the Israeli-Gaza conflict and Maine’s Jewish community, is an authentic and experienced debater, Cain said.
He’s also fresher than Collins, who hasn’t debated in six years. Jackson participated in several public forums and debates during his third-place gubernatorial run, and also debated fellow Democrats who sought to replace Platner.
“It’s just important to be yourself, tell the truth and talk to voters,” Cain said.

title: Recovery changed Biddeford-area resident’s life, now she helps others
text:
(First in a series of occasional stories on recovery.)
Today, Kelsie Fitch is healthy, committed to her own long-term recovery, helping others along that path, and living a happy life. But it wasn’t always that way. Before recovery, her life was a seemingly never-ending cycle of drug use, homelessness, arrests followed by jail time where she got sober — and then back to using when her sentence was complete.
“I couldn’t stay sober when I was released from jail,” said Fitch.
That was then. Now 33, she has been in recovery for seven years. Her life began to change when she was court-ordered to a six-month residential recovery program several years ago. She went, she said, because the alternative to the program was remaining in jail.
“I really didn’t understand what the program was or what recovery could look like,” she said. “That recovery center ended up changing my life.”
It wasn’t all clear sailing — there was a brief relapse and an additional period of time in the residential program, but Fitch wants others in the grip of substance use to know successful recovery can happen.
“Recovery gave me a life that I truly never thought was possible for me, and I hope someone who is struggling knows that their life can change for the better, too,” she said.
Now employed as housing director for a couple of women’s recovery residences and as a recovery care navigator and an alcohol and drug counseling aide for a program for those with opioid disorders, she is doing what she can to bring long-term recovery to others.
Fitch, of the Biddeford area, dropped out of high school in 10th grade. She had dabbled in alcohol and marijuana use. Then things changed. She was prescribed oxycodone after gall bladder surgery, and became enamored of it.
“Someone told me heroin could give a similar effect, and from there, one thing led to another,” Fitch said in a September interview. “I began using heroin, and eventually I was using heroin and crack cocaine. Later fentanyl became a part of that as well.”
Her use went on for two years.
“Toward the end of using, I knew I didn’t want to live that life anymore,” she said. “I didn’t like who I had become, and I didn’t feel like myself. I knew I was ready for something different, but I honestly didn’t know how to stop.”
Fitch’s recovery date is etched in her memory — June 13, 2019. A year later, she began working
at Shalom House in Portland.
“It taught me so much about mental health, and some residents were co-occurring with
substance use,” Fitch said. “I have worked in the field ever since.”
The residential program she attended — the former Layman Way Recovery Center — was York County Government’s first foray into recovery services, and provided an alternative to jail for nonviolent offenders who were in the grip of substance use. The program was operated by York County Shelter Programs Inc. through a contract with the county government.
“That program really supported me,” she said, and not only with the recovery piece — Fitch earned her high school equivalency while there. She also took advantage of a 12-step program, and continues to follow the steps.
“Ultimately, I have that choice to stay sober and be the best version of myself; it lies within the
person the ability to do well,” she said.
Early next year, the York County Recovery Center is poised to open on First County Way in Alfred. The 58-bed residential recovery center will sport a detox program, along with 30-day and 180-day residential components and an intensive outpatient program. Those with substance use issues will be able to apply.
Fitch said she’s glad to see that happening. She’s happy to see more recovery services becoming available. And she had these thoughts for folks considering recovery: “Take suggestions from people willing to help, people who have been where you are,” she said. “Really hear the words. It’s one day at a time. So cliché, but it’s true … you don’t have to have everything figured out, you just have to be willing to take that first step and accept help.”
Tammy Wells is a media specialist for York County Government.

title: The cost of Susan Collins outweighs the benefit
text:
How many federal dollars does it take to offset the rollback of constitutionally guaranteed rights of more than a half century? How many federal dollars is sufficient to offset the cost of previously defeated diseases like polio and measles to return to Maine families?
How about the cost to Mainers of legally dubious tariffs or war? And what about the cost to Mainers who stand to lose their health benefits through Medicaid, or lost food assistance?
Yes, Sen. Collins has brought home some “bacon” to Maine’s seniors, rural hospitals and first responders, but at what cost? Sen. Collins has let Maine down. It’s long past time for “Susie from The County” to return to her status in The County.
Bob Riley
Saco

title: Early voting for the November election is underway in Maine. Here’s how to do it
text:
Early voting has begun in Maine ahead of the Nov. 3 election, which features a high-profile set of races for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House, alongside State House and local contests.
Mainers can vote early for any reason from Monday through Oct. 29, and they can do so by casting a ballot in person at their local town office, returning their absentee ballot by mail or using a ballot drop box in their community.
Here are a few things to know about early voting.
Where and when can I vote early in Maine?
Early voting locations, hours and absentee ballot drop box locations for each municipality are available on the Maine Department of the Secretary of State’s website and its “Upcoming Elections” page.
On that page, voters can view and download the “Municipal Office Hours & Absentee Drop Box Locations” form, which lists each town’s office hours and drop box locations. Some towns offer early voting Monday through Friday, while others are only a few days per week or by appointment.
If a municipality does not have a listed address for a drop box, contact your town office. The “Find a Municipal Clerk or Registrar” page on the secretary of state’s website has a searchable database of contact information for local election officials.
The last day to vote early is Oct. 29, the Thursday before the Nov. 3 election. Mainers can also register to vote online or in person through Election Day. Visit registertovote.sos.maine.gov to register, update voter registration information or change party enrollment.
How do I vote by mail?
The deadline to request an absentee ballot is also Oct. 29. Absentee ballots must be returned to a municipal clerk by 8 p.m. Nov. 3, and unlike several states that allow ballots to be counted if they are at least postmarked by Election Day, only ballots received by the close of the polls on Election Day are counted in Maine.
To request an absentee ballot and find out more information about ballots for voters with disabilities and voters who are in the military or overseas, visit the “Absentee Voting” page on the secretary of state’s website.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said during a Monday morning news conference in Brunswick that laws regarding early voting and absentee ballots have not changed. That was a nod to President Donald Trump, who long criticized mail-in voting and proposed changes that were blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court but is now urging Americans to vote early.
“We have all unfortunately experienced frustration with the Postal Service and things from everyday mail to prescriptions not arriving in a timely manner,” Bellows said. “That’s why it can be so helpful to vote early.”
How do I track my absentee ballot?
Maine voters can track the status of their absentee ballot at absenteeballotrequest.sos.maine.gov.
How many Mainers have voted early so far, and what’s the breakdown by party?
The secretary of state’s office posts updated reports on absentee requests each Tuesday and Thursday. Ahead of the start of early voting, the office reported that 70,260 Mainers had requested absentee ballots, more than 45,000 ballots had been issued so far, and nearly 800 ballots had been returned and accepted.
About 57% of the absentee ballot requests were from registered Democrats, 14% from Republicans and 26% from unenrolled voters. The early gaps have narrowed in past elections as Election Day gets closer, though Democrats typically outpace Republicans in absentee voting.

title: Calling all crafters: Jesup opens self-facilitated Makerspace for community creatives
text:
BAR HARBOR — The Jesup Memorial Library has launched its Makerspace, inviting the community to explore creativity, collaboration, and new possibilities in the newly expanded historic building.
The library officially opened its expanded facility on July 19, after two years of dedicated construction and more than a decade of preparation, planning, and fundraising to create a new community space. The expansion offers full accessibility, with an elevator, a 120-person auditorium, an art gallery, a climate-controlled archival space, an interactive area for children and young teens, meeting rooms, and the Makerspace — which includes a digital lab.
The Makerspace, tucked on the first floor near the back entrance, offers a place for people to come together to work on ongoing projects, experiment with new ones, and explore digital technology alongside fellow creators. The collaborative, hands-on lab is stocked with common creative tools like scissors, hot glue guns, and paintbrushes, as well as larger tools like a chomp saw and a metal pipe cutter.
“The Makerspace is part of the joy that comes from the library’s expansion: providing a new service in the new space while retaining all the services in the historic space. We didn’t get rid of anything on the historic side; we needed to expand to offer more to our community,” said Jesup Memorial Library Director Megan Brooks.
The Makerspace offers monthly programming, with at least one adult and one youth program each month. Open studio hours are held on the first Saturday of every month, from 1-4 p.m. These drop-in hours are open to the community for creating anything, from finishing a knitting project to spending three hours on an entirely new creation. During the open studio hours, patrons may use the 3D printer with the assistance of a library technician.
Workshops and studio hours are led by Makerspace Assistant Sam Yanevskyy, a recent graduate of College of the Atlantic and an Education Technician at Conners Emerson School. In the Makerspace, Yanevskyy curates the monthly programming and hosts open studio hours to develop programs based on community input.
“I hope to support the space in serving the community with programming and functional crafting that is financially and physically accessible for everyone,” said Yanevskyy. “During the day, I work at Conners Emerson. When working with the youth members of our community, I can draw from what I see interests the students and use that knowledge to create new events in the Makerspace.”
Brooks expressed gratitude for Yansvskyy’s contributions to the Jesup Makerspace: “Sam is providing a wide perspective on what the Makerspace can offer to makers and has been heavily involved in programming and how it aligns with the community’s needs from the space.”
This month, the Makerspace is hosting two adult workshops. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, from 4-5:30 p.m., the workshop Bear Behavior: Mending Cozy Clothes will take place in the Jesup. This workshop is a collaboration with the Makerspace and Golden Hour Gear Repair, and it focuses on mending gear or layers for the winter months for both novice and experienced menders. All materials and tools will be supplied by the Makerspace.
On Thursday, Oct. 29, the Makerspace will host a Halloween Costume worktime for adults from 4:30-7 p.m. This open studio time will allow for adults to finish up any last-minute preparation for their Halloween costume debut.
“I want the Makerspace to be a creative, helpful space that is fun and safe for all users. I want the space to become a tool for the community. Part of that means designing programs specifically for the community,” said Yansvskyy.
The Makerspace is expanding to meet the community’s needs. During Conners Emerson School’s two-week break in October, the Jesup is partnering with the MDI YMCA’s youth programs. Youth participants will spend the morning at the YMCA and then head up the street to the Jesup for lunch and library fun. An aspect of the camp is theater work, where students will be asked to put on plays and small performances. Utilizing the Jesup’s Makerspace, students will have the opportunity to build their props and costumes over the course of the two-week break.
Alongside their special events, the Makerspace hosts community groups like the Island Quilters and a weekly knitting group.
“With all the suggestions we’re getting on what to put in the space, we know this is a growing place, and we know that with our current supplies and equipment, we’re just getting started. We’re not at the end … We have a history of making at the Jesup that has been happening for years. It’s wonderful to have this space that expands different types of making within the Jesup,” said Brooks.
Within the first summer season of the Jesup’s expansion, the library has been visited by thousands of patrons. The Jesup held its annual book sale for the first time in the expansion space and, for the first time since before the pandemic, inside the library. Since school started, the kids’ area has been filled with students. According to Brooks, more than 10,000 people entered the Jesup building in August alone.
“Seeing the kids’ area makes everyone’s heart sing,” said Brooks. “Everyone is coming into the building and using the library as it was envisioned when this expansion was planned. It’s been great to see the different ways people are using the building.”

title: MSSM to Host Public STEM Night
text:
LIMESTONE, Maine (WAGM) -The Maine School of Science and Mathematics in Limestone is hosting a STEM Discovery Night tonight from 6 to 8 p.m. The event is free and open to the public.
VO: School officials say students and staff will lead hands-on STEM activities designed with children in kindergarten through fifth grade in mind. Families will have the chance to explore a variety of interactive stations throughout the evening, including activities focused on circuits, engineering, motion, and chemistry. The event is designed to give young students and their families an opportunity to learn, experiment, and explore science, technology, engineering, and math in a fun, hands-on setting.
MSSM school officials said quote: “We’re really excited to welcome local families to MSSM for our first STEM Discovery Night. We wanted to create an opportunity for kids to explore STEM in a fun, hands-on way, and hopefully leave with more curiosity about the world around them. We’re excited to make events like this part of how MSSM connects with and serves the local community.”

title: US citizen who was shot by immigration agent in Chicago files lawsuit alleging he fired from behind
text:
CHICAGO — An American citizen shot by a Customs and Border Protection agent one year ago during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Monday, alleging the Maine-based agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.
Federal prosecutors initially accused Marimar Martinez, then 30, of using her vehicle to strike and box in agent Charles Exum’s SUV on Chicago’s southwest side on Oct. 4, 2025, during “Operation Midway Blitz.” Exum then exited his car and opened fire, leaving Martinez with seven gunshot wounds.
In the month after the shooting, prosecutors filed to dismiss the charges in a dramatic reversal of the closely watched case in the nation’s third-largest city.
Agent fired into rear of car, attorneys say
Her lawyers said Monday that they commissioned an expert to analyze bullet trajectories and her injuries and determined Exum wasn’t in the path of her car when he opened fire. They said he had walked several feet toward her car, contrary to statements he made to the FBI, and fired off five shots in less than a second, the last from the rear side of her vehicle.
“Charles Exum told the FBI agent on that day, within hours of the shooting, that Marimar was driving her car directly at him, that he shot her five times through the windshield, and that he ceased firing once he was no longer in the path of the vehicle. Those are three objective lies that you’ll see here today,” said one of her attorneys, Chris Parente.
Parente said there were only three bullet holes in Martinez’ windshield on the right passenger side, which indicated Martinez wasn’t driving toward the agent. He said the fourth shot was fired through the front passenger side window, adding another bullet hole in the back of Martinez’ car seat showed the agent fired the fifth shot from behind her.
“In what world can a U.S. law enforcement officer stand behind a car and fire his Glock service weapon through the rear passenger window at a young woman who’s crouched over the steering wheel?” Parente said.
CBP said in a statement to The Associated Press in response to the suit that Exum had been placed on administrative leave. Use-of-force incidents are “thoroughly investigated, reviewed, and presented” to an independent board, it added.
Exum is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the federal government, which was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act and does not allow for lawsuits against individual agents. It was not known where Exum could be reached.
Body-worn camera footage from another agent in Exum’s vehicle before the shooting captured the agents saying it was “time to get aggressive” and other profanity-laced comments by agents who were present encouraging violence, according to the complaint.
Martinez taken from hospital with bullet holes ‘leaking blood,’ suit says
The FBI arrested Martinez, taking her out of the hospital just hours after the shooting when she was “wheelchair bound and her bullet holes were leaking blood through her bandages,” according to the lawsuit. A judge ordered her release two days after her arrest.
Messages released by Martinez’ attorneys in February showed that former head of Border Patrol Greg Bovino had praised Exum for his “excellent service in Chicago” after the shooting. Other messages they released showed agents in a group chat congratulating Exum and calling him a “legend.”
Martinez was one several people shot in their cars by federal agents during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. An immigration agent shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in his car in Austin, Texas, last month, and another shot a Colombian driver in Biddeford, Maine, in July. The Trump administration has at times justified such shootings as self-defense against people allegedly weaponizing their vehicles.
Martinez appeared with her attorneys at a news conference Monday, saying the various shootings spurred her to file suit.
“If I don’t, then who else, you know? Look at what happened to Renee and all these victims,” she said, referring to Renee Good, a woman shot dead in her vehicle by a federal agent in Minneapolis in January.
“What’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t stay here and normalize what’s happening,” she said.
Story by Cybele Mayes-Osterman, a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Starbucks mislabeled 8 ‘sugar-free’ protein drinks, lawsuit alleges
text:
(AP) - Starbucks is facing a consumer lawsuit over claims that the protein drinks labeled “sugar-free” on its cafe menus may actually contain more sugar than a Reese’s peanut butter cup.
The federal lawsuit filed late Friday in Seattle alleges that eight protein beverages Starbucks sells in the U.S. contain varying amounts of sugar even though the company lists them as sugarless.
On Monday, the menu on Starbucks’ U.S. website listed a 16-ounce (0.5-liter) Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Matcha with 16 grams of sugar and a 20-ounce (0.6-liter) version of the same drink with 21 grams of sugar. By comparison, one Reese’s cup has 11 grams of sugar.
Hagens Berman, a law firm that specializes in class action cases, filed the suit on behalf of three individual consumers who bought Starbucks’ sugar-free protein drinks in California, New York and Washington.
“Consumers avoid sugar for various reasons, whether that be general health, diabetes and blood glucose levels or other factors, and for many, a staunch mislabeling like this is significant,” said Steve Berman, a co-founder and managing partner of the Seattle-headquartered firm.
The plaintiffs contend that Starbucks’ naming and marketing of sugar-free products is “false, deceptive and unlawful” and that the company violated federal labeling regulations.
Seattle-based Starbucks said the sugar in its protein drinks comes from the protein-boosted milk it uses. The company said it doesn’t add sugar to the drinks and it uses sugar-free syrup for flavoring.
On Starbucks’ website Monday, the drinks were marketed as “sugar-free,” but the company also clearly stated the amount of sugar in each beverage and that they were made without added sugar.
“We believe these claims have no merit,” a Starbucks spokesperson said Monday. “Starbucks has consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices and nutritional content across product announcements, menus, marketing materials, Starbucks.com and the Starbucks app, and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves in this matter.”
Starbucks introduced its protein drinks in September 2025 to meet consumer demand for functional beverages and catch up to rivals like Dutch Bros, which launched protein-enhanced coffee drinks in 2024.
Dutch Bros also offers a lower-sugar version of its caramel-flavored Hopscotch Protein Latte, but it’s advertised as the Hopscotch Zero Sugar Added Protein Latte. The 16-ounce (0.5-liter) iced version has 7 grams of sugar and 11 grams of protein. By comparison, a 16-ounce (0.5-liter) iced Starbucks Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte has 9 grams of sugar and 29 grams of protein.
The lawsuit seeks damages on behalf of U.S. consumers who bought the drinks. It also wants the court to order Starbucks to stop using the label “sugar-free” on products that contain sugar.

title: Weather Discussion 10/5/26
Why ‘ladybugs’ invade Maine homes in fall — and how to get rid of them
text:
This was originally published Oct. 6, 2025.
I have a ton of “ladybugs” in my home. They’re not just on the ceiling — they’re crawling along wall edges, getting past window frames and flying around erratically.
Some get stuck in my hair or fall onto my shoulder while I’m minding my own business. They’re annoying and impossible to ignore. The only redeeming thing about them is that they remind me of my dog, Lady, who I used to call Ladybug. She passed away in May.
My home faces southeast, which means it catches the morning and midday sun, warming walls and windows just enough to attract these creatures.
These are multicolored Asian lady beetles, an invasive species in the same family as Maine’s native ladybugs. Unlike the natives, which stay outdoors, these beetles often move indoors in the fall to overwinter.
They appear in many color variations, but in Maine the most common is the red or orange Succinea form, which can have anywhere from zero to 19 spots. Drawn to light-colored walls and sun-warmed windows, they often cluster in corners, along ceilings and near attics once inside.
The good news is they’re mostly harmless. They don’t chew on furniture, spread disease or reproduce indoors. The downside is that crushing them releases a strong odor and yellow stain, and they can bite, although I haven’t experienced this myself.
Aside from the obvious need to block entry points, natural repellents can help prevent beetles from entering your home. They dislike the scents of essential oils like citronella, peppermint and citrus — a few drops mixed with water in a spray bottle and applied to windowsills or door frames can be effective. You can also put a few drops on a cotton ball and place it between the window and screen.
Other strong scents from bay leaves, cloves or chrysanthemums can repel these nuisances. Since mums are already a common fall decoration, placing them inside and outside can discourage insect activity.
If they are already inside, avoid sprays because most insecticides — including pyrethrin-based ones — can irritate pets and humans. For a no-nonsense removal method, a vinegar-and-water solution works well. It kills the beetles and removes pheromones that attract others. Adding a few drops of dish soap helps the solution adhere to surfaces.
Because these insects are attracted to light, reducing outdoor lighting and using light traps indoors can help limit their activity.
Asian lady beetles may be a pest inside your home, but outdoors, they play an important role in Maine’s gardens and forests, feeding on aphids. With a few preventive measures, you can keep these seasonal visitors where they belong — out in nature and not crawling across your ceilings.

title: Christa Pike received life-saving measures after her botched lethal injection. Here’s why
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - After a failed execution, Christa Pike remains in the hospital on a ventilator in critical condition.
On Wednesday, Pike received two doses of pentobarbital and saline, but she remained alive.
During the process, witnesses described Pike as having labored breathing, snoring heavily and, at some points, sounding like she was choking.
Ambulances later arrived at Riverbend Maximum Security and took her to the hospital.
After Pike’s failed execution, people are questioning why Tennessee performed life-saving measures on Pike when they planned to execute her.
What the execution team is required to do before and during the execution process
According to Tennessee’s 2025 lethal injection protocol, team members must rely on the protocol for training.
Leading up to Pike’s execution, the execution team, IV team and physician were required to review the protocol when they were assigned. The warden is also required to review the protocol with them every year.
According to the protocol, staff must prepare four syringes, two containing 50 mg of saline and two containing 50 mg of pentobarbital.
During the execution, staff must open the blinds so witnesses can view the execution chamber. The inmate will say their last words and the pentobarbital will be administered. After a five-minute waiting period, the blinds are closed and a doctor must examine the inmate.
The document goes on to explain that if the inmate remains alive, a backup set of four syringes must be administered. The blinds must be opened again for witnesses to view the injections, and then must be closed again as medics examine the inmate to see if the inmate died.
That’s exactly what happened Wednesday night at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, according to execution witnesses and the Tennessee Department of Correction.
But what happens if the inmate still does not die?
A loophole in the protocol
That is the question the Tennessee Department of Correction prison staff were forced to deal with in real time on Wednesday evening when Pike remained alive.
The protocol mentions nothing about what happens if the execution fails, but the Eighth Amendment of the United States Constitution explains that “cruel and unusual punishments” cannot be inflicted.
Attorneys and Tennessee officials push for answers
Pike’s failed execution prompted Gov. Bill Lee to halt the one remaining execution this year and order a full investigation.
It is still unclear how Pike survived the two doses of pentobarbital, and the state protocol indicates she is the first to do so. However, it is possible she survived due to a mistake made along the way.
The Tennessee Department of Correction denies making any mistakes and has declined to answer further questions on Pike’s execution, but Lee ordered a “comprehensive” third-party review of Wednesday night’s events, which will be conducted by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton.
On Saturday, Lee announced that Frank Strada, the state’s Department of Correction commissioner, was resigning.
Pike’s legal team is also challenging the lethal injection protocol. They previously asked Tennessee to use hanging instead of lethal injection and argued that her blood disorder, vein-access issues and history of trauma could result in unnecessary suffering. Their request was denied.

title: Orono Public Library staff prepare for expansion as construction bids approach
text:
The Orono Public Library is moving closer to beginning an $8.62 million expansion, with construction bids expected in mid-October. In an Oct. 1 interview with the Maine Campus, Orono Public Library Foundation (OPLF) President James Jackson Sanborn and Library Director Laurie Carpenter discussed the challenges of the project and the community support that has shaped its development since planning began in 2023.
When the library first opened, its location changed frequently due to rising demand for a community-oriented public space. Previous locations included the Orono Christian Temperance Union, the Katahdin Building, the Keith Anderson House and the Orono High School. Now, the library is located at 39 Pine Street.
Orono community members have been at the heart of this process since 2002, when the OPLF was established and initial planning for the building began. Finally, in September 2009, the grand opening of the new public library took place.
In 2015, the foundation launched a “second chapter,” with a project that would expand outdoor spaces for visitors. Today, the foundation hopes to expand on their projects with their campaign Achieving the Vision, which includes updated child, teen and adult areas, work space for library staff and a larger community living room.
The campaign brochure highlights projected expenses of $8.62 million with about 96% being construction expenses. Carpenter and Sanborn explained that the campaign has received financial support from over 500 private donors, the town council and manager and federal funds. The rest of the money was matched by the town through fundraising efforts with $8.62 million in projected revenues.
The library’s floor plan provides a visual representation of the additional expanded areas. With expected bids from contractors in mid-October, program continuity has become a rising challenge while expansions are being completed. Depending on construction factors, the library may close for up to a month; however, Carpenter is hopeful that there will be other options in the community to move library programming so that it remains open.
“We are feeling pretty good about where we are having faced challenges,” said Sanborn.
Internal support from the board of trustees, fundraising and staff dedication has been critical during the planning process.
“The staff of the library have been key and helped us think about what the library should be and what it could be,” said Sanborn.
Externally, the support has been matched through collaborative relationships with multiple stakeholders such as the Orono school system. With active participation in building committees and focus groups, community members have dedicated their time and effort to provide feedback.
Both Carpenter and Sanborn believe in having a community space where members are able to connect with each other.
“Having a great collection is just as important as having space for people to connect,” said Carpenter.
In addition to the physical renovations, the goals of this expansion remain rooted in giving back to the community and promoting educational opportunities.
“One of our basic missions is basic literacy,” said Carpenter. “Recreational reading is important and a lifelong skill and it’s all part of the mission of the community too.”
To further encourage this effort, both Sanborn and Carpenter welcome university students into the library to receive a free library card and use the resources available as members of the Orono community.

title: Maine Forest and Logging Museum celebrates history with annual ‘Living History Days’
text:
BRADLEY, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Forest and Logging Museum held its annual Living History Days celebration over the weekend.
Historical reenactors as well as local traditional craftsmen performed demonstrations for attendees, showcasing colonial-era cooking, blacksmithing, fiber arts and other traditional crafts.
The event celebrates American history from the colonial era to modern day.
“For me, it’s honestly the interaction with the people, the children, seeing everybody coming out, have a good time, watching the reenactors, just seeing how it all comes together,” said Bryan Harper, a member of the Maine Forest and Logging Museum Board of Directors.
Harper has been involved with the event for three years.
“Part of anything like this are the volunteers, the reenactors. Without them, any non-profit or organization like ourselves, we cease to exist. It’s just a great way to give back to the community,” said Harper.
To learn more about the Maine Forest and Logging Museum, visit www.maineforestandloggingmuseum.org.
