title: Norway commits 2026 property taxes over citizens’ objections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After residents departed the Norway Select Board‘s business meeting Oct. 1 with no answers on what their tax bills will look like this year, Town Manager Jill Lathan announced Friday that contracted tax assessor John O’Donnell had committed the property taxes and set the tax rate at $10.85.
In an 8 a.m. email statement, Lathan wrote that the property taxes had been committed at at rate of $10.85 per $1,000 of assessed value.
She later clarified that “the tax commitment was officially filed October 1st to the State (of Maine). It was confirmed this morning.”
Dozens of residents have spoken out at recent Select Board meetings about issues they say resulted in revaluations recently done by O’Donnell’s appraisal firm, John E. O’Donnell & Associates containing errors and oversights.
It’s the first revaluation the town has done in 19 years..
To a person, each urged the board to rescind or delay the revaluations, or at least alter the process, to give taxpayers leeway to properly refute their updated tax cards.
Several alleged that O’Donnell’s company’s staff cut corners during the reevaluation, misrepresenting building uses, failing to measure structures and incorrectly assigning condition grades and comparative properties to determine values, among other issues.
It has also been asserted that O’Donnell has a conflict of interest, with property owners now in a position of having to challenge a private business owner who also has the power as a sworn town official to acknowledge or deny their disputes with its services.
About 1,000 Norway property owners will see a tax decreases as a result of the revaluation. But values and tax payments are increasing for more than 3,400, many significantly.
Last month Matthew Glatz, a resident of King Street who said his multiunit home value soared by 200%, created a website — A Citizen’s Guide for Fair and Transparent Property Tax Valuations, norwayparcelreview.org — which calculates how property values for every parcel in Norway changed from 2025 to 2026.
Last year, his home’s assessed value was $115,923 and his taxes were $2,363, based on a tax rate of $20.38.
Now it is valued at $349,015, and using a hypothetical tax rate of $10.96 the website calculates that this year his tax bill would be $3,825. Applying the $10.85 rate Lathan announced Oct. 2, his actual taxes will be $3,787.
On Oct. 1, as an example of one problem with his revaluation, Glatz pointed out to the board how the foundation of his house had been miscategorized. “At 15 King St., it has a sand basement floor,” he said. “The basement is only 16 by 16 feet. More than half my basement is crawlspace … The building grade does not increase when a re-evaluation occurs. You cannot change the structure or skeleton of a building.
No property owner has disputed the need for a revaluation in Norway.
But town spending has jumped by 50% over the last four years, a period overseen by three short-term, acting or interim town managers.
This year’s municipal budget was 11% higher than for the 2025 fiscal year.

title: Why I’m out canvassing for Troy Jackson
text:
Sandra Smith Congdon is a Maine Democrats campaign volunteer and Saco Democratic Committee member.
I’m out every weekend canvassing for Troy Jackson in York County with the hope that we can flip the U.S. Senate because Maine is central to that fight.
I grew up in a working-class family in the ’70s and ’80s. My father worked in construction and my mother worked in retail, both in unions that provided them with fair wages and good healthcare. They worked hard to put food on the table for our family and made sure we had what we needed and sometimes could even afford things that we “wanted.”
The reason I’m supporting Troy is because I see a lot of working-class people today who can no longer afford basic needs. Troy wasn’t my first pick to run against Susan Collins but the more I hear him speak and hear others talk about him, the more I believe he’s the right choice for Maine. His working-class roots and his experience in the Maine Senate show that he is a fighter and will work hard for Mainers.
Mostly I’m out knocking on strangers’ doors because I cannot believe what I’m seeing every day in our Capitol. The bombastic man occupying the Oval Office has staffed his cabinet with sycophants whose only qualifications are blind loyalty and public praise of their boss. His only consistent policy is maximizing financial gain for himself and the billionaires who understand his pay-to-play mindset.
He isn’t listening to, nor does he care about, working-class people. He doesn’t see that the average American is struggling to afford food, fuel, healthcare, childcare, housing and other basic needs. He doesn’t even try to hide the corruption or his all-important ego, focusing on buying or bullying his name onto whatever he can in an attempt to paint himself a legacy in D.C. vs. earning it from the American people.
But worst of all is the lack of accountability, because Republicans in Congress are unwilling to stand up to his schoolyard bullying and brazen grift. They are showing the American public very clearly that their hold on power is far more important to them than the well-being of our great nation.
We need to flip the House and the Senate in the midterms to bring back checks and balances (not to mention basic accountability) to this administration. We cannot afford another two years of expensive pet projects, a continuing war in Iran driving up fuel costs, the whittling away of our education system, legislation that makes it harder to vote, abuse and alienation of our allies, deaths of U.S. citizens at the hands of ICE and tariffs that are being passed on to American consumers. We cannot afford children going hungry because of SNAP cuts, an EPA that is enabling the destruction of the planet, whitewashing or erasing U.S. history and a lack of AI regulation that could quickly get out of human control.
I encourage you all to tune out the negative campaign ads that stretch the truth and look at how we can be better humans and get back to having an American dream again where basic needs are met and working people can even afford some wants. This will not happen with the current administration or Susan Collins’ consistent enabling. As everyone can clearly see, Collins votes with the Republicans 95% of the time and only doesn’t when her vote won’t make a difference. Collins may have been a moderate at some point during her career, but she no longer fits that definition.
Please vote for Troy Jackson and other Democratic candidates so working-class people, not just billionaires, have a shot at the American dream.

Brisbane 2032 launches a cockatoo emblem for Olympics and Paralympics
text:
Brisbane 2032 launches a cockatoo emblem for Olympics and Paralympics
The cockatoo has won out over the kangaroo, the koala and the bin chicken to become the emblem of the 2032 Olympics and Paralympics — after a bit of an embarrassing social media leak.
It's now official.
Video above: Simone Biles interview about 2028 Olympics
Days after officials in Brisbane were forced to hold a hastily-convened news conference to explain the accidental leaking of the emblem ahead of schedule, the 2032 organizing committee held an official launch on Monday.
The Olympic emblem is the crest of a pink cockatoo, an Australian bird, with the color stylized to resemble an Olympic and Paralympic flame, and a shape to resemble the host state of Queensland.
Brisbane’s Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner on Monday said the emblems “are a celebration of our city, our lifestyle.”
“They reflect the Brisbane (that) people know and love: vibrant, resilient, connected, friendly, playful and a little bit cheeky,” Schrinner said. “They are also a symbol of the excitement building across our city.
“With just under six years to go, we are already preparing to welcome the world to Australia’s lifestyle capital.”
Organizers said First Nations elements were contained within the emblems, with “cockatoos seen as messengers carrying cultural meaning and linking people to place, story and ceremony.” The emblems are separate to the Games mascot, which will be revealed closer to the Games.
An explainer video meant to go live after a planned ceremonial event briefly appeared on the event’s YouTube channel on Friday night. Screenshots of images and text soon circulated on social media.
Brisbane 2032 vice president Tim Mander and chief marketing officer Brent Hill told the weekend news conference the accidental release was a pleasant surprise. Hill embraced the unexpected opportunity, saying “the publicity has been incredible.”
Ahead of the community launch Monday evening in the downtown Southbank parklands, Brisbane 2032 chairman Andrew Liveris said the “emblems are an opportunity to promote the unique character of a Games, inviting the world to learn more, visit, invest and be part of an event unlike any other,”
For Mikaela Cojuangco Jaworski, who heads the IOC's coordination commission for the 2032 Games, the emblems represented a “vibrant expression” of the nature and character of the region. The Olympics and Paralympics will be centered on the state capital, Brisbane, but cities across the state, including the Gold Coast and the Sunshine Coast, will host competitions.
Australia has twice previously hosted the Summer Olympics, at Melbourne in 1956 and at Sydney in 2000.
The Sydney emblem design contained representations of famous landmarks including the Sydney Opera House, the city's famous harbor and beaches, as well as boomerangs, sun and rocks.

title: Late comeback falls short as Maine drops fifth straight to Sacred Heart
text:
ORONO, Maine — On Saturday, Oct. 3, the Maine Black Bears football team’s late comeback attempt fell short as they dropped their fifth straight game, losing 24-16 to the Sacred Heart University Pioneers.
Maine entered the game looking to snap a four-game losing streak and improve to 2-1 in CAA play. Instead, the Black Bears struggled to find the end zone early and were unable to overcome a Sacred Heart offense that took control in the second half. Sacred Heart Head Coach Mark Nofri said before the game that his team expected a physical challenge from Maine, calling the Black Bears a “well-coached football team” that was “big and physical.”
Maine controlled the early stages of the game. The Black Bear defense made several strong stands, including one before Maine’s first score when the Black Bears stuffed third-year quarterback Poochie Snyder and forced a turnover on downs.
This stop directly led to a Maine field goal when the Pioneers made a stop on the following drive. Redshirt second-year kicker Samuel Tremblay hit that field goal from 42 yards. He also picked up the next two scores in the game, hitting from 45 and 37 yards out, as Maine failed to reach the end zone.
The Black Bears paid for failing to score a touchdown, as the Pioneers wore down the Black Bear defense and scored their first points of the day when third-year wide receiver Dean Hangey punched it in from three yards out. Sacred Heart took the lead just before halftime when Snyder threw an 11-yard touchdown pass to fourth-year wide receiver Jason Palmieri.
Early in the third quarter, the Black Bears looked in danger of being blown away when Snyder threw a second touchdown pass, this time a six-yarder to fourth-year tight end Brendan Errity.
The teams traded possessions following this, with Maine finally finding the end zone three minutes into the third quarter. Here, the Black Bears drove 69 yards down the field, with redshirt third-year running back Nick Laughlin rushing for a touchdown from two yards out.
Sacred Heart responded with an eight-play, 38-yard drive that ended in a 40-yard field goal from second-year kicker Ryan Bocklet.
Maine attempted to find a game-tying touchdown, driving into Pioneers territory before turning the ball over on downs. Maine’s defense got the ball back, but the Black Bears again turned it over on downs, allowing Sacred Heart to run out the clock.
The game featured a two-quarterback system from Maine, with the Black Bears switching quarterbacks every other possession between redshirt second-year Eddie Buehler and redshirt third-year Caden Drezek. Buehler went 1-for-5 on his pass attempts, throwing for 13 yards and rushing for 2 yards, while Drezek was the quarterback for Maine’s final three drives, going 12-for-28 passing for 141 yards and also rushing for 19 yards.
On the other side, Snyder played every snap under center except one. Snyder threw two touchdown passes, going 21-for-27 and throwing for 207 yards. He also led Sacred Heart in rushing, putting up 73 yards against Maine.
For Maine, the Black Bears are now 1-5 and have lost five straight. Maine is also 1-2 in conference play and will have a bye next week to regroup before returning to action against the Bryant Bulldogs in Orono.
Maine will have to work to turn around a season that has quickly become a struggle after a 1-0 start. The Black Bears will need to find a way to turn their late offensive pushes into points while continuing to rely on a defense that has kept them competitive despite the team’s recent struggles.

title: Home heating costs top of mind for most Mainers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Home heating costs top of mind for most Maine residents
With heating oil prices being so high, many people in Maine are turning to wood to heat their homes.
A nonprofit wood bank in Franklin County is offering clients a discount to make it even more affordable.
Christmas has come early for Thelma Jewell in the form of firewood, and Jim Webster is her Santa Claus.
Jewell, 79, lives alone in a small house in the village of Dryden, which is in the town of Wilton.
"I was able to keep up with the oil when the prices were reasonable, but they've gone beyond anything reasonable now," Jewell said.
Jewell called the oil company Monday morning and was told oil is now $5.95 per gallon. She said she has $1,100 saved for oil this year, which would not have even filled her tank once.
Jewell, like many Mainers, is turning to wood.
The Webster Wood Bank has come to the rescue of many by delivering cords of wood at a discount so more Mainers can stay warm.
The average price for a cord of wood currently is just shy of $400. The United Methodist Economic Ministry fired up the only wood bank in Franklin County last year in Salem Township, about 20 miles north of Farmington.
The wood bank is able to offer wood cut, split and delivered at a discount thanks to grants and donations.
"We are selling our wood for $275 a cord," said Jim Webster of the United Methodist Economic Ministry.
"I got those four cords of wood for that, so that's going to get me roughly four months, and that's more than oil would have gone me one month or a month and a half," Jewell said.
Jewell said the wood bank is a godsend.
"That was a blessing. I don't know what I would have done," she said. "Thank God he's got it to sell to me that I can afford, you know."
The Webster Wood Bank expects to help 300 to 400 families this year. That is up from 250 families last year. If you'd like to learn more, you can call 207-678-2611.

title: Eastport City Council asks feds to deny application for underwater data center
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
EASTPORT, Maine — The Eastport City Council registered a formal motion to intervene with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission last week in an attempt to block a controversial subsea artificial intelligence data center proposal, DeepGreen Western Passage SPV.
The councilors, who also sent an accompanying statement to FERC that was posted a day later, joined a growing list of residents and organizations fighting the project, including the nonprofit research group the Center for Biodiversity, by registering official concern over the DeepGreen Western Passage application for 48-month preliminary permit, which was accepted for filing by the agency in August.
The August acceptance of DeepGreen’s FERC preliminary permit application by the Commission kicked off a 60-day process for community members, organizations and other relevant parties to formally intervene in the permit proceedings; that window closes this month.
In a letter to FERC posted on Sept 30, the City Council asked that FERC deny the application.
“We recognize that a preliminary permit would not authorize construction or land-disturbing activities,” councilors wrote. “Nevertheless, it would give DeepGreen priority to pursue development of this project at this location for up to four years. That is a significant procedural benefit involving waters and community interests that are central to Eastport’s economy, heritage, and future.”
The letter went on to list specific concerns, including unexplored impacts on fish, wildlife and overall marine habitat from sediment, underwater noise, electromagnetic fields and heat; access and use to waterways, resources and other waterborne assets; effect on industries like fisheries; effect on water quality, and vagueness regarding site recovery and decommissioning.
In the letter, councilors also expressed concern over project unknowns, like how much it might cost the city if the project requires emergency response or other city works or utilities. The letter also outlined a desire for accountability to the Passamaquoddy tribe, who, the council wrote, should be consulted with meaningfully before any permit is considered.
The letter also noted that “On September 9, 2026, the Eastport City Council unanimously enacted ordinance provisions prohibiting large-scale data centers, including underwater data centers, within the areas covered by those provisions. The Council expects to undertake additional work to strengthen and clarify the City’s protections.”
The ordinance ban was enacted after the City Council voted to enact a temporary moratorium on data center development.
The council raised questions about the technical experience of the developer and managing member of DeepGreen Holdings LLC, Louis Wolfson, who has not been present in person for the Eastport proceedings.
Wolfson’s background is in luxury real estate development in Needham, Massachusetts. 
DeepGreen Holdings LLC was incorporated in Delaware just weeks before preliminary permit applications were submitted to FERC by the company’s project subsidiaries, DeepGreen Western Passage SPV and DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, for similar hydrokinetic data center projects in Eastport in Maine, and Cook Inlet, Alaska.
Special project vehicles, or SPVs, are a type of legal formation developers often use when they intend to package and sell a project with all of its permits and agreements in place.
Commenters from Alaska Commercial Fisheries Conservation Alliance, who objected to the FERC docket assigned to Cook Inlet Alaska, also registered their formal objection letter to the Eastport project’s comments, citing similar concerns about impacts on local water temperature and commercial fisheries in the area. Further, ACFCA says DeepGreen used decisions by the commission in their response to these concerns that cannot be verified by the group as “genuine Commission decisions.”
In the FERC file for DeepGreen Western Passage SPV, Ocean Renewable Power Co., ORPC, a company once named by Wolfson on the preliminary permit application because of its hydrokinetic turbine technology, also filed a comment stating DeepGreen’s application language could be “interpreted that extensive discussions have happened between ORPC and DeepGreen regarding the integration of ORPC’s turbines onto DeepGreen’s proposed data center.”
Stuart Davies, chief executive officer of ORPC, stated “we are submitting this comment to clarify for FERC that ORPC has no involvement in DeepGreen’s project and that no conversations have occurred between ORPC and DeepGreen regarding the integration of ORPC turbines with DeepGreen’s proposed data center.”
In their letter to FERC, councilors also noted that DeepGreen’s proposal “does not establish
that the electricity generated would provide a direct energy or grid-reliability benefit to Eastport residents or the surrounding region.”
Eastport residents Carrie Cobb and Gary Fronheiser have also filed motions to intervene in the case, along with the nonprofit Center for Biological Diversity, Eastport Community Solar and the National Marine Fisheries Service Greater Atlantic Region.
Once the 60-day comment period closes this month, FERC will review DeepGreen’s preliminary permit application for the Western Passage, considering comments from the public, and will begin to schedule intervention hearings with those whose petitions have been accepted.
Registration of Motions to Intervene and public comment closes on Oct. 19.
This story appears as part of a collaboration to strengthen investigative journalism in Maine between the BDN and The Maine Monitor. Read more about the partnership.

title: Prosecutors claim Maine man admitted to 1984 murder of 18-year-old
text:
Prosecutors claim Maine man admitted to 1984 murder of Linda Maxwell
A Maine man accused of killing an 18-year-old Calais woman more than 40 years ago admitted the crime to a fellow inmate, according to prosecutors.
Opening statements were heard Monday in the trial of Raymond Brown, 67, of Bangor, who has been charged with the 1984 murder of Linda Maxwell.
Police said Maxwell was last seen in the Calais area on Aug. 23, 1984, after spending the evening with friends. Two days later, Maxwell's body was recovered along the shoreline of the St. Croix River in Robbinston.
Brown, formerly of Pembroke, was arrested in May 2025 after he was indicted by a Washington County grand jury.
Prosecutors said during opening statements that Brown told an inmate that he suffocated Maxwell in a bog and later dumped her body in the St. Croix River, according to WMTW media partner WABI.
Assistant District Attorney Suzanne Russell told jurors that Maxwell, her friends and Brown had been drinking heavily the night Maxwell died. Prosecutors said that Brown, who was married at the time, wanted to have sex with Maxwell. According to prosecutors, Brown was supposed to take Maxwell home that night, but killed her after she threatened to tell people he raped her. Russell said Brown planned to dump Maxwell's body in her driveway, but instead decided to leave her in the river.
Brown's attorneys questioned whether the state has proven Maxwell's death was a murder. The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner initially ruled Maxwell's death was a drowning.
The defense said Brown did not kill Maxwell, and that the state decided to focus on him.
Evidence will begin to be presented to jurors on Tuesday.

title: I hunted whitetail for years. Then one day, I became allergic.
text:
In mid-October 2003, I arrowed my largest Maine buck. It wasn’t a massive-racked, record-book contender on the same scale as some bucks that come out of Illinois, Ohio, Iowa and other big-buck-producing states, but at 200 pounds field-dressed, with nine typical points and a 141 3/8-inch Pope and Young score, it remains the largest Maine buck I’ve ever taken.
I still remember the shot. It was late in the day, and the setting sun was casting dark shadows across the heavy foliage. The buck eventually stepped onto the old tote road I had walked in on several hours earlier.
There were only a few minutes left before legal shooting hours ended. I was hunting with an old, well-used Martin WartHog compound with laminated wooden limbs and cams about the size of a 50-cent piece. I was new to bowhunting and shooting instinctively, so I needed the buck to get closer.
As luck would have it, he walked in my direction. About 30 yards away, he turned and gave me a perfect broadside shot.
I took it, but the thing that remains most vivid in my mind is watching the arrow fly like a Tom Brady Hail Mary pass to Gronk. I never thought it would reach its mark.
Of course, it did.
But the arrow flight wasn’t the most memorable part of that hunt.
The most memorable part came after I killed that buck. That’s when I discovered I was allergic to deer.
I’ve hunted since my teenage years and all my adult life. I’ve had successful hunts for bear, elk, caribou, moose, pronghorn and, of course, deer, and never had a negative physical reaction to any of them during or after the field-dressing process.
Until that day.
I’ve never been allergic to anything. They say the human body changes every seven years. I don’t know if that is factually true, but something changed because I had experienced no reaction to the deer I arrowed the year before.
That made me think the itchy, swollen eyes, congestion, wheezing, sneezing, runny nose and facial redness that occurred shortly after field-dressing the buck were just a fluke.
“Maybe he got into some poison ivy or something and it was still on his body,” I thought.
But that was wishful thinking.
I’ve experienced the same reactions to deer during every successful season since. The good thing is that the symptoms don’t last long. After taking a hot shower, I take antihistamines, which ease the congestion, wheezing and runny nose. The swollen hives take a few days to go down, but in less than a week, I’m back to normal.
To this day, I don’t know precisely what it is about deer that causes my body to react the way it does — dander, blood, saliva or urine, all of which can cause uncomfortable symptoms.
I eventually spoke with my family doctor, who suggested I see a dermatologist to determine the exact cause and what could be done about it. But since my initial reaction to that big buck, I have experienced no symptoms from other game or animals in general. I have no reaction to eating venison and have no other allergies.
I had a pretty good idea it had something to do with deer, so I declined the referral.
In time, I’ve learned to live with it.
I know the symptoms will be coming, so when I head for the woods each day, I go prepared. In my pack, I carry a nondrowsy antihistamine such as Claritin, Zyrtec or a generic equivalent. If I arrow or shoot a deer, I take one and wait about 30 minutes before touching the deer.
I also carry a painter’s mask to limit airborne particles such as dander and, as an extra precaution, swimming goggles to protect my eyes, which, other than the wheezing, seem to be affected the most.
To provide some protection from blood and other fluids, I wear elbow-length latex gloves during the field-dressing process and while getting the deer out of the woods.
If there’s a water source nearby, I wash my knife and other tools used to field-dress the deer. If not, I carry antiseptic wipes to clean them before returning them to my pack.
Finally, I always carry hypoallergenic baby wipes to wash my face, neck and other exposed skin. I even wash my hands after removing the gloves, just as an extra precaution.
While these precautions may not be medically ideal or all that can be done to relieve my annual fall curse, they reduce the effects enough that I can live with them for a few days.
I’ve since learned that deer allergies are not as uncommon as some might think. I’m not alone, and others also suffer from the same fate each fall, surprisingly including one of the cutters at the deer processor we use.
It hasn’t stopped him from doing what he does or from hunting.
And it won’t stop me, either.

title: Frats need to change if they want to stay on campus
text:
EDITORIAL: Early last week, a story came out that shook America.
A Cornell University student going by Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the university and seven current and former members of the Chi Phi fraternity chapter. The lawsuit alleges that she was drugged, raped and sexually assaulted by the seven men listed in the lawsuit.
The new detailed information, as well as some of the decisions made by Cornell surrounding her report back in 2024, has people outraged and finally ready to have difficult conversations about fraternities on campus.
Fraternities’ stated goals are to build leaders, foster brotherhood and serve their community. While that does take place, fraternities also bring a very distinct party culture to campus.
This culture is present from the beginning, when freshmen seeking to prove themselves and become brothers of the fraternity are known as “pledges.” While not every frat hazes their pledges, it is historically a problem for most. Hazing can come in many forms, but often manifests in incidents like forced consumption of drugs and alcohol, forced reckless behavior, sexual acts, public shaming or a combination of more than one of these.
On top of the way fraternities can treat their own brothers, their parties are also shrouded in hazard. While they can be fun, there is a sense of danger, and a necessity for caution to make sure horrific events like the ones that Jane Doe is alleging don’t happen to you or someone you care about.
While numbers in studies vary, there are reports that members of fraternities can be three times as likely to commit a criminal sexual act than their peers. On top of this, women who are in sororities — the organizations who are often partnered with frats and frequently attend frat events — are up to 74% more likely to be sexually assaulted than other women on college campuses.
But we don’t need to tell you that fraternities often have a reputation of bad behavior. If you’ve been on campus long enough, you know which frats to go to and which ones to avoid — and that should never be a thought people have to have.
This latest incident at Cornell has brought some people’s minds to a question that others have been pondering for a while: why are fraternities necessary on campus?
Fraternities can bring good things to campus and are not all net negatives, but with certain behaviors they bring, it can make you wonder why they are university organizations.
If fraternities stay on campus, they need to be the opposite of what their current image is. They need to be the lead group in helping fight the culture of sexual assault that can reside on a college campus. Additionally, until this culture changes, universities need to have a higher level of scrutiny concerning fraternities and not have leniency when it comes to punishment.
There needs to be systemic change, because this behavior is happening at every university, not just Cornell.

title: Ellsworth food stand owners differ on possible food sovereignty ordinance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The owners of two popular, honor-system food shops in Ellsworth are at odds over a potential food sovereignty ordinance that could allow small-scale food producers to sell directly to consumers, bypassing some state licensing and inspections requirements.
Ellsworth is weighing the adoption of an ordinance that could strip some administrative hurdles for small, local food producers to operate in the city. The move, which would apply to foods produced for home consumption or sold at some community events, could loosen certain strict state conditions like installing a commercial grade kitchen.
As of now, residents can only sell homemade food prepared with shelf-stable items, like baked goods and jams.
If passed, Ellsworth would be one of more than a hundred Maine municipalities with similar ordinances in place. The expansion of the state’s 2017 Food Sovereignty Act allows municipalities to adopt such ordinances, which has already been passed in many Maine communities and others in Hancock County such as Blue Hill, Bucksport and Trenton, among others.
Two already-established Ellsworth food producers, Brenda Ledezma of Momo’s Cheesecakes and Amy Henderson of Lincoln’s Farmstand, don’t quite agree with one another on the idea.
“I think it’s a great idea because not everybody can afford a commercial kitchen,” Ledezma said Friday. “We were lucky, we had a building off the side of our house that we could go into, but not everyone has that. I don’t see a reason why a person couldn’t cook at home and sell to other places and people. I think it’s a great idea.”
But Henderson, a registered dietician and former restaurateur, was far more concerned about the safety risks, like food-borne illnesses, that could arise from relaxed regulations.
The potential ordinance, which is now being researched by city staff, was proposed by local residents Dawn and Rob Hudson, former U.S. Department of Agriculture employees, who run a roadside farm table with free, homegrown vegetables.
The couple, familiar with the hardships brought on by food insecurity from their time with the federal government, want to expand their farmstand to include healthy, organic pre-prepared meals — priced affordably or free when needed.
But in Ellsworth, doing so would cost considerable investment, Dawn Hudson told the City Council.
“What we learned is disappointing: to offer anything that’s not shelf stable, we would need a state licensed commercial-grade kitchen,” Dawn Hudson said. “We would need to either renovate our home to add a separate kitchen because it can’t be our home kitchen, it has to be completely separate for the commercial kitchen license. Or, purchase a food trailer. Either of which would cost tens of thousands of dollars. That expense would make it impractical for us to provide the kind of high quality, affordable food we hoped to offer.”
Henderson pointed to other options. Those who want to cook commercially-regulated meals can rent spaces in community buildings or restaurants, she said.
Ledezma, who runs Momo’s from a self-serve garage on her Main Street property, thinks the ordinance could make it more accessible for people to sell food items from their homes without the financial burden of building a commercial kitchen.
Ledezma spent roughly $5,000 on new sinks and plumbing for her commercial kitchen, she said. She’s limited to bakery items, however, and cannot sell meat or seafood, Ledezma said.
If adopted, the ordinance would not eliminate all state conditions, and meat and poultry items would still be subject to state and federal regulations, according to a city memo.
Henderson, who has operated her Surry Road farmstand for roughly six years and rents a commercial kitchen space at the Veterans of Foreign Wars hall in Ellsworth, is fine with people selling bakery items from their home kitchen. She draws the line at meals.
“It opens up the whole gamut of what you can make without supervision,” Henderson said Friday. “Finding a commercial kitchen was challenging, so it was a barrier to produce meals for a while. [But] I think those barriers are there for a reason — that is a food safety thing.
Henderson — who bakes pies and desserts, foods that aren’t regulated by commercial standards, from her home kitchen — agreed that less regulations could help residents supplement their income by selling food from their home. But the risk to public safety outweighs the pros, she said.
Ledezma also said that if ordinance strips the need for a commercial kitchen, any home kitchen would still need inspections to ensure food isn’t in close contact with animals or other contaminants. Commercial licenses require annual state kitchen inspections.
“As a commercial producer, I’m ethically required to resource products that are regulated,” Henderson added. “It just comes down to food safety. [Someone] down the road who’s making cheese lasagna, even if it’s cheese lasagna — it’s just as dangerous as a meat lasagna if it is sitting on the counter longer than it’s supposed to.”

title: Workshop maps next steps for outdoor recreation in Jay region
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — More year-round, outdoor events throughout Jay, Livermore and Livermore Falls was the priority for the more than 40 people who participated in a two-day regional workshop Sept. 30 and Oct. 1.
The Recreation Economy for Rural Communities workshop at Spruce Mountain Ski Slope brought together residents and local, state, regional and federal partners to review recreation assets, assess work already underway and identify resources and next steps for future projects.
Participants worked systematically from reviewing outdoor recreation assets and community progress to identifying current priorities and resources that could support specific strategies, according to Shelley Kruszewski, regional planner with the Androscoggin Valley Council of Governments.
Examples of work already underway included upgrades at Spruce Mountain Ski Slope and the Androscoggin Land Trust’s regional wayfinding project.
The resulting action-plan priorities are organized around three broad areas: growing local capacity, developing outdoor and downtown events and experiences, and continuing to improve year-round access to outdoor recreation amenities across the three-town region.
The workshop was built on the 2025 Recreation and Facilities Master Plan for Jay, Livermore and Livermore Falls, which identified opportunities to improve recreation facilities, strengthen connections among destinations and use outdoor recreation as part of a broader regional economic development strategy.
Before the workshop, Kruszewski said the workshop process was intended to move that planning into more detailed action steps, including timelines, milestones, financial and staffing needs, responsibilities and other work needed to advance projects.
“Emphasis will be on near term and implementable next steps needed to move forward,” Kruszewski said.
Participants also examined how individual recreation sites could complement one another as part of a connected regional network rather than operate as isolated facilities.
Projects and destinations previously identified for discussion included the Livermore Falls Recreation Area, French Falls, Area Youth Sports, Spruce Mountain Ski Slope and Spruce Mountain Conservation Area.
The workshop included a community tour during which members of the workshop steering committee and federal, regional and state partners examined recreation and downtown connections firsthand.
In Livermore Falls, participants discussed ways outdoor recreation could connect with the downtown. At the Jay Recreation Area, they discussed trail connections and opportunities for outdoor programming.
Those discussions reflected a broader goal of the workshop: connecting recreation assets with town centers and creating opportunities for residents and visitors to move between trails, recreation areas, businesses and downtown destinations.
“The workshop will also provide the opportunity to focus attention on placemaking and how outdoor recreation connects to the town centers,” Kruszewski said before the event.
The workshop also gave community members an opportunity to speak directly with agencies and organizations that may be able to help identify technical assistance, partnerships and potential funding sources.
“The value of having these partners at the table is that they can hear directly from the communities about their priorities and help identify technical assistance, funding programs, partnerships or other resources that may align with those goals,” Kruszewski said.
The Recreation Economy for Rural Communities program does not directly provide project funding. Participation, however, connects communities with government agencies, technical resources, other communities pursuing similar projects and potential funding programs. Kruszewski previously said some funding opportunities are limited to communities participating in the program.
The federal planning assistance program focuses on helping rural communities strengthen outdoor recreation economies while supporting Main Street revitalization.
The program involves the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, USDA Forest Service, Northern Border Regional Commission, Appalachian Regional Commission and Denali Commission. Holly Fowler of Northbound Ventures Consulting is facilitating the local process, while Androscoggin Valley Council of Governments is coordinating with the three towns and the local steering committee.
The work also overlaps with a Tri-Town recreation branding and wayfinding project that grew out of the 2025 master plan.
Members of the Tri-Town Recreation Committee and steering committee previously supported a successful Rural Investment Project Grant application to create cohesive regional branding and wayfinding signs for recreation destinations. The Androscoggin Land Trust is leading that project.
The master plan identified promotion of key recreation areas, improved signs, co-branding and wayfinding as priorities.
The workshop’s action planning will continue beyond the two-day session. Organizers previously said the draft action plan would be refined through three post-workshop calls that will also be open to participants.
“The community’s input during the workshop becomes the centerpiece of the final deliverable of the planning process,” Kruszewski said.
She had also stressed before the workshop that local participation would be central to the process.
“This is a community-driven process,” Kruszewski said. “It only works if the community comes and shares their input.”

text:
MALIBU, Calif. (KABC) - Officials say a kayaker who caught a shark while fishing off the California coast was bitten twice as he tried to release it.
The incident was reported at 8:32 a.m. Sunday in Malibu, according to the Los Angeles County Fire Department.
Officials say the kayaker was fishing about a half mile offshore when he caught the shark. While he was trying to release it, the shark bit him and caused him to fall out of the kayak.
That’s when the shark bit him a second time, officials say.
The victim was taken to the hospital. His condition was not immediately known.

title: Alex Ovechkin says this is his final NHL season: ‘It’s hard, but let’s enjoy it’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Alex Ovechkin said Monday that his 22nd season in the NHL will be his last, beginning the farewell tour for the longtime Washington Capitals captain who holds the league’s career goal-scoring record.
Ovechkin addressed teammates to deliver the news before the team posted a message from him on social media.
“It’s sad, but it is what it is,” Ovechkin said in his locker room address. “It’s hard, but let’s enjoy it and let’s do some special things this year.”
Ovechkin signed a one-year contract this past summer and turned 41 on Sept. 17. All signs pointed to this being the end, and he said he and his family decided as much in recent months.
“I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it’s the right decision,” the Russian star said in a statement released before the Capitals’ home opener Wednesday night.
Ovechkin broke Wayne Gretzky’s goals record in April 2025 and entered this season at 929. The front office acquired Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch in trades and signed fellow forward Boone Jenner and defenseman Vincent Desharnais in free agency to add around a young core in the hopes of making another long playoff run and contending for the Stanley Cup.
“Let’s make the playoffs, let’s have fun and enjoy the moment because times fly,” Ovechkin told the team. “For young guys who are first year or experienced guys, I remember that moment, and enjoy the time. Because times fly. It seems like yesterday I was here my first year.”
Speaking to reporters later Monday, Ovechkin said this was the right time to announce his decision, two days before the home opener.
“I’m not 20 years old,” he said. “I want to play with my kids when they’re growing up. Play hockey, play soccer, play basketball. I want to be healthy enough to do that kind of stuff.”
Ovechkin has spent his entire career with Washington, winning the Calder Trophy as rookie of the year in 2005-06, the Hart Trophy as MVP three times and leading the NHL in scoring nine times. He was playoff MVP in 2018 when he led the Caps to the first Stanley Cup championship in franchise history.
There’s been speculation Ovechkin could receive an unfriendly reception on the road after he appeared in an ad for a party aligned with Vladimir Putin during the offseason. But there wasn’t much sign of that during the first two games of the season — at Carolina and at Tampa Bay.
When addressing the fallout from that last month, Ovechkin confirmed he’d be going back to live in Russia when he retired from the NHL.
In Washington’s season-opening win over the Hurricanes, Ovechkin had 12 minutes, 46 seconds of ice time, the lowest of his career in a game when he wasn’t injured or ejected.
Monday was 21 years to the day after Ovechkin made his debut with the Capitals.
“It’s been pretty good career, pretty good 22 seasons,” he said. “Obviously the goal that we have, to bring a Stanley Cup to D.C., we did it.”
Although the Capitals have designs on making the playoffs this season, within a couple hours of Ovechkin’s announcement, tickets for Washington’s regular-season home finale against Pittsburgh on April 4 were going for a minimum of $825 on StubHub. With D.C. hosting college hockey’s Frozen Four next year, the Capitals finish the regular season with three straight road games, wrapping up April 10 at Philadelphia.
The Capitals missed the playoffs in 2025-26, but Ovechkin played all 82 games and scored 32 goals. He’s reached 30 in every season of his career except 2020-21, when he played only 45 games.
Long before he broke through during the Capitals’ Stanley Cup run, Ovechkin had rejuvenated hockey in Washington, and he’ll retire as one of the city’s most accomplished athletes in any sport. The Capitals drafted him No. 1 overall in 2004, and he and Pittsburgh’s Sidney Crosby became stars almost immediately in 2005 when the league emerged from missing a season because of a lockout.
“Before we even met, we were kind of built up against each other: It’s kind of a natural thing to happen,” Crosby said. “Over the years developed a friendship with him. Have a ton of respect for him, and you play against someone that long, you’re compared and see each other enough I think that’s something that builds over time.”
Ovechkin’s combination of goal-scoring skill, physicality and boundless energy made him an instant hit, and he scored a career-high 65 goals in his third season, which earned him the first of his MVP honors.
“He’s done everything,” said Penguins center Evgeni Malkin, a fellow countryman who was picked second after Ovechkin in the 2004 draft. ”He do everything for team, for league. I hope he plays good this year, no injury, he just stay healthy, score goals and enjoy the game.”
Washington’s penchant for postseason heartache, which existed long before Ovechkin showed up, followed him for a while as well. The Capitals won the Presidents’ Trophy three times with the league’s best regular-season record, falling short in the playoffs each time before a Washington team that merely won its division finally went all the way in the playoffs.
In four postseason meetings between Crosby and Ovechkin — in 2009, 2016, 2017, 2018 — the winner won the Stanley Cup each time. Washington’s home opener Wednesday is against Pittsburgh.
“Definitely have had some great battles over the years,” Crosby said. “Obviously when you get to our age, that’s something that you have to make decisions on and for him, as long as he’s happy and enjoying it, that’s the biggest thing.”
___
Whyno reported from New York.
___
AP freelance writer Sammi Silber in Arlington, Virginia, and AP Sports Writer Will Graves in Pittsburgh contributed to this report.

title: ‘This baby is gone’: 12-year-old girl killed in crossfire at youth football game
text:
BALTIMORE (WBAL) - A 12-year-old girl was killed and a woman was injured when gunfire erupted at a youth football game.
The shooting happened Saturday in Baltimore.
Police Commissioner Richard Worley said preliminary information indicated there were two shooters who were arguing over a parking space before gunfire erupted.
Officials said a 12-year-old girl, who was not immediately identified, was shot and killed in the crossfire. A woman was also injured with non-life-threatening injuries.
Authorities say two men also walked into hospitals seeking treatment from the incident.
Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said the shooting is one of the most “disgusting things” he’s ever seen in his life.
“We will find him. We will bring them here and bring them to justice for their family, but that’s not going to bring her back. That’s not going to stop these other kids from having the trauma of seeing somebody they know get shot and killed. That’s not gonna heal these folks. Two men got into a basic argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone,” he said.
“But two men — or so-called men — got into an argument, and now this baby is gone, never going to see her full potential. Her family is going to be hurting for this for the rest of their lives. Her classmates are going to be hurting. Her community is going to be hurting because people can’t handle their conflict in a different way,” Scott continued.
There was no information on potential suspects or arrests in the investigation.

title: Crowd of students protests Cornell’s response to gang rape complaint
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — Cornell students thronged a campus plaza to protest the university’s response to allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity house, and the school’s main administration building was splashed with graffiti and damaged overnight.
At a demonstration that overflowed the large space in front of the school’s student center, students, faculty members and others wore purple ribbons and held signs with such messages as “support survivors, expel rapists” and “Justice 4 every Jane Doe” — the name by which the woman who reported the assault is known in court papers. Other people watched from pathways, windows and a nearby hill.
“Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support,” student Athena Holloway told the crowd. “How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”
Hispanic studies professor Julia Chang added to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.”
Calls for Cornell president’s resignation
Speakers faulted fraternities, the university trustees and Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff, saying he and his administration have prioritized protecting the university’s reputation over students’ safety.
“Kotlikoff, resign!” demonstrators chanted, among other slogans, as they marched to the damaged administration building to present a list of demands. They included changes to how the student code of conduct defines sexual consent, an overhaul of the student discipline system and expulsions or degree revocations for all students involved in the alleged 2024 assault of the woman known as Jane Doe, among other things.
The woman’s account of being sexually assaulted by several fraternity brothers has made clear, on and beyond campus, that “for all the strong feelings about sexual assault, .... we do not do enough to prevent it, nor to support survivors after it happens,” student Madeline Gage said.
The group began disbanding with chants including “ban the frats!”
Graffiti and broken glass at an administration building
The Ivy League school has been trying to quell a firestorm over its handling of the alleged 2024 gang rape. Early Monday, the university found signs of the anger on the very walls of its administrative headquarters.
Holes were knocked into one of the building’s glass doors, and the walls beside them were marked with red-painted messages condemning patriarchy and the Ivy League school’s handling of sexual assaults, news media photos showed. Later Monday, the graffiti was removed and the door was boarded up.
Cornell spokesperson Kyle Kimball said in a statement that the university was investigating and that “damaging property is not the answer” to Cornellians’ “frustration and strong emotions.” Campus police referred questions to his office, which declined to provide more detail on the incident.
Jane Doe alleges that she was sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity members in October 2024 after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs. She was a Cornell student at the time.
The woman recently sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others. Her lawsuit said that she became fully incapacitated as fraternity members assaulted her, and that one man sent others a message inviting them to participate.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told Cornell investigators last year, according to records reviewed by The Associated Press.
Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that some of the accused students, when interviewed by Cornell investigators, described the sexual activity as consensual.
Shortly before she went to Cornell police in November 2024, Jane Doe recorded a phone call with one of the men she says raped her. ABC News broadcast portions of that call Monday, containing only what it said was his voice, and recounted other parts of the conversation in writing.
“What y’all did would be classified as gang rape,” she told him at one point, according to the network, which said she had provided the recording to the university.
Students are demanding transparency, accountability
The suit has drawn national attention to what Cornell, its police force and the local district attorney did after she told the campus police in November 2024 she “can say with 100% confidence I was raped.”
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others. In a statement last week, the administration bristled about the “false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case.”
Students, however, have demanded more accountability and transparency, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has said Jane Doe was “failed by people and institutions” including the Cornell police and local District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.
Hochul appointed the state attorney general last week to take over a criminal investigation that Van Houten had reopened days earlier, and the governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter.
After the week’s developments, Kotlikoff released an apologetic video Saturday, saying that Jane Doe’s account “raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.”
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his support for an independent review of the university’s actions and vowed more transparency and a commitment to “finding the answers our community deserves.”
___
Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz contributed from New York.

title: The Maine Marathon was not my day, but it wasn’t a loss
text:
This is not the story I was planning to write.
When I pitched this series to Sports Editor Bill Stewart, my goal was take readers through my training and then tell the triumphant story of my race at the Maine Marathon. I would write about all the miles I crushed during the race, fighting through the pain to get to the finish line, where I would ring the PR bell and then finally, after 12 years of trying, erase my goal time of 3:47 off the chalkboard that hangs in my apartment.
Unfortunately, I don’t get to tell that story.
I ran my sixth marathon Sunday morning and the day did not go as planned. I missed every one of my time goals, nearly dropped out multiple times, and was left wondering if I ever want to do this again.
I won’t bury the lead anymore than I already have: I finished the race in 4 hours, 13 minutes, 58 seconds. I missed my ‘A’ goal by 26 minutes, my ‘B’ goal by 23 minutes and my ‘C’ goal by nearly 14 minutes.
It was not the race I was hoping for, but there was way too much good to focus only on the bad.
It was a stellar day to run a marathon. It was right around 50 degrees when the race started, ideal weather for a marathon. I chatted up friends and hung out with folks from my run group until the race started, then I went my own way, to run my own race.
I was cruising between 8:45 and 9 minutes per mile for the first 6 miles, taking in all the signs and the ocean views, and shouting out friends and high-fiving my sister Melissa when I saw her just after mile 6. I stopped at the porta potty during mile 7 and choked down my second gel (I literally choked on it for a second, yuk), and picked the pace back up in mile 8.
The hills started at mile 10, but I was feeling good, keeping my effort relaxed, and dropped down to 8:36-8:43 per mile until the half marathon. I crossed the half in 1:57, a little slower than 3:47 pace, but right on target to give it a good effort on the way back to Portland.
My race took a turn in the 17th mile while climbing the hill at Tuttle Road in Cumberland. My right knee, the one that always gives me problems during marathons, started to really hurt as I approached that hill. Every swing of that leg, every time my foot hit the ground, my knee sang in agony. Before I started to limp, I told myself it was OK to walk to the top of that hill, then get back on pace at the top.
I never did get back on pace. The final 10-plus miles of the marathon was a slog. A slow, painful slow. I jogged when I could and walked when I felt I needed to. I considered dropping out every time I saw a medical tent, but didn’t allow myself to quit. That’s one thing I can take pride in.
I was about 2.5 miles from the finish line when I looked at my watch and saw 3:47 flip to 3:48. I knew long before that I wasn’t hitting that goal, but it still hurt to see the number pass so far from the end.
I jogged the final three-tenths of a mile, determined not to walk across the finish line. I shook hands with my colleagues, waited in line for pizza that never came, then left with my sister and brother-in-law for a well deserved lunch at Wilson County Barbecue. I celebrated the day, not necessarily the race.
Ten months after signing up for this race and after 18 weeks of training, I’m ready for a bit of a break. I’m looking forward to running again, but not right away. I’m going to recover, reflect and decide what’s next.
What won’t be next is another marathon. I don’t know if I’ll ever put myself through that again, but it’s too soon after the race to say, “No way.” After all, seven years ago after running the Chicago Marathon, I said that was it, yet here we are.
If I ever do decide to try again, I’ll remember how much fun I had this summer putting in the work, and do everything I can so it doesn’t physically feel the way it did on Sunday.
That will be a story I want to tell.

WalletHub compared all 50 states using 52 measures to determine its rankings of the safest states in America for 2026.
Those measures included assaults per capita, losses from climate disasters per capita and unemployment rates.
Maine ranked third overall in the safety report, placing first for the lowest rate of assaults and third for the lowest rate of murders and nonnegligent manslaughters.
The state also ranked eighth for climate disaster losses, 12th for its uninsured population share, 14th for sex offenders, 19th for fatal workplace injuries and 25th for traffic fatalities, based on the population and exposure measures used in the report.
WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo said the safest states combine low crime rates, safe roads and strong job markets with workplace safety, disaster preparedness and residents’ efforts to protect their communities.
Vermont ranked as the safest state, supported by low unemployment, relatively low rates of violent crime and identity theft complaints, and strong road safety measures.
And there you have it! Maine’s particularly low rates of assaults and murders helped place the state near the top of WalletHub’s nationwide safety ranking.

title: Here’s where the country’s largest measles outbreak in 30+ years is
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials said Monday, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.
The U.S. is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 reported cases, according to the CDC. The nation has seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the past two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Since the beginning of last year, large outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest with 997 cases reported.
The governor of New York on Monday declared a disaster emergency because of measles cases in neighboring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extends the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and allows nurses to join doctors in ordering testing. The state has more than 100 cases this year.
Health officials say Pennsylvania’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia. There have been 1,004 cases, including 198 hospitalizations and five deaths, state officials said.
Health experts attribute such outbreaks to low vaccination rates.
It’s been decades since a U.S. state has seen an outbreak surpass 1,000 cases, stretching back to a multiyear outbreak in New York City in the early 1990s that infected more than 4,500 people.
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
Measles is highly contagious. It spreads when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, and through contaminated surfaces. It also can linger in the air for two hours. Up to 9 out of 10 people who are susceptible will get the virus if exposed, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
U.S. measles infections have been surging in recent years, as fewer kids get routine vaccines due to parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation.
Pennsylvania and New York are not the only states with a growing problem. Another is Ohio, with more than 200 cases this year. Like in Pennsylvania, some of the hardest-hit Ohio counties have significant Amish populations, which tend to have lower vaccination rates.
Meanwhile, CDC officials have quietly begun to acknowledge measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.
State officials in August announced that two unvaccinated residents died after being infected with measles.
The announcement quickly came under fire as a clash erupted between vaccine-promoting Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines.
Since then, Pennsylvania has reported three additional deaths.
But for weeks, the CDC — which Kennedy oversees — did not count any deaths on its measles data dashboard, instead saying it was seeking more information. That changed two weeks ago, when one death was finally counted, and again last week when a second was added to the agency’s tally.

title: The ego has invaded American politics
text:
Ron Snyder lives in Dexter.
Our church, like many churches, is experiencing an attendance decline that is causing financial challenges. This week I encountered a church leader who was, in my opinion, disrespectful to me and our pastor. For reference, there was nothing done that I would consider illegal, only disrespectful.
However, this caused me to decide that I needed to review the church leader’s and the church’s performance as if I were doing a business turnaround. In so doing, one must always look at the product being marketed and with whom the business is competing and then determine why the poor performer is not keeping pace.
This analysis led me to a conclusion I had previously given little thought or consideration: A church is really a business that markets behavioral laws. They may also provide shelter and lease instructors, but they also employ managers and have a management structure to manage and control their operation.
But with whom are they really competing? The clue came when my pastor said she was not allowed to talk about politics.
Who, besides churches, provides moral and behavioral rules that humans must follow? The answer was geographical leaders or government and political leaders.
In some countries, religious leaders take over governing the country’s inhabitants. In others, political leaders take control and provide laws that take precedence over religious leaders. The answer became even clearer when one looks at how they are funded. One collects tithes, the other taxes and each’s leaders decide how they are redistributed.
This turned me to the U.S. Constitution and prompted the question of, “How are we prepared?”
Surprisingly, our founders prepared us very well if we use the tools they included in our Constitution 250 years ago. First, they recognized the power struggle between religious leaders and territorial government leaders. They solved this by including freedom of religion. All church leaders were welcomed to participate in America’s leadership.
But the second part of their planning and analysis displays even more foresight. They included a plan and provision to address leaders’ egos. They provided set terms: representatives, two years; presidents, four years; senators, six years. Additionally, they provided a procedure to impeach an unsatisfactory leader during his or her elected term. And more importantly, they left administration in the hands of the inhabitants of the territory being represented: voters.
Our founders did not provide for political parties. Political parties were a method devised by egotistical government leaders to divide voters and disperse money collected in taxes. However, the Constitution’s writers did also plan for this and point us in the direction our representatives and we, the voters, need to go to make America great again.
Whether in church or state, we need to remove the egotistical leaders who want to collect our tithes and taxes and distribute them as they see fit and replace them with ones who will work for all of us and distribute our labor for the benefit of all mankind. In America, as long as political parties and churches exist, this means voters must register independent and insist on implementing ranked-choice voting.
I urge you, the voter, to truly make America great again.
Be respectful of your neighbors and insist that your representative represent you and address the ego issues that have invaded and overtaken our leadership. If they don’t, you have the choice in November. And for you Christians who believe the U.S. is a Christian country, remember Jesus was not a member of a Christian church. He was a Jewish rebel in the Jewish synagogue who took offense to the way church leaders treated mankind.
Good luck, America, and regardless of your church affiliation, God will prevail.

title: Patients’ shocking sexual assault claims lead to charges against former nurse
text:
MONROE, Wash. (KIRO) - A former nurse in Washington state is facing felony charges after several patients levied shocking claims of sexual assault against him.
Stephen Odingo, 61, faces four felony counts of indecent liberties after three women accused him of sexual assault. The women were all patients at EvergreenHealth Monroe, the hospital where Odingo worked as a nurse.
Charging documents from the Snohomish County Prosecutor’s office outline the case.
The first incident was reported in July 2024. A woman told police she checked into the medical center, and Odingo asked her to remove all her clothing. She said the nurse then “grabbed both [her] breasts and started to massage them” and “went down the front of her underwear with his hand,” according to the documents.
A second victim said that, in January 2025, Odingo repeatedly hugged her and held her hand then asked her to remove her bra. When she refused, the nurse reportedly tried to remove it himself, according to the documents.
Investigators said, in both cases, the women reported Odingo, and he was removed from their care teams.
A third victim reported Odingo just days after the second alleged incident. She told investigators she was nervous about her treatment and initially thought Odingo’s behavior was an attempt to comfort her, according to the documents.
She alleged Odingo gave her a back massage then told her, ‘Maybe you can take care of me sometime’ before kissing her on the mouth through his mask. She said the nurse later squeezed her breasts so hard she started crying after which he again tried to hug and kiss her before touching her genitals, according to the documents.
Following the third report, investigators say Odingo was suspended from work then resigned later that month.
Odingo is set to be arraigned Wednesday.
EvergreenHealth said patient safety is a priority and that it is cooperating fully with the investigation. The hospital would not comment further because this is an ongoing legal matter.

title: Maine Forest and Logging Museum celebrates history with annual ‘Living History Days’
text:
BRADLEY, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Forest and Logging Museum held its annual Living History Days celebration over the weekend.
Historical reenactors as well as local traditional craftsmen performed demonstrations for attendees, showcasing colonial-era cooking, blacksmithing, fiber arts and other traditional crafts.
The event celebrates American history from the colonial era to modern day.
“For me, it’s honestly the interaction with the people, the children, seeing everybody coming out, have a good time, watching the reenactors, just seeing how it all comes together,” said Bryan Harper, a member of the Maine Forest and Logging Museum Board of Directors.
Harper has been involved with the event for three years.
“Part of anything like this are the volunteers, the reenactors. Without them, any non-profit or organization like ourselves, we cease to exist. It’s just a great way to give back to the community,” said Harper.
To learn more about the Maine Forest and Logging Museum, visit www.maineforestandloggingmuseum.org.

title: ‘No better time than now’: Couple gets engaged during massive I-95 pileup
text:
LAKE MARION, S.C. (Gray News) - A couple traveling from Philadelphia turned chaos into a lifelong memory during a massive crash involving more than 60 vehicles.
Kevin Cossa and Meghan Quinn were traveling for vacation when they were caught in the crash on the Santee Bridge over Lake Marion.
“We just crashed, and then we got out and made sure everybody was safe. And they were telling us we needed to leave the bridge...,” Quinn said.
With traffic stopped and uncertainty all around them, Cossa decided there was no reason to wait for the perfect moment.
“I just figured that I wouldn’t find another moment as unique as that one,” Cossa said.
Right there on the bridge, he asked Quinn to marry him — and she said yes.
“He was like, ‘I was gonna do this tomorrow but no better time than now,’” Quinn said.
“I honestly, at that point in time, with so much confusion and everything going on, didn’t even know what tomorrow meant,” Cossa said.
The couple was later treated at MUSC Health Orangeburg.
“We’re grateful Kevin and Meghan are doing well and wish them safe travels, a happy engagement and many years of happiness together,” MUSC Health said on Facebook.

title: A Florida university focuses on space medicine to train future astronaut healthcare providers
text:
A Florida university focuses on space medicine to train future astronaut healthcare providers
The University of Central Florida is expanding its space medicine program to train students in providing healthcare for astronauts during missions.
"Space medicine is a relatively new field in the realm of things when you think about the history of medicine, which really started in the 1960s with the first humans flown into space," said Dr. Manny Urquieta, founder of the division of aerospace medicine at UCF.
Urquieta joined UCF two years ago after serving as chief medical officer at the Johnson Space Center in Texas. He is leading efforts to establish a master's degree in space medicine and a residency program to prepare future physicians for astronaut and pilot care.
"We are developing a new master's degree of space medicine and also a residency program so we can train the future physicians who will become more certified to take care of our astronauts and pilots," Urquieta said.
Students in the program will conduct astronaut health checks before missions, assist in selecting the next generation of astronauts and support their training.
"Once they're selected to help with their training and once they're assigned to a mission, get all the medical checks that they need to be certified for that mission. Then, once they're in space, the physicians will take care of them with telemedicine, or some of them perhaps could fly into space," Urquieta said.
Physicians trained in the program will also assist astronauts at recovery sites after their missions and beyond.
