title: Oversize load to complete the final leg of its journey from Jay to South Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A “super oversize” load, as some public safety departments have dubbed it, that has been crawling south across Maine over the past week reached its destination in South Portland on Tuesday morning.
The nearly 220-foot-long and roughly 20-foot-wide load is a heat recovery steam generator that was trucked from the former Androscoggin Mill in Jay over the course of several nights. It weighs more than 683,000 pounds.
The oversize load was originally expected to make it to South Portland within two days of its Sept. 29 departure. However, after night one of its journey, officials said it would take days longer than anticipated.
The convoy spurred road closures and attracted onlookers as it slowly wove its way through portions of Franklin, Androscoggin, Oxford, York and Cumberland counties.
For the last leg of the journey Monday night into Tuesday, the transport truck, escorted by utility crews and law enforcement personnel, was expected to depart Buxton at about 9 p.m. Monday, Maine State Police said in a news release.
The convoy crossed a Maine Turnpike bridge early Tuesday morning, a few hours after crews set up a jumper bridge — essentially steel beams put across the bridge to spread out the weight of the load.
From there, it traveled along U.S. Route 1 in Scarborough to Broadway and Elm Street in South Portland, its final destination in Maine.
At 8 a.m. Tuesday, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Transportation confirmed that the load had arrived in South Portland.
It’s the first of nine oversize loads planned for the route. Maine DOT said last week that the schedule for the eight remaining transports will be released following the completion of the first.
JGT2 Redevelopment purchased the Jay mill site from Pixelle Specialty Solutions in 2023. Tony McDonald, a JGT2 partner, said in an email that the heat recovery steam generator is among a dozen pieces of old mill equipment that the company sold to Packaging Corporation of America.
In addition to two more heat recovery steam generators, the remaining planned transports will carry three gas turbines and three gas turbine-driven electric generators, McDonald said. Some other pieces of equipment have already been removed from the site, he added.
McDonald said his company is not involved in the transport of the equipment, and a spokesperson for Packaging Corporation of America did not respond to a request for further details on Monday.
Headquartered in Illinois, Packaging Corporation of America is one of the largest producers of containerboard in the United States. It operates over 120 facilities across the country, including nine mills and dozens of plants.
This story was updated on Oct. 6 after authorities confirmed that the load had reached its destination.
Staff Writer Morgan Womack contributed to this report.

title: Yes, it's almost Prime Day again. Here's everything to know about October's deals
text:
Everything you need to know about Amazon's October Prime Big Deal Days
Mark your calendars, Big Deal Days is just a few days away.
Everything you need to know about Amazon's October Prime Big Deal Days
Mark your calendars, Big Deal Days is just a few days away.
It seems like Amazon Prime Day just happened, but believe it or not, the e-tailer’s second Prime Day event of the year is just around the corner. Amazon officially announced that this year’s Prime Big Deal Days will happen on October 6 and 7.
I’ve covered Prime Day for five years at this point, and I already know you’ll find deals on Good Housekeeping Institute-tested kitchen appliances, gifts for the holidays, Halloween decorations, stylish clothes, vacuums, and more. As the sales go live, we’ll sift through all the discounts and share the only deals worth your money. In the meantime, here are a few things to note about Prime Big Deal Days:
What is Amazon Prime Big Deal Days?
By now, you may have heard of Prime Day, Amazon's biggest sales event of the year that typically happens in the middle of summer. It runs over a couple of days and promotes steep discounts across all categories—and it’s open exclusively for Amazon Prime members.
Amazon introduced Prime Big Deal Days in October 2022, and the event has returned every fall since. Think of it as a second Prime Day before the holiday shopping rush, with many of the same standout discounts—so much so that shoppers often call it "October Prime Day."
What's the difference between Prime Big Deal Days and Prime Day?
They're practically the same event, with exclusive discounts just for Prime members, but they occur at different times of the year. Prime Day (usually happening in the summer) will slash prices on items across all categories (think home essentials, everyday appliances, and everything outside of that).
Because Prime Big Deal Days typically falls in October, the event tends to highlight hot-ticket holiday items, letting you check off your holiday shopping list early and score the hottest gifts at a discount. Think tech, TVs, toys, best-selling beauty, and more. Plus, you can score some discounts on Halloween decorations and costume accessories just in time for October 31 (thanks to Amazon’s fast shipping!).
Also, Prime Big Deal Days is typically shorter at just two days long. This past Prime Day in June 2026 was four days long for the second time in the retailer's history.
When is October Prime Day 2026?
October Prime Day—or as it's officially called, Prime Big Deal Days—kicks off on Tuesday, October 6, and runs through Wednesday, October 7. Although this savings event is technically live for 48 hours, we often see early deals popping up days and even weeks before the event.
Is it actually worth shopping October Prime Day?
Definitely. While Amazon hasn't released an official list of October Prime Day deals to the public yet, the retailer tends to offer competitive discounts across every category on the site.
Since the holiday shopping season has been progressively getting earlier and earlier, Amazon's October Prime Day is my favorite time to get my holiday gift shopping done. That’s because if you shop now, you don't have to worry about potential inventory issues and shipping delays spoiling your holidays.
During last year's Prime Big Deal Days event, we saw steep markdowns on home and beauty products like Shark vacuums, Samsung TVs, and RoC skincare, so you can expect to see similar savings during 2026's October Prime Day. And based on past events, we’d be shocked not to see some pretty good deals on Apple tech. In June, we saw 40% off the AirPods 2 Pro, the GH Institute's best overall AirPods pick.
How to shop October Prime Day
Like most Prime Day events, the best prices during Prime Big Deal Days will be reserved for Prime members only. Your subscription comes with a suite of other perks, like free two-day shipping, access to movies and shows through Prime Video, discounts on groceries, and more. But if you're not already a member, here's a hack: You can sign up for a 30-day trial to get access to all the Prime Day deals and try out all the exclusive perks for free. Just be sure to cancel before the 30-day mark to avoid charges.

- Lauren Gruber is a commerce editor who has covered the last five Amazon Prime Day events for various publications, including GH. She is dedicated to helping readers navigate the e-commerce landscape and identify which deals are worth their money.
- Amanda Fama is the senior editor of deals and trends at Good Housekeeping. She's covered Amazon Prime Day for various publications and knows the ins and outs of what to sales shop and when.

title: Nearly 684,000-pound Maine mill machine will complete its slow journey tonight
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A nearly 684,000-pound paper mill machine will start the final leg of its slow-moving journey Monday night.
The machine, a heat recovery steam generator from the former Androscoggin Mill in Jay, will depart from Buxton at 9 p.m., according to the Maine State Police.
It is expected to cross a local bridge starting at 10 p.m., requiring all other traffic to be detoured because of the size of the load — it’s 20 feet wide, more than 19 feet tall and 219 feet long.
Once across the bridge, it will crawl toward South Portland. On the way, it will have to cross a Maine Turnpike bridge, which is expected to happen between 1 and 2 a.m. Tuesday, the state police said Monday morning.
The super oversize load will reach its ultimate destination, Turner Island in South Portland, which is home to a shipping company and gas terminal, about 6 a.m.
This is the first of nine such loads. Once the heat recovery steam generator completes its journey, officials will announce a schedule for the remaining eight loads.
The load was originally expected to reach South Portland last Tuesday after a two-night journey. But after departing from Riley Road in Jay, it failed to reach a key bridge in time. It then began making a more painstakingly slow journey, traveling from Turner to Buxton over three nights.

title: US citizen who was shot by Maine-based immigration agent in Chicago files lawsuit alleging he fired from behind
text:
CHICAGO — An American citizen shot by a Customs and Border Protection agent one year ago during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Monday, alleging the Maine-based agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.
Federal prosecutors initially accused Marimar Martinez, then 30, of using her vehicle to strike and box in agent Charles Exum’s SUV on Chicago’s southwest side on Oct. 4, 2025, during “Operation Midway Blitz.” Exum then exited his car and opened fire, leaving Martinez with seven gunshot wounds.
In the month after the shooting, prosecutors filed to dismiss the charges in a dramatic reversal of the closely watched case in the nation’s third-largest city.
Agent fired into rear of car, attorneys say
Her lawyers said Monday that they commissioned an expert to analyze bullet trajectories and her injuries and determined Exum wasn’t in the path of her car when he opened fire. They said he had walked several feet toward her car, contrary to statements he made to the FBI, and fired off five shots in less than a second, the last from the rear side of her vehicle.
“Charles Exum told the FBI agent on that day, within hours of the shooting, that Marimar was driving her car directly at him, that he shot her five times through the windshield, and that he ceased firing once he was no longer in the path of the vehicle. Those are three objective lies that you’ll see here today,” said one of her attorneys, Chris Parente.
Parente said there were only three bullet holes in Martinez’ windshield on the right passenger side, which indicated Martinez wasn’t driving toward the agent. He said the fourth shot was fired through the front passenger side window, adding another bullet hole in the back of Martinez’ car seat showed the agent fired the fifth shot from behind her.
“In what world can a U.S. law enforcement officer stand behind a car and fire his Glock service weapon through the rear passenger window at a young woman who’s crouched over the steering wheel?” Parente said.
CBP said in a statement to The Associated Press in response to the suit that Exum had been placed on administrative leave. Use-of-force incidents are “thoroughly investigated, reviewed, and presented” to an independent board, it added.
Exum is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the federal government, which was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act and does not allow for lawsuits against individual agents. It was not known where Exum could be reached.
Body-worn camera footage from another agent in Exum’s vehicle before the shooting captured the agents saying it was “time to get aggressive” and other profanity-laced comments by agents who were present encouraging violence, according to the complaint.
Martinez taken from hospital with bullet holes ‘leaking blood,’ suit says
The FBI arrested Martinez, taking her out of the hospital just hours after the shooting when she was “wheelchair bound and her bullet holes were leaking blood through her bandages,” according to the lawsuit. A judge ordered her release two days after her arrest.
Messages released by Martinez’ attorneys in February showed that former head of Border Patrol Greg Bovino had praised Exum for his “excellent service in Chicago” after the shooting. Other messages they released showed agents in a group chat congratulating Exum and calling him a “legend.”
Martinez was one several people shot in their cars by federal agents during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. An immigration agent shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in his car in Austin, Texas, last month, and another shot a Colombian driver in Biddeford, Maine, in July. The Trump administration has at times justified such shootings as self-defense against people allegedly weaponizing their vehicles.
Martinez appeared with her attorneys at a news conference Monday, saying the various shootings spurred her to file suit.
“If I don’t, then who else, you know? Look at what happened to Renee and all these victims,” she said, referring to Renee Good, a woman shot dead in her vehicle by a federal agent in Minneapolis in January.
“What’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t stay here and normalize what’s happening,” she said.
Story by Cybele Mayes-Osterman, a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Maine ICE observers added to DHS database, unsealed court records say
text:
A federal immigration agent added eight Maine residents to a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database in January, including several observers of immigration enforcement activity, according to newly unsealed court records.
One woman, Caryln Williams, was held by U.S. Customs and Border Protection while returning from a trip to Quebec as a result of being in the Department of Homeland Security’s Investigative Case Management (ICM) system. An agent testified that he added her to it after her car was observed at a location where multiple people were recording federal agents on Jan. 20, according to court records in a lawsuit against DHS.
But Williams wasn’t driving her car that morning, her spouse was.
Williams was “not physically present, or in any other way present, at the scene of the Jan. 20 encounter with this ICE agent,” Williams’ attorney JoAnna Suriani said on Monday.
Williams, her partner Polyxenia Pantos, and two other Maine residents are suing DHS, accusing the agency of violating their First Amendment rights. The federal lawsuit alleges that agents threatened to add observers in Maine to a database for “domestic terrorists.” A motion from the plaintiffs filed last week, citing depositions and other evidence that remains sealed, states that an agent added Williams to the ICM system, an existing database used by DHS to document cases by Homeland Security Investigations.
Attorneys for DHS stated in a motion to dismiss the case that the agent — an HSI Boston officer, identified as “J.C.” — added eight people to ICM who “he believed posted potential threats to law enforcement.”
The plaintiffs say in their filings that six of those people were observers.
DHS has denied any allegations of wrongdoing, including the existence of a database for domestic terrorists.
A spokesperson for DHS did not address questions from a reporter about the case Monday, but maintained the agency does not run a database for domestic terrorists. Attorneys for DHS did not respond to a request for comment.
The plaintiffs asked the court in the motion to issue an injunction before trial, barring agents from retaliating against observers with threats of a database and other tactics, like driving by protesters’ homes or calling them.
“Once you are in that database, or a database like it … the reach of where that data goes, including who has access to it, and what it can be used for in the future, is, in my opinion, very chilling,” said Suriani, an attorney with the nonprofit Protect Democracy, which is representing the plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs are also asking that Williams’ classification in the ICM database be modified, so she can travel internationally without being automatically detained or subject to a second inspection by border officials.
Attorneys for DHS have said in hearings and court filings that the government has a policy to protect observers and protesters who engage in First Amendment activity, and that agents receive relevant training. In March, the government also argued that only a few agents in Maine were recorded by observers talking about a database for domestic terrorists, and that those agents violated DHS policy.
No agents were disciplined, the plaintiffs argued in court records, citing depositions that remain under seal at the government’s request. Suriani also disagreed with characterizations that the agents were “rogue.”
According to a motion filed by Williams’ attorneys, the agent identified as J.C. testified during a deposition that he added Williams to the ICM database as an “aggressive woman (who) interject(ed) herself into an arrest.” The motion alleges that he also called Williams hours after Pantos was seen recording ICE agents, identifying himself only as someone from DHS and encouraging her to tell Pantos “not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist.”
Documents filed last month by the government identify J.C. as “Mr. Coleman.” Attempts to reach Coleman through social media, email and DHS were unsuccessful.
The plaintiffs’ motion also states that agents have continued driving by the homes of people who film and protest them. One agent said in his deposition that this was meant to “show them that we knew who they were” and “have them stop following us,” according to the plaintiffs’ filing.
This is the plaintiffs’ second time asking for pretrial relief. U.S. District Judge John Woodcock denied their request for a temporary restraining order against DHS in March, ruling that he didn’t have enough evidence to merit such an emergency measure.
In their latest filing, the plaintiffs said most of the agents whom they deposed said they considered the Maine observers to be interfering with immigration arrests. Plaintiffs have denied interfering with arrests.
“The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that’s what we’re asking the court to stop,” Suriani said.
Both sides are still responding to the government’s motion to dismiss, and the plaintiffs’ motion for preliminary injunction. A hearing for either request has not yet been scheduled.
The ICM database is hosted by software company Palantir, according to a statement the company released in 2022 and recent reporting by Wired. A spokesperson for Palantir declined to comment Monday.

title: California woman arrested for allegedly spying for China
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The FBI arrested a California real estate agent as she prepared to fly to China, accusing her of secretly working for Beijing to surveil the president of Taiwan’s family in the U.S., federal officials said.
The case comes at a fraught moment for U.S.-China relations, with Taiwan persistently at the center of their military and diplomatic rivalry. Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory.
The FBI and federal prosecutors allege Wanying Zhang surveilled the house of the president’s son and sent photos, videos and license plate information for his vehicles to a Chinese government official. The federal criminal complaint does not name the alleged target, but the FBI’s rapid response account on the social media platform X said it was the president’s son. Ting-Yu Lai, the president’s elder son, lives and works in the Seattle area as an engineer.
Zhang, a 34-year-old real estate agent from Irvine who also went by the name Heather, was arrested Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport and charged with working for China as an unregistered agent, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. Zhang is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Shawn Lewis, a spokesperson for the U.S. attorney’s office.
Zhang appeared in downtown Los Angeles federal court Monday for an initial hearing to confirm she understood her rights. She has not yet been formally indicted.
Judge Steve Kim told her she was not financially eligible for a public defender and would need to hire a private attorney as soon as possible. A hearing to determine bail or whether she would be detained was scheduled for Wednesday afternoon.
Her husband, Edric Ding, was at the courthouse but declined to comment.
California records show Zhang has been a licensed real estate agent since 2016. A Zillow page shows she has sold seven homes in the last year around Orange County.
Justice Department has been arresting alleged Chinese agents
The case is the latest in a series of Justice Department prosecutions aimed at rooting out alleged covert agents advancing Beijing’s interests on American soil.
Many of the cases have centered on what the Justice Department says is China’s aggressive effort to locate and harass pro-democracy activists living in the U.S. and suppress their speech. The Justice Department also says Beijing is determined to sway American public opinion in its favor by cultivating relationships with political figures seen as having access to the levers of power.
The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.
Taiwan’s Presidential Office confirmed President Lai Ching-te’s relatives were the targets, without specifying if it was the president’s son, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression.”
“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts — which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families — as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
Federal officials say surveillance happened in September 2025
At the direction of Chinese officials, Zhang and another person flew to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, and conducted surveillance outside the target’s home, according to an affidavit with the criminal complaint. A home security camera near the target’s home recorded the pair filming the target and their family from a vehicle, the affidavit said.
Zhang then allegedly sent a Chinese official information related to the surveillance, including photos, videos and license plate information from the target’s vehicles. The affidavit said that photos like that and the location of close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese official could be useful to China if officials wished to “obtain leverage” over Taiwan’s president “during any potential conflict.”
According to the affidavit, Zhang attended the University of International Relations in Beijing, which the FBI agent writing the affidavit said is known to be affiliated closely with China’s intelligence apparatus. Many of the university’s graduates go on to work for ministries in Beijing, including the country’s intelligence apparatus.
The affidavit said Zhang and a classmate who became a Chinese government official had kept in contact since graduating around 2014, and he introduced her to another government official, and she was in contact with both in 2025.
In a post dated Sept. 2, 2025, on the Chinese language app Xiaohongshu, Zhang complained about the long wait at the Seattle airport’s security check, wondering aloud if it was the “least efficient international airport” in the U.S.
She regularly shared photos of her travels around the world and dining at high-end restaurants.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, but Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory. Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and Beijing do not belong to each other and that the “People’s Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan.”
China considers him a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace.”
While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan, notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.
In May, a Southern California mayor agreed to plead guilty to acting as an illegal agent for the Chinese government, and resigned from her city position. Eileen Wang, the mayor of Arcadia, had been charged with one count of acting in the U.S. as an illegal agent of a foreign government. She was accused of doing the bidding of Chinese officials, such as sharing articles favorable to Beijing, without prior notification to the U.S. government as required by law.
___
Wu contributed to this report from Bangkok and Stengle contributed from Dallas. Reporters Eric Tucker and Didi Tang contributed to this report from Washington.

title: Supreme Court declines to take up Maine lobster boat tracking appeal
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear a Maine lobsterman’s legal challenge to an electronic vessel tracker requirement, putting an end to the multiyear lawsuit.
The court denied a request to take up the appeal by Frank Thompson, a Vinalhaven lobsterman, Maine Morningstar reported.
In a statement, Maine Department of Marine Resources Commissioner Carl Wilson said the department believes the tracking data is critically important to the long-term sustainability of the lobster fishery.
“It will inform the lobster stock assessment, enhance offshore enforcement and support better decision-making in a range of federal management contexts,” Wilson said.
Thompson’s attorney, Matthew Gilliam with Pacific Legal Foundation, said in a statement that the denial does not diminish the importance of the issues in the suit.
“Forcing lobstermen to carry a GPS tracker on their private boats and submit to around-the-clock surveillance as a condition of keeping their license remains a serious constitutional concern,” Gilliam said. “We are committed to fighting for Fourth Amendment protections from government overreach and we will continue to pursue every lawful avenue to protect individual rights.”
At the center of the case is a 2023 requirement that all federally licensed lobster vessels must operate GPS trackers. The rule was passed by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, and implemented by the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
Thompson sued Wilson, the Marine Resources commissioner, in federal court when the rule went into effect in 2024, arguing that the tracking constituted an unreasonable search and seizure and violated his constitutional rights.
But federal judges were not persuaded. The lawsuit was dismissed by the district court, and that ruling was upheld by the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last year. With the Supreme Court declining to intervene, the 1st Circuit ruling is the final order in the suit.
The Conservation Law Foundation previously filed an amicus brief in the case, supporting the regulations and arguing that it is legal and vital to track lobster boats to ensure effective management of the industry.
“New England’s lobster population has declined dangerously,” Conservation Law Foundation Associate Attorney Sarah Shahabi said in a statement. “Tracking lobster boats provides the timely and accurate data that regulators need. This decision is a valuable step toward appropriately managing this iconic species.”
This story was published by Maine Morningstar.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Evelyn L. Winchenbach, 86, of Waldoboro, passed away at her home quietly on Nov. 19, 2025 from several medical issues that could not be cured.
Evelyn was born to Irving Spencer and Florence Seigars and was one of eight siblings.
As a foster child, she was raised by Doug and Alice Benner of Bristol and later by Barry and Verna Gould, of Waldoboro. She attended school at A.D. Gray in Waldoboro. Her first job was at Moody’s Diner in Waldoboro.
At the age of 18, she married Earl Nelson Winchenbach, and they started their family. They built a general store called Winks on Kalers Corner in Waldoboro. They later built a motel, the Village View, also on Kalers Corner. Both places were extremely known and very popular.
After Earl passed away, she met Fredrick S. Poland and was engaged to him until his passing.
Evelyn was a hard worker and often named the nicest woman someone had ever known. She was a kind, generous, caring woman, always taking in people who needed help.
Always a busy lady, Evelyn loved to cook, share time with friends, go to dances, listen to country music, sew, knit, and garden. She also loved her neighborhood and the families in it.
She is predeceased by siblings, Helen Nelson, Blanche Cunningham, Richard and Robert Spencer, Edith Achorn, and Gloria Kelly.
She is survived by sister, Irene Turner; children, Neil Winchenbach, Scot Winchenbach, Alisa Fessenden, and Lynette Platt; three grandchildren; and several great-grandchildren and great-great-grandchildren
She will always be loved, missed, and carried in our hearts. God bless you and rest in peace, amen.
There will be an indoor and outdoor celebration of life at 1 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 19 Bremen Road in Waldoboro, with a rain date of Sunday, Oct. 18. Alisa can be reached at 542-4217 if guests would like to bring something to share.

title: Bangor Adapted Baseball hosts annual game honoring first responders, local celebrities
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Local celebrities, first responders and adapted athletes took to the Mansfield Stadium in Bangor Sunday afternoon to play ball!
Bangor Adapted Baseball hosted the annual Local Heroes and Celebrity Game to recognize the efforts of those who serve their community.
“For the last five years we’ve had a local celebrity’s game here, and it’s been all about showcasing local celebrities that you see every day on TV or on the radio. This year we threw in the twist of adding some local heroes, local firefighters and there’s a couple former Navy SEALs here I believe as well,” said Bangor Adapted Baseball coach Tyler Parke.
“When we do the All-Star game it’s like the World Series. Our first practice we work really hard and we build up our confidence and getting ready for the big game,” said Ray Quimby of Bangor Adapted Baseball.
“I’m completely new, this is my first year playing. I didn’t know what it was until some of my friends that are playing today told me about it. I think I might do this again next year,” said Micheal Mayo of Bangor Adapted Baseball.
“I haven’t played baseball since I graduated in 2017 so it’s fun to pick up a bat and a glove and throw a ball around again and just get out there and have fun,” said Derek Fournier, Goalie Coach for UMaine Women’s Hockey.
It’s a tough job having to go all the way across the state or anything like that to report and make sure everybody’s well informed," said Parke. “Then you got the other side of it with the local heroes that are often underpaid and overworked to recognize them for what they do I think is incredibly important because they don’t often get recognized for what they do. It’s nice to put a face of the names and the names of the jobs.”

title: Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity
text:
Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity
The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The Nobel Assembly lauded their work and said their tool is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.
Related video: Fossilized eggs reveal new secrets about world’s biggest dinosaurs
Deisseroth, 54, is a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator and Stanford University professor in California. Hegemann, 71, is at Humboldt University in Berlin, and Nagel, 73, most recently worked at the University of Würzburg, also in Germany, the assembly said.
The work that won the 2026 Nobel Prize in medicine
Optogenetics opened what the Nobel Assembly called a new era in neuroscience following the discovery of a light-controlled switch to turn on and off nerve cells and circuits in the brain to better learn how it works. The research has started unraveling the pathways that lead to behavior and disease.
The breakthrough began when Hegemann explored how a single-celled type of green algae can swim toward light. He and Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive.
Deisseroth then worked with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
“People usually think about light as a way of collecting information to observe things,” he said. “But this is the opposite of that. This is using light to control things, to make things happen, and to do it in a very precise way.”
Deisseroth first developed tiny fibers to deliver light to cells modified with the light-sensitive gene and said there now are other techniques to switch on or off neurons being studied.
Optogenetics is mostly a research technique to learn how specific neurons and neural circuits work, which can then lead to development of treatments, including regimens for autism and schizophrenia that other scientists are pursuing, he said. A technique he called direct optogenetics is being used to test a treatment for a genetic form of vision loss called retinitis pigmentosa.
Why the research is important
Brain cells communicate in milliseconds, and optogenetics for the first time offered scientists a way to control them at the same speed in a laboratory, said Patrick Forcelli, the chairman of the pharmacology and physiology department at Georgetown University, whose lab uses optogenetics.
Now a mainstay in neuroscience labs, the field has moved from using fixed maps of brain activity to building functional wiring diagrams. It has also jump-started additional techniques to explore neural complexity.
“It has let us go from a ‘Rand McNally’ road atlas of the brain to something more akin to ‘Google Earth,’” Forcelli said in an email.
The University of Pittsburgh’s Jeremy Berg was at the U.S. National Institutes of Health in the early 2000s when it awarded Deisseroth major funding for “this vision of optogenetics that was pretty much spot-on the way it played out.”
“It’s a very precise set of tools for doing experiments about how the brain works that are pretty hard to do any other way,” Berg said.
Abdel El Manira, a member of the Nobel Assembly, said the impact of optogenetics goes beyond the understanding of a healthy brain.
“It has also helped reveal how specific brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression, addiction and dementia," El Manira said. "Yet despite these extraordinary advances, the brain still holds countless mysteries, with much more left to learn and discover. And optogenetics has given us a powerful means to take on these challenges.”
Deisseroth had just gone to bed when he learned of the award
Deisseroth, a self-described night owl, said he was up late in his Northern California home working on papers and emailing students. He had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly.
“No real sleep was achieved,” he told The Associated Press in a phone call an hour after the announcement.
He said the next task on his to-do list was to pack school lunches for his children, who were still sound asleep.
“That’s my one obligation I have in the next few hours, to make sure I make their sandwiches,” he said.
Thomas Perlmann, the secretary of the medicine committee, said he was able to reach all three winners Monday. The AP could not immediately reach Hegemann and Nagel.
Medicine prize kicks off Nobels week
The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, kicking off Nobels week. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.
Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.
Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.
After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.
___
Neergaard reported from Washington, and Ramakrishnan reported from New York. Associated Press Writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: Weakened fuel efficiency goals will cause lasting damage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Trump administration recently lowered goals for fuel efficiency in many gas-powered vehicles. The previous goal, set by the Biden administration, was for 50.4 miles per gallon in 2031. This change brings that down to 30.1 mpg. This reduction will increase emissions and accelerate climate change when we need to slow it down.
There’s another aspect of this, which is that continued reliance on fossil fuels puts us all at risk. As we’ve seen in the war with Iran, relying on fossil fuel shipments from other countries leaves us economically vulnerable.
Those of us in Maine, as well as elsewhere, are already feeling this. A recent news report (“Rising gas prices eating into profits of Mainers who drive their cars for a living,” Sept. 28) pointed out how those who drive as part of their jobs — such as with Lyft, Uber, and DoorDash — are having to make changes to their jobs now that they spend so much on gas. That will also impact their customers.
I know how much of a difference it makes to get 50 mpg, since that’s about what I get with my hybrid. Yes, I still need to buy gas, but the rising prices have had much less of an impact on me. Not everyone can afford a hybrid, but if the previous fuel standards were kept, even those without a hybrid would benefit.
As it is, this change is short-sighted, environmentally harmful, and will have lasting negative impacts on all of us. I encourage everyone to keep this in mind when voting this November.
Erica Bartlett
Portland

title: Mother and son from Bermuda named as passengers on missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
text:
Mother and son from Bermuda named as passengers on missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
The two people aboard an air ambulance that crashed in the waters off Massachusetts over the weekend while flying from Bermuda to Boston were identified Monday as a mother from Bermuda and her son.
Bermuda police said Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41, both Bermudian nationals, were aboard a Gulfstream G100 with four crew members when it went missing off Nantucket around 1 a.m. Saturday. Bermuda is about 750 to 780 miles southeast of Boston.
Searchers later found a “debris field” off the coast of the island, but with no sign of the six people on board after a 66-hour search that spanned more than 4,400 miles (7,081 kilometers), the U.S. Coast Guard suspended rescue efforts Sunday.
“While we held out hope for the best, the worst fears have been realized," Bermuda Premier David Burt said in a statement. “Let us open our hearts to the families in the hope that our expressions of love, support and compassion will bring some comfort as they attempt to deal with this terrible loss.”
Warwick Academy, the school Lottimore attended in Bermuda, remembered him as a school prefect and an “outstanding person.” Hamilton Re, the Bermuda insurance firm where he served as a senior vice president, said it had lost a “respected leader, colleague and friend.”
The names of the plane's crew have not been released, but Latitude Air Ambulance, the Ontario-based company that owned the plane, said Sunday that its staff faces the “heartbreaking reality” that all aboard the plane are now presumed dead, even if they have not been officially declared dead.
“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family,” the company said in a statement. “They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred. We are grieving their loss deeply."
Peter Byl, president of Latitude Air Ambulance, said Monday the company's immediate focus was on supporting the victims' families and cooperating fully with authorities.
“We will not speculate about the circumstances or cause of the accident while that work is underway,” he wrote in an email.
The Canadian-registered jet had departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport on a nighttime flight to Massachusetts. Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been “coming in blind” as a storm loomed. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.
Canada’s Transportation Safety Board said it will send investigators in the coming days to assist in the search for and recovery of the aircraft. The agency said it is leading the investigation into the crash with assistance from its U.S. counterpart, the National Transportation Safety Board.

title: Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt lands her next gig: Fox News contributor
text:
Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt lands her next gig: Fox News contributor
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has found her next chapter: She is heading to Fox News.
Leavitt will serve as an on-air contributor beginning Nov. 1, the network said Monday.
“Karoline’s firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape,” said the network’s CEO, Suzanne Scott.
For her part, Leavitt, in the same statement, said she looked forward “to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms.”
Leavitt, now 29, was the youngest person to hold the role of press secretary. When she left at the end of August, President Donald Trump described her as one of his “most trusted aides.”
Leavitt is not the first White House press secretary to join Fox. Kayleigh McEnany joined in 2021 and remains at the network.
And Trump has hired several Fox News personalities to key jobs in his own administration, chief among them Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

title: Women’s ice hockey splits non-conference series with St. Lawrence
text:
ORONO, Maine — On Thursday, Oct. 1, the Black Bears hosted RV St. Lawrence College in the Harold Alfond Arena. After losing two games last week to Quinnipiac at home, the team looked to bounce back and secure their first win of the new season.
St. Lawrence also entered this game at 0-2-0, which set the table for Maine to seize an opportunity and even out their record before diving deeper into conference play.
The match up was a high scoring affair. Maine set the tone early on with a lead-taking goal at the end of the first period. Third-year defender Kendall Sundby scored on a powerplay that gave Maine the lead going into period two. The goal was assisted by second-year defender Sade Sandilands and third-year forward Gracie Hanson.
Maine had the opportunity to hold this lead through the second period and push the lead further, but slipped up and gave up an unassisted goal to St. Lawrence’s first-year forward Kendall Doiron under two minutes into the period.
For the rest of the second period, Maine made it their mission to bolster the defense and not give up the lead. For the next 13 minutes of gameplay, they did just that, and it was rewarded with a Black Bear goal at the end of the period. Fourth-year forward Mikayla Boarder scored her first goal of the season to put Maine up 2-1. The goal was assisted by fourth-year forward Lily Fetch and Hanson, bringing her tally to two assists for the game.
Unfortunately, after the goal, the defense let up a bit, and gave up another unassisted, equalizer goal just minutes after their own score. St. Lawrence would tie the game 2-2 going into the third period. Second-year forward Cheyenne Degeer scored the goal for St. Lawrence.
The Saints momentum would continue early in the third. Just three minutes into the final period, Degeer would net another goal, this time assisted by second-year forward Brooke Mulvihill. The Black Bears now trailed late, and time was against them.
Minutes later, with their backs against the wall, Fetch and Hanson combined for their second assist together, sliding the puck to Boarder for her second goal of the contest. This also marked Hanson’s third assist of the game.
With the game tied 3-3, it all came down to the last few minutes. Both teams had scoring opportunities and went back and forth down the ice trying to score the game winner.
Ultimately, it was the Black Bears who struck once again. Second-year forward Mackenzie Podewell and second-year defender Lulu Rucinski combined for an assist on a set-up play for a third-year forward Stephanie Jacob goal, a score that lifted Maine to their first win of the season.
Maine earned their first win in a thriller at the Alfond, but the second game of the series would not bode so well.
The Black Bears lost 3-0 the following day, and gave up a goal in each period to let St. Lawrence escape Orono with a win of their own.
Maine Women’s ice hockey moves to 1-3-0, and will play Minnesota in an away game on Oct 9th. This will be a huge opportunity to score a big win against a good team.

title: Portland’s Taco Escobarr sues copycat Nevada restaurant
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Taco Barr LLC, on behalf of Taco Escobarr, has filed suit against a Las Vegas restaurateur for operating a restaurant under a nearly identical name.
The suit claims that Taco Escobar in Las Vegas has violated the Lanham Act, which protects trademarks and prevents companies from adopting brand names identical or too similar to ones already in use.
Taco Escobarr owner Thomas Barr learned of the Las Vegas restaurant in 2024, according to the suit, filed Oct. 2 in U.S. District Court for the District of Maine. The suit contends he read about plans for the venue in a local Las Vegas publication that included a site map with the brand name and logo for Taco Escobarr, lifted directly from Barr’s website for his own restaurant.
Barr, who has operated Taco Escobarr on Congress Street for more than 15 years, reached out to the brokerage firm listed in the article, but received no response. Shortly after, though, the Nevada restaurant dropped the second “r” in its name.
The suit notes that Las Vegas restaurateur Jeffrey Fine, owner of Taco Escobar, has publicly stated that he goes out of town on dining research trips, specifically to Maine. It quotes from a 2024 published interview of Fine: “I like exploring, traveling, and importing places that are doing well back here to Las Vegas,” Fine says. “Driving up and down the (Maine) coast, there’s lobster shacks, clam shacks, and just the whole experience of doing that inspired me, for instance, to bring a lobster roll business to Vegas.”
“Recently, our client was dismayed to learn that one of those visitors to Maine had apparently taken Taco Escobarr’s name and brand identity back home to Nevada to open a restaurant there,” attorney Stacy Stitham of Brann & Isaacson in Lewiston wrote in response to a reporter’s query. “After several efforts to reach out to establish a dialogue were met with silence, Taco Escobarr’s owner has filed suit to protect the goodwill and reputation of one of Portland’s iconic restaurants.”
After Taco Escobar opened in Las Vegas in 2025, the suit states that Taco Escobarr has received calls from customers trying to reach the Las Vegas restaurant, and social media reviewers have left negative reviews about the Portland venue, thinking they were commenting on the Las Vegas restaurant.
The suit states that Fine’s actions are “likely to cause confusion, mistake, or deception as to the affiliation, connection, or association between Taco Escobar (Vegas) and Barr,” and so “constitute trademark infringement, false designation of origin, and/or unfair competition.”
Barr’s suit seeks to prevent Fine and his associates from using Taco Escobar or any other confusingly similar business name, and asks the court for statutory and compensatory damages, “including lost profits due to diverted sales, lost goodwill, and cheapening of plaintiff’s reputation.”
Barr declined to comment and referred questions to his attorney. Fine and his management group did not immediately return calls for comment on Monday.

title: Experts warn lithium-ion batteries pose fire risk during Fire Prevention Week
text:
Maine (WABI) - The National Fire Protection Association says many phones, tablets and laptops run on rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which store a large amount of energy in a small space.
If those batteries are damaged or charged incorrectly, they can overheat, and some can explode, according to the NFPA.
Experts say it’s important to use the cord or charger that came with a device or ones approved by the manufacturer. They also recommend unplugging a device once it is fully charged.
Experts say where a device is charged matters as well.
“Because lithium-ion batteries are a newer technology, not everyone is aware of the potential dangers they present, particularly when it comes to charging them safely,” said Lorraine Carli, vice president of Outreach and Advocacy at NFPA. “Our goal for this year’s Fire Prevention Week campaign is to help people make informed choices and practice simple habits that can help greatly reduce those risks.”
Fire Prevention Week is observed throughout North America every October.
More safety tips are available at nfpa.org.

title: Court bailiff accused of selling fake CPR certifications to daycares
text:
THOMSON, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) - A Georgia man is accused of selling invalid CPR certifications to employees at daycare and adult care facilities.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigation arrested and charged James Ed Lewis, 66, of Thomson, with three counts of filing false documents and one count of theft by taking.
Kakika Eubanks, who runs Lil Bo Peep Learning Center, said the children at her daycare are like her own.
“They’re like my little ones. They’re like my own children. So I would tend to them and treat them and love them just like my own kids,” Eubanks said.
Eubanks said CPR certification is required by the state for her workers.
“CPR is required by the state. For all of my workers,” she said.
To teach the class, Eubanks called Lewis, a first responder she had known for years. Lewis provided state certificates along with training logs.
The GBI said the cards were fake and that Lewis was not certified to issue them.
“I was devastated. I was shocked. I was in disbelief. I just couldn’t believe that it wasn’t, you know, that this had happened,” Eubanks said.
Lewis turned himself in Wednesday and was booked into the McDuffie County Jail.
Law enforcement sources said the fake cards were handed out at as many as three daycares, including at Thomson’s First Methodist Church.
According to the GBI, Lewis was not certified as a CPR instructor at the time the course was provided to the businesses.
To clarify, being certified as a CPR instructor isn’t the same as being certified in CPR. Lewis is certified in CPR, according to documents.
“I was mad. I was very upset. Very upset,” Eubanks said.
Lewis was a longtime firefighter and former lieutenant. He was employed by the McDuffie County Sheriff’s Office, working security as a bailiff at the McDuffie County Government Complex, a job he retired from after he was bonded out of jail.
He informed the county Wednesday morning that he would be retiring immediately, McDuffie County Manager Brandon Burton said.
Eubanks said she had known Lewis for years.
“I’ve been knowing him for years, actually since I was little, but I found him doing a fire and safety training years ago, and he started doing our CPR and first aid training since. So he’s been doing our CPR training for years,” she said.
Eubanks said no one at her daycare had to use the CPR skills listed on the certificates.
“Thank God that we didn’t need CPR or anything during this time frame because I mean, we didn’t have the proper CPR training that we thought that we had that we trusted in him to give us,” she said.
The Thomson Police Department asked the GBI to investigate the allegations on March 24.
Preliminary information indicates several daycare businesses and adult care facilities in Thomson paid Lewis to provide CPR certification courses to their employees.
Those businesses were later told by the Georgia Department of Early Care and Learning that the courses Lewis taught, and the CPR certification cards he provided to attendees, were invalid, according to the GBI.
We have reached out to Lewis for a comment.
The investigation remains active and ongoing.
Anyone with information is asked to contact the GBI Regional Investigative Office in Thomson at 706-595-2575.
Anonymous tips can also be submitted by calling 1-800-597-TIPS (8477), online, or through the “See Something, Send Something” mobile app.

title: Early voting for the November election is underway in Maine. Here’s how to do it
text:
Early voting has begun in Maine ahead of the Nov. 3 election, which features a high-profile set of races for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House, alongside State House and local contests.
Mainers can vote early for any reason from Monday through Oct. 29, and they can do so by casting a ballot in person at their local town office, returning their absentee ballot by mail or using a ballot drop box in their community.
Here are a few things to know about early voting.
Where and when can I vote early in Maine?
Early voting locations, hours and absentee ballot drop box locations for each municipality are available on the Maine Department of the Secretary of State’s website and its “Upcoming Elections” page.
On that page, voters can view and download the “Municipal Office Hours & Absentee Drop Box Locations” form, which lists each town’s office hours and drop box locations. Some towns offer early voting Monday through Friday, while others are only a few days per week or by appointment.
If a municipality does not have a listed address for a drop box, contact your town office. The “Find a Municipal Clerk or Registrar” page on the secretary of state’s website has a searchable database of contact information for local election officials.
The last day to vote early is Oct. 29, the Thursday before the Nov. 3 election. Mainers can also register to vote online or in person through Election Day. Visit registertovote.sos.maine.gov to register, update voter registration information or change party enrollment.
How do I vote by mail?
The deadline to request an absentee ballot is also Oct. 29. Absentee ballots must be returned to a municipal clerk by 8 p.m. Nov. 3, and unlike several states that allow ballots to be counted if they are at least postmarked by Election Day, only ballots received by the close of the polls on Election Day are counted in Maine.
To request an absentee ballot and find out more information about ballots for voters with disabilities and voters who are in the military or overseas, visit the “Absentee Voting” page on the secretary of state’s website.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said during a Monday morning news conference in Brunswick that laws regarding early voting and absentee ballots have not changed. That was a nod to President Donald Trump, who long criticized mail-in voting and proposed changes that were blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court but is now urging Americans to vote early.
“We have all unfortunately experienced frustration with the Postal Service and things from everyday mail to prescriptions not arriving in a timely manner,” Bellows said. “That’s why it can be so helpful to vote early.”
How do I track my absentee ballot?
Maine voters can track the status of their absentee ballot at absenteeballotrequest.sos.maine.gov.
How many Mainers have voted early so far, and what’s the breakdown by party?
The secretary of state’s office posts updated reports on absentee requests each Tuesday and Thursday. Ahead of the start of early voting, the office reported that 70,260 Mainers had requested absentee ballots, more than 45,000 ballots had been issued so far, and nearly 800 ballots had been returned and accepted.
About 57% of the absentee ballot requests were from registered Democrats, 14% from Republicans and 26% from unenrolled voters. The early gaps have narrowed in past elections as Election Day gets closer, though Democrats typically outpace Republicans in absentee voting.

title: Multiple people hurt in hay wagon crash
text:
WELLSBURG, N.Y. (WENY) - A hayride crash in New York on Sunday left multiple people injured, authorities said.
The crash happened in Wellsburg, a village near the Pennsylvania border.
Authorities said a tractor-trailer was hauling a hay wagon when the vehicle went too fast down a road. When the driver turned the wheel, the tractor rolled over and the wagon separated from the tractor, authorities said.
The wagon then crashed, according to authorities.
Emergency responders treated 14 people for injuries at the scene. Up to five other people were taken to a hospital, and some of them suffered critical injuries, authorities said.
It remains unclear how many people were on the hayride when the crash happened.

title: Christa Pike received life-saving measures after her botched lethal injection. Here’s why
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - After a failed execution, Christa Pike remains in the hospital on a ventilator in critical condition.
On Wednesday, Pike received two doses of pentobarbital and saline, but she remained alive.
During the process, witnesses described Pike as having labored breathing, snoring heavily and, at some points, sounding like she was choking.
Ambulances later arrived at Riverbend Maximum Security and took her to the hospital.
After Pike’s failed execution, people are questioning why Tennessee performed life-saving measures on Pike when they planned to execute her.
What the execution team is required to do before and during the execution process
According to Tennessee’s 2025 lethal injection protocol, team members must rely on the protocol for training.
Leading up to Pike’s execution, the execution team, IV team and physician were required to review the protocol when they were assigned. The warden is also required to review the protocol with them every year.
According to the protocol, staff must prepare four syringes, two containing 50 mg of saline and two containing 50 mg of pentobarbital.
During the execution, staff must open the blinds so witnesses can view the execution chamber. The inmate will say their last words and the pentobarbital will be administered. After a five-minute waiting period, the blinds are closed and a doctor must examine the inmate.
The document goes on to explain that if the inmate remains alive, a backup set of four syringes must be administered. The blinds must be opened again for witnesses to view the injections, and then must be closed again as medics examine the inmate to see if the inmate died.
That’s exactly what happened Wednesday night at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, according to execution witnesses and the Tennessee Department of Correction.
But what happens if the inmate still does not die?
A loophole in the protocol
That is the question the Tennessee Department of Correction prison staff were forced to deal with in real time on Wednesday evening when Pike remained alive.
The protocol mentions nothing about what happens if the execution fails, but the Eighth Amendment of the United States Constitution explains that “cruel and unusual punishments” cannot be inflicted.
Attorneys and Tennessee officials push for answers
Pike’s failed execution prompted Gov. Bill Lee to halt the one remaining execution this year and order a full investigation.
It is still unclear how Pike survived the two doses of pentobarbital, and the state protocol indicates she is the first to do so. However, it is possible she survived due to a mistake made along the way.
The Tennessee Department of Correction denies making any mistakes and has declined to answer further questions on Pike’s execution, but Lee ordered a “comprehensive” third-party review of Wednesday night’s events, which will be conducted by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton.
On Saturday, Lee announced that Frank Strada, the state’s Department of Correction commissioner, was resigning.
Pike’s legal team is also challenging the lethal injection protocol. They previously asked Tennessee to use hanging instead of lethal injection and argued that her blood disorder, vein-access issues and history of trauma could result in unnecessary suffering. Their request was denied.

title: Alex Ovechkin says this is his final NHL season: ‘It’s hard, but let’s enjoy it’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Alex Ovechkin said Monday that his 22nd season in the NHL will be his last, beginning the farewell tour for the longtime Washington Capitals captain who holds the league’s career goal-scoring record.
Ovechkin addressed teammates to deliver the news before the team posted a message from him on social media.
“It’s sad, but it is what it is,” Ovechkin said in his locker room address. “It’s hard, but let’s enjoy it and let’s do some special things this year.”
Ovechkin signed a one-year contract this past summer and turned 41 on Sept. 17. All signs pointed to this being the end, and he said he and his family decided as much in recent months.
“I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it’s the right decision,” the Russian star said in a statement released before the Capitals’ home opener Wednesday night.
Ovechkin broke Wayne Gretzky’s goals record in April 2025 and entered this season at 929. The front office acquired Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch in trades and signed fellow forward Boone Jenner and defenseman Vincent Desharnais in free agency to add around a young core in the hopes of making another long playoff run and contending for the Stanley Cup.
“Let’s make the playoffs, let’s have fun and enjoy the moment because times fly,” Ovechkin told the team. “For young guys who are first year or experienced guys, I remember that moment, and enjoy the time. Because times fly. It seems like yesterday I was here my first year.”
Speaking to reporters later Monday, Ovechkin said this was the right time to announce his decision, two days before the home opener.
“I’m not 20 years old,” he said. “I want to play with my kids when they’re growing up. Play hockey, play soccer, play basketball. I want to be healthy enough to do that kind of stuff.”
Ovechkin has spent his entire career with Washington, winning the Calder Trophy as rookie of the year in 2005-06, the Hart Trophy as MVP three times and leading the NHL in scoring nine times. He was playoff MVP in 2018 when he led the Caps to the first Stanley Cup championship in franchise history.
There’s been speculation Ovechkin could receive an unfriendly reception on the road after he appeared in an ad for a party aligned with Vladimir Putin during the offseason. But there wasn’t much sign of that during the first two games of the season — at Carolina and at Tampa Bay.
When addressing the fallout from that last month, Ovechkin confirmed he’d be going back to live in Russia when he retired from the NHL.
In Washington’s season-opening win over the Hurricanes, Ovechkin had 12 minutes, 46 seconds of ice time, the lowest of his career in a game when he wasn’t injured or ejected.
Monday was 21 years to the day after Ovechkin made his debut with the Capitals.
“It’s been pretty good career, pretty good 22 seasons,” he said. “Obviously the goal that we have, to bring a Stanley Cup to D.C., we did it.”
Although the Capitals have designs on making the playoffs this season, within a couple hours of Ovechkin’s announcement, tickets for Washington’s regular-season home finale against Pittsburgh on April 4 were going for a minimum of $825 on StubHub. With D.C. hosting college hockey’s Frozen Four next year, the Capitals finish the regular season with three straight road games, wrapping up April 10 at Philadelphia.
The Capitals missed the playoffs in 2025-26, but Ovechkin played all 82 games and scored 32 goals. He’s reached 30 in every season of his career except 2020-21, when he played only 45 games.
Long before he broke through during the Capitals’ Stanley Cup run, Ovechkin had rejuvenated hockey in Washington, and he’ll retire as one of the city’s most accomplished athletes in any sport. The Capitals drafted him No. 1 overall in 2004, and he and Pittsburgh’s Sidney Crosby became stars almost immediately in 2005 when the league emerged from missing a season because of a lockout.
“Before we even met, we were kind of built up against each other: It’s kind of a natural thing to happen,” Crosby said. “Over the years developed a friendship with him. Have a ton of respect for him, and you play against someone that long, you’re compared and see each other enough I think that’s something that builds over time.”
Ovechkin’s combination of goal-scoring skill, physicality and boundless energy made him an instant hit, and he scored a career-high 65 goals in his third season, which earned him the first of his MVP honors.
“He’s done everything,” said Penguins center Evgeni Malkin, a fellow countryman who was picked second after Ovechkin in the 2004 draft. ”He do everything for team, for league. I hope he plays good this year, no injury, he just stay healthy, score goals and enjoy the game.”
Washington’s penchant for postseason heartache, which existed long before Ovechkin showed up, followed him for a while as well. The Capitals won the Presidents’ Trophy three times with the league’s best regular-season record, falling short in the playoffs each time before a Washington team that merely won its division finally went all the way in the playoffs.
In four postseason meetings between Crosby and Ovechkin — in 2009, 2016, 2017, 2018 — the winner won the Stanley Cup each time. Washington’s home opener Wednesday is against Pittsburgh.
“Definitely have had some great battles over the years,” Crosby said. “Obviously when you get to our age, that’s something that you have to make decisions on and for him, as long as he’s happy and enjoying it, that’s the biggest thing.”

title: Supreme Court declines to take up Maine lobster boat tracking appeal
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear a Maine lobsterman’s legal challenge to an electronic vessel tracker requirement, putting an end to the multiyear lawsuit.
The court denied a request to take up the appeal by Frank Thompson, a Vinalhaven lobsterman, Maine Morningstar reported.
In a statement, Maine Department of Marine Resources Commissioner Carl Wilson said the department believes the tracking data is critically important to the long-term sustainability of the lobster fishery.
“It will inform the lobster stock assessment, enhance offshore enforcement and support better decision-making in a range of federal management contexts,” Wilson said.
Thompson’s attorney, Matthew Gilliam with Pacific Legal Foundation, said in a statement that the denial does not diminish the importance of the issues in the suit.
“Forcing lobstermen to carry a GPS tracker on their private boats and submit to around-the-clock surveillance as a condition of keeping their license remains a serious constitutional concern,” Gilliam said. “We are committed to fighting for Fourth Amendment protections from government overreach and we will continue to pursue every lawful avenue to protect individual rights.”
At the center of the case is a 2023 requirement that all federally licensed lobster vessels must operate GPS trackers. The rule was passed by the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, and implemented by the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
Thompson sued Wilson, the Marine Resources commissioner, in federal court when the rule went into effect in 2024, arguing that the tracking constituted an unreasonable search and seizure and violated his constitutional rights.
But federal judges were not persuaded. The lawsuit was dismissed by the district court, and that ruling was upheld by the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last year. With the Supreme Court declining to intervene, the 1st Circuit ruling is the final order in the suit.
The Conservation Law Foundation previously filed an amicus brief in the case, supporting the regulations and arguing that it is legal and vital to track lobster boats to ensure effective management of the industry.
“New England’s lobster population has declined dangerously,” Conservation Law Foundation Associate Attorney Sarah Shahabi said in a statement. “Tracking lobster boats provides the timely and accurate data that regulators need. This decision is a valuable step toward appropriately managing this iconic species.”
This story was published by Maine Morningstar.

title: Maine’s next governor to inherit $1.3 billion budget shortfall
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - In January, when the next governor moves into the Blaine House, they will inherit a $1.3 billion budget shortfall.
This includes $1.085 billion from the General Fund and $256.7 million from the state highway fund.
Things that are funded include the statutory requirement to fund 55% of public education in the state as well as MaineCare funding and all the bills passed during the last legislature that need funding.

title: New Veranda restaurant planned for Portland’s Fore Street
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The owners of Veranda Thai and Vietnamese restaurants and markets in Greater Portland have leased space on Fore Street with plans to launch a new Veranda Kitchen & Bar.
Owners Hai Pham and Sonka Nguyen have filed an application with the City Council, which is scheduled to be reviewed at their Oct. 5 meeting. The owners could not be reached immediately for comment.
The application notes that the owners have operated Veranda Kitchen & Bar in Westbrook for more than 10 years. They expect the venue at 425 Fore St., in the same building as Barkada and Gelato Fiasco, will offer similar Thai and Vietnamese specialties as their Westbrook location.
The Veranda Group includes Veranda Thai and Veranda Noodle Bar, both on Veranda St.; Veranda Asian Market on Forest Avenue; and Veranda Kitchen & Bar in Westbrook.

title: Supreme Court rejects appeal over Michigan school's ban on ‘Let’s Go Brandon’ sweatshirts
text:
Supreme Court rejects appeal over Michigan school's ban on ‘Let’s Go Brandon’ sweatshirts
The Supreme Court is rebuffing an appeal from a Michigan woman fighting a school district's ban on shirts with the phrase “Let’s Go Brandon,” a jab at then-President Joe Biden with a coded reference to profanity.
Video above: Supreme Court begins new term with cases addressing climate change, immigration, and gun laws
The mother of two boys says their First Amendment rights were violated when they were told to take off the sweatshirts she bought them for Christmas in 2022.
A lower court disagreed, finding that the veiled vulgarity of the phrase, which functions as a stand-in for “F--- Joe Biden,” allows schools to ban it.
The woman's attorneys argued that the decision wrongly gives school officials wide latitude to squelch political speech based on their personal ideas of what is vulgar. The phrase itself doesn't contain any swear words or sexual implications, they said.
The school district urged the justices to reject the case, arguing that messages with lewd implications have no place in school, even if they touch on political topics. There has been evidence that some students wore clothing that read “Make America Great Again” or had messages supporting President Donald Trump, a Republican who lost the 2020 election to Biden, a Democrat.
The phrase originated in 2021, when people in the crowd at a NASCAR race chanted the obscenity directed at Biden and a TV sports reporter said they were calling out “Let’s Go, Brandon," apparently believing they were chanting for driver Brandon Brown, who had just won a race.
