title: Trump tried to make an ally out of fishermen. Some have started to turn on him
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — John Evich, a commercial fisherman in Washington and Alaska, has voted for President Donald Trump three times, viewing him as someone who would fight for his industry.
But these days, Evich is weary of the high cost of doing business at sea, with fuel prices rising and trade hostilities with Canada jeopardizing markets for the crabs that he pulls off the ocean floor.
“If somebody came along that was going to do a better job, I would vote for them in a heartbeat,” he said.
Evich’s sentiment, echoed throughout the U.S. seafood industry, is another piece of a political puzzle that is working against Trump in the midterm elections. Dissatisfaction among commercial fishermen could cause collateral damage for Republicans in competitive races in Washington, Alaska and Maine.
“Having those costs be so much higher this year has really undermined the viability of some of our fisheries,” Alaska fisherman Linda Behnken said.
Trump sought to make an ally out of fishermen during his first term with expanded fishing territory, aggressive trade moves and cutting down regulations on the water. He did so again after his second election.
But one of Trump’s government cutback efforts, cuts to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which regulates fisheries, has left the agency slower to respond to the industry’s needs, fishermen said. Staff cutbacks also resulted in the agency reducing weather balloons used to gather data fishermen rely on.
Fuel costs have also crept up during the war with Iran, pushing diesel fuel into the $6-per-gallon range when it was less than $4 per gallon a year ago — a major burden for a diesel-dependent industry. And the trade war with Canada has complicated the American seafood industry’s relationship with a country it has long been interconnected with, fishermen said.
The Trump administration has continued trying to win the hearts of fishermen with industry-friendly moves, including an early September promise to reduce more regulatory burdens in response to a 2025 executive order. And some of the industry’s key states, such as Alaska, Washington and Maine, are important to Trump politically this year because of competitive House and Senate races. But support on the water could be waning.
“I’m for whatever has to happen for the greater good in the long run for my family and my country,” Evich said.
Trump has cozied up to the fishing industry for years
Trump has positioned himself as a pro-fishing president since his first term, when one of his major moves to impact the fishing industry was the rollback of Obama-era fishing restrictions for Northeast Canyons and Seamounts National Monument off the New England coast. Biden later restored the protections, and then Trump removed them again.
The fishing industry is potentially a natural ally for Trump. A 2026 NOAA survey of commercial fishing crews found that 70% thought fishing rules were too restrictive, and Trump has fashioned himself as an enemy of bureaucracy and red tape.
But in recent months, Trump has brought disruption to the fishing industry in a time when it can ill afford it, said John Sackton, founder of SeafoodNews.com and a longtime industry analyst. He said he sees an industry that is eager to “turn the page” on the Trump administration.
“Now what’s happened is that there has been this unbelievable wave of disruption from everything — targeting NOAA and fisheries, science and even weather reporting that people rely on,” said Sackton, who also cited tariffs and the rising cost of doing business as problems Trump brought to the industry.
Fuel costs and tariffs are huge concerns for fishermen
The high price of fuel is “one of the most immediate pressures on us as commercial fishermen,” said Bonnie Brady, executive director of the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association in New York.
Nearly all of the U.S.’s commercial fishing fleet uses marine diesel fuel, which makes soaring fuel costs a burden they can’t avoid. Fuel prices are so high right now that fishermen sometimes can’t afford to leave the dock at all, she said.
“Actual dockside marine-fuel prices vary, but the magnitude of the increase is undeniable. It determines whether a trip is economically viable, what the crew earns and whether necessary vessel maintenance can be performed,” Brady said.
In Rhode Island, fisherman Chris Brown, who targets species such as fluke and squid out of Point Judith, puts it more bluntly.
“It’s huge. It’s crazy. Thank you, Donald Trump,” he said sarcastically.
Trump’s trade war with Canada is a more complicated matter because Canada exempted U.S. fish and seafood products from its counter-tariffs that followed the U.S. placing tariffs on Canadian goods. Prior to the exemption, Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, said U.S. lobstermen risked becoming “collateral damage in a broader trade dispute.”
But unease among fishermen remains, in part because Canada is the U.S.’s largest seafood trading partner. The U.S. also relies on Canada for seafood processing and manufacturing of fishing gear. For some species, such as lobster and salmon, American and Canadian fishermen fish very close to each other or even in the same waters.
A trade war with such a key partner could have negative consequences for the fishing industry, said Steve Train, a lobster fisherman from Long Island, Maine, who described himself as a “right-leaning centrist” who has voted Republican more than Democrat.
“I get the standing up to a bully concept, but too many people will be caught in the middle of this,” Train said. “Both sides need to reconsider these tariffs, and they need to reconsider soon.”
Cuts to NOAA are troubling to fishermen
NOAA Fisheries, the arm of NOAA tasked with overseeing commercial fishing, is facing a budget cut of more than 40% in the fiscal 2027 budget proposal. That would result in cuts to science programs, fisheries management and data collection.
Those cutbacks trickle down to the fishermen and result in a lack of fishing opportunities, Sackton said. Some in the fishery also have the impression NOAA is too understaffed to regulate fisheries in a timely fashion, he said.
In Sitka, Alaska, Behnken said the Trump administration’s cutbacks at NOAA have made it more difficult for her and others who rely on the agency. She said she has a lot of empathy for the workers left at the agency, who she said are “doing the work of three people, particularly at the weather service,” but it is still frustrating for fishermen.
“It’s hard to retain good people when their future at the organization is that uncertain,” said Behnken, who is executive director of the Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association.

title: Tim Stutzle powers Ottawa Senators past Boston Bruins
text:
BOSTON — Tim Stutzle had two goals and an assist and goalies Linus Ullmark and Samuel Ersson combined to stop 18 of 19 shots as the Ottawa Senators defeated the Boston Bruins 4-1 on Monday night.
Stutzle’s multi-point game moved him into sole possession of sixth place for most points in Ottawa history with 413.
Ullmark started in goal for Ottawa, but wasn’t on the ice at the start of the third period. The onetime Bruin netminder, who stopped all 10 shots he faced in the first two periods, was on the bench five minutes into the final period. Ersson made eight saves in the final period for the Senators.
Ottawa’s Michael Amadio had a goal and assist, and Drake Batherson also scored.
Boston rookie James Hagan spoiled Ottawa’s shutout bid with a goal in the third period. Jeremy Swayman made 20 saves for the Bruins, who have lost two straight after opening the season with two wins.
Boston was outshot 24-19 and failed to score on four power plays.
Stutzle came close to two short-handed goals on the same power play. He scored on the man advantage at 7:39 of the first. Seconds after Ottawa successfully shut down Boston on the power play, Stutzle scored on a 2-on-1 chance, making it 2-0.
Batherson scored 66 seconds into the second period, taking advantage of a Boston turnover and scoring with a backhand shot.
Amadio converted on a feed from Shane Pinto to give Ottawa a 4-0 lead, prompting Bruins head coach Marco Sturm to call at timeout at 14:41.
Ullmark was slow getting up after Boston’s JJ Peterka crashed into him at 4:25 of the second. The 2022-23 Venza Trophy winner with Boston is in his third season with Ottawa after being traded before the 2024-25 season.
Up next
Senators: At Detroit on Tuesday night.
Bruins: Host Utah on Thursday night.

title: Family mourns 7-year-old girl stabbed to death while walking with sister; suspect charged
text:
CHICAGO (WLS) - A Chicago family is mourning a 7-year-old girl who was stabbed to death while walking with her older sister as police say the suspect faces a murder charge.
A vigil was held Sunday to honor 7-year-old Eddimar Paola Hernandez, a day after she was stabbed to death in Chicago’s Chatham neighborhood. Family members were immediately brought to their knees the moment they returned to the spot where the little girl was attacked.
“She was happy,” said Eddimar’s stepfather, Pedro Izqueirdo, in Spanish. “She had dreams, to be big.”
Eddimar was out with her older sister Saturday morning when Chicago police say 48-year-old Shavon Gayden stabbed her in the back multiple times. The 7-year-old died at the hospital.
Security video shows bystanders rushing in, helping to detain Gayden until police arrived.
At a community vigil Sunday, Alderwoman Michelle Harris of the 8th Ward said Gayden had allegedly gotten into an altercation with staff at a nearby wireless store before allegedly attacking and killing Eddimar.
Police say Gayden is facing a first-degree murder charge.
“You send your baby out. It’s a beautiful Saturday morning, and then, they don’t come back home,” Harris said.
Eddimar’s family remembers her as a bright little girl who loved to draw, play with her siblings and wait by the window for her parents to come home from work. Her mother, Estefany Hernandez, is calling for justice.
“My daughter’s death should not be left like this,” Hernandez said in Spanish. “There must be justice for my little girl. She wasn’t bothering anyone.”
Gayden is scheduled to appear in court Monday.
Investigators have not released a motive in Eddimar’s murder.

title: What parents should know about GLP-1s for kids
text:
What parents should know about GLP-1s for kids
What parents should know about GLP-1s for kids
Drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy have transformed how we talk about weight loss.
So perhaps it’s not surprising that some doctors are prescribing the medications known as GLP-1s to address childhood obesity, too.
Related video above: How parents’ GLP-1 weight loss can affect kids
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention last year reported a 300% increase in the number of adolescents ages 12 to 17 prescribed obesity medications between 2020 and 2023, when the U.S. Food and Drug Administration expanded approval of these drugs for that age group. Thousands of children ages 8 to 11 have also been prescribed these drugs.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
Although the overall number is still small, the growing use of these relatively new medications in childhood raises numerous questions for parents and pediatricians.
Available research generally shows they can be safe and effective for some children for about a year. But researchers don’t yet have answers about their long-term effects.
Here are seven things parents should know about weight loss GLP-1s for children.
#1: Two weight loss GLP-1s are approved for children ages 12 and up
In 2020, the FDA approved the daily injection liraglutide with the brand-name Saxenda as weight loss medications for children ages 12 and older. Two years later, it did the same for the once-weekly injection semaglutide known as Wegovy.
As GLP-1s, both drugs act on hormone receptors throughout the body by mimicking glucagon-like peptide-1, a hormone produced after eating. The drugs bind to the body’s GLP-1 receptors, a process that helps regulate blood sugar and reduce appetite.
In 2023, 0.5% of adolescents with obesity ages 12 to 17 received obesity medication prescriptions including GLP-1s.
Some doctors have prescribed GLP-1s to children under 12 “off label”, meaning the drug isn’t approved and labeled by the FDA for people their ages.
The number of 8- to 11-year-olds taking drugs such as Saxenda and Wegovy was 310 times higher in June 2026 than June 2019, new data shows. In that time, 20,282 children ages 8 to 11 had been prescribed GLP-1s, according to a study published in Pediatrics.
#2: Doctors have clinical guidance for prescribing weight loss drugs to children
Since 2023, the American Academy of Pediatrics’ clinical guidelines have said doctors can consider GLP-1s as one treatment for children diagnosed with obesity.
The group recommends intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment as the most evidence-backed way to manage obesity. That could translate to 26 hours or more of face-to-face family nutrition and physical activity counseling over three to 12 months. Such treatment, however, isn’t widely available, and its demanding schedule may be impractical for people who work or go to school.
GLP-1s show promise “for children and adolescents who require an additional treatment option to manage their obesity,” the guidelines say. These drugs might be best for older children, kids with immediate and life-threatening comorbidities, and those with more severe obesity defined by a person’s body-mass-index. (BMI use is often criticized).
In certain cases, the academy’s guidelines leave room for prescribing weight loss drugs to children as young as 8.
Dr. Rebecka Peebles, vice president of adolescent medicine at Monte Nido, an organization that works to end eating disorders, said the guidelines affected how pediatricians’ prescribe GLP-1s.
“It is definitely being done more and more,” she said.
#3: There is no long-term data for weight loss GLP-1 use in children
There’s a lot scientists still don’t know about weight loss GLP-1s for children.
The main reason: limited data. A 2025 JAMA Pediatrics review found 18 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1s for people under 18 years old. Those clinical trials were for GLP-1s broadly, whether they were prescribed for weight loss, diabetes treatment or some other reason.
Of 18 trials, nine included fewer than 50 patients.
“The evidence base is meaningful but still shorter-term than we would ideally like for a chronic disease that often begins in childhood,” said Dr. Fatima Cody Stanford, a Harvard Medical School obesity medicine expert and a pediatrics professor.
That’s especially true for children under 12 because available research doesn’t answer all the long-term questions about growth, puberty, bone health, nutritional status, durability and outcomes.
There is more data on GLP-1s for diabetes, but that’s at smaller doses than what is used for weight loss.
And some research raises additional questions. A 2024 study of 82 kids ages 6 to 12, for example, found that after a year on liraglutide with lifestyle changes, children’s BMIs dropped more than they did with placebos and lifestyle changes.
Doctors have concerns about reducing a children’s body-mass index at a time when it should be increasing as they grow.
#4: Taking weight-loss GLP-1 medications is typically a long-term strategy
For adults, weight loss appears to last only as long as you are on the drugs, and people who stop the medication typically regain much of the weight they lost.
The same is generally true for children.
“They’re meant to be medicines you’re on for a very long time, if not forever, so making that decision is a big decision,” Peebles said.
Once adolescents stopped taking liraglutide for weight loss, research showed they regained weight, Stanford said.
#5: Insurance won’t always cover weight-loss GLP-1s
These medications are expensive even with discounts, so it might not be possible to pay for them without insurance footing the bill. Insurance coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss is inconsistent. Coverage can vary by state or even month and insurers often deny off-label prescriptions.
Some private insurance plans and state Medicaid programs cover pediatric weight loss GLP-1s, but typically with prior authorization after doctors document obesity-related complications and patients participate in lifestyle treatments, Stanford said.
#6: Weight loss GLP-1s come with side effects and risks, including malnutrition.
When taking GLP-1s, most children in studies reported uncomfortable or unpleasant gastrointestinal effects. Semaglutide and liraglutide list common side effects including nausea, diarrhea, constipation and vomiting.
Some rare side effects are also linked to GLP-1 medications, including pancreatic inflammation, acute kidney damage and gallbladder issues.
Children are at risk of getting malnourished when taking GLP-1s if they lose too much weight, Peebles said.
Children losing 10% of their body weight in six months is considered a warning sign of severe malnutrition, she said. But when physicians prescribe weight loss GLP-1s for a child, they are often hoping that child loses more than 10% of their body weight — sometimes even quicker than six months.
“Those things collide,” Peebles said. “When do we worry about malnutrition and what labs do we need to follow?”
A September 2026 study found that nearly 17% of children ages 10 to 17 who started a GLP-1 medication were diagnosed with at least one nutritional deficiency or deficiency-related complication within one year. The most common deficiencies in order of frequency were vitamin D, nutritional anemia and iron-deficiency anemia.
#7: Before weight loss GLP-1s, a child’s eating disorder risk should be evaluated
Doctors prescribing weight loss GLP-1s should screen for eating disorders or factors that might make someone more vulnerable to developing an eating disorder, Peebles said.
People vulnerable to developing eating disorders don’t do well with weight suppression, which is the difference between a person’s current weight and the most they’ve ever weighed.
She advised parents of children on GLP-1s to watch unusual behaviors, such as their child skipping meals and snacks, constantly pacing or exercising and becoming really rigid about mealtimes or weighing themselves.
“Parents are better at noticing these things than doctors sometimes,” she said. “They know their kids.”
Children taking GLP-1s should still be able to eat three meals a day and a snack or two, Peebles said. They should be able to keep up with their sports and activities, which means they shouldn’t be eating fewer than 2,000 calories a day, and even more if they’re very active.
PolitiFact Staff Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this report.

title: Trump tried to make an ally out of fishermen. Some have started to turn on him
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — John Evich, a commercial fisherman in Washington and Alaska, has voted for President Donald Trump three times, viewing him as someone who would fight for his industry.
But these days, Evich is weary of the high cost of doing business at sea, with fuel prices rising and trade hostilities with Canada jeopardizing markets for the crabs that he pulls off the ocean floor.
“If somebody came along that was going to do a better job, I would vote for them in a heartbeat,” he said.
Evich’s sentiment, echoed throughout the U.S. seafood industry, is another piece of a political puzzle that is working against Trump in the midterm elections. Dissatisfaction among commercial fishermen could cause collateral damage for Republicans in competitive races in Washington, Alaska and Maine.
“Having those costs be so much higher this year has really undermined the viability of some of our fisheries,” Alaska fisherman Linda Behnken said.
Trump sought to make an ally out of fishermen during his first term with expanded fishing territory, aggressive trade moves and cutting down regulations on the water. He did so again after his second election.
But one of Trump’s government cutback efforts, cuts to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which regulates fisheries, has left the agency slower to respond to the industry’s needs, fishermen said. Staff cutbacks also resulted in the agency reducing weather balloons used to gather data fishermen rely on.
Fuel costs have also crept up during the war with Iran, pushing diesel fuel into the $6-per-gallon range when it was less than $4 per gallon a year ago — a major burden for a diesel-dependent industry. And the trade war with Canada has complicated the American seafood industry’s relationship with a country it has long been interconnected with, fishermen said.
The Trump administration has continued trying to win the hearts of fishermen with industry-friendly moves, including an early September promise to reduce more regulatory burdens in response to a 2025 executive order. And some of the industry’s key states, such as Alaska, Washington and Maine, are important to Trump politically this year because of competitive House and Senate races. But support on the water could be waning.
“I’m for whatever has to happen for the greater good in the long run for my family and my country,” Evich said.
Trump has cozied up to the fishing industry for years
Trump has positioned himself as a pro-fishing president since his first term, when one of his major moves to impact the fishing industry was the rollback of Obama-era fishing restrictions for Northeast Canyons and Seamounts National Monument off the New England coast. Biden later restored the protections, and then Trump removed them again.
The fishing industry is potentially a natural ally for Trump. A 2026 NOAA survey of commercial fishing crews found that 70% thought fishing rules were too restrictive, and Trump has fashioned himself as an enemy of bureaucracy and red tape.
But in recent months, Trump has brought disruption to the fishing industry in a time when it can ill afford it, said John Sackton, founder of SeafoodNews.com and a longtime industry analyst. He said he sees an industry that is eager to “turn the page” on the Trump administration.
“Now what’s happened is that there has been this unbelievable wave of disruption from everything — targeting NOAA and fisheries, science and even weather reporting that people rely on,” said Sackton, who also cited tariffs and the rising cost of doing business as problems Trump brought to the industry.
Fuel costs and tariffs are huge concerns for fishermen
The high price of fuel is “one of the most immediate pressures on us as commercial fishermen,” said Bonnie Brady, executive director of the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association in New York.
Nearly all of the U.S.’s commercial fishing fleet uses marine diesel fuel, which makes soaring fuel costs a burden they can’t avoid. Fuel prices are so high right now that fishermen sometimes can’t afford to leave the dock at all, she said.
“Actual dockside marine-fuel prices vary, but the magnitude of the increase is undeniable. It determines whether a trip is economically viable, what the crew earns and whether necessary vessel maintenance can be performed,” Brady said.
In Rhode Island, fisherman Chris Brown, who targets species such as fluke and squid out of Point Judith, puts it more bluntly.
“It’s huge. It’s crazy. Thank you, Donald Trump,” he said sarcastically.
Trump’s trade war with Canada is a more complicated matter because Canada exempted U.S. fish and seafood products from its counter-tariffs that followed the U.S. placing tariffs on Canadian goods. Prior to the exemption, Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, said U.S. lobstermen risked becoming “collateral damage in a broader trade dispute.”
But unease among fishermen remains, in part because Canada is the U.S.’s largest seafood trading partner. The U.S. also relies on Canada for seafood processing and manufacturing of fishing gear. For some species, such as lobster and salmon, American and Canadian fishermen fish very close to each other or even in the same waters.
A trade war with such a key partner could have negative consequences for the fishing industry, said Steve Train, a lobster fisherman from Long Island, Maine, who described himself as a “right-leaning centrist” who has voted Republican more than Democrat.
“I get the standing up to a bully concept, but too many people will be caught in the middle of this,” Train said. “Both sides need to reconsider these tariffs, and they need to reconsider soon.”
Cuts to NOAA are troubling to fishermen
NOAA Fisheries, the arm of NOAA tasked with overseeing commercial fishing, is facing a budget cut of more than 40% in the fiscal 2027 budget proposal. That would result in cuts to science programs, fisheries management and data collection.
Those cutbacks trickle down to the fishermen and result in a lack of fishing opportunities, Sackton said. Some in the fishery also have the impression NOAA is too understaffed to regulate fisheries in a timely fashion, he said.
In Sitka, Alaska, Behnken said the Trump administration’s cutbacks at NOAA have made it more difficult for her and others who rely on the agency. She said she has a lot of empathy for the workers left at the agency, who she said are “doing the work of three people, particularly at the weather service,” but it is still frustrating for fishermen.
“It’s hard to retain good people when their future at the organization is that uncertain,” said Behnken, who is executive director of the Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association.

title: Why this law could leave adult children paying parents’ medical debt
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Would you ever pay a bill that wasn’t yours? Depending on which state you live in, you could be forced to pay for your parents’ debts.
It’s called filial responsibility, and you could be legally liable for unpaid bills. The laws vary state to state and historically are rarely enforced, but legal experts are concerned that could change.
Sarah Daro had no contact with her father for nearly two decades because of his addiction to drugs. When he died a few years ago, she received a call from a cremation business informing her that she was responsible for his burial.
“They said it was our responsibility to bury him. And that if we had the means, we had to pay for the burial,” Daro said.
She was told that if she refused to pay, she could face jail time or a fine. Daro, who was 28 and pregnant at the time, opted to pay the $3,000 fee.
What is filial responsibility
California, where Daro’s father died, has a filial responsibility law. The law makes adult children responsible for the care and support of their parents if the parents cannot care for themselves.
Nearly half of U.S. states have a version of the law. In Indiana, South Dakota and Louisiana, an adult child could have to pay for a parent’s food, shelter and medication. Seven states, including Kentucky, Massachusetts and Virginia, threaten jail or prison time if an adult child doesn’t pay.
Almost all of the states with the law could require financially stable adult children to support an indigent parent medically, which could include nursing home care and hospital bills.
Carla Sigler is an estate planning attorney in Louisiana, which has filial responsibility.
“Most people today are floored when they find out that they as adult children still have a responsibility to honor, respect and even provide for their parents,” Sigler said.
Sigler said the laws date back more than 100 years, to a time before Medicaid existed.
“Before you had Medicaid, you had state governments that were going broke trying to take care of these needy, aging people,” she said. “So these laws were originally enacted so nobody had to be a burden to the state budget, basically.”
Sigler said the need for filial responsibility dropped once Medicaid, Medicare and Social Security were in place, but many states kept the laws on the books.
Medicaid cuts raise concern
Attorneys say the laws have rarely been enforced for decades, but Sigler said that could change because of Medicaid cuts.
The federal government is set to cut $1 trillion from Medicaid spending by 2034 as part of the Big Beautiful Bill. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office projects millions of people will lose coverage.
If a parent is on Medicaid while in a facility, Sigler warns that adult children will need to worry about filial responsibility laws.
“It’s the gap periods people need to worry about. Before I get the Medicaid coverage, and what if it stops,” Sigler said. “When there’s no coverage, who’s gonna pay? If it’s not Medicaid, it could be you.”
Eric Carlson, with the group Justice in Aging, said the number of filial responsibility cases nationwide is currently in the “low double digits” per year. Carlson said there is no way of knowing how often the law is used to recoup money, and he suspects cases are more common than they appear because most don’t go to trial or become public.
When adult children are pursued for unpaid medical bills, Carlson said the amount could cost thousands of dollars.
A North Dakota man had to pay over $100,000 after a court ruling. And in Pennsylvania, one man paid $93,000 while another woman was sued for $300,000 — all for their parents’ unpaid nursing home bills.
Efforts to repeal the law
Pennsylvania is known for enforcing filial responsibility. State Rep. Tarik Khan (D-Philadelphia) has worked on legislation to repeal it.
Khan thinks it’s wrong for adult children to pay a debt that isn’t theirs. Pennsylvania lawmakers have made at least six other attempts to repeal or reform filial responsibility. All of them failed.
“You know corporations hate being told what to do,” Khan said. “And then you are leaving fewer options for these hospitals and nursing homes to get what they need. Now, I think we all agree in Pennsylvania that should not mean that they should be able to go after families and sue families and sick collection agencies on families.”
Idaho, Montana, Utah and Iowa have repealed filial responsibility laws, but Sigler said that’s not the norm.
“The reason you haven’t seen them repealed is because there’s lobbyists on the other side that are saying, don’t repeal that,” she said. “If you cut Medicaid, how am I gonna pay for this facility? Where’s my source of funding? They want those laws to stay on the books.”
The American Health Care Association and National Center for Assisted Living, advocacy groups for skilled nursing and assisted living facilities, said they could not comment because it is a “state-by-state issue.”
What to do if you’re contacted
Daro lives in Nevada, another filial responsibility state. She feels ready to handle the issue if it comes up again.
“I think it’s so scary because most people don’t know,” Daro said, describing her reaction to learning about filial responsibility laws. “This happened to me, it could happen to anybody.”
Those interviewed agreed nursing homes and hospitals should get paid for their services, but they said the burden should not fall to a patient’s child.
Sigler recommends contacting an attorney immediately if you receive a demand for payment of a parent’s bill. The Pennsylvania woman sued for $300,000 ended up not having to pay after her attorneys proved she didn’t have the means to do so.
If you don’t live in a filial responsibility state but your parents do, and you are sued for their bills, Sigler said to get a lawyer immediately. You may not be subject to another state’s laws, but legal guidance can help navigate the issue.
If you live in a filial responsibility state and want the law repealed, you can contact your state legislators.

title: Friends, family and fall foliage: UMaine hosts Family and Friends Weekend
text:
In Maine, there are few months more pleasing than October. Mild weather, a cool breeze and the famed foliage attract ardent peepers from all over the country. Walking through campus in the midst of fall, it’s easy to idealize the momentary bliss and forget about the impending gloom of winter. When the sun shines brilliantly, but the air is still a perfect seventy degrees, the leaves shake loose in a gentle gust and scatter impressions of crisp reds and oranges across the green grass. It is no coincidence that the University of Maine Family and Friends Weekend occurs during this time of heightened seasonal bliss.
If you were to spend some time walking around campus this past weekend, you likely would have seen clusters of families aimlessly strolling about as they moved between a variety of university-organized events. Looking around, you could see freshmen eagerly pointing out their dorm building to their parents and seniors begrudgingly guiding their family down the same path for the fourth time in four years. There is a sentimental joviality in observing these families, as parents get to experience the campus that is meant to carry their child through adolescence, and students get a break from classes to be reminded of home.
This weekend is an opportunity for the UMaine administration and faculty to put their best foot forward in the presence of the wallets which keep the gears turning. From the artisan fair in the New Balance Recreation Center to the fermentation expo at the Innovative Media Research and Commercialization Center (IMRC), the university even went as far as setting up a carnival on the mall. Parents roamed about, buying tacos and locally made ice cream from the food trucks. Younger siblings played laser tag, and an adventurous few families took a ride on the horse-drawn carriage.
I had the pleasure to interview a few of these families to hear about what it is that makes this weekend worth five-hour commutes and hotel room fees. I spoke with one family who had just left the taco stand, coming all the way from Missouri for this weekend, and they had this to say about visiting their UMaine student:
“It was good to get a hug and see him in person and know when he tells me he’s doing fine, he really is. Yeah, he’s doing okay. And it’s a beautiful time of year to be here,” said a parent.
After the fermentation expo, I interviewed fourth-year student Frances Underwood and her mother Melissa Pattavina, who drove up from Rhode Island and had a lot to say about the impact of this weekend.
“You know I always like getting to see your campus, and I like you taking us on a tour, so I sort of feel what your day-to-day life is like. It’s also nice to see your living situation and feel good that you are in a safe and happy environment,” said Pattavina. “And then I had a ton of fun doing the dying stuff today, learning more about the fermentation and understanding what it is that we see every time we open our refrigerator door and we’re wondering if something is going to come to life in there. I guess it is alive, but dying.”
Underwood also felt a similar sense of importance regarding this trip.
“I’m so happy that these two people, who are my family, came to see me this weekend. No, seriously, like I’ve been looking forward to this. I’ve been texting them for like two weeks straight, being like, When are you coming? I’m really excited,” said Underwood.
Whether you’ve had the nuclear experience with the whole family this past weekend or, like me, you’ve merely watched vicariously from the shadows and asked other people’s parents about their love for their children, Family and Friends Weekend is a very special time on campus.

title: Immigrants contribute $15B impact to Maine economy, report finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A report commissioned by the Maine Office of New Americans quantifies immigrants’ contributions to the state’s economy while warning that federal immigration enforcement could leave employers shorthanded in critical sectors.
In total, foreign-born workers generated about $2.25 billion in personal income and $177 million in state income tax revenue from 2020 to 2024, the report found. Their employment also supported nearly 74,000 jobs and nearly $15 billion in economic output.
The 26-page report, which combines U.S. Census American Community Survey data with economic modeling, is the first to quantify immigrants’ direct contributions to Maine’s workforce and their broader economic impact.
“We commissioned this report to establish a common set of facts about the vital contributions of immigrants to our economy,” said Julia Trujillo Luengo, director of the Maine Office of New Americans.
“This analysis supports what many of us already know – immigrants are key to some of our most iconic industries, from blueberry processing to lobstering and tourism. Their economic impact reaches well beyond the jobs they hold,” she added.
Cautionary tale
The report notes that federal immigration enforcement may cause employers to lose workers abruptly, with little opportunity to recruit and retrain replacements.
Without examining specific enforcement actions or predicting future enforcement activity, the report estimates a potential loss of 840 to 7,050 workers from three possible scenarios, concentrated in health care, manufacturing, construction, personal services and agriculture.
Including broader economic effects, the impact grows to roughly 1,800 to 15,100 jobs statewide and $395 million to $3.3 billion in lost annual economic output, researchers found.

title: Are self-driving cars legal for public use in Maine?
text:
No.
Maine has not enacted legislation allowing for broad use of autonomous vehicles on public roads, though it has established a regulatory framework authorizing their use in approved pilot programs.
Staffing and recruiting firm Elevation Proving Grounds, using data from the National Conference of State Legislatures, reported in July that autonomous driving was fully legal in 21 states.
Another 11 states only allowed testing or limited pilot programs, the firm found, while a few others have imposed explicit safety restrictions.
In 2018, then-Gov. Paul LePage signed an executive order to form an advisory committee on “highly automated vehicles.” The Maine Legislature also passed a resolve to allow their testing, demonstration and deployment. The state has since established rules for pilot program evaluation and approval.
In 2019, Maine lawmakers rejected broader legislation that would have established rules for registering autonomous vehicles, licensing operators and assigning liability; the bill died in committee.

title: Russia reports a worker at a Siberian plague institute got pneumonia from an unknown cause and died
text:
(AP) - Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an “unknown” cause. Local state TV said the woman died last week.
Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
The woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, southeastern Siberia. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported Monday that she died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk.
The hospital has been placed under quarantine, Mayor Maxim Modin said Friday, no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted carrying out routine tests. The hospital’s outpatient clinic kept operating as usual, he said.
Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk and met with Gov. Igor Kobzev and other officials on Friday.
Kobzev said everyone who came into contact with the woman is under medical supervision. He didn’t identify the infection and called it a suspected case of “a particularly dangerous infection.”
Rospotrebnadzor was implementing “a full range of anti-epidemic measures,” he added.
Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday the woman was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” or origin, and said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.”
The agency also said it didn’t uncover any incidents at the institute “involving pathogenic microorganisms.”
Two people who were in contact with the woman tested positive for a virus that causes a common cold and two others for COVID-19, the agency said, adding that others who were tested were all negative.
Trump says he’s concerned about the reports
In Washington, President Donald Trump said he was watching the situation with concern and said the United States would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation.
“It’s a rough disease. You know, that’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “Even with great advancement, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well anymore.”
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday he doesn’t think there is cause for alarm, but the U.S. is watching the case closely, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.
Independent local news outlet Lyudi Baikala quoted sources it did not identify as saying the 28-year-old lab technician died from pneumonic plague and that several Irkutsk hospitals were placed under quarantine.
Asked Monday to comment on the case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumors or speculation.”
Rospotrebnadzor did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov required staff to wear masks as a precaution, its director Artyom Fominykh said Saturday on Telegram, calling for calm and adding: “Better be safe than sorry.”
The World Health Organization describes pneumonic plague as a less common but severe form of plague — a disease caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals and their fleas.
“In the event of a potential laboratory exposure, it would be normal to identify individuals who might have been exposed and to monitor them according to the assessed level of risk,” said Dr. Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology at the Imperial College London.
The scale of any monitoring program would depend on “the circumstances of the exposure and the number of people potentially affected,” Gibani said in a written comment.
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia,” although because of modern living conditions and antibiotics, “its potential is therefore limited.”

title: The Maine Marathon was not my day, but it wasn’t a loss
text:
This is not the story I was planning to write.
When I pitched this series to Sports Editor Bill Stewart, my goal was take readers through my training and then tell the triumphant story of my race at the Maine Marathon. I would write about all the miles I crushed during the race, fighting through the pain to get to the finish line, where I would ring the PR bell and then finally, after 12 years of trying, erase my goal time of 3:47 off the chalkboard that hangs in my apartment.
Unfortunately, I don’t get to tell that story.
I ran my sixth marathon Sunday morning and the day did not go as planned. I missed every one of my time goals, nearly dropped out multiple times, and was left wondering if I ever want to do this again.
I won’t bury the lead anymore than I already have: I finished the race in 4 hours, 13 minutes, 58 seconds. I missed my ‘A’ goal by 26 minutes, my ‘B’ goal by 23 minutes and my ‘C’ goal by nearly 14 minutes.
It was not the race I was hoping for, but there was way too much good to focus only on the bad.
It was a stellar day to run a marathon. It was right around 50 degrees when the race started, ideal weather for a marathon. I chatted up friends and hung out with folks from my run group until the race started, then I went my own way, to run my own race.
I was cruising between 8:45 and 9 minutes per mile for the first 6 miles, taking in all the signs and the ocean views, and shouting out friends and high-fiving my sister Melissa when I saw her just after mile 6. I stopped at the porta potty during mile 7 and choked down my second gel (I literally choked on it for a second, yuk), and picked the pace back up in mile 8.
The hills started at mile 10, but I was feeling good, keeping my effort relaxed, and dropped down to 8:36-8:43 per mile until the half marathon. I crossed the half in 1:57, a little slower than 3:47 pace, but right on target to give it a good effort on the way back to Portland.
My race took a turn in the 17th mile while climbing the hill at Tuttle Road in Cumberland. My right knee, the one that always gives me problems during marathons, started to really hurt as I approached that hill. Every swing of that leg, every time my foot hit the ground, my knee sang in agony. Before I started to limp, I told myself it was OK to walk to the top of that hill, then get back on pace at the top.
I never did get back on pace. The final 10-plus miles of the marathon was a slog. A slow, painful slow. I jogged when I could and walked when I felt I needed to. I considered dropping out every time I saw a medical tent, but didn’t allow myself to quit. That’s one thing I can take pride in.
I was about 2.5 miles from the finish line when I looked at my watch and saw 3:47 flip to 3:48. I knew long before that I wasn’t hitting that goal, but it still hurt to see the number pass so far from the end.
I jogged the final three-tenths of a mile, determined not to walk across the finish line. I shook hands with my colleagues, waited in line for pizza that never came, then left with my sister and brother-in-law for a well deserved lunch at Wilson County Barbecue. I celebrated the day, not necessarily the race.
Ten months after signing up for this race and after 18 weeks of training, I’m ready for a bit of a break. I’m looking forward to running again, but not right away. I’m going to recover, reflect and decide what’s next.
What won’t be next is another marathon. I don’t know if I’ll ever put myself through that again, but it’s too soon after the race to say, “No way.” After all, seven years ago after running the Chicago Marathon, I said that was it, yet here we are.
If I ever do decide to try again, I’ll remember how much fun I had this summer putting in the work, and do everything I can so it doesn’t physically feel the way it did on Sunday.
That will be a story I want to tell.

title: Bangor golf fights thunder, lightning and hail to repeat as KVAC A champion
text:
ROCKPORT — After some key graduations a year ago, Chris Junkins wasn’t sure what type of season Bangor would have in 2026.
On Monday, the young Rams showed their potential.
Battling through hail, thunder and lightning, Bangor (160) repeated as Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference Class A champions, holding off Messalonskee (164) and Camden Hills (174) on the Par-34 front nine of Samoset Resort Golf Course.
“We lost a lot of seniors last year, so (this year) kind of felt like a rebuild after that,” said Junkins, Bangor’s head coach. “But as the year started and we started playing, you could see that our team was good, with some good young players who are helping us out.”
Junior Jacoby Harvey led the way for Bangor, shooting a 2-over 36, followed by junior Carter Catell (38) and freshman Mason Webb (42).
Play began at 3 p.m., but after only two holes, a quick but powerful hail storm hit the course, along with thunder and lightning. Each player left their golf balls on the course, hopped into their golf carts and headed back to the clubhouse.
Play resumed at 4:45 p.m., leaving players less than two hours to finish their round before dark. Playing quickly, the final group finished play at 6:30.
“The upperclassmen, we’ve been here before, but we were telling the younger players, ‘Stay patient, keep your head and don’t lose sight of what we’re looking for,'” Harvey said. “Every shot, each kid is dealing with the same thing. You just have to be mentally stronger than the other kids and we’ll do what we need to do.”
Junkins said the Rams’ experiences this season help them secure Monday’s win.
‘We were here Saturday and played two rounds on the front (nine),” Junkins said. “They were able to see the course twice. We played in wind at home. A week ago, we played in a lot of wind at Penobscot Valley (Country Club in Orono) for our pod championship. We played in the rain this year. I think all of that plays in the results at the end (of the year), learning different golf courses, giving them different opportunities to play and learn.”
Messalonskee had a strong outing from their No. 2 player, junior Greyson Dooley, who shot a 3-over 37. Junior Trent Bell shot 42, while senior Evan Hayes shot 43.
Freshman Ryan Irish (5-over 39) had the top score for Camden Hills, while senior Lila Dailey and junior Landon Reynolds each shot 45.
The postseason continues Tuesday with the KVAC Qualifier at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro. The Class A championships are scheduled for Friday, while the Class B and Class C championships will be on Saturday. All three rounds will be held at Natanis.
“That’s a big win over two big teams (today), that’s a big momentum swing,” Harvey said. “We’re not going to take (Tuesday) lightly, we’re going to try to set a new low (score), hopefully, and keep that momentum going into Friday and just do the same thing and maybe get a state championship.”

title: Vehicle fire causes significant backups on the Maine Turnpike on Monday
text:
Vehicle fire causes significant backups on the Maine Turnpike Monday afternoon
All lanes have since reopened
Vehicle fire causes significant backups on the Maine Turnpike Monday afternoon
All lanes have since reopened
A vehicle fire was causing significant traffic backups on the Maine Turnpike (Interstate 95) in Scarborough on Monday afternoon.
At 2:38 p.m., the Maine Turnpike Authority (MTA) said the left lane on the southbound side of I-95 was closed at mile 43 in Scarborough.
At 2:52 p.m., the MTA said all lanes were blocked. About 20 minutes later, one lane was open again.
Traffic was backing up significantly and drivers were urged to find another way around. Traffic was backing up onto I295 southbound as well.
All lanes reopened at about 3:40 p.m., but traffic was still backed up.
Shortly before 4:30 p.m., the MTA lifted the traffic alert associated with the vehicle fire.
It was not immediately clear if anyone was hurt or what caused the fire.

title: 'Def Comedy Jam' and 'In Living Color' actor-comedian dies at 57
text:
'Def Comedy Jam' and 'In Living Color' actor-comedian Reggie McFadden dies at 57
Actor and stand-up comedian Reggie McFadden, who got his break on HBO's Def Comedy Jam and worked on the Fox sketch series In Living Color, has died.
McFadden's sister told The Hollywood Reporter that the U.S. State Department notified the family that the comedian died in Tanzania, where he had been living for almost two decades.
His family told the media outlet that they do not know when he died or the cause.
He was 57 years old.
According to Forbes, McFadden performed stand-up on several TV shows, apart from Def Comedy Jam.
Shows included Late Night With Conan O'Brien, Late Show with David Letterman, Tough Crowd with Quinn, and Last Call with Carson Daly.
McFadden also played various characters in the fifth season of creator Keenan Ivory Wayans’ sketch comedy series In Living Color from 1993 to 1994.
USA Today said he also appeared in "Little Nicky," the Adam Sandler movie comedy, and played Officer Burt, a neighbor of Larry David's character, on HBO's "Curb Your Enthusiasm."
Born on Nov. 30, 1968, McFadden grew up in Brooklyn and decided to pursue comedy as a way to escape living in the projects, according to a bio posted online.

title: Saco unveils printed biannual city newsletter
text:
The city of Saco Communications Department is rolling out a new biannual newsletter that will be delivered to every mailbox in the city.
Saco Spotlight will feature information on local matters like leaf collection, winter parking bans, updates on infrastructure projects throughout the city and a career listings section.
It will also include a community event calendar that lists events three months in advance.
The first edition of Saco Spotlight, which is set to be delivered this week, also features a voter guide to help residents feel better informed ahead of the November election. Early voting for the election started Monday.
The purpose of Saco Spotlight, communications director Andrew Dickinson said, is simply to help residents stay informed about what’s happening in the city.
“As print publications have dwindled in Biddeford and Saco, some of our residents who aren’t as connected online are feeling like they don’t have access to what’s going on,” Dickinson said.
In the spring of 2025, the Maine Trust for Local News transitioned its southern Maine weekly newspapers — including the former Biddeford-Saco-OOB Courier — to digital-only products. Several other online publications cover the Biddeford-Saco area, including the Biddeford Buzz, Biddeford Gazette and Saco Bay News.
The spring 2027 newsletter will include a section on how the municipal budget process works, as well as other seasonal updates on things happening in the city.
“The idea of an informed community knowing how their government works has always been important to me,” Dickinson said. “While a lot of people are online, not everyone is.”
The newsletter is funded out of the city’s communications budget and has been a bit of a passion project for Dickinson, who has a background in journalism.
Over the next few months, the department will be monitoring the newsletter’s popularity and effectiveness with the intention of producing more than two issues a year. Dickinson also hopes some residents will eventually be open to the idea of an emailed newsletter.
“I’d love to see this grow in future years,” he said.
Saco Mayor Jodi MacPhail said last week that she applauds and praises the communications team for recognizing the community need for a printed newsletter and developing it.
“We understand that not everybody is on or has access to social media or pays for subscription service,” MacPhail said.
The newsletter is already making an impact on residents who aren’t as connected to the internet. Dickinson said a woman recently visited his office and told him how out of touch she feels without a printed, community-focused news source.
“I showed her a preview of the newsletter, and her eyes lit up,” Dickinson said. “That was really validating.”

title: Long-term care insurance: What it covers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Long-term care can get expensive fast, and long-term care insurance may help.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down how long-term care insurance works and what it pays for.
What long-term care insurance actually pays for
“Long-term care insurance is an insurance that pays for care,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “And what do I mean by care? Hands-on care. Bathing, dressing, going to the bathroom.”
The first step for anyone considering a policy is understanding the real cost of care, she said.
“The first thing I would suggest is, look at how much care costs. Look at your budget,” O’Rourke said.
When to buy — and why age matters
O’Rourke said there’s a window where buying in makes the most financial sense.
“You ideally would get it between 50 and 70 — 50 years old, 70 years old,” O’Rourke said. “The younger you are, the less you’re going to pay. If you’re a woman, you’re going to pay more than a guy. And the longer you wait, the higher the premium goes up.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said rising rates of chronic illness among younger adults are a factor in making the decision as well.
“Why are people in their 40s, 45, having these health issues?” Rogers said. “The state of health of the country and all of us right now is people are getting sicker at earlier ages, and we know it’s metabolic disease and metabolic disorders ... people are having insulin resistance and that’s affecting a lot of the different diseases that are showing up early. So, a lot of people who have these medical conditions are now under the age of 50. So they have to make a decision, do I pay a little bit more longer to get what I need or do I wait ‘til later and pay more.”
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck agreed that paying in earlier can pay off.
“If you can budget for it earlier and you can get it and you can pay into it longer, your benefit will end up being — there’ll be more in the account,” Cradduck said.
Understanding the elimination period
O’Rourke explained that most policies include a waiting period before benefits kick in.
“You can have an elimination period of 30 days, 60 days, 90 days, no days,” O’Rourke said. “Elimination period is, you have to pay for the care over a period of time to prove that you’re going to need it long term. Then after you’ve proved that you need that care ... you can start the clock and start putting in the claims to get paid for the care that you’re paying for.”
Cradduck said one benefit kicks in once a claim is approved.
“The beauty once you invoke the policy and once you get it started, you don’t have to pay the premium any longer,” Cradduck said.
Hybrid policies and reading the fine print
Cradduck said hybrid long-term care policies are among her preferred options because they offer more flexibility.
“There are hybrid models, and those are the ones that I really like, because if you don’t use it, then it can go into a life insurance,” Cradduck said. “Some of them are use-it-or-lose-it policies.”
Cradduck said no two policies are alike, so find out what you have.
“I’ve billed this stuff for years. I’ve seen all kinds of companies and different policies, and I’ve never seen two that are the same, never. So find out what you have, always,” Cradduck said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose urges planning in advance.
“Planning creates options. If you don’t plan in advance, you’re going to lose options. You’re going to lose having a choice, and maybe lose out on all the money that you’ve paid in,” Ambrose said.
Ambrose recommended policyholders review their paperwork with a professional.
“Pull that policy out right now and get with a local professional that can help explain exactly what you have,” she said.
How benefits are paid out
O’Rourke said policies typically set a maximum lifetime benefit and a daily payout cap.
“You have a maximum lifetime benefit and that might be unlimited. It might be a certain amount — $200,000, $300,000. And then they pay by the day,” O’Rourke said.
Cradduck described two clients with very different outcomes.
“I had one gentleman who truly needed full-time care. His policy would only pay $200 a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year,” Cradduck said. “And then I had a gentleman who was 24/7 care, 168 hours a week. So we’re talking almost $30 grand a month, and for four years, $360,000 a year. Now, the policy didn’t cover every penny, but it covered over $200,000 a year. And he could do that for 10 more years and not maximize out.”
Cradduck said the lesson is about flexibility, not guaranteed coverage.
“What people have to realize is you’re not buying care here. You’re buying the choices for the care that you’re going to need,” she said.
O’Rourke said that decision should start with a budget and a family health history.
“You have to look at, what is your budget. Do you have the money to do it? Do you have enough liquid income to be able to afford it?” O’Rourke said. “If you do have the money to afford it, do you have a family history of long-term chronic diseases — like is there Parkinson’s or Alzheimer’s or something that you’re maybe at a higher risk for needing long-term care?”
Resources
Key takeaways
- Care can be expensive — long-term care insurance may help cover some of the cost.
- Know caps and limits — know your policy, waiting periods and daily caps to understand what you will get.
- Budget for long-term premiums — check your budget to see if it’s something that you can afford and sustain.

title: Maine transportation service to reduce services for low-income riders due to funding cut
text:
Maine transportation service to cut offers for low-income riders due to funding cut
The Regional Transportation Program (RTP), a service based in Westbrook that provides services to people throughout Cumberland County, says the Maine Department of Health and Human Services has cut its 2027 funding for low-income transportation in half.
RTP says its funding from the state went from $296,220 in 2026 to $147,739 in 2027. RTP says that money pays directly for rides, especially for income-eligible residents throughout Cumberland County who have no other means of transportation.
RTP says it was already underfunded and its latest reduction is the largest of any transit provider in the state.
In 2025–2026, RTP provided more than 14,000 low-income trips under this program.
"This isn't a case of the state having less money for low-income transportation. It's a decision to take half of Cumberland County's share based on census numbers that are six years old," said Don Libby, Executive Director of RTP. "Our funding hadn't increased in over a decade. We were already underfunded, and now we are severely underfunded. That means roughly 7,000 fewer rides next year for people who can least afford to lose them. What is especially troubling is that no one from OCFS came to us to talk about what this would mean for our riders before the decision was made."
RTP says its allocation of $296,220 had not changed in more than ten years, while the costs of drivers, fuel, vehicles, and insurance continued to rise. At $147,739, program officials say they are now severely underfunded.
Libby said RTP expected to make several changes to low-income transportation services starting on Jan. 1, 2027. Those changes include reducing the number of shopper shuttles, capping the number of rides available for medical appointments, capping the number of low-income rides each person can get, and reducing service hours.
Libby said RTP is looking at options to reduce the impact on riders.
On Monday afternoon, Maine DHHS provided a response to Maine's Total Coverage.
"For efficiency and effectiveness, Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services is in the process of restructuring the Social Services Block Grant (SSBG) and Community Services Block Grant (CSBG) into one contract to align all low- income programming administered by Maine DHHS’ Office of Child and Family Services’ (OCFS) and funded by U.S. Administration for Children and Families (ACF)," the statement said.
"These changes utilize a poverty-based formula used to distribute SSBG grant dollars more equitably across the low-income transportation network, of which RTP has been a part. This formula is used in poverty-based programming in Maine and across the country and is based on published federal poverty data which looks at the percentage of the county population living under 150% federal poverty level (FPL). The Department uses the U.S. census data updated every 10 years and compared that with more recently published NIH data. The Department has, historically, followed this process as part of the basis for administering the Community Services Block Grant (CSBG) as well."

title: How hazard trees stand in the way of wildfire cleanup
text:
ROWENA Ore. (InvestigateTV) - In the blink of an eye lives can be upended by a natural disaster, and recovering from one can last long after the danger is gone.
In June 2025, a wildfire tore through the community of Rowena, Oregon. It forced 8,000 people to evacuate and destroyed more than 56 homes.
Many residents remain unable to rebuild. The fire tore through the community on June 11, leaving behind not just loss, but a new and unexpected barrier to recovery.
What didn’t burn is now what’s holding people back.
Charred trees, weakened and unstable, still stand across properties throughout the community. Known as hazard trees, they are dangerous enough to halt any rebuilding efforts. Until they are removed, construction cannot begin.
For many residents, the obstacle is not a lack of will or resources to rebuild, but the remnants of the fire itself.
Clearing the first path forward
On property after property, volunteers are stepping in to help.
Teams from Team Rubicon, a veteran-led disaster response organization, are working to remove trees and clear debris at no cost to homeowners. It is the kind of work that must happen before anything else can.
“What they’re doing is they’re actually giving us hope,” said Shane Wolfe, who helped start a nonprofit supporting the Rowena community after his father lost his home in the fire.
That hope comes in a place still grappling with trauma.
“We’re still in trauma,” Wolfe said. “Our entire lives changed, everything changed for people living here. And then also all of their families, overnight, and we’re just still in the recovery, the disaster.”
Just down the road, Wylesha Wilcox walks through what remains of her property, still taking in the scale of what was lost.
“We used to have a triplex here. So we had a mixture of like cabins and manufactured homes here. And then as you keep going, we lost 10 properties,” Wilcox said.
She plans to rebuild, but for now, the trees remain in the way.
“Until these come down, we can’t start anything,” Wilcox said.
The danger left behind
Fire-damaged trees can appear intact but are often structurally compromised, capable of falling without warning. Removing them requires skill, equipment, and money that many property owners simply do not have.
That is where volunteers step in.
Krystal Samsel, a Navy veteran and teacher, drove six hours from Washington to spend her spring break helping in Rowena.
“I live by the motto of whatever’s needed,” Samsel said. “It is great to see humanity and in the worst times humanity comes together and it’s so good. It’s so good to be part of that.”
Leading the effort on the ground is Joe Goodenough, a saw boss responsible for training and coordinating volunteer sawyers. Like many in the group, he traveled a long distance to be there. He lives in Alaska, where he drives trucks on ice roads and fights forest fires.
But Rowena is not just another deployment.
“I grew up here. I was born in The Dalles. Rowena, specifically where we’re sitting. My grandfather had a house. He lived in this neighborhood that we’re sitting in for about 45 years,” Goodenough said.
Among the trees he has helped remove was an old maple with branches that he used to swing from as a kid.
“It’s awful to come back under these circumstances. But it’s neat to be able to be a part of that whole building process. Because I know these people and they know me,” he said.
A mission that hits close to home
Goodenough has spent about a decade deploying with Team Rubicon to disaster zones across the country. The work has shown him the full scope of what fire can erase.
“Every single thing that a human being put on that site is lost,” he said. “It would be easier to rebuild on a piece of dirt out in the forest than it would at a site where a home once stood.”
But in Rowena, the work carries a different weight.
“I’ve been doing this a long time with TR and it’s always somebody else’s world, right? It’s always, you know, we’re the folks coming in to instill hope. But like, we’re instilling hope for me,” he said. “These guys are bringing my family peace, directly, you know. It’s freakin’ incredible thing to be a part of that.”
Recovery, one tree at a time
As volunteers continue their work, the community is slowly finding its footing. Progress comes incrementally, measured not in rebuilt homes yet, but in cleared lots and safer ground.
At the same time, another fire season looms.
With record low snowpack in the mountains, anxiety is building even as recovery continues. Residents are trying to prepare for what may come next while still processing what happened last summer.
For now, the work continues, one tree at a time, each one bringing the possibility of rebuilding a little closer.

title: Police say man killed wife, took children and forced family member to drive to another state at gunpoint
text:
WINFIELD, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - A man was arrested after allegedly killing his wife, taking two children and forcing a family member to drive to another state at gunpoint.
According to the Winfield Police Department, officers responded to a call about a possible homicide at 4:34 a.m. Saturday.
The suspect contacted a sheriff’s office in North Carolina and told them he had shot and killed his wife. The sheriff’s office then contacted the Winfield Police Department.
Police said when they arrived at the home, they found a woman who had been shot and killed lying in the kitchen.
After the alleged shooting, the suspect left the home with two children and held another family member at gunpoint. The family member was forced to drive to North Carolina.
The family member was able to escape and provided investigators with detailed information about the alleged shooting.
The suspect is in custody and the two children and family member are safe, according to police.
The identities of the man and his wife have not been released.

title: Maine Football fires offensive coordinator midseason
Are self-driving cars legal for public use in Maine?
text:
No.
Maine has not enacted legislation allowing for broad use of autonomous vehicles on public roads, though it has established a regulatory framework authorizing their use in approved pilot programs.
Staffing and recruiting firm Elevation Proving Grounds, using data from the National Conference of State Legislatures, reported in July that autonomous driving was fully legal in 21 states.
Another 11 states only allowed testing or limited pilot programs, the firm found, while a few others have imposed explicit safety restrictions.
In 2018, then-Gov. Paul LePage signed an executive order to form an advisory committee on “highly automated vehicles.” The Maine Legislature also passed a resolve to allow their testing, demonstration and deployment. The state has since established rules for pilot program evaluation and approval.
In 2019, Maine lawmakers rejected broader legislation that would have established rules for registering autonomous vehicles, licensing operators and assigning liability; the bill died in committee.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: Readfield vehicle explosion prompts investigation
text:
A group of individuals using Tannerite to blow up a vehicle in Readfield last week prompted an investigation from the Office of State Fire Marshall and may result in criminal charges.
The Readfield Fire Department responded to multiple reports of an explosion Sept. 27 at 846 Main St., the location of Hatch Auto Repair, according to a release from the Office of State Fire Marshall. Investigators determined the vehicle explosion was caused by several people shooting at Tannerite placed in the car.
Tannerite is an explosive often used in reactive targets for firearm practice. State law allows the use of up to 5 pounds of Tannerite for sport and target shooting only. It may not be used to explode anything other than the container in which it is mixed.
The investigation is ongoing, but fire marshal investigators are working with the Kennebec County District Attorney’s Office to determine whether charges will be brought,the release states.

title: 1 CMMC nurse reinstated after September firings at Lewiston hospital
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
One Central Maine Medical Center nurse will return to work this week after being fired in mid-September, according to union officials in a press release issued Monday night.
The nurse, who was not identified, was among 20 who had been disciplined last month for “documented violations of established hospital policies and standards,” according to CMMC officials last month.
At the time, several city leaders criticized the hospital, which is owned by California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation, saying the terminations were retaliation for a unionizing effort among the nurses.
Local leaders from across the political spectrum said the firings appeared to be related to recent union activities at the hospital, which would be in violation of state and federal law, and demanded the nurses be reinstated.
“Nurses were unlawfully disciplined for our patient advocacy,” said Hillary Ferrell, former nurse at Olympia Fields Hospital in Illinois, another Prime hospital where six nurses were terminated during a unionization effort last month. “But we will never stop speaking up for our patients. Our patients and our community deserve safe staffing and safe patient care,” she said in the press release.
At Olympia Fields, four fired nurses had been re-instated by Monday night.
Nurses at Olympia Fields won their union election with 82% support on Sept. 23 and CMMC nurses won their union election with 91% on Sept. 24.
The announcement that a single CMMC nurse will return to work came from the National Nurses Organization, an affiliate of the National Nurses United union, at almost 8 p.m. Monday night.
The group said they are continuing to fight on behalf of the remaining nurses who were either suspended or fired.
“Prime needs to reinstate all nurses who were suspended or fired,” said Katie Grinnell, a former nurse at CMMC. “Also, Prime must stop challenging our overwhelming victory at the ballot box. We won our union election by a landslide.”

title: Volunteer musicians bring live music to hospital patients
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (Aging Untold) — A group of volunteer musicians in Nashville is bringing live music to hospital rooms for patients, families and staff.
Alex King takes the music from room to room at TriStar Centennial. She has performed for patients, including Penn Pennington, for whom she first played several years ago while he was battling leukemia.
A video of their song went viral.
The performances are part of Musicians on Call, an organization that sends volunteer artists to play for patients.
Volunteers visit patients monthly
Allie Lamb takes her guitar on rounds a couple of days every month. She said seeing a kid’s face light up is rewarding.
“Give my voice in a way that matters,” she said.
Lamb encourages patients to sing along, clap and get involved during performances.
“It helps me stay positive,” Mayra Martinez, a patient, said.
The group performs more than 3,000 times a year for patients in Nashville.
