title: Redistricting battles have reshaped the 2026 midterms. How do voters in redrawn districts feel?
text:
Redistricting battles have reshaped the 2026 midterms. How do voters in redrawn districts feel?
A Dallas-area neighborhood has been carved up by redistricting, and neighbors on either side of the dividing line have very different feelings about the outcome — highlighting the impact of the nationwide battle ahead of the midterms.
Redistricting battles have reshaped the 2026 midterms. How do voters in redrawn districts feel?
A Dallas-area neighborhood has been carved up by redistricting, and neighbors on either side of the dividing line have very different feelings about the outcome — highlighting the impact of the nationwide battle ahead of the midterms.
The battle for control of Congress began weeks before a single vote was cast in the midterm elections.
In the last few months, states across the country have rushed to redraw their maps as both parties sought a partisan advantage. As a result, one in 10 voters will be casting a ballot in a newly formed district this cycle.
But how do those voters feel? In one Dallas suburb, neighbors who have found themselves on opposite sides of a new dividing line have very different opinions about redistricting.
Divided by redistricting
Raymond Alfred and Claudia Goodman live just feet apart, but their homes now sit in separate congressional districts after Texas Republicans redrew the state’s map last year. Until then, they shared the same district.
“If you look toward our west, right on our street, four doors down is our old congressional district,” Goodman said.
Goodman’s former district, centered around Dallas and its suburbs, voted for Kamala Harris by about 24 points. Her new district stretches into East Texas and would have backed Donald Trump by about 18 points.
“My vote is disrespected and diminished in its power,” Goodman said.
Alfred, however, sees the redistricting differently.
“We're never going to have any issue with the redistricting because it was put in place for our benefit,” he said.
A political arms race
The neighborhood’s division is part of a broader political strategy that began after President Donald Trump urged Texas Republicans to redraw the state’s congressional map.
“There could be some other states... we're going to get another three or four or five in addition. Texas would be the biggest one,” Trump said in July 2025. Typically, the maps are only redrawn every decade, around the time of the census.
The redistricting has triggered a political arms race, with both parties rushing to redraw maps in their favor. Nine states now have new congressional maps in place for this election, and the Cook Political Report estimates Republicans gained the upper hand.
However, political experts warn that overextending a party’s advantage can backfire.
“The reason it can backfire is if you take all your Republican-leaning voters and spread them not across 25 districts, but across 30 districts, you dilute your Republican majorities,” said Cal Jillson, a political expert at Southern Methodist University.
Jillson also noted that redistricting can exacerbate political tensions.
“It heightens the tension, it heightens the conflict, the vitriol. And we've got plenty of that in our elections,” he said.
On this Dallas street, the tension is palpable.
“There ain't no gray area in it, you know what I mean? Like somebody is going to lose,” Alfred said. “I think we — I think a lot of people want to be warm and fuzzy and say, 'No, everybody has to get a win out of this and great job,' and hand out participation awards. It don't work that way.”
Goodman disagreed.
“This is an erosion of our democracy. And the drawing of congressional district lines was never meant to serve this purpose. So, no, I do not agree that this is a perk to the victors,” she said.

title: InvestigateTV+: Potential medical breakthrough for sepsis
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ explores how sepsis attacks the body and the medical breakthrough one doctor says could potentially save lives.
Then, we take an in-depth look at how burnt trees stand in the way of rebuilding after wildfires and meet the volunteers doing dangerous work to help families move forward.
Plus, how experts say reading 1,000 books before kindergarten is not only doable but can set up a child for success.
A potential treatment to reduce sepsis deaths
Sepsis kills more than 350,000 adults and 1,800 children in the United States each year, according to the CDC. One in three adults who die in the hospital have sepsis.
A doctor in Kansas City, Missouri, has made a discovery that could drastically reduce that statistic.
Burnt trees standing in the way
In June 2025, a wildfire tore through the community of Rowena, Oregon. It forced 8,000 people to evacuate and destroyed more than 56 homes.
Many residents remain unable to rebuild. What didn’t burn is now what’s holding people back.
Charred trees, weakened and unstable, still stand across properties throughout the community. Known as hazard trees, they are dangerous enough to halt any rebuilding efforts.
Oldest bicycle factory in the nation
Wayne Sosin spent decades keeping the nation’s oldest bike maker rolling. He helped take over the more than 125-year-old family-owned company in 1987 before expanding operations from New York to Conway in 2015.
“We made a commitment to stay in America,” Sosin said.
1,000 books and counting
A Missouri six-year-old is reading more books than many people read in a lifetime.

title: Woman dies after stopping to help driver of flipped car on interstate
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A New Orleans woman died after she stopped to pull a trapped driver from a flipped car on Interstate 10 and was struck by another vehicle, according to her family.
Ka’Sheena Daniels, 31, died Sept. 25 on westbound I-10 near Elysian Fields Avenue after helping free a driver she recognized as her neighbor, said Franchon Williams, a friend who was with her.
New Orleans police said the crash began when a speeding car made a sudden lane change and flipped, prompting several drivers to stop and help the trapped driver.
Police said another vehicle then struck one of the stopped cars, pushing it into the crowd of people who had gathered to help. Multiple people were hurt, but Daniels was the only person who died.
Daniels was born and raised in New Orleans, had just celebrated a birthday and was raising her adopted son, Noah, while working in accounting, according to her mother, O’Sheenana Daniels.
“She just was that girl,” O’Sheenana Daniels said in an interview Friday. “If you needed help...and she could do it, it was done.”
Daniels left New Orleans East last Friday night to go out with close friends. The group saw a flipped car on the interstate, and Williams said Daniels recognized the driver as her neighbor.
“We see the lady. We try to help her out. My friend KK jumped out,” Williams said, referring to Daniels.
Williams said her friend pulled the woman out of the car and that only a few moments passed before Daniels was struck, causing her to fall from the interstate.
“(We’re) looking for my friend. (We’re) looking up under the cars, everywhere, and then they told me, like, ‘Well, y’all, somebody went over,’” Williams said. “They put their flashlight down there. It’s my friend. She’s just down there.”
O’Sheenana Daniels said she helped authorities locate her daughter after the crash.
“I started screaming my (baby’s) name, and she said, ‘Ma,” O’Sheenana Daniels said. “When they heard her say that, they ran where...she was calling from.”
O’Sheenana Daniels said she can’t believe her daughter’s death and struggles with the circumstances surrounding it.
“It’s sad to say, but I wish she just never would have helped (anybody),” O’Sheenana Daniels said. “I just wish she would have just kept on going about her business.”
Williams said she and Daniels had planned to start paramedic school next week. Williams said she will pursue that goal in her friend’s honor.
New Orleans police said the investigation is ongoing. Daniels’ family has set up a GoFundMe to pay for her funeral.

title: Fermentation Expo emphasizes storytelling through food at the IMRC
text:
On Saturday, Oct. 3rd, the Innovative Media Research and Commercialization Center (IMRC) was full of family, friends and students walking through numerous showcases about the power of fermentation. A SCOBY petting zoo for the kids, hydrophones playing the sounds of fermentation, make-your-own sauerkraut, tie-dying with fermented indigo— the idea that fermentation is only for an improved taste was proven wrong.
“I wanted to bring people together and build community,” said Ellie Markovitch, a communications and journalism professor at the University of Maine and the founder of the food and media lab known as Fermentation Friday. Commenting on its beginnings, Markovitch said she has “a passion for storytelling and food is a great way to bring people in.”
There was no shortage of storytelling on Saturday either. Bringing together the most fermentation-forward individuals they could wrangle, those behind the tables gave the history of their practice and the food to be consumed to the attendees of the event.
“It made me think, ‘How did this start?’ like the practice of fermentation,” said Josie Veilleux, a fourth-year student at UMaine and a fermentation novice.
“Seeing solutions to waste with the fish sauce was also really inspiring,” said Veilleux. He emphasized the dimensions of fermentation which are not as visible to the average shopper. We seem to stop our conception of fermentation at pickles and onions, but attendee Liam Fischer brought his fish and eel sauce, which are made entirely from material that is otherwise trashed.
“I was convinced to try whipped cream with eel sauce and it turned out to be the best,” Veilleux laughed.
“I had fermented once before at the Terrell house and it stunk up my dorm for a while,” attendee Shannon Macdonald added. “It really breaks down the fast-paced mindset of a lot of modern things. It’s the quality of taste over the speed and quantity.” Macdonald was exposed to the nuances of fermentation via the exposition.
“My thesis started with the question: How can I represent archaic Indigenous practices in a way that Western audiences can have some understanding?” explained Alicia Bell, a master’s student at UMaine working with fermentation to answer just that. An entire room was dedicated to Bell’s display. On the table in the center were three jars of fermenting foods, one with a hydrophone inside, and the walls were covered in microscopic photos of the fermentation process.
“It’s really made me think about how every system has a process of fermentation,” Bell said about her research. “For instance the Earth has the ocean. It is always changing and exchanging with the life inside of it— if you’ve ever gone in the ocean, you’ve been fermented!”
In the back of the IMRC, children ran around with indigo-blued hands, with the smell of the dye infecting the room. Families wandered around, watching, and a clothesline of finished crafts hangs in the center of the room.
“It is just a very giving community and students really appreciate having the time to come together to grow, skill-share, ferment, try new things and document it all,” Markovitch reflected on the student response to Fermentation Friday. “We have brought guest speakers, local businesses; we have taken students on road trips, [and] we’ve presented at the Fermentation Fair. So, we just keep going and keep doing more and more.”

title: Russia reports a worker at a Siberian plague institute got pneumonia from an unknown cause and died
text:
(AP) - Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an “unknown” cause. Local state TV said the woman died last week.
Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
The woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, southeastern Siberia. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported Monday that she died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk.
The hospital has been placed under quarantine, Mayor Maxim Modin said Friday, no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted carrying out routine tests. The hospital’s outpatient clinic kept operating as usual, he said.
Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk and met with Gov. Igor Kobzev and other officials on Friday.
Kobzev said everyone who came into contact with the woman is under medical supervision. He didn’t identify the infection and called it a suspected case of “a particularly dangerous infection.”
Rospotrebnadzor was implementing “a full range of anti-epidemic measures,” he added.
Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday the woman was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” or origin, and said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.”
The agency also said it didn’t uncover any incidents at the institute “involving pathogenic microorganisms.”
Two people who were in contact with the woman tested positive for a virus that causes a common cold and two others for COVID-19, the agency said, adding that others who were tested were all negative.
Trump says he’s concerned about the reports
In Washington, President Donald Trump said he was watching the situation with concern and said the United States would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation.
“It’s a rough disease. You know, that’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “Even with great advancement, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well anymore.”
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday he doesn’t think there is cause for alarm, but the U.S. is watching the case closely, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.
Independent local news outlet Lyudi Baikala quoted sources it did not identify as saying the 28-year-old lab technician died from pneumonic plague and that several Irkutsk hospitals were placed under quarantine.
Asked Monday to comment on the case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumors or speculation.”
Rospotrebnadzor did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov required staff to wear masks as a precaution, its director Artyom Fominykh said Saturday on Telegram, calling for calm and adding: “Better be safe than sorry.”
The World Health Organization describes pneumonic plague as a less common but severe form of plague — a disease caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals and their fleas.
“In the event of a potential laboratory exposure, it would be normal to identify individuals who might have been exposed and to monitor them according to the assessed level of risk,” said Dr. Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology at the Imperial College London.
The scale of any monitoring program would depend on “the circumstances of the exposure and the number of people potentially affected,” Gibani said in a written comment.
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia,” although because of modern living conditions and antibiotics, “its potential is therefore limited.”
——
AP reporters Matthew Lee, Will Weissert and Collin Binkley in Washington contributed.

title: Former Prince Andrew takes legal action against UK police over Epstein arrest
text:
Former Prince Andrew takes legal action against UK police over Epstein arrest
King Charles' younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against police in England over his arrest earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office following revelations from the Epstein files in the United States.
Related video: NY AG's office takes over Cornell rape investigation
Mountbatten-Windsor, 66, has asked for a judge to determine if Thames Valley Police's actions against him earlier this year were lawful. The development was first reported by Britain's The Telegraph newspaper on Sunday.
He has lodged a judicial review in relation to the search warrants that were executed at his home at the Sandringham Estate and his former home at Royal Lodge in Windsor.
A court hearing will be held on Thursday, British media reported Monday.
Thames Valley Police confirmed to CNN on Monday that it was "engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court" and would not comment further with legal proceedings ongoing.
CNN has also reached out to the UK Judicial Office for comment.
The former Duke of York became the first senior royal in centuries to be arrested in February, the latest extraordinary development in a yearslong scandal over his ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which obliterated his reputation and has thrown the royal family into crisis.
He was detained by police on his 66th birthday at his new home on his brother's Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England, on February 19. He was taken to Aylsham police station where he was questioned for almost 12 hours before being released under investigation. No charges were filed; police have said their investigation is still ongoing.
Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest came after the force previously said it was assessing whether the former prince had shared confidential information with Epstein during his decade as a UK trade envoy.
Mountbatten-Windsor has vehemently denied any and all wrongdoing in his dealings with Epstein, and has denied any personal gain from his role as a trade envoy, according to British media reports.
He stepped down from official royal duties in 2019 following a calamitous interview with the BBC over his friendship with Epstein. But headlines related to the late financier continued to plague the disgraced royal. In 2025, King Charles stripped his younger brother of his title as prince, following public outcry after the release of a posthumous memoir by Virginia Giuffre, a prominent accuser of Epstein who alleged that Mountbatten-Windsor had sexually assaulted her as a teenager.
Giuffre – who the prince claims never to have met – died by suicide in April 2025 at the age of 41. In addition to denying all allegations against him, Mountbatten-Windsor has also previously insisted he never witnessed or suspected any of the behavior of which Epstein is accused.

title: A new Supreme Court term begins with cases on climate change, immigration and gun rights
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court’s new term begins Monday with cases on climate change, religious rights and President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration high on the agenda.
Here’s a look at what’s in store:
Climate change
The high court is starting its term with a major climate change case. The justices will hear an appeal from energy companies trying to block dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold them liable in court for damage related to climate change.
Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in a case out of Boulder, Colorado, where local officials say the industry should help shoulder the escalating costs of disasters linked to climate change.
The companies, Suncor and ExxonMobil, say lawsuits aren’t the way to deal with the global issue. They have the backing of the Trump administration, which argues the litigation is a power grab intended to impose regulations on emissions.
Assault weapons bans
About a dozen states have banned semiautomatic rifles like AR-15s, which are often called assault weapons. They say the guns are disproportionately used in mass shootings, and banning them helps reduce gun violence.
Challengers say those laws violate the Second Amendment. They argue that AR-15s and other similar weapons are among the most popular and commonly owned guns in the country.
The conservative-majority court has expanded gun rights in recent years, and four justices had signaled that it was only a matter of time before the court took up the issue. The case will be considered in December.
Immigration
The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump’s wide-reaching crackdown.
One is about deportations of migrants who can’t be quickly sent back to their home countries. The Trump administration has been sending thousands to other countries where they have no ties, under a series of often-secret agreements.
The Supreme Court will consider overturning lower court orders allowing them a chance to object. The justices have allowed the flights to continue in the meantime.
The other case is over the administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants who have been living in the U.S. illegally, even if they’ve been in the country for years.
The administration argues it can hold people without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have considered the issue disagree.
Voting
A Republican push to enforce strict Arizona voting laws will also come before the justices this term.
One measure requires people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form, and another calls for regular purges of the voter rolls to remove people if their citizenship could not be confirmed.
It comes as Trump has failed to get legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for registering to vote through Congress. Arguments are set for December.
Religious rights
Catholic preschools that can’t take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November. It’s the justices’ latest case involving religious rights.
St. Mary Catholic Parish says it’s been left out of the state’s universal preschool program over its faith-based admissions policies, which exclude kids from LGBTQ+ families.
Colorado says religious schools are welcome to participate but have to follow nondiscrimination laws. The program was created by a 2020 ballot measure and provides public funding for preschool at schools selected by parents.

title: Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt lands her next gig: Fox News contributor
text:
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has found her next chapter: She is heading to Fox News.
Leavitt will serve as an on-air contributor beginning Nov. 1, the network said Monday.
“Karoline’s firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape,” said the network’s CEO, Suzanne Scott.
For her part, Leavitt, in the same statement, said she looked forward “to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defied my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms.”
Leavitt, now 29, was the youngest person to hold the role of press secretary. When she left at the end of August, President Donald Trump described her as one of his “most trusted aides.”
Leavitt is not the first White House press secretary to join Fox. Kayleigh McEnany joined in 2021 and remains at the network.
And Trump has hired several Fox News personalities to key jobs in his own administration, chief among them Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

title: Robert Kelker-Kelly, known for roles in major soap operas, has died at 62
text:
Robert Kelker-Kelly, former star of ‘Days of Our Lives,’ ‘General Hospital’ and ‘Another World,’ has died, reports say
Actor Robert Kelker-Kelly, known for his roles in “Days of Our Lives” and two other major soap operas, has died at age 62, according to reports.
The cause and manner of death have not yet been publicly reported, but TMZ was the first to report that a Missouri medical examiner had confirmed that Kelker-Kelly died on Oct. 3.
Variety and USA Today have also confirmed with police that Kelker-Kelly has died. The St. Peters Police Department in St. Charles County, Missouri, said it was called on Oct. 3 for an unconscious male who was having a medical event and had become unresponsive, the Variety report states. St. Peters, Missouri, is located outside of St. Louis. Both Variety and USA Today report that police said he experienced chest pains before becoming unresponsive.
Related video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
Kelker-Kelly got his start in soap opera acting when he played Sam Fowler on “Another World” in 1987. He would also later go on to play Stavros Cassadine on “General Hospital."
Kelker-Kelly was one of the actors to star as Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives,” and his character was known for his steamy and dramatic relationships with Hope Williams Brady, played by Kristian Alfonso, and Billie Reed, played by Lisa Rinna. Kelker-Kelly took on the role of Bo in 1992 after Peter Reckell. Reckell originated the role in the early 1980s and then later returned as Bo Brady in 1995.
People and Entertainment Weekly both report that Kelker-Kelly was also a professional pilot.
He was married to actress Linda Rattner from 1988 to 1992. Then, from 1997 to 2013, he was married to “Days of Our Lives” costar Miriam Parrish, who played Jamie Caldwell. Both of the marriages ended in divorce, People reports.

title: Jeffries says House Democrats reaching to flip Trump districts in attempt to repeat their 2018 sweep
text:
Jeffries says House Democrats reaching to flip Trump districts in attempt to repeat their 2018 sweep
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday his party is on track to win back control of the House, confident it can overcome a fundraising disadvantage and reach deep into conservative areas to flip congressional districts won by President Donald Trump just two years ago.
In a conference call with reporters, Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats seize the majority, compared this midterm election to 2018, when Democrats swept to power during Trump's first term in the White House.
Related video above: Here are the Senate races to watch
“House Democrats are poised to take back the majority,” he said.
Jeffries, who is from New York, said that when Democrats took control of the House in 2018, most of the seats they flipped were in districts where Trump won in 2016.
“In 2026, we're poised to do the same thing,” he said.
His comments were the latest display of confidence from Democrats with a month to go until the midterm elections on Nov. 3. The party is working to expand the map by going on offense in Republican-held districts, while Trump hits the trail in a red-state sprint to boost voter enthusiasm and shore up support from his base.
Republicans have a sizable cash advantage as House Speaker Mike Johnson steers the party closer to Trump to try to keep the majority. Trump is promising voters $5,000 cash dividends if the Republicans win, though it's not at all certain that Congress would unleash the estimated $1 trillion-plus for such an outlay. Over the weekend, Trump announced $90 payments to seniors to help pay Medicare premiums.
Jeffries said Republicans are “failing and flailing."
“The American people are not buying what MAGA Republicans are trying to sell,” he said.
With the House narrowly split, just a few seats could determine which party holds the gavel. Early voting is underway. Republicans are under pressure because of high gas prices stemming from the war with Iran.
Jeffries said a Trump-led redistricting effort to draw more favorable Republican districts in Texas, Florida and other states backfired in some places. At the same time, the House Democrats’ campaign arm announced late last week it was adding eight districts to its map of districts in play, including those in Kansas, Oklahoma, Virginia and Washington state.
“The Republican gerrymander scheme has failed,” Jeffries said.
Jeffries cautioned, however, that “anything and everything” is possible, and urged Democrats to remain focused. “We can’t afford to take anything for granted,” he said.
Johnson, the Republican speaker, has been crisscrossing the country and insisted Republicans will be able to protect their majority. He stumped for Republicans in California last week and he is scheduled to be in more than 40 districts across some 20 states in the final weeks before November.
Jeffries, who was also in Western states over the weekend, said he too will be traveling in the weeks ahead.

title: Grieving family fights fake obituaries for teenage son
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - The details in the obituaries were vague, some were totally wrong. Brett Tinch found himself correcting lies about his teenage son Noah’s life.
“I started seeing these posts, obituaries, and none of the information was accurate. The middle name was wrong,” Brett Tinch said. “There’s one out there that says he’s 32 years old.”
The rising sophomore was actually one day away from his 19th birthday, in Colorado with his mother. The family says he was helping grandparents clean out a property they had just sold, and he was doing what he loved - fly fishing.
“They believe that he had gotten a fly stuck in a rock and he had bent down to pick it up, he hit his head and lost consciousness and he drowned,” Brett Tinch said.
The father of two wasn’t planning on sharing those difficult details, but he knew he had to fight the fake facts with the painful truth.
“It’s an unfortunate situation, and it’s the last thing a family wants to deal with when a loved one has passed,” Dr. Lisa Blue, the director of the Artificial Intelligence Strategies for Eastern Kentucky University, said. “The family’s best strategy is to be proactive, and control the narrative by posting an obituary on an official news site, or a platform, or a funeral home website as soon as possible.”
Blue said the AI-generated obituaries are published anonymously, some overseas, with no repercussions for inaccurate information.
“These fake obituaries are then published to these low-quality, high-volume content sites in the hopes of generating ad revenue. So the more odd these obituaries seem, the more likely they’re gonna get clicks, and every one of those clicks generates a small income stream for the poster,” Blue said.
Blue said grieving families should publish the real obituary early and widely.
Use the funeral home’s website or a reputable obituary platform and ask friends to share that link only.

title: Ask ACE: What governance structures help an ESOP succeed as it grows?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Q: What governance structures help an ESOP succeed as it grows?
ACE advises: One of the biggest mistakes growing ESOPs make is assuming employee ownership will create alignment on its own. It will not. An employee stock ownership plan needs clear layers of governance, and each layer needs to know its job.
At the top, you need strong fiduciary oversight. That usually means having a trustee and board that understand they are there to protect the company’s long-term health, not manage daily operations. Their roles are to oversee risk, leadership succession, major decisions and the business’s integrity.
Next comes management. Management should run the company, execute strategy and produce clear financial and operational reporting. If the board has to chase basic information, step into routine decisions or untangle confusion about who owns what, the governance structure is not keeping pace with the business.
Then there is leadership depth inside the business. Department leaders and frontline managers need defined authority, accountability and decision rights. If too much still lives with one founder, CEO, or a few long-tenured people, the ESOP may be employee-owned on paper, but it is still overly dependent in practice.
Finally, employee-owners need education. They do not need to govern the company day to day, but they should understand what drives value, what weakens margin, and how their work connects to ownership.
A healthy ESOP works when those layers support each other. The board governs, management runs the business, leaders lead, and employee-owners understand how value is built and protected. That is what turns ownership into a real advantage.

title: Robert Charles “Bob” Thibodeau
text:
Robert Charles “Bob” Thibodeau, 75 of Warren, Maine, passed away on Sept. 22, 2026 at his home with his loving family by his side.
Bob was born on November 9, 1949, in Rumford, the son of Albert Wilfred Thibodeau and Emma Caroline (Mooney) Thibodeau. He grew up in Rumford and following high school, joined the United States Navy in 1969. He served aboard the USS Patterson, later became a member of the Naval Reserve, and was awarded the National Defense Service Medal.
Bob had a long career in law enforcement. He began his career as a deputy with the Knox County Sheriff’s Office and later worked at the Maine State Prison in Thomaston, where he retired. Following retirement, he continued working with the Knox County Jail and Northeast Transport.
Bob loved hunting and fishing and spent much of his life enjoying the outdoors. He had a special love for his Wirehaired Pointing Griffon hunting dogs and the many years he spent hunting with them. Bob was also a competitive clay target shooter who earned state and club championship titles in skeet and side-by-side shooting at Varney’s Clay Sports in Richmond.
One of Bob’s favorite places was the family camp in Lambert Lake, Maine, where he especially enjoyed spending time with his wife, Pam, and making many lasting memories together.
Bob was a proud lifetime member of Union Lodge No. 31, Ancient Free and Accepted Masons, in Union.
He was predeceased by his parents, Albert Wilfred Thibodeau and Emma Caroline (Mooney) Thibodeau, and his granddaughter, Emma Thibodeau.
Bob is survived by his wife, Pamela Jean Abbott Thibodeau, of Warren; his children, Tammy Pacenza and her husband, Michael, of Newburgh, N.Y.; Robert Thibodeau II and wife Judith, of Old Orchard Beach; and Shannon Marie Crute, of Rockland.
He is also survived by his grandchildren, Gavin Pacenza, Alexi Gallipeau, Joseph Gamage, Jacob Thibodeau, Shawn Crute, Trevor Crute, Calob Crute, and Maxim Crute.
He is also survived by his siblings, Patsy Rinaldo and her husband Rick, of North Carolina; John Alfonse Thibodeau and his wife, Deirdre, of Rockland; and Susan Ames and her husband, Bruce, of Kenduskeag.
A memorial service will be held to celebrate Bob’s life on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026 at 11 a.m. at the Union Masonic Hall No. 31, at 149 Sennebec Road in Union.
In lieu of flowers please consider making a donation in Bob’s name to the Mount Olivet Scholarship or Building Fund, 149 Sennebec Road, Union, ME 04862 or to any animal shelter of your choosing.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home, Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a condolence, please visit Bob’s Book of Memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: October is just another month at this Halloween-themed bar in Portland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — On a wall by the fireplace in the lobby of the Ramada Plaza on Riverside Street, a sign with an outline of a dog’s head points in the direction of Zero Bar & Grille.
Not until you go past the fitness center and the ice machine, down a hallway of rooms and through two doors is there any indication that this isn’t going to be your typical hotel bar.
Even as you approach the door, passing windows with decals in the shape of skulls, bats and spiderwebs, you’d have no reason to think they’re anything other than seasonal decorations this time of year. But they won’t be coming down in November.
Zero, named after owner Liv True’s miniature Australian shepherd who is named after the ghostly dog in “The Nightmare Before Christmas,” is a year-round Halloween-themed bar and restaurant. That’s a lot more apparent from the entrance at the side of the building, where the hands and legs of giant skeletons dangle from the roof overhang, flanked by gargoyles.
Anyone who knows True, with the haunted house she has tattooed on her upper arm and the skull-shaped trinkets that filled her Portland home before she brought them here, isn’t surprised that this is what she decided to do with her bar.
Still, she said, “my daughter thought I was nuts.”
Zero opened just over a year ago, but True has been imagining it a lot longer.
As a bartender in the same sprawling space when it was Seasons Grille, she would think about how she could do things better: bring in pool tables and make use of the back room, where there are now dartboards, pinball machines and, on Tuesdays, country swing dance classes.
When the venue’s lease became available, she jumped on it and, with the help of her regulars from the bar, went to work tearing up carpet, scrubbing down the kitchen and covering the walls and surfaces with spiders, bats, witches, ghosts and skulls in all forms. A giant skeleton greets people at the door and two human-sized ones, including a child in a high chair, sit at table 13, often joined by families in the flesh for dinner.
“Everybody, when they hear Halloween, they think scary, spooky,” True said, but that’s not what she’s going for. “It’s more fun, cute Halloween.”
Although the theme attracts other fans of the holiday, True has broadened the customer base by filling up the calendar with bands and weekly events, including karaoke and cribbage. Receptionists at the hotel said guests appreciate that there’s always something to do at night.
Two sessions of bingo on Thursdays — the first with a music theme, followed by a “naughty” one — bring in the biggest weekday crowds.
Two women who met working at Market Basket were there last week well before it started, as they always are, at the same table in the lounge. Bingo, they said, isn’t the only thing that brings them back. The staff have become like friends, and you can count on the DJ to turn even your worst day around. They love the food, especially the buffalo chicken pizza, and the decor, because it’s something different.
Aside from Halloween weekend itself and the Zombie Prom on Oct. 24 (the biggest event last year after True’s own 50th birthday party), she doesn’t know if she’ll see a big spike in business this month in the lead-up to the holiday.
Things have been picking up since Labor Day, now that there’s less competition for music fans who want to go to outdoor shows while they can, she said. She’s also gotten a boost from a TikTok video, posted by Maine influencer Jessica Annè this summer, that has over 90,000 views.
Between the startup costs and the $10,000 loss from a break-in this spring, she thinks it will be another year before she makes back the money she’s put into it. She still works her day job, bookkeeping for Overhead Door Co., her family’s business.
True doesn’t have to worry about a lull after Halloween though. Two weeks later, it’s Friday the 13th, when people will be invited to come dressed up as their favorite character from a horror film.
After that, she’ll get out the Santa hats and light-up sweaters for the skeletons and start decorating for Christmas.

title: New Supreme Court term begins with cases on climate change, immigration and gun rights
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court’s new term begins Monday with cases on climate change, religious rights and President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration high on the agenda.
Here’s a look at what’s in store:
Climate change
The high court is starting its term with a major climate change case. The justices will hear an appeal from energy companies trying to block dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold them liable in court for damage related to climate change.
Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in a case out of Boulder, Colorado, where local officials say the industry should help shoulder the escalating costs of disasters linked to climate change.
The companies, Suncor and ExxonMobil, say lawsuits aren’t the way to deal with the global issue. They have the backing of the Trump administration, which argues the litigation is a power grab intended to impose regulations on emissions.
Assault weapons bans
About a dozen states have banned semiautomatic rifles like AR-15s, which are often called assault weapons. They say the guns are disproportionately used in mass shootings, and banning them helps reduce gun violence.
Challengers say those laws violate the Second Amendment. They argue that AR-15s and other similar weapons are among the most popular and commonly owned guns in the country.
The conservative-majority court has expanded gun rights in recent years, and four justices had signaled that it was only a matter of time before the court took up the issue. The case will be considered in December.
Immigration
The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump’s wide-reaching crackdown.
One is about deportations of migrants who can’t be quickly sent back to their home countries. The Trump administration has been sending thousands to other countries where they have no ties, under a series of often-secret agreements.
The Supreme Court will consider overturning lower court orders allowing them a chance to object. The justices have allowed the flights to continue in the meantime.
The other case is over the administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants who have been living in the U.S. illegally, even if they’ve been in the country for years.
The administration argues it can hold people without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have considered the issue disagree.
Voting
A Republican push to enforce strict Arizona voting laws will also come before the justices this term.
One measure requires people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form, and another calls for regular purges of the voter rolls to remove people if their citizenship could not be confirmed.
It comes as Trump has failed to get legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for registering to vote through Congress. Arguments are set for December.
Religious rights
Catholic preschools that can’t take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November. It’s the justices’ latest case involving religious rights.
St. Mary Catholic Parish says it’s been left out of the state’s universal preschool program over its faith-based admissions policies, which exclude kids from LGBTQ+ families.
Colorado says religious schools are welcome to participate but have to follow nondiscrimination laws. The program was created by a 2020 ballot measure and provides public funding for preschool at schools selected by parents.

title: Tim Stutzle powers Ottawa Senators past Boston Bruins
text:
BOSTON — Tim Stutzle had two goals and an assist and goalies Linus Ullmark and Samuel Ersson combined to stop 18 of 19 shots as the Ottawa Senators defeated the Boston Bruins 4-1 on Monday night.
Stutzle’s multi-point game moved him into sole possession of sixth place for most points in Ottawa history with 413.
Ullmark started in goal for Ottawa, but wasn’t on the ice at the start of the third period. The onetime Bruin netminder, who stopped all 10 shots he faced in the first two periods, was on the bench five minutes into the final period. Ersson made eight saves in the final period for the Senators.
Ottawa’s Michael Amadio had a goal and assist, and Drake Batherson also scored.
Boston rookie James Hagan spoiled Ottawa’s shutout bid with a goal in the third period. Jeremy Swayman made 20 saves for the Bruins, who have lost two straight after opening the season with two wins.
Boston was outshot 24-19 and failed to score on four power plays.
Stutzle came close to two short-handed goals on the same power play. He scored on the man advantage at 7:39 of the first. Seconds after Ottawa successfully shut down Boston on the power play, Stutzle scored on a 2-on-1 chance, making it 2-0.
Batherson scored 66 seconds into the second period, taking advantage of a Boston turnover and scoring with a backhand shot.
Amadio converted on a feed from Shane Pinto to give Ottawa a 4-0 lead, prompting Bruins head coach Marco Sturm to call at timeout at 14:41.
Ullmark was slow getting up after Boston’s JJ Peterka crashed into him at 4:25 of the second. The 2022-23 Venza Trophy winner with Boston is in his third season with Ottawa after being traded before the 2024-25 season.
Up next
Senators: At Detroit on Tuesday night.
Bruins: Host Utah on Thursday night.

title: Healthcare advocacy group launches bus tour in Bangor
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Polling shows healthcare affordability is a major issue for voters this election.
One group is traveling the nation hoping to mobilize voters against Republicans, saying the current administration has taken a wrecking ball to the system.
Protect Our Care’s “Sick Of It” Fix Healthcare Now bus tour kicked off Monday in Bangor.
It was the first of nearly 40 stops the organization’s bus, dubbed Care Force One, is making coast to coast.
The group is bringing together local advocates at each stop to protest Medicaid cuts and changes to the Affordable Care Act while promoting the restoration of tax credits to lower premiums and extending out of pocket pay caps to people with private insurance.
“These cuts affect everybody because it’s a health care system. And so doctors and hospitals have to charge more to make up for the money they’re not getting. So that means pretty much everybody is facing higher health insurance premiums,” said Laura Packard, cancer survivor.
“If we had a system like a Medicare for all system or some other form of universal health care like every other industrialized country in the world has, we could actually provide some comfort and relief to people so they wouldn’t have to worry about slipping and falling on the ice and then looking at bankruptcy because of it. So this is really, really important,” said Maine CD2 candidate Matt Dunlap.
Dunlap also said the cost of gas is limiting affordable healthcare as many Mainers need to travel to get to medical appointments.
The bus plans to make 35 stops in 15 states over the next four weeks.

title: 4 teens charged in murder of 16-year-old shot after high school football game, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Police in Tennessee say four teenagers have been charged after a 16-year-old boy was killed in a drive-by shooting after a high school football game.
Cameron Frierson, 16, was killed in a drive-by shooting Aug. 21 after he went to a football game at Pearl-Cohn High School, according to Nashville police. It was around 10:30 p.m. when police say someone in a white sedan drove by and began shooting, hitting Cameron multiple times as his brother stood close by.
Now, police say four teenagers — ages 16, 17, 17 and 18 — have been arrested in connection with the killing. All four are charged with criminal homicide and engaging in a criminal conspiracy.
Police say all of the suspects were inside the white sedan when the shots that hit Cameron were fired. The investigation into a motive for the gunfire is ongoing.
‘I miss him so much’
Cameron’s parents spoke with WSMV after his death, describing their son as a teenager who was “truly being a kid” on the night he was killed.
Cameron was a student at Hunters Lane High School and the oldest of seven siblings. His mother, Brittany Frierson, said he loved football, cars and fashion. He had a dream of getting an HVAC degree and owning his own business.
“I miss him so much. I miss the laugh and his smile,” Frierson said.
Cameron’s mother said he worked two jobs but had the night off Aug. 21. He had been looking forward to going to the football game with his friends all week. She said no mother should ever have to worry about their child not coming home from a school football game.
“It could have been anybody’s child. It’s not right for us to live in the city and not enjoy the city. He was 16, just like any other 16-year-old,” Frierson said. “They weren’t doing anything wrong. Gun violence and these kids is serious.”

title: Brian Chester McLain
text:
Brian Chester McLain, 73, of New Harbor, passed away peacefully at Maine Medical Center on Oct. 2, 2026 following a period of declining health. He was born in Damariscotta on July 11, 1953, the son of Doris Thompson McLain and Harry S. McLain.
Brian grew up in Bristol, attending Bristol High School as a member of one of its final classes before graduating from Lincoln Academy. He was a fourth-generation lobsterman, proudly following in his father’s footsteps. He began fishing from the family dock in Pemaquid and later made New Harbor his homeport.
Fishing was not simply Brian’s livelihood; it was a huge part of his life and who he was. During his more than 60 years on the water, he owned several fishing boats and played a large role in the construction of his beloved f/v Silver Bullet. Over the years, Brian lobstered, groundfished, seined, scalloped, and especially loved winter shrimp dragging. He participated in numerous research projects and could often be found on the boat alongside scientists, sharing his knowledge and experience.
Brian was also passionate about passing that knowledge on to the next generation. He welcomed young fishermen aboard his boat and participated in lobstering apprenticeship programs, helping introduce others to the work and traditions that meant so much to him.
Brian was a longstanding board member of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, serving from 1984-2013 and eventually as second vice president. During his many years with the association, Brian advocated for the lobstering industry and the fishermen who depended on it. In recognition of his dedication and going above and beyond in support of the industry, Brian was honored with the Golden V-Notch Award in 2005.
Brian was a lifelong member of the Samoset Fish & Game Club and enjoyed fundraising for the club for many years, especially during Olde Bristol Days. He loved lobster bakes on his dock and heading north to ice fish, hunt, and snowmobile. For many years, he participated in a candlepin bowling league at DePatsy’s. Brian also enjoyed keeping his mind busy, often coming up with his own inventions to make life easier. Over the years, he created many things at home, including his very own oyster shucker. Later in life, he enjoyed mackerel fishing, freshwater fishing, cheering on his New England sports teams, following NASCAR, going to the casino, and simply hanging out in his garage with “the guys.”
Brian is survived by his wife, Heather; daughter, Sheila McLain; grandchildren, Jared McLain and Anna Brackett; brother, David McLain and his wife, Linda; nephew, Billy McLain and his wife, Kimberly; niece, Tammy Holmes and her husband, Rusty; five stepchildren, Andrea Hauck, Darrell Fossett, Brett Smith, Branden Smith, and Brock Smith; step-grandchildren; grandnieces and grandnephews; cousins and many dear friends.
The family would like to extend their heartfelt thanks to Dennis Lane and the Bristol first responders for their dedication, care, and support of Brian over the last several years.
A celebration will take place in the spring. In lieu of flowers, donations in Brian’s memory may be made to Bristol Fire and Rescue, 104 South Side Road, New Harbor, ME 04554.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for his family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.

title: Troy Jackson campaigns in Bangor ahead of first televised debate with Sen. Susan Collins
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - During his stop in Bangor Sunday for a canvass launch event statewide, Democratic U.S. Senate Candidate Troy Jackson replied to questions regarding his tight Senate Race with Maine Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins.
A NYT poll updated on October 2nd shows both Jackson and Collins are tied at 50%.
Collins had criticized Jackson for spreading “baseless lies” amid allegations following a report by ProPublica last month.
The report said that Collins was allegedly at the center of an FBI probe involved in “pay-to-play” scheme with Naval Defense Company Navatek.
Collins denies the claims, saying they are the allegations are “categorically false.”
Jackson said that Collins needs to stand up and take accountability.
“She should worry about who she takes money from. I don’t take corporate money. I don’t trade votes for things like that. That’s on her. I don’t know what else to say about it, but I’m sure she is very concerned about it,” said Jackson,
Ahead of the first televised debate Thursday, Jackson also spoke about how he is preparing ahead of time.
“Your record is always something I felt very strongly about. I am very excited to be able to be on the debate stage and talk about the things that I’ve done compared to the things that she’s done. She can defend her, and. I’ll defend mine. I’m proud of what I fought for.”
A full statement sent to WABI from Susan Collins campaign can be found below:
“Troy Jackson took hundreds of thousands of dollars of corporate money when he was Maine Senate President. Tobacco money, pharmaceutical companies, electric companies — you name it. It is the height of hypocrisy for him to lecture anyone on campaign money. These are seven year old allegations and the Biden led FBI and the FEC both said there was no indication that Senator Collins had done anything wrong. Troy just doesn’t know what he is talking about.”
WABI and WAGM will be hosting a debate between Jackson and Collins on Tuesday, October 13th at 7 p.m.
It will be streamed on-air and online.

title: Nolo changes from a hurricane to a typhoon after crossing the international date line
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Nolo has changed from a strong hurricane to a typhoon after it crossed the international date line.
Nolo was a Category 3 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kph) Sunday morning Hawaii time before it crossed the agreed-upon line in the Pacific Ocean that separates one day from the next. Names of tropical cyclones vary by the parts of the world where they occur.
Monday morning Japan time, Typhoon Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (162 kph) and was moving west at 19 mph (30 kph), according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.
“The good news is there’s a large, vast ocean, so even though it is still going to be strong, it’s not near any land,” said John Cangialosi, a senior hurricane specialist with the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami.
Tropical cyclones with winds over 74 mph (119 kph) are called hurricanes in the northern Atlantic Ocean and the central and eastern Pacific. They are typhoons in the North Pacific, while the South Pacific and Indian Ocean use just the generic term tropical cyclone no matter the strength of the storm.
Nolo is forecast to keep moving west and gradually weaken.
Nolo skirted Hawaii as a hurricane a week ago. It then lost some of its punch and became a tropical storm, before regaining hurricane strength on Friday.
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hurricane Rachel continued heading westward on a path away from Mexico.
As the storm moved further out to sea, it was sending dangerous waves and swells back to the coast of west-central Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula, according to the hurricane center.

title: US Supreme Court does not take up case regarding lobster boat GPS tracking
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (WABI) - The US Supreme Court has declined to take up a case affecting the nation’s lobster industry.
The rule at issue lets fishery managers require electronic vessel trackers on federally permitted lobster boats, in the water and at the dock.
The First Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the rule last year.
Opponents called it “unconstitutional” in their appeal.
Supporters say tracking provides timely, accurate data for regulators as the New England lobster population declines.
Attorney Matthew Gillam from Pacific Law Group, who represents the Maine fisherman who challenged the rule said in a statement to WABI, ”While we are disappointed that the Supreme Court declined to hear Mr. Thompson’s cert petition, today’s decision does not diminish the importance of the issues presented. Forcing lobstermen to carry a GPS tracker on their private boats and submit to around-the-clock surveillance as a condition of keeping their license remains a serious constitutional concern. We are committed to fighting for Fourth Amendment protections from government overreach and we will continue to pursue every lawful avenue to protect individual rights."

title: MaineCare will cover traditional Wabanaki healing practices
text:
Tribal health clinics soon will be able to bill MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, for traditional Wabanaki healing practices.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services announced Friday that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) granted the state a waiver to try new and expanded Medicaid coverage.
Tribal health clinics in Maine already provide traditional practices, including smudging, sweat lodges, talking circles and other ceremonies to patients. But they have to use other revenue sources to cover the costs.
That will change, likely by 2028, once tribal leaders and state officials work out the particulars of what will be covered under the waiver.
“I think this really gives merit and weight to what we always knew was good medicine for our people,” said Theresa Cochran, health director for the Mi’kmaq Nation.
The primary purpose of the waiver was to add MaineCare coverage for treatment of incarcerated people up to 60 days before they reenter society.
As Dr. Courtney Pladsen, MaineCare’s medical director, set out to draft the application, she was committed to maximizing the benefit. Tribal leaders in consultation meetings told Pladsen that other states had expanded Medicaid coverage in this way, and wondered if Maine might do the same.
“When I had read the other waivers and talked to other states about the opportunity, it just seemed like a no-brainer,” Pladsen said.
Maine joins Arizona, California, New Mexico and Oregon, which had similar waivers approved in 2024. It’s the first eastern state to take the step. CMS last week approved a similar request from Utah, bringing the total to six states nationwide.
The expansion must be budget neutral, under the terms of federal approval. The hope is that upstream interventions prevent downstream costs, Pladsen said, and any reimbursements under the program are billed to the federal agency, not the state.
“Our communities should never have to choose between the medicine of our ancestors and the coverage that makes care possible,” William Smith, board chairman of the National Indian Health Board, a national advocacy nonprofit, said in a statement. “(The) decision honors both, and it honors the trust and treaty obligations this country owes to Tribal Nations.”
Tribal members and their families seeking care from one of the five clinics operated by tribal governments in Maine, or from Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness, a statewide public health nonprofit, will be eligible. Over half of Wabanaki Public Health’s clients are on MaineCare, said the organization’s co-CEO Lisa Sockabasin, including 100% of those at its Bangor-based detox center.
Cochran’s department serves almost 600 people, while the statewide Wabanaki public health agency reaches over 7,000 people annually.
Sockabasin said the tribal health providers are looking to extend care beyond just treatment for substance use to fields including chronic disease and mental health as well.
“Tribal healing practices have been in our communities for thousands of years,” said Sockabasin, who is Passamaquoddy. “And those tribal ceremonies and practices and tradition provide immense healing for our community.”
Over the next year, leaders from healthcare providers will work with state Medicaid officials to determine exactly what practices will be covered by Medicaid, and how much clinics will be reimbursed for them.
Tribal knowledge-keepers have continued to use ceremonies to heal members of their communities even without a mechanism of government financial support, leaders emphasize. And they always will. Although there’s never a charge for those ceremonies, they do consume resources.
“Rather than having them adapt their cultural practices to our systems, we need to adapt our systems to their cultural practices,” Pladsen said.
It is an odd moment, Sockabasin acknowledged, in which traditional practices that are typically shared relationally within communities are to be assigned a dollar value.
But it’s also an opportunity for collaboration and for mutual growth, she said.
“We’re becoming more aware, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people, on what it takes to heal. We are both learning.”
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: Early voting for the November election is underway in Maine. Here’s how to do it
text:
Early voting has begun in Maine ahead of the Nov. 3 election, which features a high-profile set of races for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House, alongside State House and local contests.
Mainers can vote early for any reason from Monday through Oct. 29, and they can do so by casting a ballot in person at their local town office, returning their absentee ballot by mail or using a ballot drop box in their community.
Here are a few things to know about early voting.
Where and when can I vote early in Maine?
Early voting locations, hours and absentee ballot drop box locations for each municipality are available on the Maine Department of the Secretary of State’s website and its “Upcoming Elections” page.
On that page, voters can view and download the “Municipal Office Hours & Absentee Drop Box Locations” form, which lists each town’s office hours and drop box locations. Some towns offer early voting Monday through Friday, while others are only a few days per week or by appointment.
If a municipality does not have a listed address for a drop box, contact your town office. The “Find a Municipal Clerk or Registrar” page on the secretary of state’s website has a searchable database of contact information for local election officials.
The last day to vote early is Oct. 29, the Thursday before the Nov. 3 election. Mainers can also register to vote online or in person through Election Day. Visit registertovote.sos.maine.gov to register, update voter registration information or change party enrollment.
How do I vote by mail?
The deadline to request an absentee ballot is also Oct. 29. Absentee ballots must be returned to a municipal clerk by 8 p.m. Nov. 3, and unlike several states that allow ballots to be counted if they are at least postmarked by Election Day, only ballots received by the close of the polls on Election Day are counted in Maine.
To request an absentee ballot and find out more information about ballots for voters with disabilities and voters who are in the military or overseas, visit the “Absentee Voting” page on the secretary of state’s website.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said during a Monday morning news conference in Brunswick that laws regarding early voting and absentee ballots have not changed. That was a nod to President Donald Trump, who long criticized mail-in voting and proposed changes that were blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court but is now urging Americans to vote early.
“We have all unfortunately experienced frustration with the Postal Service and things from everyday mail to prescriptions not arriving in a timely manner,” Bellows said. “That’s why it can be so helpful to vote early.”
How do I track my absentee ballot?
Maine voters can track the status of their absentee ballot at absenteeballotrequest.sos.maine.gov.
How many Mainers have voted early so far, and what’s the breakdown by party?
The secretary of state’s office posts updated reports on absentee requests each Tuesday and Thursday. Ahead of the start of early voting, the office reported that 70,260 Mainers had requested absentee ballots, more than 45,000 ballots had been issued so far, and nearly 800 ballots had been returned and accepted.
About 57% of the absentee ballot requests were from registered Democrats, 14% from Republicans and 26% from unenrolled voters. The early gaps have narrowed in past elections as Election Day gets closer, though Democrats typically outpace Republicans in absentee voting.

title: ‘The Breadwinner‘ Contains Some of the Worst Product Placement Ever
text:
‘The Breadwinner‘ Contains Some of the Worst Product Placement Ever
“You gotta put in work.”
That’s the lesson learned by Nate Bargatze’s character in The Breadwinner, the comedian’s first attempt to translate his hit standup act to the big screen. Bargatze plays an ordinary guy named Nate (next-level galaxy-brain casting) who loves his family in a disinterested sort of way. He’s the breadwinner, you see, while his wife Katie (Mandy Moore) performs the traditional housewife duties of cooking and cleaning and taking the kids to and from school.
Then Moore’s character becomes a successful inventor and needs to go on a prolonged business trip, which means Nate must take a sabbatical from his job to care for their three daughters — with predictably disastrous results in the short term, and valuable life lessons learned about the importance of “showing up” in the long term. Hence: “You gotta put in the work.”
That may not be the only way in which Bargatze is “putting in the work” in The Breadwinner, which was a flop in theaters but is currently among the most-watched films on Netflix. He plays a salesman onscreen — and he works as a salesman throughout the movie as well. The Breadwinner is as much a story as it is a shameless vehicle to pitch viewers a whole bunch of products and chain retailers. This movie is selling stuff to the audience from literally its very first shot to its very last. I am hard-pressed to think of another recent film with so much egregious product placement.
Don’t believe me? See for yourself.

title: Portland man sentenced to 16 years in prison for fatal West End stabbing
text:
PORTLAND — Debra Kelly felt a rush of relief as the man who killed her son walked out of the courtroom.
She sat quietly on a Cumberland County Courthouse bench Monday as the judge read the sentence for the Portland man who was charged in the fatal stabbing: He will serve 16 years in prison on one count of manslaughter for killing 43-year-old Matthew Merrick.
“When I’m holding his picture, I feel like his soul is here,” Kelly said. “It makes me realize that justice is happening.”
Domingus Nobrega, 49, killed Merrick in November 2024 at the apartment they shared on Marshall Street in the city’s West End. A witness reported seeing Nobrega stab Merrick, and the medical examiner’s office determined Merrick died from stab wounds to his chest.
Nobrega was originally charged with murder in the killing. He agreed in August to plead guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter.
Kelly stood beside a photo of Merrick when she addressed the courtroom Monday afternoon, telling the judge how much she loved her son. She said Merrick would have turned 45 on Oct. 1.
Friends and family have said Merrick grew up in the Portland area and worked as a self-taught cook.
Kelly said in an interview after the hearing that her son was a kind and jovial man who checked in with her often. She wore a necklace and earrings with cardinal symbols because the bird reminds her of Merrick.
“I’m relieved,” Kelly said of the sentencing. “It feels like a weight off my shoulders. I can carry on. That’s the good part.”
Investigators say a woman who was staying at Nobrega and Merrick’s apartment saw the stabbing, and that Nobrega took her into another room, gave her drugs and asked her to blame the killing on someone else. She later identified Nobrega through a photo lineup while speaking with police.
During the hearing Monday, Nobrega brought a hefty file of documents, some of which he wanted to file in the courthouse. Superior Court Justice John O’Neil said those records referred to debts, expatriation and renouncing his citizenship. O’Neil agreed they could be added to Nobrega’s courthouse file but said he could not make rulings on any issues in the documents.
Kelly said she never met Nobrega, but she sometimes visited his and Merrick’s apartment to take her son angel food cake, his favorite dessert. She said she would have wanted Nobrega to receive a longer sentence if prosecutors had more evidence.
Attorney William Maselli, who represents Nobrega, said after the hearing that the plea deal was negotiated in good faith by both sides.
Assistant Attorney General Kate Bozeman said during the hearing that the agreement resulted in a lesser sentence than prosecutors would’ve typically asked for because of “the loss of some of our witnesses and the evidence that they brought with them, as well as the desire to have some finality for Matthew’s family.”

title: Tim Stutzle powers Ottawa Senators past Boston Bruins
text:
BOSTON — Tim Stutzle had two goals and an assist and goalies Linus Ullmark and Samuel Ersson combined to stop 18 of 19 shots as the Ottawa Senators defeated the Boston Bruins 4-1 on Monday night.
Stutzle’s multi-point game moved him into sole possession of sixth place for most points in Ottawa history with 413.
Ullmark started in goal for Ottawa, but wasn’t on the ice at the start of the third period. The onetime Bruin netminder, who stopped all 10 shots he faced in the first two periods, was on the bench five minutes into the final period. Ersson made eight saves in the final period for the Senators.
Ottawa’s Michael Amadio had a goal and assist, and Drake Batherson also scored.
Boston rookie James Hagan spoiled Ottawa’s shutout bid with a goal in the third period. Jeremy Swayman made 20 saves for the Bruins, who have lost two straight after opening the season with two wins.
Boston was outshot 24-19 and failed to score on four power plays.
Stutzle came close to two short-handed goals on the same power play. He scored on the man advantage at 7:39 of the first. Seconds after Ottawa successfully shut down Boston on the power play, Stutzle scored on a 2-on-1 chance, making it 2-0.
Batherson scored 66 seconds into the second period, taking advantage of a Boston turnover and scoring with a backhand shot.
Amadio converted on a feed from Shane Pinto to give Ottawa a 4-0 lead, prompting Bruins head coach Marco Sturm to call at timeout at 14:41.
Ullmark was slow getting up after Boston’s JJ Peterka crashed into him at 4:25 of the second. The 2022-23 Venza Trophy winner with Boston is in his third season with Ottawa after being traded before the 2024-25 season.
Up next
Senators: At Detroit on Tuesday night.
Bruins: Host Utah on Thursday night.

title: Monday Five and Five: County Champions and a Big Week Ahead
text:
The Monday Five and Five: PVC Champions, Top-10 Runs and Big Rematches Ahead
Another week of fall sports is in the books across Aroostook County, and this one had a little bit of everything.
We saw County champions crowned on the golf course, local runners compete against one of the largest cross country fields they will see all season, a goal scored with less than a second remaining, and plenty of offense on the soccer field.
Now, with the regular season moving deeper into October, some familiar County matchups are coming back around and the stakes continue to grow.
Here is this week's Monday Five and Five.
The Five Best From Last Week
5. Hailey Plant Beats The Clock For Presque Isle
This one was about as dramatic as a regular-season soccer game can get.
Presque Isle and Foxcroft Academy appeared headed toward a 2-2 finish Tuesday before Hailey Plant scored the game-winner with less than one second remaining, giving the Lady Wildcats a 3-2 victory.
Carrlyn Buck and Emily Collins also scored for Presque Isle, while Delanie Cyr added two assists.
4. Ava Ezell Puts Together A Six-Goal Week
Houlton's Ava Ezell had a big week offensively for the Lady Shires.
Ezell scored four goals and added an assist in Houlton's 6-1 victory over Van Buren on Tuesday.
She came back Saturday with two more goals as Houlton defeated Old Town 4-2.
That gave Ezell six goals and an assist across the two Houlton victories.
3. Katahdin Scores 16 In Saturday Sweep
Both Katahdin soccer teams filled the net Saturday against East Grand.
The Cougar boys earned a 7-0 shutout, led by three goals and an assist from Conor Schmidt. Leighton Rodgerson added a goal and two assists, while Gage Phillips recorded the shutout in net.
Katahdin's girls followed with a 9-1 victory.
Add it together and the two Cougar teams scored 16 goals in one afternoon.
2. County Runners Make Their Mark At Festival Of Champions
Aroostook County runners went to Belfast Saturday and held their own against a massive Festival of Champions field.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault finished seventh overall in the boys race with a time of 16:01.17, while Emma Graves placed eighth in the girls race at 19:06.96.
Houlton/GHCA put four runners inside the top 66 and finished ninth among 79 scoring boys teams.
Presque Isle had Lillian Johnson finish 19th and Aleah Rideout take 23rd, helping the Wildcats finish 12th in the girls team standings.
It was a strong showing for County cross country against competition from throughout Maine and New England.
1. Presque Isle Sweeps The PVC Golf Titles
Championship performances earn the top spot this week.
Patrick Collins shot a 74 at Hermon Meadows to capture the PVC boys individual championship, winning by two strokes.
Alice Korzekwa made it a Presque Isle sweep, shooting an 86 to win the girls championship.
Presque Isle also finished second in the team competition and qualified for the state championship.
Two individual champions and a state tournament berth made Thursday a big day for Wildcat golf.
Five Big Things To Watch This Week
5. Presque Isle Hits The Road
The Wildcats have a busy Class B North soccer week away from home.
The Presque Isle boys are scheduled to visit Orono Monday before the girls make the same trip Tuesday. The boys then head to Foxcroft Academy Thursday.
Saturday brings another road doubleheader, with Presque Isle scheduled to face Ellsworth in girls soccer at noon and boys soccer at 2 p.m.
With October underway, every one of those games becomes another opportunity to build momentum heading toward the postseason.
4. A Big Home Week For Caribou
Caribou also has plenty on the schedule.
The Vikings are set to host John Bapst in a makeup doubleheader Monday before Fort Kent comes to Caribou for Senior Night games later in the week.
The boys host Fort Kent Wednesday night, with the girls matchup following Thursday.
Then Hermon comes north Saturday for another Class B doubleheader, with the girls scheduled for noon and the boys at 2 p.m.
3. Fort Fairfield And Central Aroostook Meet Again
Thursday night should provide another good County doubleheader when Fort Fairfield visits Central Aroostook.
The girls are scheduled for 5 p.m., followed by the boys at 7.
Central Aroostook is coming off a sweep of Easton, while Fort Fairfield's girls beat Van Buren last week and the Tiger boys closed Saturday with a scoreless double-overtime tie against Bangor Christian.
It is another County rivalry worth keeping an eye on as the regular season moves toward its final weeks.
2. Presque Isle Golf Heads To States
After sweeping the PVC individual championships, Presque Isle now turns its attention toward the state tournament.
The Wildcats qualified as a team, while Patrick Collins and Alice Korzekwa are also among the individual qualifiers following their PVC championship rounds.
The MPA currently lists the Class B and Class C team and individual championships for Saturday, October 10, at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro.
After what Collins, Korzekwa and the Wildcats accomplished at Hermon Meadows, state championship weekend will be one of the biggest events involving a County team this week.
1. Two Big Rematches In Ashland
Tuesday may provide the most interesting night of County soccer this week.
Katahdin's boys return to Ashland after the Cougars won the first meeting 2-1 in double overtime earlier this season. Conor Schmidt scored both goals in that game, including the winner.
Then Central Aroostook and Ashland meet again in girls soccer.
Their first matchup was one of the best County games we have seen this fall, with Ashland edging Central Aroostook 3-2 in a meeting between two of the top teams we had been following in Class D North.
Two rematches, two established storylines and four familiar County programs make Ashland the place to watch Tuesday.

title: Police say man killed wife, took children and forced family member to drive to another state at gunpoint
text:
WINFIELD, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - A man was arrested after allegedly killing his wife, taking two children and forcing a family member to drive to another state at gunpoint.
According to the Winfield Police Department, officers responded to a call about a possible homicide at 4:34 a.m. Saturday.
The suspect contacted a sheriff’s office in North Carolina and told them he had shot and killed his wife. The sheriff’s office then contacted the Winfield Police Department.
Police said when they arrived at the home, they found a woman who had been shot and killed lying in the kitchen.
After the alleged shooting, the suspect left the home with two children and held another family member at gunpoint. The family member was forced to drive to North Carolina.
The family member was able to escape and provided investigators with detailed information about the alleged shooting.
The suspect is in custody and the two children and family member are safe, according to police.
The identities of the man and his wife have not been released.
