title: The Latest: Soldiers seriously wounded in Iranian drone strike tell AP the US military failed them
text:
U.S. soldiers wounded in the Iran war’s deadliest strike yet on American troops are raising concerns publicly, many for the first time, about whether commanders underestimated the threat. Some of those wounded also said the military medical system failed them. The Pentagon has so far released few details about the Iranian drone strike on Port Shuaiba in Kuwait that killed six soldiers on March 1, the day after the U.S. and Israel started the war against Iran.
Now entering its eighth month, the war— and its upheaval of the economy — is dragging down Republican candidates as Americans begin voting in the midterm elections. President Donald Trump takes his GOP rescue mission on Monday Nebraska, where ranchers are rebelling against record diesel prices and Trump’s plans to import more beef. Democrats meanwhile are expressing confidence that Trump’s redistricting efforts will backfire.
The Latest:
US is monitoring Russian health scare tied to plague institute
Rubio, who doubles as Trump’s National Security Advisor, says he doesn’t think there is cause for alarm after Russian officials quarantined a hospital and confirmed they are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an “unknown” cause.
But Rubio said the U.S. is closely watching the case, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.
“There’s very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia, obviously,” Rubio said. “But like anything else, something like that gets out.”
Marco Rubio says the Saudis and Yemeni government ‘have a right to defend themselves’
The secretary of state said it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels to try to reclaim territory.
Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the U.S., Rubio told reporters that Saudi Arabia and the U.S. have a defense agreement but wouldn’t offer more details.
He says the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis have come under attack, and “they have a right to defend themselves.”
He says the coalition’s offensive is a counter to that, and the U.S. “expected that would happen, and that’s what happened.”
The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
Marco Rubio downplays US moving bombers from UK base
The U.S. secretary of state told reporters Monday that that Pentagon “is constantly reallocating resources” as he downplayed the significance of removing American bombers from a U.S-run base in England that has been used to attack Iran.
The move came after an investigation into a suspected terror plot on the base.
“I wouldn’t just directly tie that to the move that was made,” Rubio said as he prepared to depart for a multi-stop diplomatic mission that begins in Iceland.
“It’s not unusual to see rotations happen and moving into the different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployment, changing out and new people coming in, in planes coming in, old planes going out,” Rubio said. “So, birds are changing all the time.”
AP-KFF poll: Rural MAGA voters support Trump’s immigration policies
Rural Republicans who consider themselves MAGA supporters are about twice as likely as rural, non-MAGA Republicans to see a benefit to Trump’s immigration policies, the AP-KFF survey found.
About two-thirds of rural MAGA Republicans say Trump’s immigration policies have had a positive impact where they live. Roughly half say the Trump administration has “not gone far enough” on deporting immigrants in the country illegally, while about half say the actions have been “about right.”
Katherine Reed, a 27-year-old Republican who supports the MAGA movement, believes the administration’s policies have had a positive impact by reducing violent crime nationwide, saying, “It’s made life for people a lot safer.”
She believes if someone comes to America, they should “respect the law of the land” and do it legally. “I want really amazing people to become Americans,” Reed said. “That’s the whole point of America.”
Soldiers seriously wounded in Iranian drone strike tell AP the US military failed them
As the war with Iran enters its eighth month, U.S. soldiers wounded in its deadliest strike yet on American troops are raising concerns publicly, many for the first time, about whether commanders underestimated the threat. Some of those wounded also said the military medical system failed them. The Pentagon has released few details about the Iranian drone strike on Port Shuaiba in Kuwait that killed six soldiers on March 1, the day after the United States and Israel started the war against Iran.
The Associated Press spoke with 13 soldiers, primarily officers, serving in key positions of responsibility there or familiar with high-level briefings. Many said the Pentagon did not take Iranian threats seriously enough as it launched Operation Epic Fury. Some of the wounded soldiers said they’ve faced inadequate medical care and bureaucratic barriers since then. Several soldiers spoke on the record — rare for troops still in the Army — others on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.
By Julie Watson, Jack Brook, Konstantin Toropin and Russ Bynum
An Army investigation was done in June and remains unreleased
The Army declined to comment on the AP’s reporting on the Port Shuaiba strike, saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation into the attack. The Pentagon also declined to comment.
“Out of respect for the primary next of kin who will be scheduled for briefs on the official findings of the completed investigation, we will not comment on specific details, individual accounts, or leaked portions of the report at this time,” the Army said in a statement.
The Army completed its investigation of the attack in June, but has yet to release a report due to the need to redact sensitive information, said an official familiar with the Army’s investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because the report has not been released.
“We have the right to know what really happened,” said Tina Marzan, whose husband, Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert Marzan, was killed in the strike.
By Julie Watson, Jack Brook, Konstantin Toropin and Russ Bynum
Families of killed soldiers demand answers, wounded still struggle for medical care
Nine U.S. service members wounded in a March 1 drone strike on a U.S. military site in Kuwait that killed six troops spoke to The Associated Press about what they describe as a medical system that left them fighting to get treatment on their own. The soldiers’ criticism comes against the backdrop of years of disinvestment and drawdowns in the Middle East driven by multiple administrations and political leaders who sought to end U.S. involvement in the region.
The Pentagon has said all soldiers were treated appropriately and evaluated by physicians who followed the health industry’s standards.
Chief Warrant Officer 4 Rodney Bearman, who had shrapnel embedded from his face to his legs, said they waited 10 days for treatment in Germany only to learn they wouldn’t be hospitalized because they weren’t documented as wounded in combat, and so were told to get outpatient care.
“Never did I think that if I was wounded that these things would happen,” said Bearman, who has served for over three decades, including in Afghanistan. “Some sacred trust that I thought would never be broken was broken.”
By Julie Watson, Jack Brook, Konstantin Toropin and Russ Bynum
Sen. Raphael Warnock launching midterm blitz that includes 2028 early primary states
The Georgia Democrat plans to campaign with Democratic candidates for Senate, governor and possibly other offices across eight states beginning Tuesday in New Hampshire, which falls third in Democrats’ 2028 presidential primary calendar.
Nevada is second on Warnock’s itinerary and for Democrats in 2028. The senator has two separate stops planned in South Carolina, Democrats’ first presidential primary state. Also on the list is the early primary state of Michigan, along with Mississippi, North Carolina, Wisconsin and Ohio.
Spokeswoman Elena Radding said Warnock will be “calling out Trump’s corruption” and “leaving voters hopeful for the next generation of Democratic leadership.”
Warnock, who is also the senior minister at Atlanta’s Ebenezer Baptist Church, where Martin Luther King Jr. served, has not ruled out a presidential bid. He’s already spent recent months traveling the country on a book tour — another common move for potential national candidates.
AP-KFF poll: Trump’s immigration crackdown divides rural voters
Voters in rural parts of the country are divided on whether Trump’s immigration policies have benefited or harmed their communities, according to a newly released AP-KFF survey of more than 2,000 rural voters.
About one-third of rural voters said the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement had been positive for their community and about a third said it had been negative. The remaining 3 in 10, roughly, said it had no impact.
Laura Leigh Taylor, a 37-year-old farmer who voted for Trump in 2024, said she disapproves of the wide-ranging scope of Trump’s immigration crackdown, which resulted in a friend’s hardworking father being deported.
“I understand getting rid of the rapists and the murderers,” she said. “But all the people that fell in between that really weren’t doing nothing but taking care of their family.”
Trump campaigning in Nebraska, where ranchers are rebelling over fuel prices and beef imports
President Donald Trump is taking his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska. He’ll campaign Monday alongside GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who’s being challenged by an independent candidate backed by national Democrats.
The race between the former Nebraska governor and independent Dan Osborn initially was not expected to be competitive, but voters across the country are frustrated with Trump’s handling of the economy, including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. Rural voters in particular are hurting, and ranchers have rebelled against Trump’s efforts to increase imports of foreign beef.
“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”

title: Franklin County Sheriff’s Report, September 26th – October 2nd
Creating a culture of respect: “Walk a Mile in Her Shoes” event returns to UMaine
text:
Across the nation, campus culture has been at the forefront of conversations this week. For many students, instances of sexual and domestic violence can be difficult to report or discuss for fear of not being believed. It can be hard to draw attention to these issues, and knowing how to do so in a respectful way can be even harder. One event aiming to eliminate this stigma, called “Walk a Mile in Her Shoes,” took place Thursday, Oct. 1.
Throughout the week, there was a campout on the mall, which was intended to highlight the 24-hour helplines operated by Partners for Peace and Rape Response Services. Both events were organized by the Sigma Phi Epsilon chapter at the University of Maine to raise awareness of these issues, especially among those who may not fully understand them. Mason Hartery, a second-year student studying financial economics and finance, serves as the “Brothers Engaged Against Sexual Assault” chairman for SigEp and began planning the event in July.
This was the second year that the “Mile in Her Shoes” event was hosted at UMaine, and it is meant to simulate the experience of a woman walking home from a night out in high heels. Men are the only competitors in the event. Hartery said this is because they “will never know what it’s like to be a girl coming home from a night out.” The event aims to “open guys’ eyes to the other side of things.” The playful nature of the event is meant to bring campus together, but Hartery reiterated that “it’s important to remember the why.”
The proceeds are split between Rape Response Services and Partners for Peace, both of which had resource tables at the event, along with the university’s Conduct Office and Title IX Student Services.
Hartery placed a lot of the focus on the larger purpose of the event, and he feels as though “[Walk a Mile] is bigger than SigEp and the organizations that participate.” When talking about the message that the event presents to campus, Hartery said it’s about “showing people that these issues are larger than them and showing the importance of community and support on campus.”
Although it was not planned in response to recent events, “Walk a Mile in Her Shoes” served as a reminder that in dark times, finding solace in community is essential for morale. When it feels like these instances constantly make the news and the only thing that is done about it is a statement, with no actions to follow, it can be disheartening and easy to lose faith.
UMaine offers confidential advisors who are trained in issues such as domestic and sexual violence. In addition to this, the Counseling Center is free to all students and appointments can be set up by phone. As for resources outside of campus, Rape Response Services has trained individuals available by phone at +1 (800) 871-7741 to talk about sexual assault and Partners for Peace has a 24-hour abuse helpline that can be reached at +1 (800) 863-9909. These organizations also provide emergency shelter in addition to other resources.
So is this another one-off support event to check a box? Hartery specified that the BEASA chairman holds “multiple events a semester to support both organizations” and that “[Walk a Mile] is their biggest, so it gets more attention.”
Last year, the event raised more than $900 for the organizations. Though resources for those affected by abuse and sexual violence are available in many forms, it is particularly important for campus organizations to support their peers. Additionally, Hartery said that it is “important for the general community” on campus to know they are supported and that the chapter aims to make “campus as comfortable and welcoming as possible.”

title: Millions automatically enrolled in Trump Accounts. Here’s how you can claim it for your child
text:
(Gray News) – The U.S. Department of the Treasury announced automatic enrollment is complete for Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under age 18.
American children born between Jan. 1, 2025 and Dec. 31, 2028 are eligible for $1,000 in seed money for the accounts.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said millions had already enrolled, with more than 60 million more eligible children now having an account ready to be claimed.
“This is a transformative milestone in the Trump Administration’s effort to give every American child the opportunity to build generational wealth and jump-start their financial future,” Bessent said.
How to claim your child’s account
A parent or guardian must claim the account to manage it and allow contributions from family, friends and employers:
- Download the official Trump Accounts app (iOS and Android)
- Verify identity and relationship to the child
- Review the child’s information and accept the account terms
Eligible children must also have their Trump Account claimed to receive the one-time $1,000 seed contribution from Treasury.

title: Haunted trails and trunk-or-treats: Western Maine readies for Halloween fun
text:
Western Maine communities are filling the October calendar with harvest celebrations, Halloween parties, trunk-or-treats and other seasonal activities. Here is a guide to some of the events announced so far.
Oct. 10
Haunted Chandler Farm, 31 Chandler Road in Strong, will hold its annual Trunk or Treat from 4 to 5:30 p.m. Oct. 10. Vehicle setup begins at 2 p.m. Organizers are inviting participants to decorate their trunks and are hoping to have 35 vehicles take part in the free event. 
Oct. 15-17
McLaughlin Garden and Homestead, 97 Main St. in Paris, will hold its 13th annual Jack-O’-Lantern Spectacular from 6 to 8:30 p.m. Oct. 15-17. This year’s theme is “Enchanted Forest,” with hand-carved and illuminated pumpkins displayed throughout the garden. Admission is $8 per person or two for $15 and includes warm spiced apple juice.
Oct. 17
Wilton Free Public Library will hold Harvest Day from 10:30 a.m. to noon at 6 Goodspeed St. The annual fall celebration will feature a cider press, face painting, games, crafts, animals and other seasonal activities.
Livermore Falls will hold the Hillside Annual Pumpkin Walk from 5-8 p.m. Oct. 17 at the Livermore Falls Recreation Field. Families are invited to walk among illuminated pumpkins, and costumes are encouraged but not required. Children and families can carve pumpkins earlier in the day from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. at AMVETS Post 33 in Jay. The finished pumpkins will be displayed at the recreation field during the evening walk. Organizers are also seeking donations of pumpkins, carving kits, battery-operated pumpkin lights, food and beverages, monetary contributions and volunteers.
The Sandy River & Rangeley Lakes Railroad will hold its Ghost Train in Phillips, with the Little Ghost Train for younger children from 5-6 p.m. and the regular Ghost Train from 6:30-9 p.m. at Sanders Station, 128 Bridge St. Related activities at the Phillips Area Community Center, 21 Depot St., will include a costume contest, popcorn, fortune telling, face painting, potions and treats. Community groups will also create themed scenes along the railroad route.
Oct. 24
Friends of Starling Hall and Fayette Central School will hold Halloween activities from 3:30-5 p.m. At Starling Hall, 2769 Main St., children can walk through a Hundred Acre Woods-themed Trunk or Treat, collect treats from decorated vehicles, hear Halloween stories at the fire station and enjoy popcorn and drinks.
Fayette Central School, 2023 Main St. in Fayette, will offer additional Halloween games and activities during the same time, organized by school and library staff.
Farmington Recreation Department will hold its Indoor Spooktacular from 3:30-6 p.m. at the Farmington Community Center, 127 Middle St. Children can trick-or-treat indoors, wear costumes, take family photos, play mini fall games and vote for their favorite exhibit. The free event is open to children 15 and younger. Children must be registered for one of five half-hour sessions between 3:30-6 p.m. Businesses, clubs and organizations may also sign up to create exhibits.
Oct. 28
Treat Memorial Library in Livermore Falls will hold a Story Time Pumpkin Tea Party at 10:30 a.m. Inspired by the children’s book “Mr. Pumpkin’s Tea Party,” the program will include stories, songs, rhymes and a seasonal craft. Costumes are encouraged but optional.
Oct. 29
The Jay-Niles Memorial Library in Jay will show “Frankenweenie” from 4-5:45 p.m. The Halloween-themed family movie screening is free.
Oct. 30
Jay-Niles Memorial Library will hold Halloween Storytime at 10:30 a.m. Costumes are encouraged, with child-friendly costumes requested. The program will include spooky music, a story, a craft and other activities and is free and open to all.
Treat Memorial Library will hold its annual Halloween Spooktacular beginning at 4 p.m. The event will feature games, spooky snacks, autumn crafts, interactive storytelling and a Skeleton Scavenger Hunt through the library. The program is free and open to the public.
Oct. 31
The Jay Recreation Committee, Androscoggin Land Trust and community partners will hold the fourth annual Halloween Boo Bash from 10 a.m. to noon at French Falls Park in Jay. Organizers say more than 250 children have participated in each of the event’s first three years. Individuals, families and organizations are invited to help provide activities and treats.
Paris Parks & Recreation will hold its Halloween Festival from noon to 3 p.m. at Moore Park. The free event will feature a costume contest, pumpkin decorating, a caramel apple bar, carnival games, face painting, cotton candy and popcorn.
Bethel’s Trick or Treat Street will be held from 1-3 p.m. along Greenwood Avenue and the Municipal Center lawn. Families can collect candy from participating businesses and community organizations. A pumpkin decorating contest will begin at 1 p.m., with a costume contest and awards ceremony following at 3 p.m. The event will be held rain or shine.
Jay-Niles Memorial Library will hold a Trunk-or-Treat from 3-5 p.m. at 983 Main St. Families can visit decorated vehicles and collect Halloween treats during the free community event.
The Maine Mineral & Gem Museum, 99 Main St. in Bethel, will hold Halloween at Maine Mineral and Gem Museum from 4-8 p.m. Admission will be free during the event, with goodie bags for visitors and glowing dinosaurs hidden throughout the exhibits for a Halloween scavenger hunt.
Our Village Market, 1798 New Vineyard Road in New Vineyard, will hold its fourth annual Trunk or Treat from 4-7 p.m. Oct. 24. Families are invited to attend the community Halloween event, and residents or organizations interested in bringing a decorated vehicle may contact Sherry or Lexi at Our Village Market at 207-652-2277.
Kingfield’s seventh annual Trunk or Treat will be held from 5:30-6:30 p.m. at the Gateway parking lot, 171 Main St. Families are invited to come in costume and collect treats from decorated vehicle trunks and tables. Community members may participate by decorating a vehicle or setting up a Halloween-themed table. For more information, contact Leanna Targett at 207-491-8092.
Livermore Falls will host a trunk-or-treat behind the Town Office from 4-6 p.m. Oct. 31. Also, the Livermore Falls Fire Department will hold its Haunted House will host its Haunted House from 5-8 p.m. at the fire station, 15 Park St. The department will transform the station into a Halloween walkthrough with themed displays and spooky surprises for families and groups.
Wilton’s annual Trunk or Treat and Halloween Walk will run from 6-7:30 p.m. Trunk or Treat will be held at Kineowatha Park, while participating homes along High Street will be marked for families taking part in the Halloween Walk. Wilton Parks & Recreation is accepting candy and monetary donations and is seeking additional participants to decorate vehicles. High Street residents who want to participate may contact Wilton Public Safety at 207-645-3876 or [email protected].

title: Hartland murder case inches to trial amid discovery disputes, competency issues
text:
SKOWHEGAN — Attorneys for a 70-year-old Garland woman charged in the shooting death of her 78-year-old sister in Hartland were in court Monday asking a judge to further sanction prosecutors for failing to hand over information when they were required to.
The mental competency of Bonnie Coombs, meanwhile, has also been called into question. At the request of her court-appointed attorneys, James Howaniec and Mitchel Roberge, Superior Court Chief Justice Robert E. Mullen last week ordered an evaluation of Coombs.
Coombs’ mental state has “declined significantly” during her 17 months in the Somerset County Jail, wrote Howaniec in a court filing. Unless she is deemed incompetent, the evaluation should not delay an upcoming trial, he wrote. A report is due to the court by the end of October.
The competency determination and a slew of evidentiary issues raised by Coombs’ attorneys need to be straightened out before trial, which was recently postponed. It is now set to start the first week of December at the Somerset County Superior Court.
Coombs is charged with one count of intentional or knowing murder in connection with the April 9, 2025, death of her sister, Velma Withee.
Three days after Withee is believed to have died, Withee’s son and daughter-in-law discovered her body between a pickup truck and camper trailer outside her home at 456 Canaan Road in Hartland, police affidavits state. Police and prosecutors believe Coombs was the last person to see Withee alive, although they have not publicly pointed to a clear motive for the killing.
The two were seen together on Withee’s route for her trash collection business April 9, 2025, and the clothes she was wearing that day matched the clothes on her dead body. Investigators found blood and a small caliber bullet in Coombs’ vehicle that matched Withee’s DNA profile.
Police characterized voicemails that Coombs left for Withee after her death as attempts to make it seem like she was unaware of what happened. Police also believe Coombs knew more than she should have about the circumstances of Withee’s death before that information became public.
Coombs was arrested in June 2025, two months after her sister’s death. She pleaded not guilty and has been held in jail without bail since.
The trial had been set to begin this week, but Mullen delayed it in August as part of an order sanctioning prosecutors from the Office of the Maine Attorney General for failing to provide certain information to the defense in a timely fashion.
The judge ruled that prosecutors did not disclose the existence of a jailhouse informant to Coombs’ lawyers for months and excluded evidence from that person from being introduced at trial. He also ruled a Maine State Police detective’s analysis of cell tower and cellphone records would be excluded from trial, unless Coombs takes the witness stand.
Among the issues raised at Monday morning’s hearing was whether prosecutors can call another state police detective — not acting as an expert witness — to testify about the cell tower data.
Roberge argued that would basically be a backdoor maneuver to get around the sanction Mullen imposed and said the data should not be introduced at trial whatsoever.
Assistant Attorney General Kate Bozeman said the other detective would be testifying in amore limited way. And, she said, the records prosecutors would present would show, without any expert knowledge or training, just that Coombs’ phone pinged a tower in Hartland the morning after Withee’s death.
In another dispute over the exchange of discovery, Coombs’ lawyers asked Mullen on Monday to prohibit prosecutors from bringing in any expert testimony about an analysis regarding gunshot residue in Coombs vehicle. In the SUV, detectives found Withee’s blood and one of two bullets they believe killed her.
But Howaniec said prosecutors and police did not test samples collected in June 2025 for gunshot residue until nearly a year later, only after he hired his own expert to provide an opinion.
Testing subsequently requested by the state and conducted in Pennsylvania found only one unknown particle in the samples from the vehicle. Prosecutors provided him with a report in May.
If Coombs killed Withee in the vehicle, there should be millions of particles of gunshot residue, Howaniec said. He and Roberge want to point out that apparent discrepancy as they challenge prosecutors’ theory that Coombs shot her sister in the car, where the blood and bullet were found.
“We’re going to be raising questions about the forensic evidence in this case, the forensic analysis,” Howaniec said. “We’re going to be raising questions about possible contamination of the crime scene … but also the analysis of the interior of that Ford Explorer.”
Bozeman said that even though investigators did the testing after the discovery deadline this spring, prosecutors still should get a chance to offer a response to the expert Coombs’ attorneys want to call to testify. And Coombs was not unfairly prejudiced by any delay because her attorneys already have an expert lined up to testify, Bozeman said.
Mullen did not make rulings Monday on either the cellphone data or the gunshot residue experts, along with two other requests from Howaniec and Roberge to exclude evidence.
At the close of the two-hour hearing, he called them “interesting issues” and asked the lawyers to provide him with relevant case law by the end of the week.
Maine prosecutors’ handling of discovery is not a new issue but has come into focus recently. In a Supreme Judicial Court decision last month on a criminal appeal, Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill put prosecutors on notice, expressing her “increasing alarm at the frequency with which the state of Maine is violating its simplest discovery obligations.”
Roberge cited Stanfill’s statement in a court filing about the gunshot residue report.
“We’ve gotten so much late discovery in this case,” Howaniec said.

title: US military says latest strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean kills 4
text:
US military says latest strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean kills 4
The U.S. military said it attacked a boat suspected of being used to smuggle drugs in the Caribbean Sea on Sunday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its yearlong campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America.
Related video: What matters to veterans and military families ahead of the midterms?
The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 235 in 70 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” in September 2025. As with most of the military’s statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes.
The military did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. A video posted on X showed what appeared to be an explosion destroying a moving boat, which the military said was a go-fast vessel.
The Trump administration is pursuing deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama in August that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March.
President Donald Trump has said the U.S. is in “armed conflict” with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing smugglers.

title: ‘Days of Our Lives’ actor Robert Kelker-Kelly dead at 62
text:
(Gray News) — “Days of Our Lives” actor Robert Kelker-Kelly died Saturday. He was 62.
TMZ was the first to report his death.
Kelker-Kelly was best known for playing Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives” from 1992 to 1995, according to his IMDb page.
His character arc often revolved around Lisa Rinna’s character Billie Reed.
Earlier this year, Rinna revealed in her memoir “You Better Believe I’m Gonna Talk About It” that the two did not get along on set, going so far as to say Kelker-Kelly was “verbally abusive” and “manipulative.”
Kelker-Kelly also appeared in other series including “Port Charles,” “Touched by an Angel” and “General Hospital.”
According to TMZ, Kelker-Kelly was also a professional pilot.
Kelker-Kelly died at his home in St. Peters, Missouri, according to Deadline. St. Peters police responded to his home for a report of an unconscious man who was not breathing.
Deadline reported the actor complained of chest pain shortly before coming unresponsive, police said. His official cause of death has not been revealed.

title: Healthcare advocacy group launches bus tour in Bangor
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Polling shows healthcare affordability is a major issue for voters this election.
One group is traveling the nation hoping to mobilize voters against Republicans, saying the current administration has taken a wrecking ball to the system.
Protect Our Care’s “Sick Of It” Fix Healthcare Now bus tour kicked off Monday in Bangor.
It was the first of nearly 40 stops the organization’s bus, dubbed Care Force One, is making coast to coast.
The group is bringing together local advocates at each stop to protest Medicaid cuts and changes to the Affordable Care Act while promoting the restoration of tax credits to lower premiums and extending out of pocket pay caps to people with private insurance.
“These cuts affect everybody because it’s a health care system. And so doctors and hospitals have to charge more to make up for the money they’re not getting. So that means pretty much everybody is facing higher health insurance premiums,” said Laura Packard, cancer survivor.
“If we had a system like a Medicare for all system or some other form of universal health care like every other industrialized country in the world has, we could actually provide some comfort and relief to people so they wouldn’t have to worry about slipping and falling on the ice and then looking at bankruptcy because of it. So this is really, really important,” said Maine CD2 candidate Matt Dunlap.
Dunlap also said the cost of gas is limiting affordable healthcare as many Mainers need to travel to get to medical appointments.
The bus plans to make 35 stops in 15 states over the next four weeks.

title: A look inside the oldest bike company in America
text:
CONWAY, S.C. (InvestigateTV) — Sparks fly, tools turn, and workers assemble parts of made-to-order industrial-grade bicycles, recreational bikes, and trikes at the Worksman Cycles factory in Conway.
“We made a commitment to stay in America,” Sosin said.
Today, his bikes are mostly built in America with some necessary help from imported and domestic parts.
“We’re as close to made in America as you can get,” Sosin said. “We weld our frames, we powder coat our frames here, we assemble the bikes, we build the wheels, and that’s highly unusual because virtually every other bicycle sold in the United States is an imported bike in its complete form.”
Sosin gave a tour of the process, from powder-coating specialty frames to hand-building the wheels and assembling the bikes themselves.
Sosin said he enjoys making rides for everyone to enjoy.
“We make adult tricycles for seniors, and we also do tricycles for people with ability challenges,” Sosin said. “That’s been one of my favorite things to get involved in. It’s very gratifying.”
The company is also building opportunities so all groups can succeed.
“We tapped into a few different special communities like the deaf community and given those people a great opportunity, and they turned out to be wonderful workers for us, so that’s been very rewarding to us as well,” Sosin said.
Sosin takes pride in what they build and believes a bike is more than a machine.
“If we were manufacturing a product I didn’t believe in, or didn’t find fun or rewarding, I’d probably be retired at this point,” Sosin said. “It’s been a great ride.”
When asked about his favorite part of being on a bike, Sosin said, “It’s just freedom. It reminds me of being a kid again, the wind in your hair, whatever hair is left.”

title: Tap ensemble in Myrtle Beach brings adults back to dance after decades
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A tap ensemble in South Carolina is made up of adults who are returning to tap dancing after stepping away for careers and family responsibilities.
Michele Selvanto-Kowalski spent more than 45 years teaching tap in New Jersey before moving to Myrtle Beach in 2014. She teaches all ages at Coastal Dance Center.
“I get chills when I teach it, I get chills when I talk about it,” Selvanto-Kowalski said.
Selvanto-Kowalski said the adults in her classes impress and inspire her the most.
“Their passion in the tap class, they just kept going and going… and that’s when I said, ‘You know what?’ Something clicked and said, ‘Let’s do this,’” Selvanto-Kowalski said.
Carolina Rhythm Tap Ensemble
Selvanto-Kowalski created a group for adults called the Carolina Rhythm Tap Ensemble.
“It gives them an opportunity to get out there and maybe pursue a dream that they always had but couldn’t do,” Selvanto-Kowalski said.
Aging Untold expert Katherine Ambrose said the ensemble is proof it’s not too late to return to a passion.
“When you pause a dream for work and family, it’s so great to be able to come back to it, and doing it with a group adds connection and belonging, which is important at every stage,” Ambrose said.
Some of the dancers in the ensemble grew up tap dancing but stopped to focus on careers, family and children.
Weekly practice and performances
The women practice choreography once a week and take tap classes to perfect their technique before performing in the community.
Ambrose said tap dancing also provides brain-and-body fitness.
“Tap is brain-and-body fitness at the same time. We’re talking balance, coordination, rhythm and memory all working together, and it can boost stability and confidence in everyday life,” Ambrose said.

title: One of these 8 sites could hold Aroostook’s next jail
text:
Eight properties are in the running to be the location of Aroostook County’s next jail.
The sites, submitted in response to a land search launched by the county last month, include both public and privately owned land along or near the Route 1 corridor. They include three parcels in Caribou, two in Houlton and one each in Presque Isle, Limestone and Fort Fairfield.
The potential jail properties were included in a document summarizing responses to the county’s request for land proposals that County Administrator Justin Tibbetts shared with the Bangor Daily News on Monday. They have not been previously reported.
The wealth of bidders gives Aroostook County options as it moves to replace its 137-year-old jail in downtown Houlton that federal corrections experts have called overcrowded and unsafe. County administration will review sites over the next few weeks with SMRT Architects & Engineers, Tibbetts said.
The County hired SMRT in May to design its next jail. The company can evaluate up to five locations under the terms of its contract.
The sites cost from $1 to more than $1.8 million. The cheapest bidders are towns or quasi-governmental agencies who are seeking to reap the economic benefits of housing the jail and not one-time profits from a land deal.
Two towns, Houlton and Fort Fairfield, submitted bids, as did the Loring Development Authority, which controls most of the former Loring Air Force base in Limestone.
Houlton’s proposed parcel is the biggest, comprising 115 acres in the Houlton Industrial Park and along Route 1. The document does not specify a specific address or price, but the town indicated it would sell the property for low to no cost.
Fort Fairfield submitted a 33-acre lot at the end of Cheney Grove, an industrial area off Route 161 and near Route 1A. The town’s asking price is $1.
The Loring Development Authority offered a 33.6-acre portion of the former Air Force base known as the Tactical Alert Site. The authority also indicated it would sell the property for low to no cost and that it had potential alternative sites on the former base.
The remaining five bidders are all private landowners. They include a “15+” acre site on the Access Road in Houlton for $375,000, a 15-acre plot at 34 Woodland Road in Caribou for $139,900, an 19-acre parcel that borders both Montgomery Avenue and Route 1 in Caribou for $725,000, a 54-acre former mobile home park on Route 1 along the northern outskirts of Presque Isle for $1.3 million and a 73-acre lot between Cary Medical Center and the NAPA Auto Parts store in Caribou for $1.83 million.
A consultant estimated in a needs assessment released last summer that the price tag to construct the jail could range from $91 million to $112 million, depending on its size, but construction costs have risen since.
In that assessment, the consultant recommended that the jail be located either in Houlton or in the vicinity of Presque Isle and Caribou, more central to The County’s population centers.
The report concluded that population shifts have made the existing jail’s location “less than ideal.” The jail was originally built in Houlton because of a former statutory requirement for the facilities to be in the county seat, but that puts it at least a two-hour drive away from many towns in the St. John Valley.
“There were indications from some agencies located to the north that a number of arrests are regularly not made in an effort to reduce trips to the current jail,” the report noted.
Presque Isle, Aroostook County’s biggest city, declined to submit a proposal for the jail to be built on municipal land, citing that it did not have a “suitable parcel” that could accommodate it.
But in a letter sent by City Manager Sonja Eyler to county leaders obtained by the BDN, Eyler outlined that the city’s council “unanimously” supports locating the jail in central Aroostook to “create a facility that is more accessible to the people and systems it must serve.”
Moving the jail outside of Houlton would require a referendum, one of the major points the town referenced to keep the facility in the county seat.
“There’s really no other viable option to keeping [the jail] in Houlton,” Houlton Town Councilor Fred Grant said in a Sept. 22 special meeting in which the Council approved its proposal.
A bond referendum to fund construction of the facility could come before voters as early as next year.

title: 1 CMMC nurse reinstated after September firings at Lewiston hospital
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
One Central Maine Medical Center nurse will return to work this week after being fired in mid-September, according to union officials in a press release issued Monday night.
The nurse, who was not identified, was among 20 who had been disciplined last month for “documented violations of established hospital policies and standards,” according to CMMC officials last month.
At the time, several city leaders criticized the hospital, which is owned by California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation, saying the terminations were retaliation for a unionizing effort among the nurses.
Local leaders from across the political spectrum said the firings appeared to be related to recent union activities at the hospital, which would be in violation of state and federal law, and demanded the nurses be reinstated.
“Nurses were unlawfully disciplined for our patient advocacy,” said Hillary Ferrell, former nurse at Olympia Fields Hospital in Illinois, another Prime hospital where six nurses were terminated during a unionization effort last month. “But we will never stop speaking up for our patients. Our patients and our community deserve safe staffing and safe patient care,” she said in the press release.
At Olympia Fields, four fired nurses had been re-instated by Monday night.
Nurses at Olympia Fields won their union election with 82% support on Sept. 23 and CMMC nurses won their union election with 91% on Sept. 24.
The announcement that a single CMMC nurse will return to work came from the National Nurses Organization, an affiliate of the National Nurses United union, at almost 8 p.m. Monday night.
The group said they are continuing to fight on behalf of the remaining nurses who were either suspended or fired.
“Prime needs to reinstate all nurses who were suspended or fired,” said Katie Grinnell, a former nurse at CMMC. “Also, Prime must stop challenging our overwhelming victory at the ballot box. We won our union election by a landslide.”

title: Early voting starts Monday across Maine. Here’s how to do it.
text:
Mainers can vote early by absentee ballot at all municipal offices starting Monday through almost the rest of October ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
High turnout is expected again in a state where nearly 61% of eligible voters cast ballots in the 2022 midterm, according to the U.S. Elections Project. Only Oregon was higher.
Chiefly driving out voters this year will be Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ race for a sixth term against Democrat Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash. It’s one of the biggest races in the country and already the most expensive in Maine history, with more than $176 million in ad reservations since Jackson became the nominee in late July.
That election, along with others for governor, Congress and the Maine Legislature, will be taking shape as Mainers vote. Collins and Jackson have agreed to four debates. The first one is Tuesday, the day after early voting begins.
Maine allows no-excuse absentee voting, and that system doubles as the state’s form of early voting. You can fill out an absentee ballot in person at your municipal office now through Oct. 29, the Thursday before the election.
If you want to vote absentee and return your ballot by mail or in person to your local clerk, you can request one through the state’s online form or at your municipal office. The state recommends allowing seven to 10 days to get your ballot if you request one less than a month before the election.
New voters and those who have moved from one municipality to another can register to vote online until 5 p.m. on Oct. 13. Registrations sent by mail, including those from voter registration drives, must reach your town clerk by that same day. You can also register at any Bureau of Motor Vehicles office until 5 p.m. on Oct. 27.
Voters can register in person at their city or town office at any time up to and including Election Day. You can also register at your polling place on Nov. 3. If you do that, you must show proof of residence at your address, such as an ID or a utility bill.

Central Maine Power may defer work on Bridgton substation
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Power may defer ongoing work on a substation in Bridgton if a proposed $70 million temporary rate hike is not approved.
The substation, which serves 1,900 customers in the Bridgton area, is currently in the middle of an upgrade, a CMP spokesperson said. The substation has structures with rotting poles, with work being done on the poles following temporary actions to shore up the structures. Design and permitting work for the project is complete.
If the rate hike is not approved, work on the substation could be deferred.
This comes as the Maine Public Utilities staff recommended against approving the request on Sept. 26, which would add about $7 per month to the average household bill.
The increase was requested in April to soften the “significant financial distress” hitting the utility, which saw its financial outlook downgraded this summer to “negative” under a $100 million cash flow deficit.
This is not the first infrastructure project CMP has delayed amid the dispute over the rate increase. Work on the Baldwin Resiliency Project, a large-scale plan to upgrade the power grid in Baldwin, Sebago and Steep Falls, was delayed until certainty around the funding could be established.
Bridgton Town Manager Donald Kasprzak said Bridgton was aware of the substation that would be affected should CMP choose to delay work. Kasprzak said the town would “certainly like” to see the substation upgrade move forward, but the town’s priority was stabilizing CMP rates for residents and business owners.

title: Maine ICE observers added to DHS database, unsealed court records say
text:
A federal immigration agent added eight Maine residents to a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database in January, including several observers of immigration enforcement activity, according to newly unsealed court records.
One woman, Caryln Williams, was held by U.S. Customs and Border Protection while returning from a trip to Quebec as a result of being in the Department of Homeland Security’s Investigative Case Management (ICM) system. An agent testified that he added her to it after her car was observed at a location where multiple people were recording federal agents on Jan. 20, according to court records in a lawsuit against DHS.
But Williams wasn’t driving her car that morning, her spouse was.
Williams was “not physically present, or in any other way present, at the scene of the Jan. 20 encounter with this ICE agent,” Williams’ attorney JoAnna Suriani said on Monday.
Williams, her partner Polyxenia Pantos, and two other Maine residents are suing DHS, accusing the agency of violating their First Amendment rights. The federal lawsuit alleges that agents threatened to add observers in Maine to a database for “domestic terrorists.” A motion from the plaintiffs filed last week, citing depositions and other evidence that remains sealed, states that an agent added Williams to the ICM system, an existing database used by DHS to document cases by Homeland Security Investigations.
Attorneys for DHS stated in a motion to dismiss the case that the agent — an HSI Boston officer, identified as “J.C.” — added eight people to ICM who “he believed posted potential threats to law enforcement.”
The plaintiffs say in their filings that six of those people were observers.
DHS has denied any allegations of wrongdoing, including the existence of a database for domestic terrorists.
A spokesperson for DHS did not address questions from a reporter about the case Monday, but maintained the agency does not run a database for domestic terrorists. Attorneys for DHS did not respond to a request for comment.
The plaintiffs asked the court in the motion to issue an injunction before trial, barring agents from retaliating against observers with threats of a database and other tactics, like driving by protesters’ homes or calling them.
“Once you are in that database, or a database like it … the reach of where that data goes, including who has access to it, and what it can be used for in the future, is, in my opinion, very chilling,” said Suriani, an attorney with the nonprofit Protect Democracy, which is representing the plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs are also asking that Williams’ classification in the ICM database be modified, so she can travel internationally without being automatically detained or subject to a second inspection by border officials.
Attorneys for DHS have said in hearings and court filings that the government has a policy to protect observers and protesters who engage in First Amendment activity, and that agents receive relevant training. In March, the government also argued that only a few agents in Maine were recorded by observers talking about a database for domestic terrorists, and that those agents violated DHS policy.
No agents were disciplined, the plaintiffs argued in court records, citing depositions that remain under seal at the government’s request. Suriani also disagreed with characterizations that the agents were “rogue.”
According to a motion filed by Williams’ attorneys, the agent identified as J.C. testified during a deposition that he added Williams to the ICM database as an “aggressive woman (who) interject(ed) herself into an arrest.” The motion alleges that he also called Williams hours after Pantos was seen recording ICE agents, identifying himself only as someone from DHS and encouraging her to tell Pantos “not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist.”
Documents filed last month by the government identify J.C. as “Mr. Coleman.” Attempts to reach Coleman through social media, email and DHS were unsuccessful.
The plaintiffs’ motion also states that agents have continued driving by the homes of people who film and protest them. One agent said in his deposition that this was meant to “show them that we knew who they were” and “have them stop following us,” according to the plaintiffs’ filing.
This is the plaintiffs’ second time asking for pretrial relief. U.S. District Judge John Woodcock denied their request for a temporary restraining order against DHS in March, ruling that he didn’t have enough evidence to merit such an emergency measure.
In their latest filing, the plaintiffs said most of the agents whom they deposed said they considered the Maine observers to be interfering with immigration arrests. Plaintiffs have denied interfering with arrests.
“The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that’s what we’re asking the court to stop,” Suriani said.
Both sides are still responding to the government’s motion to dismiss, and the plaintiffs’ motion for preliminary injunction. A hearing for either request has not yet been scheduled.
The ICM database is hosted by software company Palantir, according to a statement the company released in 2022 and recent reporting by Wired. A spokesperson for Palantir declined to comment Monday.

title: Letter: Support election workers, and vote
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Elections are always complex. Now they have been made fraught. Outcomes have always been anxiety making. Now we are forced to contend with the process itself. Mainers vote. In fact, we are consistently a leader in the nation in voter participation.
Until recently, protecting and facilitating our citizens’ voting rights was a bipartisan effort. In the past years, our governor, secretary of state, and attorney general have had to join other “blue state” officials in going to court to protect the privacy of our own voter data and our state’s right to conduct elections.
Conducting elections has always presented logistical challenges. Now it presents personal danger — from a riled up and resentful minority of Americans and the full force of a federal government ruled by a party desperately running scared of losing its majority.
Behind the scenes, there are our neighbors working to facilitate a regular process and reliable results, as they always have. They have always been on the frontlines, now they are in the crosshairs of especially nasty voter suppression efforts.
We here in Maine are fortunate in election officials and workers faithful to our national and state constitutions, to their oaths, to their mission, and to our communities. For the good of the nation and us all. They deserve our admiration, support, and protection.
As early voting begins, and the weeks culminate in Election Day, let us honor our hard won rights and our brave neighbors’ hard work — with our full and respectful participation.
Annlinn Kruger
Bar Harbor

title: The ego has invaded American politics
text:
Ron Snyder lives in Dexter.
Our church, like many churches, is experiencing an attendance decline that is causing financial challenges. This week I encountered a church leader who was, in my opinion, disrespectful to me and our pastor. For reference, there was nothing done that I would consider illegal, only disrespectful.
However, this caused me to decide that I needed to review the church leader’s and the church’s performance as if I were doing a business turnaround. In so doing, one must always look at the product being marketed and with whom the business is competing and then determine why the poor performer is not keeping pace.
This analysis led me to a conclusion I had previously given little thought or consideration: A church is really a business that markets behavioral laws. They may also provide shelter and lease instructors, but they also employ managers and have a management structure to manage and control their operation.
But with whom are they really competing? The clue came when my pastor said she was not allowed to talk about politics.
Who, besides churches, provides moral and behavioral rules that humans must follow? The answer was geographical leaders or government and political leaders.
In some countries, religious leaders take over governing the country’s inhabitants. In others, political leaders take control and provide laws that take precedence over religious leaders. The answer became even clearer when one looks at how they are funded. One collects tithes, the other taxes and each’s leaders decide how they are redistributed.
This turned me to the U.S. Constitution and prompted the question of, “How are we prepared?”
Surprisingly, our founders prepared us very well if we use the tools they included in our Constitution 250 years ago. First, they recognized the power struggle between religious leaders and territorial government leaders. They solved this by including freedom of religion. All church leaders were welcomed to participate in America’s leadership.
But the second part of their planning and analysis displays even more foresight. They included a plan and provision to address leaders’ egos. They provided set terms: representatives, two years; presidents, four years; senators, six years. Additionally, they provided a procedure to impeach an unsatisfactory leader during his or her elected term. And more importantly, they left administration in the hands of the inhabitants of the territory being represented: voters.
Our founders did not provide for political parties. Political parties were a method devised by egotistical government leaders to divide voters and disperse money collected in taxes. However, the Constitution’s writers did also plan for this and point us in the direction our representatives and we, the voters, need to go to make America great again.
Whether in church or state, we need to remove the egotistical leaders who want to collect our tithes and taxes and distribute them as they see fit and replace them with ones who will work for all of us and distribute our labor for the benefit of all mankind. In America, as long as political parties and churches exist, this means voters must register independent and insist on implementing ranked-choice voting.
I urge you, the voter, to truly make America great again.
Be respectful of your neighbors and insist that your representative represent you and address the ego issues that have invaded and overtaken our leadership. If they don’t, you have the choice in November. And for you Christians who believe the U.S. is a Christian country, remember Jesus was not a member of a Christian church. He was a Jewish rebel in the Jewish synagogue who took offense to the way church leaders treated mankind.
Good luck, America, and regardless of your church affiliation, God will prevail.

title: This program promotes reading for kids before they get into kindergarten
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - A Missouri six-year-old is reading more books than many people read in a lifetime.
Pew Research in the past found that the average American reads about 12 books a year. An elementary student outside of St. Louis crushed this number by reading 1,000 books before he entered kindergarten.
Malachi Henderson, 6, started kindergarten in the fall, shortly after completing the 1,000 Books Before Kindergarten program at the St. Louis County Library.
The program is designed to encourage childhood literacy through reading amongst caregivers and children.
The program encourages reading by allowing families to track each and every book. And the more books you read, the better the prizes get.
“If we can get children excited about reading and thinking it’s something fun that they want to do when they’re young, they’ll keep striving as they are learning, even when it is a little bit difficult,” said Laura Polak, who helps run the program for the library system. “By third grade, they’re learning by reading, so building this foundation early on really sets children up for future success.”
Childhood literacy is a critical predictor of long-term academic and life success.
Studies have shown that third graders not reading at grade level are four times more likely to drop out of high school. Lower proficiency in reading can also lead to lower income, poor health outcomes, and even higher incarceration rates.
Malachi’s mom, Angel Dallas, said as a child she often observed her own mother reading around the house.
“I grew up in a home where we had books and things to read and we were always at the library and I always saw my mom reading and it was just very inspiring to me at a young age,” said Dallas.
So, when Dallas was pregnant with Malachi, she began reading to him. Once he was born, she discovered the library’s program and slowly began crossing books off the list.
When Malachi was three-years-old, he was reading on his own, she said.
“Reading is the foundation for every other subject possible and that’s why it was always important for me for Malachi to know how to read, to recognize words to know different words,” she said. “His language is also advanced and teachers are telling me that he’s on track to be in the gifted program when he gets into elementary school.”
Malachi and his mother now share the same passion for reading, always making room for a new book on the shelf.
Hundreds of libraries nationwide participate in the program and you can find a list of branches in your state as well as resource to start the journey at home on 1000booksbeforekindergarten.org.

title: 2 people killed, including a student, after Florida school bus rolls over in crash, sheriff says
text:
WINTER HAVEN, Fla. (AP) — A school bus flipped over onto its roof during a multivehicle crash in central Florida on Monday morning, killing two people — including a 10th grade girl — and injuring several others, authorities said.
Some 39 people were on the school bus that was headed to Winter Haven High School in Winter Haven when an oncoming car crossed the center line and caused the crash, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said at a news conference.
“It was a horrible crash,” Judd said. “It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life.”
The bus had been traveling along a Winter Haven road shortly after 6 a.m. when an oncoming car crossed the center line and crashed into the side of the bus near the rear wheels, Judd said. The impact ripped the tire off the bus and caused it to crash head-on into an oncoming Jeep, which caught on fire.
One person in the Jeep died. Judd said five to seven people were transported to the hospital with potentially traumatic injuries and that one person remained in critical condition early Monday.
The bus was transporting 39 people in all — 37 high school students, the bus driver, and the bus driver’s daughter. Judd said first responders spent the first several hours getting people to the hospital, identifying them and reuniting students with their parents.
“I think this is the most horrific bus tragedy we’ve had in decades, as far back as I can remember,” Judd said.
Just over a month ago on Sept. 3, another Polk County school bus was involved in a crash in Lakeland. Authorities said no students were on the bus at the time, and one person had injuries that were not life-threatening.
Polk County Public Schools Superintendent Frederick Heid said students practice drills on how to leave a bus that is involved in an accident.
“This event could have been far worse. You can see the condition of the bus, you can see its current positioning,” Heid said. The sheriff and superintendent held their news conference directly in front of the overturned bus, which had come to rest in a ditch beside the road.
Justin Sharpless, chairman of the Polk County school board, asked the community to come together to support the family of the girl who died, as well as the school and school staff.
“There are really no words that can take away the pain of losing a young person,” he said.

title: Good 4 ME: Guacamole Chicken Melt
text:
Hannaford Dietitian Mary Lavanway has a recipe for a Guacamole Chicken Melt.
4 Servings | Active Time: 0:05 | Total Time: 0:15
Ingredients:
- 4 Boneless, Skinless Chicken Breasts, about 2 lbs.
- 2 tsp. Chili Powder
- Salt and Pepper, to taste
- 2 Tbsp. Olive Oil
- 1 cup Guacamole
- 1/2 cup Shredded Mexican Cheese Blend
Directions:
- Place oven rack 6 inches from broiler. Heat broiler on high.
- One at a time, add chicken breast to a resealable plastic bag. Using a meat tenderizer or heavy rolling pin, flatten breast to an even 1/2-inch thickness. Transfer flattened breast to a plate and repeat.
- Season chicken breasts with chili powder and salt and pepper, to taste.
- In a 12-inch oven-safe skillet, heat oil on medium. Cook chicken breasts 4-5 minutes per side, until fully cooked.
- Top with guacamole and cheese. Broil 1-2 minutes, until cheese is melted and bubbly.

title: NBA is experimenting with smart basketballs and official wrist wearables in select preseason games
text:
NBA is experimenting with smart basketballs and official wrist wearables in select preseason games
The NBA is experimenting with two pieces of technology in the lead-up to the season, the league announced Monday.
Select exhibition games will include a smart basketball that has a Bluetooth sensor in it and can collect data for future use in real-time officiating decisions. The league said the information from the Wilson-developed connected balls will be for research only and not affect calls made during those games.
Officials in select games will also use wrist wearables to communicate with the replay center in designated situations, including replay reviews, scoring changes and clock malfunctions.

title: Augusta Schools propose closing Hussey Elementary, expanding Farrington
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Augusta superintendent’s office has formally announced plans to close Hussey Elementary and expand Farrington Elementary, but the decision is ultimately up to local voters on election day.
The proposal calls for additions to Farrington Elementary and the closure of the Lillian Hussey School. The planned additions to Farrington include a universal pre-k model, 19 new classrooms and a designated STEM space.
The total cost of the project is about $53.5 million, to be reimbursed by the state. Superintendent Mike Tracy, of Augusta Schools, said construction would not be paid for by Augusta taxpayers.
Tracy said the project was approved under the state’s prior district funding model, making it the last project in Maine to qualify for full state reimbursement.
“I think it’s a once in a lifetime opportunity, especially with the law that just changed where local towns will have to have a local share for any future building projects,” Tracy said. “So, the fact that we’re on the last project at 100% state funded is a really big deal.”
The new state rule requiring a local contribution started July 1.
If approved, the district says construction would begin in summer 2028 and finish in summer 2030.

title: VIDEO: Take a flight with Jake, the air traffic controller who flies himself to work
text:
Meet Jake, the air traffic controller who flies himself to work
Jake Hutzler spends his workdays directing planes from an airport tower. Once a week, he gets there by strapping a propeller to his back and taking to the skies of Colorado.
Before his commute, the 28-year-old air traffic controller lays out a large wing on the road outside his apartment complex, fires up the motor and starts running. Within seconds, his feet leave the ground.
Meet Jake in the video player at the top
For the next 20 minutes, Hutzler flies at a leisurely 35 mph above the expansive fields around Pueblo, a city near the Front Range mountains. He soars over a highway, a water tower, and finally the airport while listening to his favorite music.
Before taking off, Hutzler calls the tower where he works and lets his colleagues know he's coming. Once airborne, he keeps them updated on where he's at and how high he's flying.
“I’m very small, and I don’t show up on radar,” Hutzler said, “so they’ll want to kind of keep track of my location and get updates on my progress.”
As the airport comes into view, he waits for the OK to land on the airport’s ramp. Pulling down on toggles to slow down the paramotor, he lets his feet dangle and meets the ground with a brief jog. He packs up the wing, strips off his jacket to reveal his collared work shirt and begins his shift telling planes when it's safe to land and take off.
‘A view that almost nobody gets to experience’
For someone who has been fascinated with flying since childhood, it's a particularly satisfying commute. Hutzler says it's as close as you can get to flying like a bird.
“In a paramotor, you have a view that almost nobody gets to experience,” he said. “You have no cockpit, nothing in front of you. You’re just sitting there in the air and total freedom to go wherever you want.”
Want more content like this? Subscribe to our News We Love newsletter here.
His grandfather used to take him up in a small four-seat aircraft. In college, Hutzler put in about 20 hours toward getting a pilot's license, but the costs were too high for him to continue.
Everything changed when he came across a viral video of a man flying a paramotor to McDonald’s and eating his hamburger on the flight home.
“After I saw that, I was like, ‘I’m sold,’” he said. “I gotta do that.”
Flying became a family affair
Hutzler started training to fly the contraption — also known as powered paragliding — in 2021 in Florida and later became an instructor.
Part of the appeal is just how accessible paramotors are. There’s no license required and the price tag is a fraction of the cost of many other forms of flying. However, they're still subject to federal rules on ultralight vehicles, including that they can only be operated during the day and fliers must avoid congested cities and towns.
The sport became a part of Hutzler's life story. He trained the woman he would go on to marry, and when he was ready to propose he used fake engine trouble on his paramotor to lure her to the contraption, where he had left a ring. On their wedding day, their paramotors were with them at the altar. Now he’s looking forward to the day their 2½-year-old daughter is old enough to go on a tandem ride.
But after Hutzler started working in air traffic control earlier this year, his job left him less time to fly.
The solution: Start flying to work.
He approached his manager about commuting by paramotor and they went through the rule book and made sure he'd have two-way communication with the tower when he entered their airspace. He made his first flight to work in June and has been doing it ever since, weather permitting.
But paramotoring is a very fair-weather sport. It only takes about 10 mph (16 kph) of wind — basically a light breeze — to keep Hutzler on the ground. It can also be problematic if the sun heats the ground and causes updrafts — making for an extremely bumpy ride.
The airborne commute isn't actually faster
With the time needed to set up the paramotor and put away all the gear, the trip takes slightly longer than driving to work. But, he said, it’s so much more fun.
“You could be having your favorite song playing in your headphones, and you just can relax and take in this awesome experience,” he said.
___
Golden reported from Seattle. Associated Press transportation writer Josh Funk contributed from Omaha, Nebraska.

title: Pres. Trump promises checks for seniors
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is promising government payments to senior citizens, with just a month to go until the midterm elections.
It’s a move aimed at helping those on Medicare, so the president is promising $90 checks to more than 20 million seniors.
The White House said the $90 payments for seniors will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund. Medicare Part B enrollees can expect to receive a one-time payment sometime this month - either by direct deposit - or by a check in the mail.
To be eligible, seniors must be living in the U.S. and not be already receiving premium assistance from Medicaid.
In addition, seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage are also not eligible for the payment.
Senator Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) accused the president of trying to bribe the electorate. He issued a statement:
“This year, Trump handed seniors a $200 monthly Medicare premium for the first time ever, and he also shoveled $20 billion in extra payments to insurance companies selling private Medicare plans, This is another desperate attempt by a failed president to escape Americans’ revulsion with his failed agenda, amounting to one tank of Trump-inflated gas.”
President Trump has also promised to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. That payment - which would cost more than $1 trillion - would need approval from Congress, although the president has indicated he thinks he might be able to issue those checks without lawmakers approval.
