title: Anger in Japan grows after US Marine is arrested over the killing of a woman on Okinawa
text:
TOKYO (AP) — The arrest of a U.S. Marine on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman on Okinawa has drawn condemnation from Japan’s leaders and renewed protests against the heavy American military presence on the southern island.
The alleged killing could complicate Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to strengthen Japanese military defense on the island and to work more closely with the U.S. military to deter China in the region.
Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island’s capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.
Security camera footage showed a man wearing a black top, trousers and white sneakers entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone.
Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported.
“I’m outraged and flabbergasted to hear that a suspect came to the (entertainment area) after committing a murder,” Kenji Higa, who lives in Okinawa City, told the Okinawa Times.
There is longstanding anger over the behavior of some Americans
People in Okinawa have long been wary of the U.S. presence on the island but many have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China.
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America’s military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today.
There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.
After the 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members, huge crowds protested the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. There was also anger over the rape of a teenage girl by a U.S. service member in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the crime.
About 160 people gathered at a protest Sunday in Naha, condemning the crime and renewing demands that U.S. military bases be removed from the island.
One sign read: “We’ve had enough of this!”
Japanese officials condemn the crime
“The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters Sunday night in Naha. “It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged.”
Koja said the case underscored the ineffectiveness of past disciplinary measures taken by the U.S. military following similar crimes.
“I’m enraged by the loss of a precious life of an Okinawan resident,” Koja told Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and U.S. Consul General in Naha, Andrew Ou on Monday when he summoned them to the prefectural government. He demanded that U.S. officials take effective preventive measures.
Watson replied: “I recognize the serious incident caused significant concern and anxiety among the residents of Okinawa, our neighbors” and that “we are committed to being good neighbors … and earning the trust of the Okinawan people.”
In Tokyo, Takaichi condemned the crime and demanded full cooperation and tougher disciplinary and preventive measures by the United States.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi also summoned U.S. Forces Japan Commander Lt. Gen. Stephen Jost to his ministry, while Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi expressed his outrage to the U.S. ambassador to Japan, George Glass.
The suspect will face Japanese justice
Glass, on X, expressed his condolences Sunday to the victim’s family and said the United States is cooperating with Japanese authorities.
On Monday, he said he is telling U.S. military commanders of the need “to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity” and that he and Watson discussed the “next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities.”
Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base.
Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect’s case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in coming weeks.
If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.

title: Special education needs growing more complex, Farmington schools find
text:
FARMINGTON — Regional School Unit 9 is seeing increasingly complex special education needs, even as its overall identification rate remains relatively steady, driving expansion of specialized programs, staffing, training and transportation services.
Director of Special Services Cynthia Bernstein said the district has seen significant changes in the types of services students require over the past five years.
Identification of students with specific learning disabilities has decreased by nearly 31% during that period, while autism identification has increased nearly 26%. Identification under other health impairments, including attention challenges or anxiety, has increased 67%.
Bernstein said the local increase in autism reflects a broader rise in diagnoses as well as students entering the district with existing needs.
“Each year students who transfer into the district come to us with these challenges, including new kindergarten students and this year pre-K students,” Bernstein said.
She also pointed to the effects of disrupted education during the COVID-19 pandemic and difficulty accessing services outside school.
“Families are struggling with accessing necessary community support, rural options are few, to help their children learn and use the life skills we are teaching in school,” she said.
While the overall percentage of RSU 9 students identified for special education has remained relatively consistent, Bernstein said the level and type of support needed has changed.
Life skills program services have increased, and include adaptive behavior services for eligible students. Speech and language, occupational therapy and physical therapy services expand as students’ developmental needs require them, while day treatment services continue across grade levels as students grow older.
The changing needs are shifting resources toward behavioral, adaptive and executive-functioning supports and have required smaller, more individualized programs.
RSU 9 has also reduced out-of-district placements by 50% over five years, although additional students would be placed outside the district if space were available.
Asked how the district is serving students whose needs might otherwise require an outside placement, Bernstein said the number changes from year to year.
“The district is focusing on solutions for students whose skills require a program that is more specialized than what can be provided in a public school building,” she said.
That work includes development of such a program as part of the special education services offered by Mt. Blue. The district’s special services budget has increased 19.5% over five years, from about $7.02 million in fiscal 2022 to about $8.38 million for fiscal 2027.
Bernstein identified staffing, training and transportation as the primary factors behind the increase. “The necessary expansion of programs has increased the need for skilled staff,” she said.
Training is provided before and throughout the school year so employees can develop and practice skills needed to serve students. The district also contracts with staffing companies when required positions cannot be filled by educators hired directly by RSU 9.
Transportation needs have also become more specialized. Based on student needs many times this is individualized in separate vehicles.
Staff preparation has been another major focus. More than 135 employees received SafetyCare training before the school year began, 22 educational technicians were being trained as behavioral health professionals, and nine professional staff members were receiving training to administer the Woodcock-Johnson V Test of Achievement.
Bernstein said staff training is one of the department’s strengths.
“I would say the things that we do best … are probably getting staff trained,” she said. The district is also evaluating whether its current safety training adequately addresses staff needs.
Bernstein said RSU 9 moved more training from the school year to the summer two years ago to reduce staff absences from classrooms and programs, a change that increased costs. During the past year and a half, the district has gathered staff feedback, reviewed administrator observations and examined changing student needs.
“These factors influenced the district’s investigation of additional behavior support programs that provide a more specific focus on student trauma and functional backgrounds and skills,” Bernstein said.
RSU 9 is also expanding services for younger children. The district is providing special education services for 4-year-olds through school-based pre-K programs, an adaptive skills pre-K and kindergarten program and community settings.
Bernstein said the district is preparing to take on services for 3-year-olds next year as well. The combination of younger students entering services and more students requiring intensive programming means the district will continue tracking staffing, space and program needs as it plans for future years.
RSU 9 includes Chesterville, Farmington, Industry, New Sharon, New Vineyard, Starks, Temple, Vienna, Weld and Wilton.

title: President Trump says he might be visiting Maine before Election Day
text:
President Trump says he might be visiting Maine before next month's election
President Donald Trump left the White House on Monday to fly to Nebraska, where he will be campaigning for incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, who faces a strong challenge from independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Before he boarded Marine One, Trump spoke with reporters and said he will be campaigning in Michigan, where former Congressman Mike Rogers (R) is squaring off with Abdul El-Sayed (D) for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
Trump was then asked if he will visit Maine, where incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins is facing a challenge from former State Senate President Troy Jackson (D) as she seeks a sixth term.
"I don't know about Maine. I think we're going to Maine, too," Trump said. "But I'm going to Michigan in about a week and a half."
On Wednesday, Trump will make his second stop in Texas within the span of a week to campaign for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn in the primary but still faces a tough test in the general election against Democratic State Rep. James Talarico.
Trump has also visited Oklahoma, Alabama and Ohio within the past week.
"We're sort of scheduled to be someplace almost every night," the president said.
The race between Collins and Jackson in Maine could help determine the balance of power in the Senate, as the Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber. Both Senate candidates are set to take part in an hourlong debate on WMTW Channel 8 at 8 p.m. Thursday.
Maine also has another race that could sway the balance of power in Congress, as State Auditor Matt Dunlap (D) and former Gov. Paul LePage (R) are running to represent the 2nd Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives. Incumbent Congressman Jared Golden (D) announced in November 2025 that he would not be seeking reelection. Democrats need a net gain of three seats to take control of the House. Dunlap and LePage participated in an hourlong debate on WMTW Channel 8 last week.

title: Portland band Small Pond creates a lush indie sound
text:
My love for the Portland-based indie rock band Small Pond started as an ember a few months ago. Now I’m all in and can’t wait to see them perform live.
Consider yourself enthusiastically nudged to get on board. This is a band that makes dreamy yet fully formed indie rock that is mesmerizingly delicate but delivers a harder edge when it needs to.
Small Pond has a pair of upcoming performances in Maine: one in Portland on Thursday and the other a week later during the All Roads Music Festival in Belfast.
Coming to know Small Pond’s music has been exquisite as I’ve made my way through a discography that started in 2022 with the seven-song release “Let it Fall Like it Should.”
A year later, Small Pond played at The Press Room in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, and released it as a live album. This is another sublime place to start your listening journey.
Small Pond also covered a popular Third Eye Blind song in a way that stopped me in my tracks. But we’ll get to that.
The band is lead singer and guitarist Molly McDevitt, Colin McKenna on drums and vocals, guitarist Ian Howard and Joe Murphy on bass.
The full-length album “Soft Burn” releases on Oct. 21 so the two shows will likely feature some of its tracks, including the scintillating single “Silver Coin.”
In a press release, McDevitt described the track as watching a relationship from the outside, catching yourself not showing up the way you want to for the people who matter and sitting in that discomfort instead of looking away.
If you’re a phony, I’m a fake
Beat the bars of the cage I made
Tuck in for sleep and accept our fate
We only talk now when it’s late
We only talk when it’s too late
“Soft Burn” opens with “Background Noise,” which is anything but. It’s a smart, pull-you-in tune with McDevitt’s vocals front and center, singing about things like shooting stars in outer space while the buzz of an electric guitar whirs and drums and bass offer sturdy scaffolding.
“Darlene” is an ethereal three-and-a-half minutes of sonic bliss.
The band’s manager told me to not sleep on the second half of the album, and he was right.
“The Cat Died on a Tuesday Night” has a darkness to it as McDevitt captures a complicated time between two people who need to figure a few things out. The layer of electric guitar is a key element added to a cauldron of a song that comes in for a surprisingly quiet landing.
“Soft Burn” ends with the title track, perhaps the album’s most upbeat, with a tempo that offers the speedups and slowdowns of a rollercoaster on medium speed.
Now about that Third Eye Blind song.
In January, Small Pond released a 5-song covers EP called “You Should Know Me Better Than That.” It features “Mammas Don’t Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Cowboys,” (written by Ed and Patsy Bruce and later recorded by Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson), “I Should Live in Salt” (The National), “The Moonlight Song” (Blaze Foley), “Between Days” (Red House Painters) and, much to my surprise and delight, “How’s It Going To Be,” the 1997 Third Eye Blind hit, which I’ve always had a soft spot for. The ’90s were sometimes a complicated time for music, but this track holds up.
Small Pond slowed it down about 30 percent, to where it floats in a cloud of lush vocals and muted electric guitar licks.
Conversely, Small Pond sped up the Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson version of “Mammas Don’t Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Cowboys.” They gave it some drum beats and electric guitar and put a skip in its step.
Small Pond formed in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in 2022. However, McDevitt recently moved to Portland which, as far as I’m concerned, means we get to claim the band as local.
Small Pond’s current schedule includes the Portland and Belfast shows, followed by gigs in Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania and Washington, D.C.
Connect with Small Pond at smallpond.band , Instagram and Bandcamp.
IF YOU GO
8 p.m. Thursday. Portland House of Music, 25 Temple St., Portland, $12 in advance, $15 day of show, 21-plus. statetheatreportland.com.
All Roads Music Festival in Belfast on Oct. 17. Small Pond’s set is at 6:15 p.m. on the Legion Hall stage. Festival passes are $55, $10 youth. Full schedule and tickets at allroadsmusicfest.com.

title: Why I’m out canvassing for Troy Jackson
text:
Sandra Smith Congdon is a Maine Democrats campaign volunteer and Saco Democratic Committee member.
I’m out every weekend canvassing for Troy Jackson in York County with the hope that we can flip the U.S. Senate because Maine is central to that fight.
I grew up in a working-class family in the ’70s and ’80s. My father worked in construction and my mother worked in retail, both in unions that provided them with fair wages and good healthcare. They worked hard to put food on the table for our family and made sure we had what we needed and sometimes could even afford things that we “wanted.”
The reason I’m supporting Troy is because I see a lot of working-class people today who can no longer afford basic needs. Troy wasn’t my first pick to run against Susan Collins but the more I hear him speak and hear others talk about him, the more I believe he’s the right choice for Maine. His working-class roots and his experience in the Maine Senate show that he is a fighter and will work hard for Mainers.
Mostly I’m out knocking on strangers’ doors because I cannot believe what I’m seeing every day in our Capitol. The bombastic man occupying the Oval Office has staffed his cabinet with sycophants whose only qualifications are blind loyalty and public praise of their boss. His only consistent policy is maximizing financial gain for himself and the billionaires who understand his pay-to-play mindset.
He isn’t listening to, nor does he care about, working-class people. He doesn’t see that the average American is struggling to afford food, fuel, healthcare, childcare, housing and other basic needs. He doesn’t even try to hide the corruption or his all-important ego, focusing on buying or bullying his name onto whatever he can in an attempt to paint himself a legacy in D.C. vs. earning it from the American people.
But worst of all is the lack of accountability, because Republicans in Congress are unwilling to stand up to his schoolyard bullying and brazen grift. They are showing the American public very clearly that their hold on power is far more important to them than the well-being of our great nation.
We need to flip the House and the Senate in the midterms to bring back checks and balances (not to mention basic accountability) to this administration. We cannot afford another two years of expensive pet projects, a continuing war in Iran driving up fuel costs, the whittling away of our education system, legislation that makes it harder to vote, abuse and alienation of our allies, deaths of U.S. citizens at the hands of ICE and tariffs that are being passed on to American consumers. We cannot afford children going hungry because of SNAP cuts, an EPA that is enabling the destruction of the planet, whitewashing or erasing U.S. history and a lack of AI regulation that could quickly get out of human control.
I encourage you all to tune out the negative campaign ads that stretch the truth and look at how we can be better humans and get back to having an American dream again where basic needs are met and working people can even afford some wants. This will not happen with the current administration or Susan Collins’ consistent enabling. As everyone can clearly see, Collins votes with the Republicans 95% of the time and only doesn’t when her vote won’t make a difference. Collins may have been a moderate at some point during her career, but she no longer fits that definition.
Please vote for Troy Jackson and other Democratic candidates so working-class people, not just billionaires, have a shot at the American dream.

title: MaineHousing grants $2.7M to warming shelters from Presque Isle to Biddeford
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MaineHousing has awarded more than $2.7 million to 12 organizations to support short-term warming shelters across the state this winter, from Presque Isle to Biddeford.
The funding is the largest amount and the most beds supported — 474 — since the program began five years ago. The grants will support shelters in eight of Maine’s nine Homeless Response Hubs, which operate in all of the state’s 16 counties.
Most of the facilities will operate overnight through April 30.
Funding can be used for staffing, supplies, transportation, extended operating hours and other costs.
“Dangerous winter weather can put lives at risk, especially for people experiencing homelessness or housing instability,” said MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan. “These grants help communities open safe, heated spaces before severe cold arrives.”
Grant recipients will work with municipalities, emergency management officials and community partners to connect people with safe, warm shelter when conditions become hazardous.
MaineHousing also administers the Home Energy Assistance Program and Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which help eligible households with heating costs and emergencies.
With heating costs rising, MaineHousing encourages eligible households to apply early and explore assistance before they’re faced with an emergency.
Residents seeking information about heating assistance and emergency heating support are urged to visit MaineHousing’s website or contact a local community action agency.
Additional information is available in the Maine Department of Energy Resources’ Winter Heating Guide.
